Lecture notes

The distilled modules for every week: a framing paragraph, the core ideas, a worked anchor with its assumptions, a read-closely / skim / skip reading map, common misconceptions, a self-test, a prompt that transfers the idea to your fermentation experience, and a closed-book teach-back with a calculation and assumption check. All 64 figures are injected at the core idea each belongs to.

Phases 1-3: Molecular foundations, metabolism in depth, and quantitative physiology (weeks 1-18).

Distilled modules: the content you need, a worked anchor, a reading map that tells you what to read closely and what to skip, misconceptions, and a self-test. Written to replace cover-to-cover reading, not to replace reading.

On the numbers before you read any of them. Every number in these modules — ribosome counts, pool sizes, half-lives, turnover times — is written from working knowledge and is an order-of-magnitude figure. Before any of them enters a notebook, a figure or a proposal, check it against BioNumbers or the primary source and cite that, not these notes. Treat the modules as a map of what matters and a scaffold for reasoning; treat the textbooks and the databases as the authority for values.

Every worked anchor states the assumptions it rests on, and every figure built from simulated rather than measured values says so in its title. Treat a calculation here as a conditional inference, not a result.

Running case study — Your Fercaf thesis: from process performance to cell metabolism

This is a case from your own work, not a claim that the thesis measured intracellular metabolism. Use it throughout the course to practice moving from a process observation to a biological hypothesis, then asking what evidence would distinguish that hypothesis from alternatives.

What the thesis reports

  • Process: semi-continuous cassava retting in a moving-tray reactor, described as 60 kg/day, with eight trays and 2.5 kg of chips fed per tray each hour. The chips were 1–1.5 mm thick. The starter is named as Lactobacillus plantarum, Bacillus subtilis, and Aspergillus oryzae in most passages (8 L of each culture; 24 L total), but one starter-preparation passage says Aspergillus niger (printed p. 46 / PDF p. 70). No strain identifiers or independent identity check are given; treat the fungal identity as unresolved. The broth was circulated; the validation operated at an 8-hour tray residence time.
  • Factors varied: residence time (8 or 12 hours), water-to-cassava loading, and broth-water replacement. The reported selected condition was 8 hours and a 7:1 water-to-substrate ratio. The replacement interval is inconsistent in the thesis: the abstract and methods say 25% at every residence time (8 hours), while the validation procedure says 25% every 4 hours; it was run for five days. Treat the interval as unresolved until the laboratory records are checked.
  • Measurements: counts for L. plantarum and B. subtilis, gravimetric A. oryzae, broth pH, cyanogenic compounds in broth and flour, flour yield, moisture, swelling power, and whiteness. The reported validation averages include 35% flour yield, 13% moisture, 10.4% swelling power, and 83.5% whiteness.

Keep the levels of explanation separate. The thesis reports process outcomes and microbial measurements. Its explanations—such as starch hydrolysis supplying glucose, L. plantarum acidifying the broth, or a consortium member limiting conversion—are hypotheses unless the corresponding substrate, metabolite, enzyme, or flux was directly measured. pH alone does not identify which acids were produced or quantify their rates.

A first evidence audit

The thesis's standard table gives whiteness a minimum of 87 and moisture a maximum of 13%; its validation discussion reports 83.5 whiteness and 13% moisture, while the abstract and conclusion describe the product as meeting the standard. The whiteness result appears below the stated threshold. Treat the compliance claim as unresolved until you check the exact standard scope, the reported metric, and the underlying result. This is a useful example of checking a conclusion against its own criteria.

There is also a ratio-notation issue worth resolving before any calculation. The abstract and conclusion describe water-to-substrate as 7:1. The methods narrative uses the reciprocal substrate-to-water 1:7: that is the same condition if the basis is stated, not a second value. The methods table, however, is headed “Rasio air terhadap substrat” and lists 1:7 and 1:12, so its label and values conflict; Table 4.1's separate Run 2 is 1:8, a different tested condition. The uncertainty is the table labelling and which run is being compared, not the reciprocal arithmetic. Check the experimental records, state kg water per kg fresh cassava, and do not silently normalize the labels.

Checked against the thesis. The process, 8-hour residence time, five-day validation, 35% yield, 13% moisture, 10.4% swelling power and 83.5% whiteness are all in the source. The starter volumes and the two bacterial names are in the source, but the fungal name is not consistent: most passages say A. oryzae, one starter-preparation passage says A. niger (printed p. 46 / PDF p. 70), and there are no strain identifiers. The 25% replacement is stated at every residence time in the abstract and methods, and every 4 hours in the validation procedure (printed p. 103 / PDF p. 127); both are in the source, so neither interval is settled. The whiteness result is below the SNI minimum of 87 in Table 4.8, while the abstract and conclusion say the product meets SNI. These are source-level issues, not transcription errors. See [TK4092] Table 3.4, Table 4.1, Table 4.8, validation pp. 101–109, conclusion p. 111.

What this case can teach across the module

  • Weeks 8–18: draw a carbon and redox map from cassava starch to sugars, biomass, acids, and any other products. Mark every quantity the thesis measured and leave the rest as unknown; then ask what a full carbon balance would require.
  • Weeks 20–29: build a small, explicitly hypothetical network and ask what FBA could predict. The thesis's pH and cell counts do not determine intracellular fluxes. Propose time-resolved sugar, organic-acid, gas, and 13C-labeling measurements that could constrain them.
  • Weeks 32–39: treat the mixed starter as an ecological system. The species-specific counts are useful, but the thesis also reports contamination and limitations in some counting methods. Ask what selective assays, controls, or strain-specific molecular measurements would be needed to distinguish the intended organisms from contaminants.
  • Weeks 47–52: connect tray residence time, circulation, water use, and product recovery to organism physiology. A process optimum need not be a cellular metabolic optimum; ask which process variables changed the cells' environment and which changed only handling or recovery.

Case teach-back

  1. Explain in your own words what the study optimized and what it did not measure about intracellular metabolism.
  2. Calculate the water requirement from the reported loading ratio for a stated cassava mass. First resolve the ratio notation; write units and show the interpretation you chose.
  3. Name one metabolic explanation for the observed pH or product outcome, one competing explanation, and the measurement that would distinguish them.
  4. Audit one conclusion against its data and criterion. Record any mismatch without forcing the evidence to fit the conclusion.

Source within your thesis: Chapters III–V, especially the methods and variation tables, the microbial-growth and pH results, Table 4.8, and the validation discussion (printed pages 43–54 / PDF 67–78, 57–80 / PDF 81–104, 81–109 / PDF 105–133, and 111 / PDF 135). Use the original tables and figures when extracting numerical data; the summary above is an orientation map.

Week 1 — The cell as a chemical plant

This week is a translation exercise, not a biology lesson. You already think in reactors, holdups, residence times and recycle loops; the cell is all of those at a scale where the numbers are unfamiliar. The aim is that by Friday you can state the size, composition and timescales of a cell from memory, say which compartment a pathway could live in and what that costs, and defend a host choice with numbers rather than with habit.

Core ideas

1. The cell as a reactor, with numbers you should memorise

An E. coli cell is roughly a cylinder 2 µm long and 0.8 µm across, so about 1 µm³ = 1 femtolitre. It is 70% water; the dry mass is around 3×10⁻¹³ g, of which 55% is protein, 20% RNA, 3% DNA, and the rest lipid, murein and small molecules. That gives about 2.5 million protein molecules and 10,000–70,000 ribosomes per cell depending on growth rate. Doubling time on glucose minimal medium is 40–60 minutes; on rich medium, 20. A yeast cell is 30–50 times larger by volume and divides in 90–140 minutes. The single most useful derived number: one molecule per E. coli cell is about 1.7 nM, because 1/(6.02×10²³ × 10⁻¹⁵ L) = 1.66×10⁻⁹ M. Carry that conversion; you will use it weekly.

2. Compartments are the engineering decision, not the biology trivia

E. coli has cytoplasm and, because it is Gram-negative, a periplasm between inner and outer membranes. The periplasm is oxidising, so it is where disulfide-bonded proteins fold correctly, and it is a secretion destination industrially. Yeast adds mitochondrion (acetyl-CoA, TCA, iron-sulfur clusters, and its own genome), endoplasmic reticulum (membrane-bound cytochrome P450s and their reductase — the reason terpenoid and alkaloid routes go to yeast), peroxisome (beta-oxidation, and a useful isolated compartment for toxic intermediates), vacuole (storage and degradation), and the nucleus. Each compartment you put a pathway into creates a transport problem for every substrate, product and cofactor the pathway needs, and the cofactor pools differ between compartments. That is the trade: compartmentalisation gives you isolation and the right chemical environment, and charges you transport.

3. Every molecule crossing a membrane is paid for, in one of two currencies

Transport against a gradient costs either ATP directly — the ABC transporters hydrolyse it — or the proton-motive force, which symporters and antiporters spend and which respiration paid ATP-equivalents to build. The PMF is an electrochemical gradient with two components, the pH difference and the membrane potential, together worth roughly 150–200 mV in a respiring bacterium. The group translocation route is a third option: the phosphotransferase system phosphorylates glucose during transit at the cost of one PEP, which is why PTS uptake halves the ceiling on any PEP-derived product. Carry one sentence from this week: nothing enters or leaves a cell for free, and the bill is paid in ATP, in PMF, or in a glycolytic intermediate. Week 8 quantifies the PMF, week 15 works the transport stoichiometries, and week 12 connects it back to oxygen.

4. What the cell is made of, and what making it costs

Four macromolecule classes. Proteins: 20 amino acids, peptide bonds, about 4 ATP-equivalents per residue to polymerise. Nucleic acids: 4 bases each, phosphodiester bonds, expensive per monomer because the bases themselves are costly to synthesise. Lipids: fatty acids on a glycerol or sphingoid backbone, built from acetyl-CoA and reduced with NADPH, so they are the most reduced and therefore most expensive cell component per gram. Polysaccharides: murein in the bacterial wall, glycogen as storage. The orders matter: protein dominates the mass and therefore dominates the biosynthetic demand, which is why amino acid supply and the twelve precursors govern growth yield. You will build this into a biomass equation in week 16.

5. The bacterial growth laws, which almost everything later rests on

Ribosome content scales linearly with growth rate. These are E. coli figures and the organism matters: a cell at µ = 0.2 h⁻¹ devotes perhaps 10% of protein to ribosomes, and one at µ = 1.5 h⁻¹ nearly 40%, from the classical composition tables of Bremer and Dennis and the growth laws of Scott et al. (Science 2010, 330:1099–1102). Take the numbers for any other organism, or for E. coli under stress or in a non-minimal medium, from a source for those conditions. The proteome behaves as a budget partitioned between a ribosomal sector, a metabolic sector that supplies precursors, and an unused or housekeeping remainder — and the sectors sum to one. Three consequences you will meet repeatedly. Overflow metabolism in week 13 is the cell choosing a pathway that yields less ATP per glucose but more ATP per gram of protein invested. Proteome-constrained models in week 31 formalise exactly this budget. And metabolic burden in week 34 is quantitatively just the fraction of that budget your pathway takes, which is why the week 1 copy-number calculation is the foundation of the burden argument rather than an arithmetic curiosity. Learn the linear ribosome relation as a number now; it explains more of what follows than any single fact in the course.

6. Timescales, and why 'steady state' is defensible

Enzyme turnover: 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁵ s per catalytic cycle. Metabolite pool turnover: ATP about 1 s, glycolytic intermediates seconds, amino acid pools minutes. Transcript half-life: 2–8 minutes in bacteria. Protein half-life: hours, or dilution by growth if the protein is stable. Generation time: tens of minutes to hours. This hierarchy is the entire justification for flux balance analysis in week 23: metabolite pools equilibrate in seconds while the growth state changes over hours, so treating metabolism as quasi-steady is sound. It is also why metabolomics in week 27 is brutally hard — you must stop metabolism faster than ATP turns over.

7. Host selection as a design decision

Five questions decide a host, in roughly this order. Does it natively supply the precursor and cofactor your pathway needs, or can it be made to? Does it tolerate the product at the titre your economics requires? Is the genetic toolkit mature enough that a build cycle takes weeks rather than months? Is there a fermentation and regulatory record at scale? And can it use the feedstock you can actually buy? Note that tool maturity ranks third, not first — which is why C. glutamicum beats E. coli for amino acids despite weaker tools, and why food applications go to lactic acid bacteria despite far weaker tools. You will build the full comparison matrix in weeks 40–46.

8. The central dogma as a set of engineering handles

DNA → RNA → protein, with each arrow a place you will intervene. Gene copy number and promoter strength set transcription; ribosome binding site and mRNA secondary structure set translation initiation, which is usually the real bottleneck; codon usage sets elongation; folding and proteolysis set how much active enzyme results. The practical consequence to internalise now: transcript abundance is a poor predictor of flux, because four independent steps sit between the transcript and a working catalyst. This is why the omics integration in week 39 is harder than it sounds, and why the week 34 tuning problem is quantitative rather than a matter of 'more promoter'.

9. The vocabulary that the whole course runs on

Titre: product concentration, g/L, which sets downstream cost. Rate or productivity: g L⁻¹ h⁻¹, which sets how much plant you need. Yield: g product per g substrate, which sets raw material cost and is usually expressed as a fraction of the theoretical maximum. Specific rates carry a q and are per gram dry weight per hour: qS for uptake, qP for production, qO₂ for oxygen. µ is specific growth rate in h⁻¹. Y with subscripts is a yield coefficient. Learn to say which of titre, rate and yield a given intervention improves — most interventions improve one and damage another, and week 51 is where you find out which one the economics punishes.

Worked anchor

How many copies of an enzyme does a cell need to carry a given flux? Take 2 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ and an enzyme running at 50 s⁻¹.

Flux per cell = 2 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ × 3×10⁻¹³ gDW = 6×10⁻¹³ mmol/h = 6×10⁻¹⁶ mol/h. Per second: 1.67×10⁻¹⁹ mol/s × 6.02×10²³ = 1.0×10⁵ molecules/s. Copies needed = 1.0×10⁵ / 50 = 2,000. Mass = 2,000 × 45,000 g/mol / 6.02×10²³ = 1.5×10⁻¹⁶ g = 0.15 fg, against roughly 180 fg of protein per cell — so 0.08% of the proteome.

The lesson is scale: one enzyme step is cheap, but a twelve-enzyme pathway at ten times this flux needs about 10% of the cell's protein, and that is where burden starts to bite. Keep this calculation; it recurs in weeks 31 and 34.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • single cell dry mass 3×10⁻¹³ g and 180 fg protein per cell
  • the enzyme runs at its full kcat in vivo, one catalytic site per molecule
  • subunit mass 45 kDa
  • flux carried by this one step alone

Common misconceptions

  • That a bigger cell is a better factory. Yeast's larger volume comes with a slower doubling time and a lower surface-to-volume ratio for transport; neither is obviously better and the choice depends on the chemistry.
  • That tool maturity picks the host. It ranks behind precursor supply, tolerance and industrial record — a fast build cycle is worth little if the strain dies at 30 g/L.
  • That the periplasm is wasted space. It is an oxidising compartment with no equivalent in the yeast cytosol, and for disulfide-bonded products it is the reason to choose E. coli at all.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. From memory: cell volume, dry mass, protein fraction, and the nanomolar concentration of a single molecule per E. coli cell.

A. About 1 µm³ = 1 fL; dry mass roughly 3×10⁻¹³ g; protein about 55% of dry mass, so ~1.65×10⁻¹³ g, giving around 2.5 million protein molecules; and one molecule per cell ≈ 1.7 nM, from 1/(6.02×10²³ × 10⁻¹⁵ L).

Q. Name four yeast compartments and one product class you would deliberately target to each, with the transport problem that creates.

A. Cytosol: most pathways by default; no transport problem, but competition with native metabolism. Mitochondrion: acetyl-CoA-derived products and anything needing the TCA intermediates directly; the problem is importing substrates and exporting product across two membranes, and the cofactor pools differ from the cytosol. Endoplasmic reticulum: membrane-bound P450 chemistry, so terpenoids and alkaloids; the problem is that soluble substrates must reach a membrane-embedded active site and NADPH must be supplied at the cytosolic face. Peroxisome: isolation of toxic or volatile intermediates, and beta-oxidation chemistry; the problem is that peroxisomal import is restricted to folded proteins via PTS signals and small-molecule transport is poorly characterised.

Q. A pathway runs at 5 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ through an enzyme with kcat 20 s⁻¹ at half saturation. What fraction of the proteome does that one step need?

A. Effective rate 10 s⁻¹. Flux per cell = 5 × 3×10⁻¹³ mmol/h = 1.5×10⁻¹² mmol/h = 2.5×10⁵ molecules/s. Copies = 2.5×10⁴. At 45 kDa that is 1.9×10⁻¹⁵ g ≈ 1.9 fg, about 1% of the 180 fg protein complement. One step at 1%; a ten-step pathway at this flux approaches 10%, which is where growth rate starts to fall measurably.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Map the cell-as-reactor idea onto your cassava fermentations. Which organism(s) were used in each run, what entered and left the cells, and what measurements would let you distinguish growth from product formation?

Week 2 — Water, bonds and the chemistry of the cytosol

The chemistry of the solvent everything happens in. Engineers routinely skip this and then misread a pH-dependent titre collapse as a biological mystery. The week's payload is small and permanent: the four weak interactions and their energies, the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, and the mechanism by which a weak-acid product poisons the cell that makes it.

Core ideas

1. The hydrophobic effect is entropic, and that is the whole point

A non-polar solute in water forces the surrounding water molecules into a more ordered cage, which costs entropy. Aggregating non-polar surfaces together releases that ordered water, so the driving force for protein folding, membrane formation and substrate binding is largely the entropy of the released water rather than any attraction between the non-polar groups themselves. Consequences you will use: the hydrophobic core of a protein is not glued, it is squeezed; a bilayer assembles spontaneously; and a hydrophobic product will partition into the membrane rather than stay in the aqueous phase, which is the week 15 toxicity problem.

2. Four weak interactions, with their energies

Hydrogen bond, 4–30 kJ/mol depending on geometry and environment. Ionic interaction, 2–20 kJ/mol in water (far stronger in a protein interior where the dielectric is low, which is why buried charges are rare and catalytically interesting when present). Van der Waals, about 1–4 kJ/mol per contact but numerous. Hydrophobic effect, context-dependent and entropy-driven. Compare these with a covalent bond at 350–450 kJ/mol and with thermal energy RT ≈ 2.6 kJ/mol at 310 K. Two conclusions: individually these interactions are barely above noise, so specificity comes from many of them acting together over a complementary surface; and a protein's folded state is only 20–60 kJ/mol more stable than its unfolded state, which is a handful of hydrogen bonds.

3. pKa and Henderson-Hasselbalch, derived not memorised

For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Take logarithms and rearrange: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). At pH = pKa the two forms are equal, and that is where buffering capacity is maximal because adding acid or base moves the ratio least on a log scale. Useful pKa values: phosphate 2.1/7.2/12.3, so phosphate buffers near neutrality; carbonate 6.4/10.3; acetate 4.76; lactate 3.86; citrate 3.1/4.8/6.4; the imidazole of histidine about 6.0, which is why histidine does general acid-base catalysis at physiological pH; cysteine thiol about 8.4, lowered substantially in an active site.

4. The weak-acid mechanism, which is the week's real content

Only the undissociated acid HA is lipophilic enough to cross a membrane by passive diffusion; the anion A⁻ cannot. Outside the cell at low pH, a substantial fraction of the product is HA. It diffuses in. Inside, where pH is near 7.2, it dissociates, releasing a proton into the cytosol and leaving an anion that cannot leave. The cell must now pump that proton back out at the cost of ATP, and the anion accumulates. The net effect is a collapsing pH gradient and an ATP drain that grows with titre. This single mechanism explains why organic acid fermentations have a titre ceiling, why they are run near neutral pH with base addition, and why that choice then creates a salt burden and an acidification step downstream. It is the clearest example in the course of a biological limit that is purely physical chemistry.

5. Osmolarity, water activity, and the other end of the titre problem

High product or salt concentrations lower water activity, and the cell responds by accumulating compatible solutes — glycine betaine, trehalose, proline — at metabolic cost. For a neutralised organic acid process the salt concentration at high titre can be the binding constraint rather than the acid itself. Rule of thumb: above roughly 1 osmol/L most industrial hosts are under measurable stress. This is why 'just raise the titre' has a physical ceiling independent of the pathway.

Worked anchor

Lactic acid, pKa 3.86. Compute the undissociated fraction at pH 6.0 and at pH 4.5.

f(HA) = 1/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)). At pH 6.0: 1/(1 + 10^2.14) = 1/(1 + 138) = 0.0072, so 0.7%. At pH 4.5: 1/(1 + 10^0.64) = 1/(1 + 4.37) = 0.186, so 19%.

A 1.5 unit drop in pH raises the inhibitory species 26-fold at the same total titre. Now the second half: at equilibrium of HA across the membrane, with internal pH 7.2 and external 4.5, the anion accumulates internally by roughly 10^(7.2−4.5) = 500-fold relative to the external anion. That concentration is physically unreachable, so the cell never attains the equilibrium — it arrests or dies first. Which tells you the real design choice: ferment near neutral pH and pay for base and downstream acidification, or engineer tolerance and pay in strain development.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • pKₐ 3.86 at the relevant temperature and ionic strength
  • only the undissociated acid crosses the membrane
  • cytoplasmic pH held at 7.2 while external pH falls
  • activities approximated by concentrations

Common misconceptions

  • That the anion is the inhibitor. It is the undissociated acid that crosses the membrane; the anion is what gets trapped. Getting this backwards leads to the wrong engineering conclusion about pH.
  • That buffering capacity scales with concentration alone. It also depends on how close pH is to pKa — a 100 mM buffer two units from its pKa is nearly useless.
  • That the hydrophobic effect is an attraction between non-polar groups. It is the entropy of the water released when their surfaces are buried.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Derive Henderson-Hasselbalch from the dissociation equilibrium without looking.

A. Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Take log₁₀ of both sides: log Ka = log[H⁺] + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Multiply by −1: pKa = pH − log([A⁻]/[HA]). Rearrange: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

Q. At pH 5.0, what fraction of acetic acid (pKa 4.76) is undissociated, and what does that imply for an acetate process?

A. f(HA) = 1/(1 + 10^(5.0−4.76)) = 1/(1 + 10^0.24) = 1/(1 + 1.74) = 0.36, so 36% is the membrane-permeant, inhibitory species. At pH 7 the same calculation gives 0.6%. Acetate processes therefore cannot be run acidic: the strain is poisoned by its own product long before the stoichiometric ceiling, so you run near neutral and pay for base and for downstream acidification, or you engineer tolerance.

Q. Why is the free energy of protein folding only 20–60 kJ/mol, and what does that predict about point mutations?

A. It is the small difference between two large opposing terms — the favourable burial of hydrophobic surface and hydrogen bonding against the large conformational entropy lost on folding. Because the net is small, a single buried hydrophobic-to-polar substitution costing 5–15 kJ/mol removes a substantial fraction of the margin, and two or three such mutations unfold the protein. This predicts that random mutagenesis libraries lose function mainly by destabilisation rather than by active-site damage, which is why stability is engineered first.

Week 3 — Protein structure and folding

The catalyst is encoded, folded, degraded and evolvable — four properties your reactor catalysts never had. This week builds the structural vocabulary you need to read an enzyme's datasheet critically, and it plants the two facts that govern protein engineering in week 37: folding is marginally stable, and activity and stability trade against each other.

Core ideas

1. Four levels, and which interactions hold each

Primary is the covalent sequence, which determines everything else. Secondary is local backbone hydrogen bonding: α-helix with 3.6 residues per turn and i to i+4 bonding, β-sheet parallel or antiparallel with inter-strand bonding, and turns. Tertiary is the three-dimensional fold, held by the hydrophobic core, plus hydrogen bonds, ionic pairs and sometimes disulfides. Quaternary is subunit assembly, which matters to you because it determines whether a gene deletion removes the activity — a heteromeric complex is an AND in the gene-protein-reaction rule of week 21, and that distinction is a leading source of false essentiality predictions.

2. Folding is marginally stable, and that is a design constraint

ΔG of folding is typically −20 to −60 kJ/mol: the difference between two large numbers, each hundreds of kJ/mol. A single buried hydrophobic-to-polar substitution can cost 5–15 kJ/mol, so a handful of such mutations unfolds a protein. Two consequences. First, random mutagenesis libraries lose activity mostly by destabilising the fold, not by hitting the active site — which is why week 37's campaigns begin by raising stability to create a mutational buffer. Second, thermostability engineering is additive and achievable, because you are adding small increments to a small number.

3. The active site is a small, strained, unrepresentative part of the protein

Catalytic residues are frequently charged in hydrophobic environments, held in strained geometries, and conserved far beyond what stability requires. That is the structural origin of the stability-activity trade-off: the active site is optimised for catalysis at the cost of being locally suboptimal for folding. When you look at a structure, the residues within 5 Å of the substrate are the ones you cannot freely mutate; the surface is where most tolerated variation lives.

4. Disulfides, the periplasm, and why secretion sometimes decides the host

Disulfide bonds form in oxidising environments. The bacterial cytoplasm is reducing, so a protein needing disulfides will not fold correctly there — it must go to the periplasm, which has the Dsb oxidation machinery, or to the eukaryotic ER. This is not a detail: it decides host and compartment for whole product classes, and it is why 'express it in E. coli' fails for many secreted eukaryotic proteins regardless of codon optimisation.

5. Protein lifetime is set by growth, not by degradation, for most enzymes

Bacterial proteins are mostly stable: active degradation targets misfolded, tagged or regulatory proteins, while a well-folded metabolic enzyme is removed principally by dilution as the cell divides. Its effective half-life is therefore ln2/µ — about 42 minutes at µ = 1.0 h⁻¹ and 3.5 hours at µ = 0.2 h⁻¹. Three things follow. At steady state the enzyme concentration is its synthesis rate divided by (µ + kdeg), so a slow-growing cell accumulates more enzyme from the same promoter, which is why expression level and growth rate cannot be varied independently. Switching off a promoter does not remove an enzyme quickly; it dilutes it over several generations, which bounds how fast dynamic regulation in week 36 can act downwards. And a degron tag, which imposes real degradation, is the remedy when you need faster removal than dilution provides.

6. Inclusion bodies: a rate problem, not a sequence problem

Folding competes with aggregation. The nascent chain exposes hydrophobic surface; if folding is slower than synthesis, those surfaces find each other instead of their own core. So the remedies all work by slowing synthesis relative to folding: lower temperature, weaker promoter or less inducer, co-expressed chaperones, or periplasmic export. Note the diagnostic implication, which is the single most useful troubleshooting fact in the course: high transcript with low activity is most often resolved by separating soluble from insoluble protein and running a gel — a one-day experiment that halves the hypothesis space.

7. Reading a structure, and reading a predicted structure

A crystal structure is a model fitted to density, with a resolution and an R-factor you should check; side-chain positions at 2.8 Å are far less certain than the backbone, and loops are often missing entirely. A predicted structure carries a per-residue confidence, is generally reliable for the fold and the core, and is unreliable exactly where you most want it: flexible loops, induced-fit rearrangements, ligand positions, and the effect of mutations. Use prediction to locate the active site and the conserved core; do not use it to argue that a substitution will work.

Worked anchor

Estimate how many destabilising mutations a protein tolerates. Take ΔG(folding) = −40 kJ/mol and an average destabilising substitution at −8 kJ/mol.

Five such substitutions bring ΔG to roughly zero, at which point half the protein population is unfolded at equilibrium and, in vivo, the unfolded fraction is degraded or aggregates. In practice soluble expression collapses well before that, typically after two or three.

Now the library arithmetic that follows: error-prone PCR at an average of 3 substitutions per gene, with perhaps a third of random substitutions destabilising by this much, means a large fraction of your library is already non-functional before you ask anything about activity. That is the quantitative reason week 37 recommends raising stability first, and the reason a library's useful size is far smaller than its nominal size.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • two-state folding at equilibrium, ΔG = −40 kJ/mol
  • an average destabilising substitution costs 8 kJ/mol
  • substitution effects additive and independent
  • roughly a third of random substitutions destabilise by that much

Common misconceptions

  • That more disulfides means more stable. In a reducing cytoplasm an unformed disulfide is worse than none, and misoxidised pairs are a common cause of aggregation.
  • That an AlphaFold model settles a mechanistic question. It predicts a fold well and a ligand pose or a mutational effect poorly, which is exactly where mechanism lives.
  • That inclusion bodies mean the gene is wrong. They usually mean synthesis outpaced folding, which is a rate problem fixed by expression conditions.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Name the four catalytic strategies' structural requirements and explain why active-site residues are often locally destabilising.

A. Covalent catalysis needs a positioned nucleophile, often with a residue network lowering its pKa. General acid-base needs an ionisable group with a pKa near the operating pH, usually histidine. Metal catalysis needs a coordination geometry held by several ligating residues. Proximity needs a rigid scaffold holding two substrates in register. All four require charged or polar residues in constrained, frequently buried, geometries — which is locally unfavourable for folding, since burial of charge is costly and strain is energetically expensive. Hence the stability-activity trade-off: the active site is optimised for catalysis at the fold's expense.

Q. Your protein needs two disulfide bonds. Where do you express it, and why does the cytoplasm fail?

A. The periplasm of E. coli, using a signal peptide and the Dsb oxidation system, or a eukaryotic host's endoplasmic reticulum. The bacterial cytoplasm is maintained reducing by thioredoxin and glutaredoxin systems, so cysteines stay reduced and the disulfides either do not form or form incorrectly, giving misfolded protein and aggregation. Engineered oxidising-cytoplasm strains exist as a third option.

Q. Transcript is abundant, activity is low. What is the first experiment, and what does each outcome rule out?

A. Fractionate the lysate into soluble and insoluble and run a gel. Protein present in the insoluble fraction means it is being made but misfolding, which rules out transcription, translation and degradation problems and points at expression rate, temperature or chaperones. Protein absent from both fractions means it is not being made or is degraded immediately, which rules out aggregation and points at translation initiation, codon usage or proteolysis. Protein soluble and abundant means the problem is downstream of expression entirely: cofactor, substrate supply, thermodynamics or inhibition.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Pick an enzyme or phenotype relevant to cassava conversion or fermentation. What evidence would distinguish low gene expression from poor folding, instability, or low catalytic activity?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Week 4 — Enzyme catalysis

Mechanism before kinetics. Knowing which catalytic strategy an enzyme uses tells you what its rate is sensitive to, which cofactor it will demand from your pathway, and what engineering it will tolerate. The week also teaches you to read a kinetic record sceptically, which is the skill Brief 1 grades.

Core ideas

1. Catalysis is transition-state stabilisation, and the arithmetic is exponential

Rate ∝ exp(−ΔG‡/RT). At 310 K, RT = 2.577 kJ/mol, so every 5.9 kJ/mol of barrier reduction buys a factor of ten. A 30 kJ/mol reduction buys about 10⁵; real enzymes achieve 10⁸ to 10¹⁷, which means barrier reductions of 45–100 kJ/mol. The enzyme achieves this by binding the transition state more tightly than the substrate — binding energy is paid back as catalysis. Crucially, the barrier falls equally in both directions, so the equilibrium constant is unchanged. State this crisply when asked; confusing catalysis with equilibrium shifting is the commonest conceptual error in interviews.

2. Four catalytic strategies and their canonical examples

Covalent catalysis: a nucleophilic residue forms a transient covalent intermediate — serine proteases, with the Ser-His-Asp triad in which the histidine deprotonates the serine and the aspartate orients the histidine. General acid-base catalysis: a residue donates or accepts a proton in the transition state, which is why histidine at pKa ≈ 6 is so common. Metal ion catalysis: a bound metal polarises a substrate or lowers the pKa of water, as zinc does in carbonic anhydrase to generate hydroxide at neutral pH. Proximity and orientation: holding two substrates in the correct geometry, which converts an unfavourable entropy of association into a binding event paid for once.

3. Cofactors are a pathway-level constraint, not an enzyme detail

Learn which chemistry each cofactor enables, because that is how you predict a pathway's demand. NAD⁺/NADH: two-electron hydride transfer, catabolic, held oxidised. NADP⁺/NADPH: the same chemistry, biosynthetic, held reduced — the separation is enforced by enzyme specificity and is the central cofactor problem of the course. FAD: one- or two-electron, handles radicals and oxygen. Coenzyme A: acyl group activation as a thioester, which is energetically rich. Thiamine pyrophosphate: decarboxylation and two-carbon transfer. Pyridoxal phosphate: essentially all amino acid chemistry — transamination, decarboxylation, racemisation. Biotin: carboxylation, which is how CO₂ gets fixed at the anaplerotic node. Tetrahydrofolate: one-carbon units. When you look at a new pathway, total its cofactor demand before anything else; that total often decides the host.

4. EC numbers as a prediction tool

The first digit gives the reaction class: 1 oxidoreductase, 2 transferase, 3 hydrolase, 4 lyase, 5 isomerase, 6 ligase, 7 translocase. From the class alone you can usually predict the cofactor requirement — a 1.x.x.x needs a redox cofactor, a 6.x.x.x needs ATP, a 4.1.1.x is a decarboxylase and so releases CO₂ and probably costs you a carbon. Use this to sanity-check a pathway you are reading for the first time, before you look anything up.

5. Why assay conditions make published parameters incomparable

Enzyme rate follows Arrhenius over the stable range, with activation energies typically 40–60 kJ/mol, which corresponds to a Q₁₀ of roughly 2 — so a measurement at 25 °C rather than 37 °C is about half as fast before anything else differs. Above the stability limit the rate collapses as the protein unfolds, so the apparent optimum is a competition between catalysis and denaturation and is not a thermodynamic property. pH dependence is usually bell-shaped: two ionisable groups, one that must be protonated and one deprotonated, give a plateau between their pKa values, and the apparent kcat and KM can have different pH profiles because they report on different ionisation states. Ionic strength and buffer identity shift both, and some buffers coordinate metals or inhibit outright. Put these together and a sevenfold spread in reported kcat for one enzyme needs no further explanation — which is the quantitative basis for the week 4 scepticism and for Brief 1.

6. Why published kinetic parameters disagree, and what to do

Four mechanistically distinct causes. Assay conditions — pH, temperature, ionic strength, buffer identity — easily span sevenfold. Enzyme preparation: tags, partial misfolding, proteolysis, or an inactive fraction, all of which depress apparent kcat unless active-site titration was done. Cofactor or metal saturation differing between preparations. And a different substrate, isoform or orthologue reported under the same EC number. The correct response is never to average: tabulate values with their conditions, exclude the non-comparable ones with the exclusion stated, and carry a range into any model. If a conclusion flips across that range, the study's output is that the parameter must be measured.

Worked anchor

How much rate does a 32 kJ/mol barrier reduction buy at 310 K, and what does that mean practically?

Enhancement = exp(ΔΔG‡/RT) = exp(32,000/(8.314 × 310)) = exp(12.42) = 2.5 × 10⁵.

If the uncatalysed reaction has a half-life of 100 years, the catalysed half-life is 100 × 365 × 24 / 2.5×10⁵ hours ≈ 3.5 hours. Still far too slow for a metabolic step, which tells you that 32 kJ/mol is a modest enzyme and that real central-metabolic enzymes must be doing considerably more — typically 60–90 kJ/mol of barrier reduction.

Use this both ways: it calibrates your sense of what catalysis costs, and it tells you that an engineered enzyme improved by 10-fold has gained only 5.9 kJ/mol of transition-state stabilisation, which is one hydrogen bond. That is why directed evolution works in small increments.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • 310 K, transition-state theory with an unchanged prefactor
  • barrier reduction is the only change between catalysed and uncatalysed
  • first-order decay, so the half-life scales inversely with rate

SourceTreatmentWhy
Berg Ch 9Read closelyCatalytic strategies in full, with the four canonical systems. The most useful single chapter this week; read the serine protease and carbonic anhydrase mechanisms until you can draw them.
Berg Ch 8 §8.1–8.3Read closelyFree energy, the active site, and the relationship between binding and catalysis. Sets up next week's kinetics.
Microbiology Ch 8.1SkimEnergy, matter and enzymes at an introductory level. Read the regulation sections; the thermodynamics is covered better in Berg.

Common misconceptions

  • That enzymes shift equilibria. They lower the barrier in both directions; ΔG° is a state function and is untouched.
  • That kcat is a property of the enzyme. It is a property of the enzyme under stated conditions with a stated substrate and preparation, which is why the same EC number spans orders of magnitude.
  • That a high kcat means a fast step in vivo. Flux depends on kcat, enzyme abundance and the substrate saturation, and an enzyme at 5% saturation is slow however high its kcat.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. What rate enhancement does 24 kJ/mol of barrier reduction give at 310 K?

A. exp(24,000/(8.314 × 310)) = exp(9.31) ≈ 1.1×10⁴, roughly ten thousand fold. Each 5.9 kJ/mol is a factor of ten at this temperature, so 24 kJ/mol is about four decades.

Q. From its EC number alone, 4.1.1.31 — what does this enzyme do, what cofactor is likely, and what does it cost in carbon?

A. Class 4 is a lyase; 4.1 cleaves carbon-carbon bonds; 4.1.1 is a carboxy-lyase, meaning a decarboxylase or, run in reverse, a carboxylase. 4.1.1.31 is PEP carboxylase. Since it fixes CO₂ onto PEP to give oxaloacetate it gains a carbon rather than losing one, and unlike pyruvate carboxylase it needs no biotin and no ATP — it uses the phosphate transfer potential of PEP instead. The general lesson is that the class alone predicts both the chemistry and whether carbon is gained or lost.

Q. Two laboratories report kcat differing fivefold. Give four distinct causes and say which value you would model.

A. Assay temperature and pH, worth about two-fold for a 12 °C difference alone; enzyme preparation differences including tags, misfolding and an inactive fraction that depresses apparent kcat unless active-site titration was done; cofactor or metal saturation differing between preparations; and a different substrate, isoform or orthologue reported under the same EC number. Model neither value alone: tabulate both with conditions, exclude the non-comparable one if there is a reason to, and carry the remaining range into an ensemble. If the conclusion flips across that range, the output of the study is that the parameter must be measured.

Week 5 — Enzyme kinetics I

Your own reaction engineering, re-pointed. Michaelis-Menten is the quasi-steady-state approximation you already derive; the new material is knowing where it fails, fitting it honestly, and understanding which parameters a given experiment can and cannot identify. This week and Brief 1 together are where your quantitative credibility is established.

Core ideas

1. Derive it, do not memorise it

For E + S ⇌ ES → E + P with rate constants k₁, k₋₁ and kcat: set d[ES]/dt = k₁[E][S] − (k₋₁ + kcat)[ES] ≈ 0, with [E]T = [E] + [ES]. Substituting gives [ES] = [E]T[S]/(KM + [S]) where KM = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁, and v = kcat[ES] = Vmax[S]/(KM + [S]). Note what KM is and is not: it is a ratio of rate constants, equal to the dissociation constant only in the rapid-equilibrium limit where kcat ≪ k₋₁. Reporting KM as 'the affinity' is sloppy and occasionally wrong.

2. What each parameter means physically

Vmax = kcat[E]T, so it scales with how much enzyme you express and tells you nothing intrinsic. kcat is the turnover number, the rate at saturation per active site. KM is the substrate concentration at half-maximal rate, and tells you the regime the enzyme operates in: compare it with the intracellular concentration from week 27 and you know whether the step is substrate-sensitive. kcat/KM is the apparent second-order rate constant for free enzyme and free substrate, governs the rate at low substrate — which is the regime of most intracellular metabolites — and is the quantity under selection for substrate discrimination. Its ceiling is the diffusion limit, about 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹.

3. Where the QSSA fails inside a cell

Two conditions. First, enzyme concentration comparable to substrate concentration: for low-abundance metabolites this is common, the free-substrate assumption breaks, and you need the total QSSA. Second, substrate changing on the ES relaxation timescale — during a rapid transient, or in the instationary labelling experiments of week 29. A third issue is not a QSSA failure but matters more: the irreversible form is simply wrong near equilibrium, and most central-metabolic reactions operate near equilibrium. Use the reversible rate law with the Haldane relation, which ties the kinetic parameters to Keq and keeps the model thermodynamically consistent. This is a requirement in week 30, not an elegance.

4. Most metabolic enzymes have two substrates, and the mechanisms are distinguishable

Single-substrate kinetics is the exception; a dehydrogenase has a substrate and a cofactor, a kinase has a substrate and ATP. Three mechanism classes. Sequential ordered: both substrates bind before any product leaves, in a fixed order — typical of NAD-dependent dehydrogenases, where the cofactor binds first. Sequential random: both bind before catalysis but in either order. Ping-pong: the first substrate binds, a product leaves carrying a group onto the enzyme, then the second substrate binds — transaminases are the standard case, with the amino group parked on pyridoxal phosphate between half-reactions. Why you care: the mechanism determines whether one substrate's concentration affects the other's apparent KM, and therefore whether raising a cofactor pool will raise flux. For a kinetic model in week 30, assuming ordered kinetics for a ping-pong enzyme gives qualitatively wrong cofactor sensitivity.

5. The reversible rate law and the Haldane relation, in the form you will type

Write these at the top of every kinetic notebook, because prose descriptions of them are useless at the keyboard. For a one-substrate, one-product reversible step:

v = ( (Vf/K_S)·[S] − (Vr/K_P)·[P] ) / ( 1 + [S]/K_S + [P]/K_P )

where Vf and Vr are the forward and reverse maximal rates and K_S and K_P the respective Michaelis constants. The Haldane relation ties them to the equilibrium constant:

K'eq = (Vf · K_P) / (Vr · K_S)

The consequence is the reason this matters. Since ΔrG′° = −RT ln K′eq, the thermodynamics fixes K′eq, which fixes one combination of the four kinetic parameters — so only three are independent. Fit all four freely and you will produce a model that implies an equilibrium constant contradicting measured thermodynamics, which is unphysical however well it fits. In practice: fit three parameters and compute the fourth, or parameterise directly in terms of K′eq. At equilibrium, setting v = 0 recovers [P]/[S] = K′eq, which is the one-line check that your implementation is correct — run it before trusting any simulation.

6. The four inhibition mechanisms, read off the data

Competitive: inhibitor binds free enzyme, apparent KM rises by (1 + [I]/Ki), Vmax unchanged; raising substrate relieves it. Uncompetitive: inhibitor binds only ES, both apparent Vmax and KM fall by the same factor so Vmax/KM is unchanged; raising substrate makes it worse. Non-competitive: binds both equally, Vmax falls, KM unchanged. Mixed: binds both with different affinities, both parameters change by different factors. The engineering reading matters more than the taxonomy: a competitively inhibited step can be relieved by increasing its substrate pool, an intervention available to you; an uncompetitively inhibited one cannot, so it is the harder bottleneck.

7. Fit properly, and know what you cannot determine

The double-reciprocal plot distorts the error structure: it compresses high-substrate points and enormously inflates the leverage of the low-substrate points, which are the noisiest. Unweighted regression on transformed data therefore gives biased parameters and dishonest intervals. Fit the untransformed data by weighted non-linear least squares with an error model you have stated, and report confidence intervals. On identifiability: Vmax is well determined if your highest substrate concentrations approach saturation; KM is inferred from the curvature and is correlated with Vmax, so it needs points near KM itself. Design the titration by where the model is sensitive to the parameter you care about — a D-optimal argument you already know.

8. Reading a double-reciprocal plot — for diagnosis, never for fitting

The replot patterns are heavily examined and are worth knowing cold, provided you keep the distinction: read the pattern to identify a mechanism, then fit the untransformed data to get the numbers.

On a 1/v against 1/[S] plot, with lines at several inhibitor concentrations: • Competitive — lines intersect on the y-axis. Slope rises with [I], y-intercept (1/Vmax) unchanged, x-intercept moves toward the origin. • Uncompetitive — parallel lines. Slope unchanged, y-intercept rises with [I]. • Non-competitive (pure) — lines intersect on the x-axis. Slope and y-intercept both rise, x-intercept (−1/KM) unchanged. • Mixed — lines intersect to the left of the y-axis, above or below the x-axis depending on the relative affinities for E and ES.

Secondary replots, which is where the examiner usually goes next: plot slope against [I] and the x-intercept gives −Ki for competitive and mixed inhibition; plot y-intercept against [I] and the x-intercept gives −Ki′, the ES-binding constant, for uncompetitive and mixed. For pure non-competitive the two are equal. For multi-substrate mechanisms the same plot distinguishes classes: ping-pong gives parallel lines when one substrate is varied at fixed concentrations of the other, while both sequential mechanisms give intersecting lines — which is the single most common multi-substrate examination question.

9. Diffusion and immobilisation distort everything above

Shuler's immobilised-enzyme sections introduce what week 48 develops: when the catalyst is in a particle, the interior sees less substrate than the bulk, so a Michaelis-Menten fit to bulk concentration returns an apparent KM that is transport-contaminated and larger than the intrinsic value. The effectiveness factor quantifies the penalty, and the Thiele modulus tells you the regime. You already know this machinery from heterogeneous catalysis; the only new thing is that the kinetics inside is saturable rather than power-law.

Worked anchor

An enzyme has kcat 85 s⁻¹ and KM 40 µM; its substrate sits at 15 µM in vivo.

Fraction of Vmax: v/Vmax = S/(KM + S) = 15/55 = 0.273, so 27% of capacity. Per-enzyme rate: 85 × 0.273 = 23.2 s⁻¹. To carry 1.5 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹: flux per cell = 1.5 × 3×10⁻¹³ = 4.5×10⁻¹³ mmol/h = 7.5×10⁴ molecules/s, so copies = 7.5×10⁴/23.2 ≈ 3,200.

Now the interpretation, which is the part that matters. The enzyme is far from saturation, so its flux is strongly substrate-sensitive — a two-fold rise in substrate gives nearly a two-fold rise in rate. That makes it a candidate for control, and it also means this step's flux can be raised by pushing its substrate pool rather than by expressing more enzyme. Contrast with an enzyme at 94% saturation, where expressing more is the only lever. Week 31's control analysis formalises this intuition.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • irreversible Michaelis-Menten, no product or feedback inhibition
  • one substrate limiting, the rest saturating
  • in vivo kcat equals the in vitro value
  • 3×10⁻¹³ gDW per cell

Reading map

Common misconceptions

  • That KM is a dissociation constant. It equals Kd only when kcat ≪ k₋₁; otherwise it is a kinetic quantity.
  • That a Lineweaver-Burk plot is just a presentational choice. Fitting on it biases the parameters, measurably, which Brief 1 asks you to quantify.
  • That irreversible Michaelis-Menten is adequate for metabolism. Most central reactions run near equilibrium, where the irreversible form overestimates flux and violates thermodynamics.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Derive Michaelis-Menten from the QSSA, then state the two in vivo conditions under which it fails.

A. Set d[ES]/dt = k₁[E][S] − (k₋₁+kcat)[ES] = 0 with [E]T = [E]+[ES]; substituting gives [ES] = [E]T[S]/(KM+[S]) with KM = (k₋₁+kcat)/k₁, and v = kcat[ES]. It fails when enzyme concentration is comparable to substrate concentration, common for low-abundance metabolites, requiring the total QSSA; and when substrate changes on the ES relaxation timescale, as in a fast transient or instationary labelling. Separately, the irreversible form is simply wrong near equilibrium, which is where most central-metabolic reactions sit.

Q. Apparent Vmax and KM both fall threefold at 50 µM inhibitor. Which mechanism, what is Ki, and why does more substrate not help?

A. Uncompetitive: both parameters fall by the same factor, so Vmax/KM is unchanged, and on a double-reciprocal plot the lines are parallel. The factor is (1 + [I]/Ki′) = 3, so Ki′ = 25 µM. Raising substrate increases the concentration of ES, which is precisely the species the inhibitor binds, so the inhibition deepens — the opposite of the competitive case and the reason this is the harder bottleneck to engineer around.

Q. You can add three data points to a titration. Where do you put them if KM is the parameter you need, and why?

A. Clustered around [S] ≈ KM, where the curvature carries the information about KM and where the model's sensitivity to it is greatest, with at least one point well above saturation retained to pin Vmax — since the two parameters are correlated, a poorly determined Vmax degrades KM. If the error is absolute rather than relative, shift the cluster upward because the low-substrate points are then relatively noisier. This is a D-optimal design argument: put points where the derivative of the response with respect to the uncertain parameter is largest.

Week 6 — Enzyme kinetics II: allostery and regulation

The cell's own control system — the thing that will fight every pathway you build. Allostery converts a modest concentration change into a large activity change, which is why feedback inhibition is such an effective regulator and why removing it is usually the first intervention in a biosynthetic strain. The week also kills a myth you will meet in older literature.

Core ideas

1. Cooperativity, and what the Hill coefficient actually says

A cooperative enzyme's rate-versus-substrate curve is sigmoid rather than hyperbolic: binding at one site changes the affinity of the others. The Hill equation, v/Vmax = Sⁿ/(K + Sⁿ), fits this empirically, and n is bounded above by the number of sites. It is not a count of sites, nor of molecules bound simultaneously; only n equal to the site number would indicate fully concerted all-or-none binding. A tetramer with n = 2.8 is strongly but not infinitely cooperative. The physiological point: a four-fold change in ligand moves a hyperbolic enzyme from 20% to 50% saturation but a cooperative one from roughly 5% to 80%, so cooperativity turns a dial into a switch.

2. MWC and KNF: two models, one observable

The concerted (MWC) model posits that the whole oligomer flips between a tense T state and a relaxed R state, with all subunits switching together; ligand binds R preferentially and so pulls the equilibrium. The allosteric constant L = [T]/[R] in the absence of ligand sets the baseline, and effectors act by changing L. The sequential (KNF) model allows subunits to change individually, with ligand binding inducing a conformational change that alters neighbours' affinity. MWC explains positive cooperativity elegantly and cannot produce negative cooperativity; KNF can produce both. Distinguishing them requires structural and binding data, not kinetics alone — which is worth knowing because papers often assert one without the evidence.

3. The two canonical systems, and why each is taught

Haemoglobin is taught because it shows cooperativity's physiological purpose: the sigmoid curve means oxygen is loaded in the lung and unloaded in tissue over a narrow pressure range, which a hyperbolic binder could not do. Aspartate transcarbamoylase is taught because it shows feedback architecture: CTP, the pathway's end product, inhibits the first committed step, while ATP activates it, so the enzyme integrates two signals and balances purine against pyrimidine synthesis. Study ATCase as the template for every biosynthetic regulation you will meet in week 14.

4. Covalent modification and zero-order ultrasensitivity

Phosphorylation cascades give a second control layer with different properties: slower, amplifiable, and capable of extreme steepness. When the modifying and demodifying enzymes are both saturated with their substrate — the zero-order regime — the fraction modified becomes an extremely steep function of the kinase/phosphatase ratio, far steeper than any Hill coefficient from binding alone. This is a switch built from two ordinary enzymes, and it is worth understanding because dynamic pathway control in week 36 uses the same logic.

5. Feedback inhibition architectures, and what to delete

End-product inhibition acts on the first committed step, because inhibiting anywhere later wastes carbon on intermediates that accumulate. For branched pathways there are three solutions: isozymes, each inhibited by a different end product; concerted inhibition, requiring all end products together; and cumulative inhibition, where each product contributes partial inhibition. Knowing which architecture a pathway uses tells you what a feedback-resistant design must do — deleting one isozyme achieves nothing if two others remain, which is exactly why amino acid strain lineages took decades. Note also that the useful mutation often removes cooperativity rather than affinity, because the sigmoid is what makes the inhibition sharp.

6. PFK is not the pacemaker of glycolysis

Older textbooks name phosphofructokinase as the rate-limiting step. Control analysis in week 31 shows this is wrong in its strong form: control is distributed across the pathway, sums to one, and redistributes the moment you amplify anything. PFK is heavily regulated — ATP inhibits, AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate — but heavily regulated is not the same as rate-controlling. Regulation keeps a flux at its set point; control determines how flux responds to a perturbation. Keep the two words distinct; conflating them is the single most common error in metabolic engineering reasoning.

Worked anchor

Why is a sigmoid better than a hyperbola for regulation? Compare saturation at two ligand concentrations, L and 4L, taking the midpoint at 2L.

Hyperbolic (n = 1): at L, v/Vmax = L/(2L + L)... using K at the midpoint 2L, saturation = L/(2L+L) = 0.33 at L, and 4L/(2L+4L) = 0.67 at 4L. A four-fold ligand change doubles activity.

Cooperative (n = 4): saturation = Lⁿ/(Kⁿ + Lⁿ) with K = 2L. At L: 1/(16 + 1) = 0.06. At 4L: 256/(16 + 256) = 0.94. The same four-fold ligand change takes the enzyme from 6% to 94% — effectively off to effectively on.

That is the whole argument for cooperativity, and it is also the argument for removing it when engineering: a feedback-resistant allele that abolishes cooperativity flattens the response so the enzyme stays active as the end product accumulates.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • Hill form with an integer coefficient, not a mechanism
  • K placed at the stated midpoint
  • binding at equilibrium, no competing ligand

Reading map

SourceTreatmentWhy
Berg Ch 10Read closelyRegulatory strategies in full, with ATCase and covalent modification. The week's core text.
Berg Ch 7SkimHaemoglobin. Read the cooperativity and Bohr effect sections for the physiological argument; skip the clinical variants.
Voet Ch 12 §4Read closelyControl of enzyme activity, with better MWC algebra than Berg. Read if you want to implement the model, which week 6's notebook asks you to do.
Berg Ch 16 §16.2SkimThe effector list for PFK and pyruvate kinase. Skim now, and read properly in week 9 when you have the pathway.
Palsson Ch 2 §2.4Read closelyProteins and their many states: the PFK bound-state reconstruction. Short, and it shows you how regulation is represented stoichiometrically, which nothing else in your stack does.

Common misconceptions

  • That the Hill coefficient counts binding sites or bound molecules. It is an empirical steepness measure bounded by the site count.
  • That regulated means rate-limiting. Regulation holds a flux at a set point; control determines the response to perturbation, and the two frequently sit on different enzymes.
  • That removing feedback always raises flux. It often raises the intermediate pool instead, until something downstream becomes limiting or an intermediate becomes toxic.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Write the Hill equation and state precisely what n means and what it does not.

A. v/Vmax = [S]ⁿ/(K + [S]ⁿ), or equivalently fractional saturation = [S]ⁿ/(K₀.₅ⁿ + [S]ⁿ). n is an empirical measure of the steepness of the binding curve, bounded above by the number of binding sites, and equal to that number only in the limit of fully concerted all-or-none binding. It is not the number of sites, not the number of molecules bound simultaneously, and not a mechanism — two different mechanisms can give the same n.

Q. A branched pathway uses cumulative inhibition. What must a feedback-resistant design achieve, and why is deleting one isozyme insufficient?

A. Under cumulative inhibition each end product contributes partial inhibition of the shared first step, and the effects compound, so relieving one product's contribution leaves the others intact and the step still substantially inhibited. A resistant design must abolish the binding of every contributing effector, which usually means engineering the allosteric site of that single enzyme rather than deleting genes. Deleting an isozyme is the right move only under the isozyme architecture, where each end product inhibits its own dedicated copy of the first enzyme — and even then the other isozymes keep carrying flux, which is why amino acid strain lineages required several generations of changes.

Q. Distinguish regulation from control in one sentence each, using PFK as the example.

A. Regulation is the cell's mechanism for holding a flux at a set point in the face of changing conditions — PFK is inhibited by ATP and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, so glycolytic flux tracks energy demand. Control is the quantitative sensitivity of steady-state flux to a change in an enzyme's activity, measured by the flux control coefficient, and PFK's is typically small — so PFK regulates glycolysis strongly while controlling it weakly, which is why overexpressing it does little.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Identify a plausible regulated step in starch breakdown or fermentation. What pattern across substrate levels or growth states would suggest allostery or feedback rather than simply too little enzyme?

Week 7 — Nucleic acids and the central dogma

The information layer, studied for what it does to your pathway rather than for its own sake. Four dials sit between a gene and a working enzyme — transcript level, translation initiation, elongation rate, and folding or degradation — and phase 6 turns all four. The week closes with Paper 1, so budget two sessions for consolidation and two for the examination.

Core ideas

1. Transcription in bacteria, in the detail you will actually use

RNA polymerase holoenzyme is core plus a sigma factor; the sigma determines promoter recognition, so swapping sigma factors switches whole regulons. A σ70 promoter has a −35 and a −10 hexamer with a spacer, and promoter strength is largely how well those elements match consensus — which is why promoter libraries are built by mutating them. Termination is either intrinsic, via a GC-rich hairpin followed by a U-tract, or Rho-dependent. What matters for engineering: promoter strength spans perhaps 1,000-fold across a good library; terminators are not perfect and read-through into downstream genes is a real and frequently unnoticed artefact; and transcription and translation are coupled in bacteria, so a stalled ribosome can terminate transcription prematurely.

2. Translation initiation is the usual bottleneck

The ribosome binds the Shine-Dalgarno sequence roughly 8–13 bases upstream of the start codon, and initiation rate depends on how accessible that region is — meaning the mRNA's secondary structure around the start matters as much as the SD sequence itself. This is why computational RBS design predicts expression better than promoter strength does, and why the first thing to vary in a tuning library is the 5′ untranslated region. A practical consequence worth internalising: the same RBS in front of a different gene gives a different expression level, because the folding of the start region depends on the downstream sequence. Context dependence is not noise; it is the mechanism.

3. Elongation, codon usage, and what rare codons actually do

Each codon is read by a tRNA whose abundance varies hugely. A rare codon stalls the ribosome, which slows elongation, causes queuing, raises the chance of premature termination and of co-translational misfolding, and can deplete the rare tRNA pool to the host's detriment. Codon adaptation indices quantify how well a gene matches the host's tRNA pool. Two cautions: codon optimisation is not a universal fix, because some slow codons are functional — rare-codon clusters can act as folding pauses — and optimisation algorithms can accidentally introduce strong secondary structure or internal SD-like sequences.

4. mRNA stability and why transcript level misleads

Bacterial transcript half-lives are typically 2–8 minutes, set by endonucleolytic cleavage and secondary structure. A measured steady-state transcript level is therefore a ratio of synthesis to degradation, and two genes with the same level can have very different synthesis rates. Combined with the independence of the four dials, this gives the week's key conclusion: transcript abundance is a weak predictor of flux. It is the reason week 39's omics integration is harder than it looks, and the reason that 'the gene is highly expressed' is never an adequate answer to 'why is flux low'.

5. Operons, and the structural difference that decides host

Bacteria transcribe polycistronic messages: one promoter, several genes, one transcript, with independent ribosome binding sites. This is extremely convenient for pathway engineering — one promoter controls a whole module, and relative expression is set by the individual RBSs. Eukaryotes do not do this in the same way: yeast needs a promoter and terminator per gene, or a 2A peptide or internal ribosome entry strategy. Add introns, capping, polyadenylation and nuclear export, and the result is that a yeast pathway construct is substantially larger and more complex than the equivalent in E. coli. That is a real cost in the host decision, set against yeast's compartments and P450 capability.

Worked anchor

A plant gene is expressed in E. coli from a strong promoter. Transcript is abundant; protein is not. Enumerate the explanations and order the experiments.

Six mechanistically distinct causes: rare codons stalling elongation; mRNA secondary structure occluding the RBS so initiation fails despite high transcript; rapid transcript turnover with high synthesis masking a short half-life; misfolding and aggregation into inclusion bodies; proteolytic degradation; and a toxic product selecting for non-expressing escape mutants that now dominate the culture.

Order by information gained per day, not by elegance. First, fractionate soluble from insoluble and run a gel — one day, no new construct, and it splits the hypothesis space roughly in half between 'protein made but insoluble' and 'protein not made'. If insoluble: lower temperature, weaken expression, try chaperones. If not made: vary the 5′ UTR and test codon-optimised synthesis. Only then consider degradation, with a protease-deficient strain, and escape, with flow cytometry on the population.

That ordering principle is the answer interviewers want, more than the list itself.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the promoter performs as specified and the transcript measurement is sound
  • the six causes are not mutually exclusive and may act together
  • ranking is by information per day for this host, not in general

Berg Ch 30SkimProtein synthesis. Read the initiation section closely — that is where the engineering lever is — and skim elongation and termination.

Common misconceptions

  • That a strong promoter guarantees expression. Initiation of translation, not transcription, is usually what limits a heterologous protein.
  • That codon optimisation always helps. It can remove functional pause sites and can introduce secondary structure; it is a hypothesis to test, not a fix to apply.
  • That an abundant transcript means an abundant protein. Four independent steps and a degradation rate sit in between, which is why flux and transcript correlate so weakly.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Where between gene and active enzyme is the rate most often limited, and what is the evidence for your answer?

A. Translation initiation. The evidence: ribosome profiling shows initiation, not elongation, as the step with the widest dynamic range between genes; RBS and 5′ UTR variation produces larger expression changes than promoter variation across comparable libraries; and computational models of initiation predict protein level better than transcript level does. The caveat worth stating is that this is the modal answer rather than the universal one — for a codon-pathological heterologous gene, elongation can dominate, and for an aggregation-prone product the limit is after translation entirely.

Q. Why does the same RBS give different expression in front of different genes?

A. Because initiation rate depends on the accessibility of the ribosome binding site and start codon, and accessibility depends on the secondary structure of the whole 5′ region — which includes the first tens of bases of the coding sequence. A downstream sequence that pairs with the SD region occludes it. This is why RBS strength is context-dependent rather than an intrinsic property, why RBS calculators take the coding sequence as input, and why silent substitutions in the first few codons are a standard tuning lever.

Q. You have one day to diagnose high transcript and low activity. What do you do, and what does each outcome rule out?

A. Fractionate soluble from insoluble protein and run a gel, because it costs a day, needs no new construct, and splits the hypothesis space roughly in half. Insoluble protein present rules out transcription, translation and degradation, pointing at expression rate, temperature or chaperones. No protein in either fraction rules out aggregation, pointing at translation initiation, codon usage or proteolysis. Abundant soluble protein rules out the whole expression axis and points downstream — cofactor, substrate supply, thermodynamic infeasibility or inhibition — each of which has its own next experiment.
