Week 8 — Bioenergetics

Thermodynamics you already own, applied to a system held far from equilibrium that charges a toll in ATP at every step. Get the conventions right this week and phases 3 and 4 become arithmetic; get them wrong and you will misread published numbers for a year. The week's three deliverables: fluency with the three Gibbs energies, a complete account of the respiratory chain's proton stoichiometry, and a settled understanding of why NADPH is not interchangeable with NADH.

Core ideas

1. Three Gibbs energies, and only one of them answers the question

ΔrG° is the chemical standard state: 1 M, 1 bar, each species with its own protonation and metal-binding state. ΔrG°′ is the transformed biochemical standard: pH fixed, specified ionic strength and temperature, water and H⁺ activity taken as unity, and all protonation states of a metabolite summed into one pseudo-species — which is why the biochemical and chemical literatures appear to disagree about the same reaction. ΔrG′ = ΔrG°′ + RT ln Q is the actual driving force, and it is the only one of the three that tells you whether a reaction can run forward in a cell. Memorise RT = 2.577 kJ/mol at 310 K, so a ten-fold concentration ratio is worth 5.93 kJ/mol and a thousand-fold is worth 17.8. Since intracellular metabolites span roughly 1 µM to 10 mM, the RT ln Q term routinely reaches 20–30 kJ/mol and frequently dominates ΔrG°′ entirely. Never judge feasibility from a tabulated value alone.

2. ATP as a currency, and why its hydrolysis energy is quoted over a range

The phosphoryl transfer potential of ATP comes from three contributions: electrostatic repulsion between the phosphates relieved on hydrolysis, better resonance stabilisation in the products, and more favourable solvation of the products. ΔrG°′ for ATP hydrolysis is quoted anywhere between −28 and −36 kJ/mol, and the spread is real rather than sloppy: it depends on free magnesium, which chelates the phosphates and changes the species distribution, and on pH. In vivo, with ATP/ADP ratios near 10 and phosphate near 10 mM, ΔrG′ is closer to −50 kJ/mol. Note where ATP sits in the phosphoryl hierarchy: PEP, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, creatine phosphate and acetyl phosphate are all above it, which is precisely how substrate-level phosphorylation works — a higher-potential donor hands its phosphate to ADP.

3. NADH and NADPH: same chemistry, separate pools, and this is the pivot of the course

The two differ only by a 2′-phosphate on the adenosine ribose, and both transfer a hydride. But the cell holds NADH largely oxidised — NAD⁺/NADH around 10 to 1,000 depending on condition — to serve as an electron acceptor for catabolism, while NADPH is held largely reduced, NADPH/NADP⁺ near 10 to 100, to serve as a biosynthetic reductant. Enzyme specificity for the 2′-phosphate keeps the pools separate. The engineering consequence governs much of what follows: a pathway requiring NADPH cannot draw on glycolytic NADH, and must instead be supplied by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, by NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase or malic enzyme, or by a transhydrogenase. Each of those carries a distinct cost — carbon, TCA flux, or proton-motive force — and choosing between them is a recurring design decision from week 10 onwards.

4. The respiratory chain, with the proton stoichiometry that actually matters

Electrons enter from NADH at Complex I, which in E. coli is NuoA-N and translocates about 4 H⁺ per 2 e⁻, or at the non-proton-pumping NADH dehydrogenase II, which translocates none. They pass to the quinone pool, then to a terminal oxidase. Count the oxidase carefully, because this is where most people go wrong: cytochrome bo₃ separates 4 charge equivalents per 2 e⁻, not 2 — two protons are actively pumped, and two more are consumed from the cytoplasm to make water while quinol oxidation releases two to the periplasm, and a proton consumed on one side contributes to the gradient exactly as a proton released on the other does. Cytochrome bd pumps none but still separates 2 equivalents by the same scalar mechanism, with much higher oxygen affinity. FADH₂-linked substrates including succinate enter at the quinone pool and bypass Complex I entirely, which is why they yield less. ATP synthase then runs the gradient down with H⁺/ATP set by the c-ring: E. coli's c₁₀ ring gives 10 H⁺ per 3 ATP from rotation, plus one for phosphate release — about 4.3 per ATP. Multiply through and the effective P/O for NADH is roughly 1.9 with Complex I plus bo₃, and roughly 0.5 with NDH-II plus bd — a four-fold range set by which enzymes are expressed, not a single textbook number. You will meet this stoichiometry again as a reaction name: in BiGG models the oxidase is CYTBO3_4pp, and the 4 is exactly this count.

5. Why P/O uncertainty propagates straight into your model

When ATP is the binding constraint, predicted biomass yield scales nearly linearly with ATP availability — so a factor of two in P/O moves a predicted growth yield by nearly a factor of two. Genome-scale models handle this not by resolving the physics but by fitting: growth-associated and non-growth-associated maintenance, GAM and NGAM, are regressed from measured growth yields across a chemostat series, which absorbs the P/O uncertainty into empirical parameters. State that plainly when asked whether genome-scale models are predictive: they are, conditionally on calibration, and the calibration is where the energetics hides.

6. Energy charge, and deliberate uncoupling as a tool

Adenylate energy charge is ([ATP] + ½[ADP])/([ATP] + [ADP] + [AMP]), and cells hold it near 0.85–0.95 with remarkable tenacity, because adenylate kinase equilibrates the three pools and many enzymes respond to the ratio rather than to ATP alone. Two engineering implications. First, an intervention that consumes ATP does not simply lower ATP, it shifts the whole adenylate distribution and triggers regulation. Second, this can be exploited: an uncoupler or a futile cycle creates ATP demand, which pulls glycolytic flux, and that is occasionally a deliberate strategy when the limitation is low glycolytic rate rather than low capacity downstream.

Worked anchor

ATP per glucose, and the honest range.

Per glucose: glycolysis yields 2 ATP and 2 NADH; pyruvate dehydrogenase yields 2 NADH; the TCA cycle yields 2 GTP, 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂. So 4 ATP-equivalents, 10 NADH, 2 FADH₂.

At P/O 2.5 for NADH and 1.5 for FADH₂: 4 + 25 + 3 = 32 ATP. At 2.0 and 1.2: 4 + 20 + 2.4 = 26.4. At 1.0 and 0.6: 4 + 10 + 1.2 = 15.2.

Now do it from the proton stoichiometry, for E. coli using Complex I and cytochrome bo₃: 4 + 4 = 8 charge equivalents per NADH oxidised, and at 4.3 H⁺ per ATP that is 1.86 ATP per NADH. Succinate's FADH₂ enters at the quinone pool, so it drives only the oxidase's 4 equivalents, giving 0.93 ATP. Total: 4 + (10 × 1.86) + (2 × 0.93) = 24.5 ATP per glucose. (The 2.5/1.5 band above is the mitochondrial convention; the E. coli chain pumps fewer protons per NADH, so the two calculations are not meant to agree. The range, not the point value, is the conclusion.) Now switch to NDH-II and cytochrome bd: 2 equivalents per NADH, so 0.47 ATP each, giving 4 + 4.7 + 0.93 = 9.6.

That ten-to-twenty-five range, from one organism with one substrate, is the honest answer — and it is why genome-scale models of E. coli predict ATP maxima in the twenties rather than at either extreme, since they carry both routes and let the optimisation choose.

When you see '38 ATP per glucose' in an older text, it assumed P/O ratios of 3 and 2 that nobody now defends. Write the derivation with your assumptions stated and you will be right in a way a quoted number never is.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • complete oxidation with no overflow metabolism
  • the stated P/O ratio or proton stoichiometry, 4.3 H⁺ per ATP at a c₁₀ ring (c/3 + 1)
  • GTP counted as ATP
  • no maintenance drain

Common misconceptions

  • That ΔrG°′ decides feasibility. The concentration term usually dominates it, so a reaction at +15 kJ/mol standard can run forward comfortably and one at −15 can sit near equilibrium.
  • That ATP hydrolysis releases 30.5 kJ/mol. That is a standard-state figure at a particular free magnesium and pH; in vivo it is closer to −50 kJ/mol and the textbook number should never be used in a ΔrG′ calculation without correction.
  • That 38 ATP per glucose is the answer. It assumes P/O ratios nobody defends. The defensible answer is a derivation with stated assumptions; for E. coli using its efficient chain it lands near 30, and near 11 using the uncoupled one.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Write the three Gibbs energies with their standard states, and say which answers whether a reaction runs forward in a cell.

A. ΔrG°: chemical standard state, 1 M and 1 bar, species defined individually with their own protonation and metal-binding. ΔrG°′: transformed biochemical standard, pH fixed at 7, specified ionic strength and temperature, water and H⁺ activity unity, protonation states summed into one pseudo-species. ΔrG′ = ΔrG°′ + RT ln Q: the actual driving force at prevailing concentrations, and the only one that answers the question — the RT ln Q term reaches 20–30 kJ/mol in a cell and frequently dominates.

Q. A reaction has ΔrG°′ = +14 kJ/mol. What product-to-substrate ratio makes ΔrG′ = −4, and name three ways a cell achieves it?

A. Need RT ln Q = −18 kJ/mol, so ln Q = −18/2.577 = −6.98 and Q = 9.3×10⁻⁴: products roughly 1,000-fold below substrates. Three mechanisms: rapid consumption of the product by the next enzyme, which is what pathway structure provides; stoichiometric coupling to ATP hydrolysis or another strongly favourable transformation in the same reaction; and removal of the product by export, compartmentalisation, volatility or precipitation. A fourth, which is really the first again: a high-capacity downstream sink.

Q. Your pathway needs 4 NADPH per product. Name three supply routes and the distinct cost of each.

A. The oxidative pentose phosphate pathway: 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate with one CO₂ released, so the cost is carbon — four NADPH costs two carbons. A transhydrogenase: the membrane-bound PntAB translocates one proton per NADPH produced, so the cost is one H⁺ of proton-motive force rather than half a carbon — which is the comparison to make, and it usually favours the transhydrogenase unless oxygen transfer is the binding constraint. An NADP-dependent GAPDH or isocitrate dehydrogenase: redirects existing flux, so the cost is a changed NADH balance that respiration was relying on, or a constraint on TCA flux. Which one is right depends on whether the process is carbon-limited, oxygen-limited or ATP-limited — a question week 52 answers, not week 8.

Week 9 — Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis

The chassis. Every product you design draws from twelve precursors, most made here, and every yield calculation starts from this stoichiometry. Learn the pathway as an accounting object rather than a sequence of names: what goes in, what comes out, what it costs in ATP and redox, and where the regulation sits. By Friday you should be able to write all ten reactions with cofactors from memory and build the stoichiometric matrix by hand.

Core ideas

1. The two phases, and why the investment phase exists

The preparatory phase spends 2 ATP to phosphorylate and cleave glucose into two triose phosphates; the payoff phase recovers 4 ATP and 2 NADH. Net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate per glucose. The investment looks wasteful until you see its three purposes: phosphorylation traps the sugar inside the cell, since the phosphorylated form cannot cross the membrane; it lowers the activation barrier to cleavage by destabilising the hexose; and it creates the handle for the substrate-level phosphorylation that follows. Carry the ten reactions as a sequence of chemical transformations — phosphorylation, isomerisation, phosphorylation, cleavage, isomerisation, oxidative phosphorylation, transfer, mutation, dehydration, transfer — rather than as ten names.

2. The three irreversible steps and what they regulate

Hexokinase or glucokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase are the thermodynamically irreversible steps, and they are the regulated ones because reversible steps near equilibrium cannot control flux. PFK is inhibited by ATP and PEP and activated by AMP and ADP, making it an energy sensor; in many organisms fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is a potent activator. Pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, which is feedforward activation — upstream signal anticipating downstream demand. Note the distinction you settled in week 6: these enzymes regulate glycolysis strongly and control it weakly, which is why overexpressing PFK does little and why the 'pacemaker' language in older texts is wrong.

3. Gluconeogenesis and the cost of futile cycling

Reversing glycolysis requires bypassing the three irreversible steps: pyruvate carboxylase plus PEP carboxykinase replaces pyruvate kinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase replaces PFK, and glucose-6-phosphatase replaces hexokinase. If both enzymes of a pair are active at once the net result is ATP hydrolysis with no chemical change — a futile cycle. Cells suppress this by reciprocal regulation, but it is never complete, and a deliberate futile cycle is occasionally used to create ATP demand. Quantitatively: a cycle running at 1 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ burns 1 mmol ATP gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹, which is about 5% of maintenance — detectable but rarely decisive unless the cycle is fast.

4. Three routes from glucose to pyruvate, compared properly

Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas: 2 ATP, 2 NADH per glucose. Entner-Doudoroff: 1 ATP, 1 NADH and 1 NADPH, using fewer enzyme steps and substantially less protein per unit flux. Phosphoketolase: 1 ATP per glucose with acetyl phosphate as a product, and no net NADH if the acetyl phosphate goes to acetate. The comparison that matters is not ATP per glucose but ATP per gram of enzyme invested: ED yields half the ATP but needs far less protein, which is why it dominates in Pseudomonas and Zymomonas, organisms operating where carbon is cheap and proteome is the binding constraint. This is the week-1 growth laws showing up in pathway choice, and it is the same logic that explains overflow metabolism in week 13.

5. The twelve precursors, which you should now commit to memory

Glucose-6-phosphate, fructose-6-phosphate, ribose-5-phosphate, erythrose-4-phosphate, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, 3-phosphoglycerate, phosphoenolpyruvate, pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, 2-oxoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, oxaloacetate. Six of these come from glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, six from the TCA cycle and its node. Every biomass component and nearly every product derives from them, which is why the biomass objective function in week 16 is written in their terms and why a yield calculation begins by asking which precursors a product needs and how many carbons are lost reaching them.

6. The matrix, and the first thing it tells you

Write the reactions as columns and the metabolites as rows, with stoichiometric coefficients as entries, and you have S. Two immediate checks: every column must balance elementally and in charge, which catches most transcription errors; and the null space of S contains every steady-state flux distribution, so its dimension tells you how many fluxes must be fixed by measurement or assumption before a unique solution exists. For glycolysis alone with its exchanges the null space is small and interpretable by inspection, which is exactly why Palsson teaches it on this pathway. Build it by hand this week, and build it in a notebook as you read rather than afterwards: print the matrix as a labelled DataFrame and assert that every column sums to zero for C, H, O, N, P and charge before you trust anything downstream. Reading about a carbon rearrangement in prose is weaker than watching its column balance in Python. In week 20 you will compare yours against the published core model, and every difference will teach you something.

Worked anchor

How much carbon does the cell lose on the way to acetyl-CoA, and why does that bound every acetyl-CoA-derived product?

Glucose (6 C) → 2 pyruvate (3 C each), no loss. Pyruvate dehydrogenase: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO₂, so one carbon of three is released at each of two pyruvates. Carbon reaching acetyl-CoA: 4 of 6, or 67%.

Therefore any product built purely from acetyl-CoA has a hard carbon ceiling of 2/3 C-mol per C-mol of glucose through this route, before any consideration of redox or ATP. For a C4 product from 2 acetyl-CoA, that is 1 mol product per mol glucose maximum; for a C₁₆ fatty acid needing 8 acetyl-CoA, 0.5 mol per mol glucose.

Now the engineering response, which is why this calculation appears in every acetyl-CoA paper: either fix the lost CO₂ back in with a carboxylation, or use a route that avoids the decarboxylation entirely — a phosphoketolase route to acetyl phosphate, or a reversed glyoxylate shunt. Each recovers carbon and costs something else. Doing this arithmetic before reading the paper tells you what problem the authors were solving.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • carbon accounting only; redox and ATP ignored
  • pyruvate dehydrogenase is the only route to acetyl-CoA
  • no anaplerotic return of carbon from the TCA cycle

Microbiology Ch 8.2Read closelyEntner-Doudoroff and the phosphoketolase pathway, which Berg does not cover and which you need for the three-route comparison and for week 43.
KEGG map00010 — glycolysisRead closelyThe canonical interactive map, organism-specific and free. Use it beside Berg rather than instead of it: KEGG gives topology and gene associations, Berg gives mechanism.
Palsson Ch 2 §2.1–2.2Read closelyThe stoichiometric matrix built on exactly this pathway. Reproduce Tables 2.1 and 2.2 by hand — it is the single most transferable exercise in the week.
Shuler Ch 5 §5.3SkimAn engineer's summary with the overall stoichiometries. Useful as a check on your own accounting rather than as a primary read.

Common misconceptions

  • That the irreversible steps are irreversible because the enzymes are one-directional. They are irreversible because ΔrG′ is strongly negative under cellular conditions; a different enzyme with a different mechanism runs the reverse reaction.
  • That ED is simply worse than EMP. It yields less ATP per glucose and more ATP per gram of protein, and which matters depends on whether carbon or proteome is limiting.
  • That phosphorylating glucose is purely about trapping it. It also destabilises the hexose for cleavage and creates the handle for substrate-level phosphorylation.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Write the net stoichiometry of glycolysis including cofactors and protons, and say where each ATP is made and spent.

A. Glucose + 2 NAD⁺ + 2 ADP + 2 Pi → 2 pyruvate + 2 NADH + 2 ATP + 2 H⁺ + 2 H₂O. Spent: 1 ATP at hexokinase, 1 at phosphofructokinase. Made: 2 at phosphoglycerate kinase and 2 at pyruvate kinase, one each per triose, so 4 gross and 2 net. NADH is produced at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, which is also where inorganic phosphate enters.

Q. Why does Entner-Doudoroff persist despite yielding half the ATP?

A. It requires substantially less enzyme protein per unit of catabolic flux, so under proteome-limited aerobic conditions it delivers more ATP per gram of protein invested even though it delivers less per glucose. Organisms occupying niches where carbon is plentiful and growth rate is set by protein allocation — Pseudomonas, Zymomonas — favour it. It also yields NADPH rather than only NADH, which suits oxidative-stress tolerance and reductive biotransformations.

Q. A product is built from 3 acetyl-CoA. What is its carbon ceiling from glucose through pyruvate dehydrogenase, and how would you raise it?

A. Each acetyl-CoA costs a decarboxylation, so from 1.5 glucose (9 C) you get 3 acetyl-CoA (6 C) having lost 3 as CO₂: a ceiling of 2/3 C-mol per C-mol, giving 0.67 mol product per mol glucose for a C6 product. Raise it by fixing the CO₂ back with a carboxylating reaction, or by avoiding the decarboxylation entirely with a phosphoketolase route to acetyl phosphate or a reversed glyoxylate shunt. Each recovers carbon at a cost in ATP or redox, and which is preferable depends on the host's energetics.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Draw the central-carbon route from an available cassava-derived sugar into a major fermentation product. Identify one branch point where carbon could instead support biomass or another product.

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Week 10 — The pentose phosphate pathway and the NADPH economy

The pathway that decides whether a reductive product is affordable. Most cofactor-driven yield failures trace back to this week, and the central skill is computing the glycolysis-to-pentose split required by a stated NADPH demand, together with the carbon that split costs.

Core ideas

1. Two branches with entirely different characters

The oxidative branch — glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, lactonase, 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase — is irreversible and generates 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate while releasing one carbon as CO₂, leaving ribulose-5-phosphate. The non-oxidative branch — ribulose-5-phosphate epimerase and isomerase, then transketolase and transaldolase — is fully reversible and simply rearranges carbon skeletons without redox chemistry, interconverting pentoses with fructose-6-phosphate, erythrose-4-phosphate, sedoheptulose-7-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Reversibility is why the pathway can run in several directions depending on what the cell needs, and why its flux is impossible to determine from extracellular rates.

2. The carbon rearrangement, worth doing on paper once

Three pentoses, fifteen carbons, become two fructose-6-phosphate and one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate: twelve plus three, fifteen carbons conserved. Transketolase moves two-carbon units, transaldolase moves three. Work this through by hand once, tracking individual carbons, then immediately encode the three reactions in your notebook and confirm the columns balance — the transketolase and transaldolase coefficients are the ones most often mistyped. Two things then become permanent: you will never again mis-state the stoichiometry, and you will understand why 1-¹³C glucose resolves the pathway's flux — because the oxidative branch specifically releases glucose C1 as CO₂ while glycolysis retains it and places it at C3 of pyruvate, giving distinguishable labelling downstream. That is the week 28 argument, and it is visible here.

3. Four flux modes, and the condition that selects each

Mode 1, NADPH only: oxidative branch runs, pentoses recycle completely to F6P and GAP, net result is glucose oxidised to CO₂ with NADPH produced. Mode 2, ribose only: non-oxidative branch runs in reverse from F6P and GAP to make R5P without any NADPH, used when nucleotide demand is high and reductant is not. Mode 3, both: oxidative branch runs and the pentose is used directly for biosynthesis. Mode 4, NADPH plus ATP: pentoses recycle through to pyruvate with glycolytic ATP generation. Knowing the modes lets you answer the question a model will put to you: what does the cell do when it needs ribose but not NADPH, or the reverse?

4. The carbon cost of NADPH, which is the week's central number

Two NADPH per decarboxylation means that supplying 2n NADPH costs n carbons. Twelve NADPH requires six glucose-6-phosphate cycled and releases six CO₂ — one whole glucose equivalent of carbon — even with perfect recycling of the pentoses, because the loss is intrinsic to the NADPH-generating step. This single calculation is why strains needing heavy NADPH acquire a transhydrogenase, an NADP-dependent GAPDH, or a non-decarboxylating route: each converts a carbon cost into an ATP or redox cost, which is usually cheaper. Compute this for your own target before reading any strain paper and you will know what the authors were fighting.

5. R5P and E4P: the pathway's other job

Ribose-5-phosphate is the nucleotide precursor, so every growing cell needs a flux of it proportional to its RNA and DNA synthesis — and RNA content scales with growth rate, so pentose demand rises with µ. Erythrose-4-phosphate, available only from the non-oxidative branch, is one of the two aromatic amino acid precursors with PEP. That makes the non-oxidative branch, and transketolase in particular, a standard overexpression target in aromatic strains: the shikimate pathway cannot run faster than E4P is supplied, however much you amplify the shikimate enzymes themselves.

6. The glutathione couple as a redox buffer

NADPH reduces oxidised glutathione (GSSG) to two GSH via glutathione reductase, and the GSH/GSSG couple is held at high ratio and high total concentration — millimolar — so it buffers the cell's reducing environment and absorbs oxidative insults. Two consequences. The thiol-reducing environment of the cytoplasm, which blocks disulfide formation from week 3, is maintained by this system at NADPH's expense. And oxidative stress consumes NADPH that your pathway wanted, which is one reason a producing strain under stress underperforms its NADPH budget.

Worked anchor

A product requires 14 NADPH per mole. What does supplying it from the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway cost, and what are the alternatives worth?

Two NADPH per G6P with one CO₂ released, so 14 NADPH needs 7 G6P cycled and releases 7 CO₂. The 7 ribulose-5-phosphate produced carry 35 carbons and recycle intact through the non-oxidative branch into F6P and triose phosphates, so the only carbon loss is those 7 decarboxylations — slightly more than one glucose equivalent.

Compare: a transhydrogenase supplying all 14 NADPH from NADH costs no carbon but spends proton-motive force for each, raising oxygen demand by roughly 14 × (H⁺ per NADPH) / (H⁺ per O) worth of extra respiration. An NADP-dependent GAPDH converts glycolytic NADH production directly to NADPH at no carbon and no PMF cost, but removes the NADH the respiratory chain was using for ATP, so the cell must make that ATP elsewhere.

The decision rule: if the process is carbon-limited and oxygen transfer has headroom, take the transhydrogenase. If oxygen transfer is the constraint — which week 49 will tell you — take the carbon loss instead. There is no context-free answer, and saying so is the correct answer.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • two NADPH per G6P through the oxidative branch
  • the non-oxidative branch recycles pentose carbon intact
  • transhydrogenase at 1 H⁺ per NADPH
  • no competing biosynthetic demand on the pentose pool

Common misconceptions

  • That recycling the pentoses recovers the lost carbon. The CO₂ is released at the dehydrogenase step and is gone; recycling conserves only the remaining 5 carbons of each pentose.
  • That the pentose pathway is 'the NADPH pathway'. It has four flux modes, one of which makes no NADPH at all, and labelling studies of glucose-limited aerobic E. coli put the oxidative branch at only about 35–60% of total NADPH supply, with NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase supplying much of the rest. Quote that range rather than assuming the pathway dominates.
  • That amplifying shikimate enzymes raises aromatic flux. It usually does not, because E4P supply from the non-oxidative branch limits first — which is why transketolase is the standard target.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. State the oxidative branch stoichiometry and compute the carbon cost of 10 NADPH.

A. G6P + 2 NADP⁺ + H₂O → ribulose-5-phosphate + CO₂ + 2 NADPH + 2 H⁺. Ten NADPH requires 5 G6P cycled and releases 5 CO₂, so five carbons — a little under one glucose equivalent. The five pentoses (25 C) recycle intact to F6P and triose phosphates, so no further carbon is lost.

Q. Why can extracellular rates never reveal the pentose phosphate split ratio?

A. Carbon entering the oxidative branch returns to glycolysis as fructose-6-phosphate and triose phosphate, so the cycle has no distinct external signature apart from CO₂, which has several other sources. The cycle flux lies in the null space of the external stoichiometry: it can take any value without changing any measurable uptake or excretion rate. Resolving it requires labelling, because the oxidative branch releases glucose C1 as CO₂ while glycolysis retains it, giving different downstream mass isotopomer distributions.

Q. An aromatic amino acid strain has ample shikimate pathway expression and low titre. What do you suspect and what do you amplify?

A. Precursor limitation rather than pathway capacity: the shikimate route needs erythrose-4-phosphate plus PEP, and E4P comes only from the non-oxidative pentose phosphate branch. Amplify transketolase, and consider transaldolase, to raise E4P supply; address PEP availability separately by replacing PTS uptake with a permease plus glucokinase, or by attenuating pyruvate kinase. Confirm the diagnosis by measuring intracellular E4P and PEP before building anything.

Week 11 — TCA cycle, anaplerosis and the glyoxylate shunt

The branch point that decides whether carbon becomes product, biomass or CO₂. Most C4 product designs live or die on the anaplerotic reactions studied this week, and the host differences at that node are the single clearest case in the course of biology dictating a host choice.

Core ideas

1. Pyruvate dehydrogenase: the committed, irreversible gateway

Three enzymes in one complex: E1 decarboxylates pyruvate onto thiamine pyrophosphate, E2 transfers the acetyl group to lipoamide and then to coenzyme A, E3 reoxidises the lipoamide using FAD and then NAD⁺. The result is acetyl-CoA, CO₂ and NADH, and it is effectively irreversible — which is why acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate and why the carbon lost here cannot be recovered without a carboxylation elsewhere. The complex is inhibited by its own products, acetyl-CoA and NADH, so a cell with high reducing power throttles entry to the cycle. Note the oxygen sensitivity of the anaerobic alternative, pyruvate formate lyase, which produces formate rather than CO₂ and NADH — a different carbon and redox outcome from the same node, and the basis of week 13.

2. Eight reactions, two decarboxylations, and the real yield

Per acetyl-CoA entering: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂. The two decarboxylations are at isocitrate dehydrogenase and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, and they are what make the cycle a carbon-destroying machine in the service of energy production. Regulation sits at citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, all responding to energy charge and NADH. For engineering, learn which intermediates are drawn off for biosynthesis — oxaloacetate for aspartate and the aspartate family, 2-oxoglutarate for glutamate and the glutamate family, succinyl-CoA for porphyrins and for lysine via one route — because every carbon drawn off must be replaced.

3. Anaplerosis is replacement, and the node is where host choice is decided

Drawing intermediates off the cycle depletes it, so carbon must be put back: that is anaplerosis. The PEP-pyruvate-oxaloacetate node in E. coli has four reactions. PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ onto PEP to give oxaloacetate, using PEP's own phosphate potential and needing no ATP or biotin. PEP carboxykinase runs the reverse, consuming oxaloacetate and making ATP, and is gluconeogenic. Malic enzyme decarboxylates malate to pyruvate with NAD or NADP reduction, and is cataplerotic. Pyruvate kinase connects PEP to pyruvate. Now the crucial difference: E. coli lacks pyruvate carboxylase, while C. glutamicum and S. cerevisiae have it. Since pyruvate carboxylase fixes CO₂ onto pyruvate rather than PEP, it does not compete with the PTS or with aromatic pathways for PEP — which is a substantial part of why C. glutamicum dominates lysine and why it is attractive for C4 diacids.

4. The glyoxylate shunt: the bypass that conserves carbon

Isocitrate lyase cleaves isocitrate to succinate and glyoxylate; malate synthase condenses glyoxylate with a second acetyl-CoA to give malate. The net effect is to convert two acetyl-CoA into one C4 without either decarboxylation, which is what makes net biosynthesis from acetate or fatty acids possible — without it, growth on acetate is impossible, because every acetyl-CoA entering the cycle would be fully oxidised. For engineering, it is a recurring target for C4 products precisely because it conserves the carbon the cycle would release. It is tightly regulated, typically by phosphorylation of isocitrate dehydrogenase to divert flux, and derepressing it is a standard intervention.

5. Two routes to succinate, and why the reductive one wins

Oxidatively, succinate is four steps from citrate through two decarboxylations, so carbon is lost and the yield is poor. Reductively, oxaloacetate is reduced through malate and fumarate to succinate, fixing CO₂ at the carboxylation step and consuming NADH rather than producing it. Since succinate (γ = 3.50 per C-mol) is more oxidised than glucose (4.00), electrons are in surplus and can pay for fixing an extra fully oxidised carbon — which is why the reductive route has a stoichiometric ceiling of 1.71 mol/mol against roughly 1.0 for the oxidative, and why every serious succinate strain uses carboxylation. The general lesson, which recurs in week 17: for products more oxidised than the substrate, CO₂ fixation is the yield mechanism rather than an environmental talking point.

6. Where the cycle is not a cycle

Under anaerobic or strongly fermentative conditions, many bacteria run the TCA as two branches rather than a cycle: an oxidative arm from citrate to 2-oxoglutarate supplying glutamate, and a reductive arm from oxaloacetate to succinate acting as an electron sink. 2-Oxoglutarate dehydrogenase is often repressed, breaking the ring. This matters because a model with a closed cycle will predict fluxes an anaerobic cell cannot carry, and because the reductive arm is exactly the route a succinate strain exploits. When reading a flux map, check first whether the cycle is closed under the condition reported.

Worked anchor

Compute the maximum anaerobic succinate yield from glucose, with and without CO₂ fixation, and explain the difference.

Without fixation, through the oxidative route: glycolysis gives 2 PEP and 2 NADH; reducing oxaloacetate to succinate needs 2 NADH per succinate, so 2 succinate would need 4 NADH while glycolysis supplies 2. The redox balance caps the route near 1.0 mol/mol, with an oxidised co-product such as acetate acting as the electron sink for the shortfall.

With PEP carboxylase fixing one CO₂ per succinate and the reductive arm carrying the flux, the classical ceiling is 1.71 mol succinate per mol glucose, equal to 1.12 g/g.

Why the surplus exists: glucose carries 24 available electrons per mole; succinate carries 14 per mole. 24/14 = 1.71. Succinate being more oxidised than glucose means the electron budget permits more product than the carbon budget of glucose alone would allow — provided the extra carbon comes from CO₂.

Real strains reach 1.3–1.6 mol/mol, because reaching the ceiling needs either a supplementary reductant, a dual-phase aerobic-anaerobic process, or a hydrogen-rich co-substrate, and because the carboxylase must compete kinetically with pyruvate kinase for PEP. That competition is why PEP carboxylase overexpression and pyruvate kinase attenuation appear together in so many designs.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • anaerobic, with no external electron acceptor
  • redox balance closed on the stated products only
  • CO₂ freely available for fixation
  • no maintenance or biomass demand

Common misconceptions

  • That the TCA cycle is always a cycle. Under anaerobic conditions it frequently runs as two branches with 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase repressed, and a model assuming closure will overpredict.
  • That anaplerosis is a detail of cofactor bookkeeping. It is the specific reaction set that decides whether a C4 product is feasible in a host, and E. coli's lack of pyruvate carboxylase is a genuine disadvantage for that product class.
  • That the glyoxylate shunt makes energy. It conserves carbon at the cost of the NADH and FADH₂ the bypassed steps would have made, which is exactly the trade you want for a product and exactly the wrong trade for growth.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Name the four reactions of the PEP-pyruvate-oxaloacetate node in E. coli, their directions, and the host difference that matters.

A. PEP carboxylase: PEP + CO₂ → oxaloacetate, anaplerotic, no ATP or biotin needed. PEP carboxykinase: oxaloacetate + ATP → PEP + CO₂, gluconeogenic. Malic enzyme: malate → pyruvate + CO₂ with NAD or NADP reduction, cataplerotic. Pyruvate kinase: PEP → pyruvate + ATP. The difference: E. coli lacks pyruvate carboxylase, which C. glutamicum and S. cerevisiae possess, and which carboxylates pyruvate rather than PEP — so it does not compete with the PTS or with aromatic biosynthesis for PEP.

Q. Why is growth on acetate impossible without the glyoxylate shunt?

A. Acetate enters metabolism only as acetyl-CoA, which in the ordinary cycle is fully oxidised to two CO₂ per turn, so no net carbon is available for biosynthesis — every carbon that enters leaves as CO₂. The glyoxylate shunt bypasses both decarboxylations, converting two acetyl-CoA into one C4 compound and so permitting net synthesis of the precursors the cell needs. Growth on fatty acids has the same requirement for the same reason.

Q. Why does an E. coli succinate strain need a carboxylating reaction, and which carboxylase would you pick in each host?

A. Because succinate is more oxidised than glucose, the electron budget allows more product than glucose's carbon alone supports — but only if the extra carbon comes from CO₂, raising the ceiling from about 1.0 to 1.71 mol/mol. In E. coli the available option is PEP carboxylase, usually overexpressed and often paired with pyruvate kinase attenuation so the carboxylase wins the competition for PEP; a heterologous pyruvate carboxylase is an alternative that avoids that competition. In C. glutamicum or yeast, use the native pyruvate carboxylase for exactly that reason.

Week 12 — Respiration, electron transport and aeration

Where biology meets your mass transfer course. The oxygen demand you compute this week becomes the kLa calculation in week 49 and the vessel cost in week 52, and the chain's branching is why a single P/O number was never going to be enough.

Core ideas

1. E. coli's respiratory chain branches at both ends, and that is the point

Entry: NADH dehydrogenase I (Nuo), translocating roughly 4 H⁺ per 2 e⁻, or NADH dehydrogenase II (Ndh), translocating none and simply passing electrons to the quinone pool. Exit: cytochrome bo₃, low oxygen affinity, separating 4 charge equivalents per 2 e⁻ — two pumped and two scalar, which is why its BiGG reaction is named CYTBO3_4pp — or cytochrome bd, high oxygen affinity, separating 2 by the scalar route alone. Combine the options and the equivalents per NADH range from 8 down to 2, so with E. coli's c₁₀ ATP synthase at 4.3 H⁺ per ATP the effective P/O spans roughly 1.9 down to 0.5. The cell chooses by condition: high oxygen favours the efficient combination, low oxygen forces the high-affinity bd oxidase. A model with a fixed P/O therefore mispredicts systematically at low dissolved oxygen, and that is a real source of error in microaerobic process modelling.

2. Anaerobic respiration, ranked by what it is worth

With oxygen absent, many bacteria respire on alternative terminal acceptors, and the ATP yield follows the reduction potential. Nitrate is the best, close enough to oxygen to support substantial growth; then DMSO and TMAO; then fumarate, which is the weakest and which doubles as the reductive TCA arm from week 11. Note the regulatory hierarchy: cells express these in order of preference, so a medium containing nitrate will suppress fumarate respiration. For engineering, this matters in two ways — an unintended electron acceptor in your medium can break a growth-coupled design by giving the cell an escape route, and deliberately supplying one is a way to control redox state.

3. From electron balance to oxygen demand, which is the week's transferable skill

Oxygen uptake is not an independent parameter to be looked up; it follows from the electron balance. Electrons entering as substrate must leave as product, as biomass, or as water via the respiratory chain. So: available electrons in substrate consumed, minus those in biomass formed, minus those in products formed, divided by four, gives moles of oxygen. Do it this way and the number is consistent with your yields by construction, which is the whole point. Working in degrees of reduction per C-mol — glucose 4.00, biomass 4.20, acetate 4.00, ethanol 6.00, succinate 3.50 — makes the arithmetic routine, and week 17 formalises it.

4. Oxygen as a substrate with almost no solubility

Air-saturated water at 30 °C holds about 0.21 mM dissolved oxygen, roughly 7 mg/L. A dense culture consumes that in a few seconds, which is why oxygen must be supplied continuously and why it is the usual limiting nutrient in aerobic fermentation. At steady state OTR = kLa(C − C) must equal OUR. The critical dissolved oxygen concentration — below which the organism's respiration becomes oxygen-limited rather than substrate-limited — is typically 1–5% of saturation for bacteria, which is low enough that a setpoint of 20–30% gives comfortable margin. The consequence to carry forward: raising C by oxygen enrichment or head pressure is usually cheaper than raising kLa by agitation, because power input scales steeply and brings shear and heat penalties with it.

5. Microaerobic operation as a deliberate choice

Some products are made best at low dissolved oxygen, because the cell's product spectrum shifts with redox state: restricting oxygen raises NADH, which drives reductive routes that are unavailable to a fully respiring cell. This is used industrially for several reduced products, and it changes the process problem from supplying oxygen to controlling it precisely at a low setpoint, which is harder. The trade is that growth and ATP yield fall, so titre and rate suffer while yield on the reduced product rises — the titre-rate-yield triangle appearing in its most physical form.

6. Heat, which is the constraint people forget

Roughly 460 kJ is released per mole of oxygen consumed, nearly independent of substrate, which makes oxygen uptake a direct proxy for heat generation. At an OUR of 100 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ that is about 13 kW per cubic metre, so a 50 m³ vessel generates several hundred kilowatts of heat requiring removal through a jacket or coils whose area scales as volume to the two-thirds. That is why large aerobic fermenters are sometimes heat-limited rather than oxygen-limited, and why the energy balance from Doran Ch 5 belongs in a process design rather than only in an examination.

Worked anchor

Compute the oxygen demand of a producing strain from first principles, then the kLa it requires.

A strain grows at µ = 0.25 h⁻¹ with YX/S = 0.45 g/g on glucose and makes acetate at 0.20 g per g glucose. Biomass is CH₁.₈O₀.₅N₀.₂.

Per gram of glucose: available electrons in = 0.133 mol e⁻ (24 per mole, 180 g/mol). Biomass at γ = 4.2 per C-mol and 24.6 g per C-mol carries 0.171 mol e⁻ per gram, so 0.45 g carries 0.077. Acetate at γ = 4.0 and 30 g per C-mol carries 0.133 per gram, so 0.20 g carries 0.027. To oxygen: 0.133 − 0.077 − 0.027 = 0.029 mol e⁻, and oxygen accepts 4, so 0.0073 mol O₂ per g glucose.

Substrate uptake qS = µ/YX/S = 0.25/0.45 = 0.56 g gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹, so qO₂ = 0.0073 × 0.56 × 1000 = 4.1 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹.

At 40 gDW/L: OUR = 164 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹. Required kLa = OUR/(C* − C) = 164/(0.21 − 0.04) = 965 h⁻¹.

That is comfortable at bench scale and at or beyond the limit of a large production vessel — which is precisely the conflict week 49 designs around, and the reason the answer to 'can we scale this' is often decided in week 12 rather than in the fermentation hall.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • biomass CH₁.₈O₀.₅N₀.₂ at 24.6 g per C-mol and γ = 4.2
  • the electron balance closes on biomass, acetate and oxygen alone
  • steady state, no accumulation of intermediates
  • the kLa correlation applies at this scale and broth viscosity

Common misconceptions

  • That P/O is a constant. In E. coli it varies four-fold, from about 2.4 to 0.6, with which dehydrogenase and which oxidase are expressed, and those shift with dissolved oxygen.
  • That you look up qO₂. It follows from the electron balance given your yields, and computing it that way guarantees internal consistency — looking it up guarantees the opposite.
  • That oxygen limitation is only about supply. The critical dissolved oxygen concentration is strain-specific and often very low, so a culture at 2% saturation may be perfectly unlimited while one at 10% with poor mixing is not.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Why does E. coli switch terminal oxidase at low oxygen, and what does that do to ATP yield?

A. Cytochrome bo₃ has lower oxygen affinity and separates 4 charge equivalents per 2 e⁻; cytochrome bd has much higher affinity and separates 2. At low dissolved oxygen the cell switches to bd in order to keep respiring at all, accepting half the charge separation per electron pair and therefore a lower effective P/O and lower ATP yield per glucose. This is one reason microaerobic operation shifts the product spectrum, and one reason a fixed-P/O model mispredicts at low oxygen.

Q. A strain at 35 gDW/L has qO₂ = 5 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹. What kLa is needed at C* = 0.21 mM and a 0.04 mM setpoint, and is it feasible at 30 m³?

A. OUR = 5 × 35 = 175 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹; kLa = 175/0.17 = 1,029 h⁻¹. A large stirred tank typically delivers 200–500 h⁻¹ before power and shear become limiting, so this is not feasible as stated. Remedies: oxygen enrichment or head pressure to raise C, a lower setpoint if the critical oxygen concentration permits, or a lower specific demand by capping growth rate through the feed — and raising C is usually cheapest because power scales steeply.

Q. How much cooling does that fermentation need per cubic metre?

A. About 460 kJ per mole of oxygen consumed. At 175 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ = 175 mol m⁻³ h⁻¹, heat generation is 80.5 MJ m⁻³ h⁻¹ = 22 kW per cubic metre. For 30 m³ that is 670 kW of cooling duty, through a heat transfer area that scales only as volume to the two-thirds — which is why large aerobic fermenters are sometimes heat-limited before they are oxygen-limited.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Relate aeration and oxygen transfer in your fermentation to respiratory versus fermentative metabolism. What dissolved-oxygen or off-gas measurements would support the explanation?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Week 13 — Fermentation routes and redox balancing

Anaerobic metabolism is a redox-balancing exercise with ATP as the prize. By Friday you should be able to write a product spectrum that balances electrons, detect what is missing from one that does not, and explain why fermentation persists in the presence of oxygen. The week closes phase 2, so budget two sessions for consolidating the pathway atlas into something you will actually reuse in phase 4.

Core ideas

1. The anaerobic pyruvate node, and the choice the cell makes there

Without a terminal electron acceptor, glycolytic NADH must be reoxidised by reducing something the cell made itself, and the options at the pyruvate node determine the product spectrum. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate directly, consuming one NADH and making no ATP beyond glycolysis. Pyruvate formate lyase cleaves pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and formate without redox chemistry, and the acetyl-CoA can then go to ethanol, consuming two NADH, or to acetate via phosphotransacetylase and acetate kinase, consuming none but making an extra ATP. So the cell trades ATP against redox: acetate is the ATP-rich, electron-poor option and ethanol the reverse, and the ratio it chooses is set by how much NADH needs disposing of. That is the whole logic of mixed-acid fermentation.

2. Mixed-acid fermentation, and why hydrogen matters to your balance

E. coli anaerobically produces a mixture: ethanol, acetate, formate, lactate, succinate, and from formate via formate hydrogen lyase, CO₂ and H₂. The hydrogen is the trap for a careless balance: it carries electrons and no carbon, so omitting it leaves carbon closing while electrons do not. Succinate is the other subtlety, since its formation fixes CO₂ and consumes NADH, making it an electron sink that also conserves carbon. When you see a published anaerobic product spectrum, check first whether gas was measured; a great many are reported without it and cannot be balanced as published.

3. Homolactic and heterolactic fermentation, with the numbers

Homolactic: glucose through the EMP pathway to 2 pyruvate, both reduced to lactate by LDH. Net 2 ATP, 2 lactate, no CO₂, and a theoretical mass yield of 1.0 g/g since 180 g of glucose becomes 180 g of lactate. Heterolactic: glucose through the phosphoketolase pathway to lactate plus ethanol plus CO₂, with 1 ATP per glucose and roughly half the mass yield. Homolactic is therefore the chassis for lactate, which is why lactate production uses homofermentative lactobacilli. The limit in practice is not stoichiometry but pH: the undissociated acid mechanism from week 2 sets a titre ceiling well before the carbon runs out, which is why these processes run neutralised and pay for it downstream.

4. Overflow metabolism: fermentation in the presence of oxygen

Above a critical growth rate, E. coli excretes acetate and yeast excretes ethanol even when oxygen is abundant. The modern explanation is proteome allocation, not any deficiency: respiration yields more ATP per glucose but requires more protein per unit of ATP flux, because the respiratory chain and TCA enzymes are expensive. Above a threshold flux the cell gets more ATP per gram of protein invested by fermenting part of the carbon, so it does. This is the week-1 growth laws cashed out, it explains the Crabtree effect and the Warburg effect by the same mechanism, and it is why proteome-constrained models in week 31 reproduce the acetate switch without any ad hoc bound. The process consequence is direct: suppress overflow by holding growth below the critical rate with a controlled feed, which is week 50's exponential feeding.

5. Redox balancing as a design constraint and as a diagnostic

Two uses, and you should practise both. As a constraint: when designing an anaerobic pathway, the NADH produced by glycolysis must equal the NADH consumed by your route plus any remaining sinks, or the design cannot carry flux — which is the stoichiometric basis of growth coupling in week 26, where you delete every sink but the product. As a diagnostic: given a measured product spectrum, compute carbon and electron closure separately and read the pattern. Carbon short with electrons complete implicates a carbon-bearing, electron-poor stream, almost always CO₂. Both short by a similar factor implicates biomass under-reporting. Both high by a similar factor implicates one over-reported stream. Electrons short with carbon complete implicates H₂ or another reduced gas.

Worked anchor

Close a mixed-acid balance, and name what is missing.

Per 100 mol glucose: 60 ethanol, 60 formate, 50 acetate, 20 lactate, 30 succinate.

Carbon in: 600 C-mol. Out: ethanol 120, formate 60, acetate 100, lactate 60, succinate 120 = 460 C-mol, so 77% recovery.

Electrons, using γ per C-mol (glucose 4.00, ethanol 6.00, acetate 4.00, lactate 4.00, succinate 3.50, formate 2.00): in 2,400. Out: ethanol 60×2×6 = 720; acetate 50×2×4 = 400; lactate 20×3×4 = 240; succinate 30×4×3.5 = 420; formate 60×1×2 = 120. Total 1,900, so 79%.

Both balances short by a similar factor points at a stream carrying both carbon and electrons in roughly biomass proportion — and indeed biomass is entirely absent from this spectrum. Assigning the missing 140 C-mol to biomass at γ = 4.2 supplies 588 electrons, which brings electrons to 2,488, slightly over. The small excess sits within the uncertainty of the biomass formula, and the residual can be trimmed by noting that succinate formation fixes CO₂, so some of the carbon came from outside glucose.

The method is the lesson: read the pattern of the two closures before you guess at a missing stream. Both short in proportion means biomass; carbon short alone means CO₂; electrons short alone means H₂.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the listed products are everything the analytics measured
  • γ per C-mol as tabulated
  • no biomass term in the balance
  • the sample is representative of the whole fermentation

Berg Ch 16 §16.1SkimNAD⁺ regeneration and the logic of fermentation. Short; read it for the framing and move on.

Common misconceptions

  • That overflow metabolism is oxygen limitation. It happens with oxygen in excess, and the explanation is proteome efficiency — more ATP per gram of protein from fermentation than from respiration above a threshold flux.
  • That a product spectrum without gas measurement can be balanced. Formate, CO₂ and H₂ carry carbon and electrons in different proportions, and omitting them makes the balance uninterpretable rather than merely incomplete.
  • That homolactic fermentation's 1.0 g/g ceiling is reachable. The undissociated acid poisons the cell long before the carbon runs out, which is why the real constraint is pH tolerance.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Write the homolactic and heterolactic equations and compute ATP and mass yield for each.

A. Homolactic: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 CH₃CHOHCOOH, via EMP, net 2 ATP, no CO₂, mass yield 180/180 = 1.0 g/g. Heterolactic: C₆H₁₂O₆ → lactate + ethanol + CO₂, via phosphoketolase, net 1 ATP, mass yield roughly 90/180 = 0.5 g/g for lactate alone. Homolactic is therefore the lactate chassis, with twice the ATP and twice the yield; the trade is that homofermentative lactobacilli are nutritionally fastidious, so complex medium cost partly offsets the yield advantage.

Q. A product spectrum closes to 95% on carbon and 101% on electrons. What is missing and how do you know?

A. A carbon-bearing, electron-poor stream — almost certainly CO₂, because it carries carbon and no available electrons, so omitting it depresses carbon closure while leaving electrons intact or slightly high. Measure it by off-gas integration rather than inferring it. Had both balances been short by a similar factor the diagnosis would instead be under-reported biomass; had electrons alone been short, H₂ or another reduced gas.

Q. Why does a cell ferment when oxygen is available, and what does that imply for process control?

A. Because respiration yields more ATP per glucose but requires more protein per unit of ATP flux; above a critical flux the cell obtains more ATP per gram of protein invested by fermenting part of the carbon. It is a proteome allocation optimum, not a defect. The process implication is that overflow is controllable by rate rather than by oxygen: hold the specific growth rate below the critical value with an exponential or feedback-controlled feed, and the carbon stops going to acetate — which is why fed-batch exists and why simply adding more air does not fix acetate.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Write a carbon and electron balance for a fermentation product you measured. Which unmeasured by-products could make an apparent yield or redox balance misleading?

Week 14 — Biosynthesis and the precursor tree

Biosynthesis is where industrial metabolic engineering began and where most of its money still is. It is also the source of every coefficient in a biomass equation, so this week does double duty: it teaches the pathways you may engineer, and it generates the numbers week 16 needs. Treat it as a costing exercise — each amino acid has a price in precursors, NADPH and ATP, and that price is what decides a theoretical yield.

Core ideas

1. Nitrogen enters by two routes with different prices

Glutamate dehydrogenase aminates 2-oxoglutarate directly using NADPH, costs no ATP, and has a high Km for ammonium — so it works only when nitrogen is plentiful. The glutamine synthetase–glutamate synthase couple (GS-GOGAT) first makes glutamine at the cost of one ATP, then transfers the amide nitrogen to 2-oxoglutarate, consuming NADPH. The net is one extra ATP per ammonium assimilated, bought in exchange for a far lower Km. That is a clean example of a pattern you will meet repeatedly: the cell pays energy for affinity. Once nitrogen is in glutamate and glutamine, transaminases distribute it, which is why these two metabolites are the nitrogen hub and why glutamate is the most abundant intracellular metabolite in most bacteria at 50–100 mM.

2. The amino acid families, organised by precursor

Learn them as a tree rooted in the twelve precursors, not as twenty separate pathways. Glutamate family from 2-oxoglutarate: glutamate, glutamine, proline, arginine. Aspartate family from oxaloacetate: aspartate, asparagine, methionine, threonine, lysine, isoleucine — the industrially dominant family. Pyruvate family: alanine, valine, leucine. Serine family from 3-phosphoglycerate: serine, glycine, cysteine. Aromatic family from erythrose-4-phosphate plus PEP: phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan. Histidine, alone, from PRPP and ATP. Two engineering consequences follow directly. The aspartate family shares a committed step, aspartokinase, so a lysine strain and a threonine strain compete at the same branch point. And the aromatic family's dependence on E4P plus PEP explains why those strains always involve transketolase and PTS interventions, as week 10 established.

3. Branch-point regulation and what a feedback-resistant design must achieve

Three architectures solve the problem of regulating a branched pathway from a shared step. Isozymes: several copies of the first enzyme, each inhibited by a different end product — E. coli's three aspartokinases are the textbook case, inhibited respectively by lysine, threonine and methionine-related signals. Concerted inhibition: the first step is inhibited only when all end products are present together. Cumulative inhibition: each product contributes partial inhibition and the effects compound. Which architecture is present determines the intervention. Under isozymes you must address every copy that carries flux, which is precisely why industrial lysine strains took several strain generations rather than one deletion. Under cumulative inhibition deletion helps nothing and you must engineer the allosteric site itself. And note from week 6 that the most useful mutations often abolish cooperativity rather than affinity, because the sigmoid is what makes the inhibition sharp.

4. Nucleotides: expensive, regulated, and salvaged

Purines are built onto PRPP stepwise, consuming glycine, glutamine, aspartate, formate from tetrahydrofolate and CO₂, at a cost of several ATP; pyrimidines build the ring first and attach PRPP afterwards. Both routes are expensive — on the order of 5–10 ATP-equivalents per nucleotide including the amino acid precursors — which is why salvage pathways exist and why they matter industrially: a fast-growing production strain spends a substantial share of its biosynthetic budget on RNA, and RNA content rises with growth rate (the week 1 growth laws again). The regulatory point worth carrying: PRPP sits at the junction of purine, pyrimidine, histidine and tryptophan synthesis, so its pool is contested and its availability constrains several product classes at once.

5. Costing an amino acid, which is the week's transferable skill

The procedure: identify the precursors and their count, the NADPH consumed, the ATP consumed, the carbons lost as CO₂, and any nitrogen assimilation cost. Then convert to a theoretical yield on glucose. For lysine: oxaloacetate plus pyruvate, 4 NADPH, 1 ATP, with one CO₂ fixed at the anaplerotic step. Published ceilings cluster near 1.0 mol lysine per mol glucose when anaplerosis carboxylates and NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway, rising towards 1.3 if a non-decarboxylating NADPH route is assumed — so state your assumptions, because the number is assumption-dependent and an interviewer is testing whether you know that. Best published strains reach about 0.55 g/g, roughly two thirds of theoretical, with the gap going to biomass, maintenance, by-products and the carbon lost supplying NADPH.

6. Where sulfur and one-carbon units come from, briefly

Sulfate assimilation is costly: reduction to sulfide consumes ATP for activation and several NADPH, which is why cysteine and methionine are among the most expensive amino acids and why methionine remains a hard industrial target. One-carbon units ride on tetrahydrofolate at several oxidation levels and feed purine synthesis, thymidylate, and methionine's methyl group via S-adenosylmethionine. You need this only at the level of knowing that these are expensive and regulated — but if your product is a methylated natural product, SAM supply becomes a first-order design constraint and you should recognise it immediately.

Worked anchor

Cost phenylalanine from glucose, and see where the constraint sits.

Precursors: erythrose-4-phosphate (C4) plus two phosphoenolpyruvate (C3 each) enter the shikimate pathway, giving chorismate, then prephenate, then phenylpyruvate, then transamination to phenylalanine (C9).

Carbon: 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 carbons in, 9 in the product, so one CO₂ released at the prephenate dehydratase step. Carbon efficiency of the route itself is 90%.

Now trace back to glucose. E4P comes from the non-oxidative pentose phosphate branch; PEP comes from glycolysis. If uptake is by the PTS, one PEP per glucose is consumed just to bring the sugar in — so the two PEP the pathway needs come at the expense of PEP that would otherwise be available, and the theoretical yield is roughly halved relative to a non-PTS strain. Published maxima are near 0.3 g/g with PTS and near 0.5 g/g with a permease-plus-glucokinase replacement, the difference being almost entirely this PEP accounting.

The lesson is the one week 15 develops: for a PEP-derived product, the transporter is a stoichiometric decision, not a logistics detail. Before designing anything in the shikimate pathway, do this arithmetic — it tells you that the first intervention is at the membrane and the second is at transketolase, and only the third is in the pathway itself.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the shikimate route as drawn, one CO₂ at prephenate dehydratase
  • uptake by the PTS, so one PEP is spent on transport
  • no competing drain on E4P or PEP

Common misconceptions

  • That deleting a feedback-inhibited enzyme relieves the inhibition. It removes the enzyme; you need an allele that still catalyses but no longer binds the effector, which is a point mutation in the allosteric site rather than a knockout.
  • That all amino acids cost about the same. Cysteine, methionine, tryptophan and histidine are several times more expensive per mole than alanine or glycine, which matters when a product or a medium is dominated by one of them.
  • That NADPH demand for an amino acid is a fixed number. It depends on which route the organism uses and on whether the dehydrogenases are NAD or NADP dependent, which differs between hosts.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Compare GDH and GS-GOGAT for ammonium assimilation, and say when each is used.

A. GDH aminates 2-oxoglutarate with NADPH, costing no ATP, but has a high Km for ammonium, so it operates when nitrogen is abundant. GS-GOGAT costs one additional ATP per ammonium — glutamine synthetase consumes it — but has a much lower Km, so it operates under nitrogen limitation. The cell therefore pays one ATP for affinity, which is a recurring pattern. In a defined medium with excess ammonium, expect GDH to dominate; in a fed-batch running nitrogen-limited, expect the GS-GOGAT route and the associated extra ATP demand to appear in your energy balance.

Q. Name the precursors of the aromatic amino acids and state the two interventions this implies before any shikimate pathway change.

A. Erythrose-4-phosphate and phosphoenolpyruvate. First, raise E4P supply by overexpressing transketolase, and possibly transaldolase, since the non-oxidative pentose phosphate branch is the only source and it usually limits before the shikimate enzymes do. Second, raise PEP availability by replacing PTS uptake with a permease plus glucokinase, or by attenuating pyruvate kinase, since PTS consumes one PEP per glucose imported. Only after those does amplifying the shikimate pathway itself pay.

Q. Best lysine strains reach about 0.55 g/g against a theoretical near 0.81 g/g. Where does the missing third go?

A. Biomass, which must be made and carries carbon away from product; maintenance, which consumes substrate at no product yield and dominates at low growth rate; by-products such as organic acids and trehalose; and carbon lost as CO₂ supplying the 4 NADPH per lysine through the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway — roughly two carbons per lysine if that is the sole NADPH route. The last item is why later strain generations targeted NADPH supply and anaplerosis rather than the lysine pathway itself.

Week 15 — Lipids, membranes, transport and uptake

Substrate must get in and product must get out. Uptake kinetics sets your maximum rate; export, or its absence, sets your toxicity ceiling. Most failed strain designs fail at the membrane rather than in the pathway, and this week is where you learn to spot that before building anything.

Core ideas

1. The bilayer, and why a hydrophobic product is a membrane problem

A phospholipid bilayer is about 4 nm thick with a hydrophobic interior equivalent to a thin oil phase, and its fluidity is tuned by fatty acid chain length and unsaturation — which is how cells adapt to temperature and to solvents. A hydrophobic product partitions into that interior according to its octanol-water coefficient, so the aqueous titre you measure is not the concentration the membrane experiences. As it accumulates the bilayer disorders, the proton-motive force leaks, membrane proteins lose activity, and the cell arrests. This is why alcohols above about C4, terpenoids and many aromatics have titre ceilings well below their stoichiometric ones, and why the countermeasures are efflux pumps, membrane engineering, or in situ product removal rather than more pathway flux.

2. Fatty acid synthesis: the acetyl-CoA and NADPH sink

The cycle extends a growing chain by two carbons per round, using malonyl-CoA as the extender and consuming two NADPH per round. A C16 fatty acid therefore costs 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 ATP for the carboxylations and 14 NADPH. Two consequences. Lipid is the most expensive cell component per gram, which is why lipid content matters in a biomass equation. And malonyl-CoA, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, is held at very low concentration and tightly regulated — which is why flavonoid, polyketide and fatty-acid-derived products are so often precursor-limited at the first step, and why acetyl-CoA carboxylase overexpression appears in so many of those papers.

3. Four transport modes, with their energy source and stoichiometry

Passive diffusion: no carrier, no energy, down-gradient only, and significant only for small uncharged species — oxygen, CO₂, water, the undissociated acids of week 2. Facilitated diffusion: a carrier gives specificity and rate but still only down-gradient. Primary active transport: ATP hydrolysed directly, as in ABC transporters, typically one ATP per solute. Secondary active transport: the proton-motive force spent via symport or antiport, so the cost is indirect but real, and the stoichiometry is usually one H⁺ per solute. Group translocation: the phosphotransferase system, chemically modifying the substrate during transit. Always ask which mode a substrate uses before computing a yield, because the answer changes the ATP balance and sometimes the carbon balance too.

4. The PTS, and why it is a stoichiometric decision

Write the chain out: PEP phosphorylates EI, which phosphorylates HPr, which phosphorylates EIIA, then EIIB, which phosphorylates the glucose as EIIC translocates it. Net: one PEP consumed per glucose imported, arriving as glucose-6-phosphate. Glycolysis makes 2 PEP per glucose, so after PTS uptake only 1 remains — halving the ceiling for any PEP-derived product, as the week 14 phenylalanine calculation showed. Replacing the PTS with a galactose permease plus glucokinase restores both PEP at the cost of one ATP, which must come from somewhere; in practice that means the replacement pays off in aerobic strains with ATP to spare and not in anaerobic ones. The PTS also has a second role: its phosphorylation state is the sensor for catabolite repression.

5. Catabolite repression and the mixed-feedstock problem

When glucose is present, the PTS components are largely dephosphorylated, which lowers cyclic AMP and so lowers activation of promoters for alternative carbon sources, while EIIA inhibits the uptake systems for those sources directly. The result is a hierarchy: glucose first, then a lag, then the second sugar. For a lignocellulosic feedstock containing glucose and xylose this is a direct economic problem, since the diauxic lag wastes fermenter time and the xylose may be left unconsumed. The three standard remedies: delete or modify the PTS so the sensing is broken, express the xylose system constitutively, or split the task between two strains in co-culture — each with its own costs, and the first often reducing growth rate on glucose.

6. Export, efflux and compartments

Product leaves by passive diffusion if it can, by a native transporter if one happens to exist, or not at all — in which case the product accumulates to toxicity and must be recovered by lysis. Engineering export means either finding an efflux pump that accepts the product, which is a screening problem, or using a host with relevant native transporters. In yeast there is a further option: place the pathway in a compartment, which isolates a toxic intermediate from the cytosol but creates a transport problem for every substrate and cofactor the pathway needs. Note that cofactor pools differ between compartments, so a pathway moved to the peroxisome may lose its NADPH supply unless a shuttle exists — a failure mode that has caught several published designs.

Worked anchor

Does replacing the PTS pay? Compute the ceiling for a PEP-derived product both ways.

With PTS: glucose → 2 PEP, minus 1 PEP consumed in uptake, leaves 1 PEP. Ceiling: 1 mol product per mol glucose.

Without PTS, using GalP permease plus glucokinase: glucose enters on the proton-motive force (one H⁺, which the cell must regenerate by respiration) and is phosphorylated by glucokinase at the cost of 1 ATP. Both PEP remain. Ceiling: 2 mol per mol — but you are now 1 ATP short, and if the only way to make it is to run 1 PEP through pyruvate kinase, you are back towards 1.

So the question is where the compensating ATP comes from. Aerobically, respiration supplies it at the cost of a little extra oxygen demand, and the ceiling genuinely approaches 2 — which is why galP-glk strains are the standard in aerobic aromatic production. Anaerobically there is no such source, so the replacement buys little.

Two further costs that papers often omit: glucose uptake rate usually falls after PTS deletion, because the permease is slower, so titre rises while productivity may fall; and catabolite repression is disrupted, which may be desirable for mixed feedstocks or undesirable for regulation you were relying on. State both when you propose this intervention — it is the sort of balanced answer that distinguishes a considered design.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • GalP plus glucokinase fully functional at the required flux
  • proton-motive force regenerated by respiration
  • one ATP per phosphorylation
  • a stoichiometric ceiling, with kinetics and regulation set aside

Common misconceptions

  • That measured titre is the concentration the cell experiences. A hydrophobic product partitions into the membrane, so the bilayer sees far more than the aqueous phase reports.
  • That PTS replacement is a free doubling of yield. It restores PEP but costs an ATP and usually slows uptake, so it pays aerobically and rarely anaerobically.
  • That moving a pathway to a yeast compartment is simply isolation. Cofactor pools differ between compartments, so NADPH supply must be checked or arranged — several published designs failed exactly here.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Write the PTS stoichiometry for glucose and state the yield consequence for a PEP-derived product.

A. PEP + glucose(out) → pyruvate + glucose-6-phosphate(in), via the EI, HPr, EIIA, EIIB, EIIC phosphorelay. One PEP is consumed per glucose imported. Since glycolysis produces 2 PEP per glucose, only 1 remains for a PEP-derived product, halving the stoichiometric ceiling from 2 to 1 mol per mol. Replacement by a permease plus glucokinase restores both PEP at the cost of 1 ATP, which pays off aerobically where respiration can supply that ATP.

Q. A hydrophobic product is limited at 8 g/L, well below its stoichiometric ceiling. Give three mechanisms and a countermeasure for each.

A. Membrane partitioning disordering the bilayer and dissipating the proton-motive force — countered by membrane engineering, by evolved tolerance, or by in situ product removal that keeps the aqueous concentration low. Inhibition of specific membrane proteins including transporters and respiratory complexes — countered by identifying and overexpressing the affected component, or again by ISPR. Absence of an export route, so the product accumulates intracellularly far above the measured aqueous titre — countered by screening efflux pumps or by choosing a host with relevant transporters, and diagnosed by measuring the intracellular concentration rather than inferring it.

Q. Why does catabolite repression matter economically for a lignocellulosic feedstock, and what are the options?

A. Because the hydrolysate contains glucose and xylose, and repression causes sequential rather than simultaneous use: a diauxic lag wastes fermenter time, lowering volumetric productivity, and the xylose may be incompletely consumed, lowering yield on total sugar. Options: break the sensing by modifying or deleting PTS components, express the xylose uptake and catabolic genes constitutively, or split the sugars between two strains in co-culture. Each has a cost — PTS modification commonly reduces growth rate on glucose, constitutive expression imposes burden, and co-culture adds process complexity and stability risk.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Choose a substrate or product in your system and reason through its membrane transport. How could uptake or export become limiting even when the pathway enzymes are present?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.
