Week 16 — Biomass composition and the biomass equation

Biomass is a product with a formula. Until you can write that formula from composition data you cannot write an honest yield, a biomass objective function, or a defensible maximum titre. This week converts the biosynthesis of week 14 into coefficients, and it produces the single most reused artifact of phase 3.

Core ideas

1. The elemental formula and what it is for

E. coli biomass is conventionally written CH₁.₈O₀.₅N₀.₂, sometimes with phosphorus and sulfur appended, and a C-mol of it weighs about 24.6 g including ash. Its degree of reduction is γ = 4 + 1.8 − 2(0.5) − 3(0.2) = 4.2 per C-mol. Note how close that is to glucose at 4.00: aerobic growth on glucose is nearly redox-neutral before any product forms, which is why the oxygen demand in such a culture is modest and why making a reduced product changes the oxygen picture so sharply. The formula varies between organisms and with growth condition by perhaps ±10% in each coefficient, which propagates into every electron balance you compute — so quote it with its source and treat closures to better than a few per cent with suspicion.

2. From macromolecular composition to precursor demand

The conversion is mechanical and you should do it once by hand. Take a composition — for fast-growing E. coli roughly 55% protein, 20% RNA, 3% DNA, 9% lipid, 6% murein, 5% glycogen, 2% other by dry weight. For protein: 0.55 g per gDW divided by an average residue mass near 110 g/mol gives about 5.0 mmol of amino acid residues per gDW, which you then distribute across the twenty amino acids by their measured abundance and trace back to the twelve precursors using the week 14 tree. Repeat for RNA at about 330 g/mol per nucleotide, giving 0.6 mmol, and for lipid and murein similarly. The output is a precursor demand vector in mmol per gDW, and that vector is the biomass reaction's left-hand side.

3. The energy cost, and why the measured number exceeds the computed one

Polymerisation alone: 4 ATP-equivalents per peptide bond, roughly 2 per nucleotide added, plus activation costs for lipid. For the composition above that totals about 23–26 mmol ATP per gDW. Measured growth-associated maintenance in E. coli models is 50–60 mmol ATP per gDW — two to three times higher. The difference covers transcript turnover, protein folding and degradation, transport of precursors into the cell, maintenance of membrane potential during growth, futile cycling, and all the inefficiency the model does not represent explicitly. Say this plainly when asked: GAM is a fitted residual, not a computed cost, and that is a limitation of genome-scale models rather than a defect of your arithmetic.

4. GAM, NGAM and the Pirt relation

Growth-associated maintenance sits inside the biomass reaction, scaling with biomass formed. Non-growth-associated maintenance is a separate ATP hydrolysis reaction with a fixed lower bound, scaling with time rather than growth. The Pirt relation, 1/Y_apparent = 1/Y_true + m/µ, separates them from data: regress reciprocal apparent yield against reciprocal growth rate across a chemostat series, and the intercept gives the true yield while the slope gives the maintenance coefficient. Two warnings from week 18's problem set: two dilution rates cannot resolve this — you need four to six — and the regression is extremely sensitive to residual substrate measurements near the detection limit, which is where most published maintenance coefficients are weakest.

5. Composition changes with growth rate, and what that does to a model

RNA content rises steeply with growth rate — from perhaps 10% of dry weight at µ = 0.1 h⁻¹ to over 30% at µ = 1.5 h⁻¹ — because ribosomes are RNA-rich and ribosome content scales with growth rate. Protein content falls correspondingly. So the precursor demand vector is not a constant: a fast-growing cell needs proportionally more ribose-5-phosphate and nucleotide precursors, and less of the amino acid precursors, than a slow one. A genome-scale model with a single fixed biomass objective function is therefore exactly right at one growth rate and approximately wrong everywhere else. Good practice is to use a composition measured near your condition and to state the growth rate at which it was measured.

6. What a wrong biomass equation does, and how to check yours

Errors propagate asymmetrically. Getting the energy coefficients wrong changes predicted growth yield almost proportionally. Getting a minor precursor wrong changes little, unless that precursor becomes limiting in a knockout, in which case it changes an essentiality call. Getting the elemental formula wrong corrupts every electron balance downstream. The check is to benchmark: compute your own coefficients, then compare against a published model's and explain every discrepancy larger than about twenty per cent. Most differences will trace to composition source or to how ash, lipopolysaccharide and glycogen were handled — and understanding why is worth more than agreeing.

Worked anchor

Build the protein term of a biomass equation and compute its ATP cost.

Protein is 0.55 g per gDW. Average residue mass in a polymer is about 110 g/mol, so residues = 0.55/110 = 5.0×10⁻³ mol = 5.0 mmol per gDW.

ATP cost of polymerisation: 2 ATP-equivalents to charge each tRNA (ATP → AMP + 2Pi counts as two) plus 2 GTP per elongation cycle, so 4 per residue: 5.0 × 4 = 20 mmol ATP per gDW from protein alone.

RNA: 0.20 g per gDW at 330 g/mol gives 0.61 mmol nucleotides; at roughly 2 ATP each for polymerisation, 1.2 mmol. DNA at 0.03 g adds about 0.1 mmol. Lipid and murein add a few more. Total polymerisation ≈ 22–24 mmol ATP per gDW.

Against a measured GAM near 55 mmol per gDW, your computed figure accounts for roughly 40%. Do not treat that as an error in your arithmetic: it is the honest statement that more than half of the energetic cost of growth is not in polymerisation at all, and is captured empirically.

One more check worth doing: 5.0 mmol of amino acid residues per gDW at a typical amino acid mass means protein synthesis consumes the equivalent of about 0.5 g of amino acids per gram of biomass, which must all come from the twelve precursors — so when you trace those 5 mmol back through the week 14 tree, the dominant precursor demands will be pyruvate, oxaloacetate, 2-oxoglutarate and 3-phosphoglycerate. That ordering tells you which parts of central metabolism a growing cell is really pulling on.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • protein 0.55 g per gDW, mean residue 110 g/mol
  • 4 ATP-equivalents per residue polymerised
  • polymerisation only; precursor synthesis costed separately
  • composition measured in one condition and applied here

Common misconceptions

  • That the biomass equation is a measured reaction. It is a modelling construct assembled from composition data, with fitted energy terms — which is why two models of the same organism disagree on it.
  • That one biomass composition serves all conditions. RNA content more than doubles across the growth rate range, so the precursor vector shifts systematically.
  • That a close match to a published biomass equation validates yours. Both may inherit the same composition measurement from the 1970s; what validates yours is explaining the differences, not minimising them.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Compute the degree of reduction of CH₁.₈O₀.₅N₀.₂ and explain its closeness to glucose.

A. γ = 4(1) + 1(1.8) − 2(0.5) − 3(0.2) = 4 + 1.8 − 1 − 0.6 = 4.2 per C-mol, against glucose at exactly 4.00. The closeness means converting glucose into biomass is nearly redox-neutral, so aerobic growth without product formation has a modest oxygen demand — the electrons mostly stay in the biomass. It also means that any product more reduced than 4.2 creates an electron deficit that must be paid by oxidising additional substrate, and any product more oxidised creates a surplus that can be put towards CO₂ fixation.

Q. Why is measured GAM two to three times the computed polymerisation cost?

A. Polymerisation accounts for roughly 23–26 mmol ATP per gDW, while fitted GAM is 50–60. The gap covers transcript synthesis and turnover, protein folding and proteolysis, transport of precursors across the membrane, maintenance of the proton-motive force during growth, futile cycling, and the general inefficiency the model represents nowhere else. GAM is therefore a fitted residual rather than a computed cost, which is a stated limitation of genome-scale models and should be described as such rather than defended.

Q. Your biomass coefficients differ from a published model's by 40% on lipid. What do you check?

A. First, the composition source and the growth condition it was measured under, since lipid fraction varies with growth rate, temperature and medium. Second, whether lipopolysaccharide and membrane lipid were counted together or separately, which is a common bookkeeping difference in Gram-negatives. Third, the assumed average chain length and degree of unsaturation, which changes the acetyl-CoA and NADPH demand per gram substantially. Fourth, whether ash was subtracted consistently. Then test sensitivity: if the predicted growth yield barely moves across the two lipid values, record the discrepancy and proceed; if it moves materially, the composition becomes a measurement you need.

Week 17 — Stoichiometry, yields and data reconciliation

The most useful thing you bring to an interview: the ability to compute, on paper and in ten minutes, the best any strain could possibly do — and then to show that published data does not close. This week is almost entirely your own discipline applied to biological data, and it produces two portfolio artifacts.

Core ideas

1. Elemental balances, done the engineer's way

Write the growth and production stoichiometry as a chemical equation: a C-mol of substrate plus ammonia plus oxygen gives biomass plus product plus CO₂ plus water. Balance C, H, O and N, which gives four equations. Count your unknowns — typically the yields of biomass, product, CO₂ and water on substrate, plus oxygen. With four balances and five unknowns you need one measurement to close, which is exactly why a single measured yield plus elemental balances determines everything else. This is the method Doran Ch 4 develops and it is strictly more powerful than the degree-of-reduction shortcut, because it tells you water and oxygen too.

2. Degree of reduction as the fast route

γ per C-mol, referenced to CO₂, H₂O and NH₃: carbon contributes 4, hydrogen 1, oxygen −2, nitrogen −3. Glucose 4.00, ethanol 6.00, acetate 4.00, lactate 4.00, glycerol 4.67, succinate 3.50, butanol 6.00, methane 8.00, biomass 4.20. The available-electron balance says electrons in substrate equal electrons in biomass plus product plus those passed to oxygen. For a maximum yield calculation set biomass to zero and oxygen to zero, and the ceiling follows immediately as γ_substrate/γ_product per C-mol. It is the thirty-second version of the elemental balance and it is what you do at a whiteboard.

3. Which constraint binds, and what that tells you to do

For each product compute both ceilings — carbon and electrons — and see which is lower. Ethanol: electrons allow 2 mol per glucose, carbon allows 3, so electrons bind at 0.511 g/g, with the two CO₂ released precisely to balance electrons. Acetate: both give 3 mol, so neither is slack and the route is intrinsically efficient. Butanol: electrons allow 1, carbon 1.5, electrons bind. Succinate: more oxidised than glucose, so electrons are in surplus and CO₂ fixation raises the carbon ceiling above what glucose alone supports. The engineering reading: where electrons bind, look for a cheaper electron source or a less reduced product; where carbon binds, attack decarboxylations; where both bind simultaneously, yield is not your problem and titre and tolerance will be.

4. Theoretical maximum by linear programming, and why it differs

Set up the same problem as an LP over a stoichiometric network with the product exchange as the objective, and you get a ceiling that accounts for cofactor and ATP constraints the hand calculation ignores. The two should agree where the hand calculation's assumptions hold, and differ where they do not — typically because the network cannot actually balance ATP or NADPH at the hand-calculated optimum. When they disagree, the LP is usually right and the discrepancy tells you which cofactor is binding. Running both and reconciling them is Brief 4, and the reconciliation is the result rather than either number.

5. Closing a real balance, and gross error detection

Measured data almost never closes. The procedure: compute carbon and electron closure separately, then read the pattern, as week 13 established — carbon short with electrons complete implicates CO₂; both short in proportion implicates biomass; electrons short alone implicates H₂ or a reduced gas; both high implicates one over-reported stream. Then localise properly: with more measurements than degrees of freedom the system is redundant, and redundancy lets you compute a test statistic that identifies which measurement is inconsistent with the others rather than merely that something is. The cardinal rule, which examiners test: a balance is reconciled by finding the missing stream, never by scaling the measured ones.

6. Titre, rate and yield — and the thresholds that matter

Yield sets raw material cost and cannot be bought back with equipment. Titre sets the water load and therefore every downstream separation cost, and below a product-specific threshold a separation becomes infeasible rather than merely expensive. Rate sets annual throughput and therefore capital per kilogram, and is the parameter most readily substituted by capital. For a commodity the ranking is yield, titre, rate; for a high-value product it inverts towards titre first, because substrate is negligible and purification dominates; and for an existing plant rate leads because capital is sunk. Learn to state the regime before giving the ranking — that is the whole content of week 52 previewed here.

Worked anchor

Derive ethanol's ceiling twice, then do succinate to see the contrast.

Ethanol by carbon: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂. Four of six carbons retained, so 0.667 C-mol/C-mol; mass yield 2(46.07)/180.16 = 0.511 g/g.

Ethanol by electrons: glucose carries 24 available electrons; ethanol carries 12 per mole (2 C × 6). 24/12 = 2 mol ethanol, identical. Electrons balance exactly with nothing to spare — the two CO₂ are released precisely because they carry carbon and no electrons, which is the signature of a redox-neutral fermentation. Neither constraint is slack, and that is why ethanol's theoretical yield is approached so closely in practice: there is no cofactor slack to waste.

Succinate by electrons: succinate (C₄H₆O₄) has γ = 3.50 per C-mol, so 14 electrons per mole. 24/14 = 1.71 mol per glucose. By carbon alone, glucose supplies only 6 carbons and succinate needs 4, so 1.5 mol. The electron ceiling exceeds the carbon ceiling — which is only reachable if extra carbon comes from CO₂ fixation, and that is exactly what PEP carboxylase does. With fixation the answer is 1.71 mol/mol, 1.12 g/g; without it, redox limits the route near 1.0.

The general rule to carry: when the electron ceiling exceeds the carbon ceiling, CO₂ fixation is the yield mechanism and your design must include a carboxylation. When the carbon ceiling is lower, attack the decarboxylations instead.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • redox-neutral fermentation with no biomass or maintenance
  • γ per C-mol as tabulated
  • a stoichiometric ceiling, so kinetics and tolerance are excluded

Common misconceptions

  • That a balance can be closed by scaling a measurement. Scaling discards the only information the discrepancy contains, which is that something is unmeasured.
  • That the degree-of-reduction ceiling is always the right answer. It ignores ATP and cofactor constraints, so the LP answer is often lower and the difference identifies the binding cofactor.
  • That carbon yield above 1 C-mol/C-mol is impossible. It requires CO₂ fixation and a product more oxidised than the substrate, which succinate from glucose satisfies.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Derive ethanol's 0.511 g/g twice and say what the agreement of the two routes tells you.

A. By carbon: 2 ethanol and 2 CO₂ per glucose, so 92.14/180.16 = 0.511 g/g. By electrons: glucose 24 available electrons, ethanol 12 each, so exactly 2 mol with nothing left over. The agreement means neither constraint is slack — the two CO₂ are released precisely to balance electrons — which is the signature of a redox-neutral fermentation and the reason real ethanol processes reach 90%+ of theoretical. Contrast a more reduced product such as butanol, where the electron ceiling falls below the carbon ceiling and the gap must be paid for.

Q. A fermentation closes to 88% on carbon and 103% on electrons. Diagnose and order the investigation.

A. Carbon short with electrons complete or slightly high implicates a carbon-bearing, electron-poor stream, overwhelmingly likely CO₂. Order by information per unit effort: integrate off-gas CO₂ first; then check volatile losses to the exhaust; then extend the analytical method for unmeasured soluble by-products; then verify biomass gravimetrically with a measured carbon content rather than an optical density correlation; then audit feed concentration, evaporation and sampling volumes. If closing carbon with measured CO₂ leaves electrons at 103%, that residual sits within the uncertainty of the assumed biomass formula and should be reported as such, not adjusted away.

Q. Rank titre, rate and yield for a commodity product, and name two circumstances that reverse the ranking.

A. Yield, then titre, then rate. Yield sets raw material cost, the largest operating line, and cannot be substituted by capital. Titre sets water load and downstream cost. Rate sets capital per kilogram and is the most substitutable. It reverses for a high-value product, where substrate is negligible and purification dominates, putting titre first; and for an existing plant, where capital is sunk and rate determines sellable output. It also reverses where titre falls below a separation's feasibility threshold, at which point titre is a constraint rather than an elasticity.

Week 18 — Growth kinetics and physiological states

Growth is autocatalysis with a catalyst whose composition changes. Everything in phase 4 is parameterised by what you learn to measure this week, and the week's real lesson is about identifiability: which parameters a given experiment can determine, and which it cannot however good the fit looks. Paper 2 is sat at the end.

Core ideas

1. The balances, and why they are the ones you already write

Batch: dX/dt = µX and dS/dt = −µX/Y − mX, with µ a function of S. Chemostat with a sterile feed: dX/dt = (µ − D)X and dS/dt = D(S₀ − S) − µX/Y − mX. Setting the derivatives to zero gives the steady state, and the first consequence is the one that makes the chemostat valuable: µ = D. You set the growth rate by turning a pump. Washout follows when D exceeds the maximum µ attainable at S₀. All of this is a CSTR with a self-reproducing catalyst, and nothing in the mathematics is unfamiliar — the biology is in the form of µ(S) and in the maintenance term.

2. Monod, and its honest status

µ = µmax S/(Ks + S) is empirical, not mechanistic: it has the Michaelis-Menten form because saturation is a general property of carrier-mediated uptake, but it describes whole-cell growth rather than one enzyme, and Ks is not a binding constant for anything. It fails in predictable ways — at very low substrate where maintenance dominates, under multiple limitation, during transients where the cell's composition lags, and for inhibitory substrates, where Haldane-type or other forms are used instead. Use it as a convenient interpolation and say so; treating Ks as a physical constant of the organism is a common and visible error.

3. Identifiability, which is the week's real content

Here is the thing worth internalising. In batch culture the substrate is far above Ks for nearly the whole run, so µ sits at µmax and carries essentially no information about Ks. The substrate passes through S ≈ Ks only briefly at the end, when biomass is high, sampling is sparse, and measuring a low residual concentration is hardest. Fitted µmax and Ks therefore come out strongly correlated with a wide, often meaningless, interval on Ks — and a fit that looks beautiful can still be telling you nothing about one of its parameters. Demonstrate this to yourself with a joint confidence region rather than two standard errors; the ellipse's tilt is the correlation, and seeing it once changes how you read every published parameter pair.

4. Designing the experiment that does resolve the parameters

A chemostat series at four to six dilution rates spanning roughly 0.1 to 0.8 of µmax resolves what batch cannot. Low dilution rates carry the maintenance information, because the Pirt term m/µ dominates there. Mid-range rates carry Ks, because that is where S is comparable to it. High rates near washout bound µmax. The substrate assay must be validated near its detection limit, since residual concentrations at low D are small and the whole maintenance estimate rests on them. State the replicate structure and the number of volume changes before each sample — five is a common minimum — because a chemostat result without those numbers is not a steady-state result.

5. Product kinetics: Luedeking-Piret and what it classifies

qP = αµ + β separates product formation into a growth-associated term and a non-growth-associated one. Three classes follow: growth-associated, where β ≈ 0 and product tracks growth, as for ethanol; non-growth-associated, where α ≈ 0 and product forms in stationary phase, as for many secondary metabolites; and mixed. The crossover point µ = β/α tells you where half the product is non-growth-associated, and that number decides the process: below it, a two-stage process with a growth phase then a production phase makes sense; above it, growth-coupled operation gives more product per unit time at the cost of carbon spent on biomass. The decision is settled by which of yield and volumetric productivity the economics punishes, which is week 52.

6. Physiological states you must be able to recognise

Overflow metabolism above a critical growth rate, which week 13 explained as proteome allocation and which fed-batch feeding is designed to avoid. Diauxie on mixed substrates, from the catabolite repression of week 15. The Crabtree effect in yeast, the same proteome logic with ethanol as the product. The stringent response under amino acid starvation, which shuts down ribosome synthesis and changes the biomass composition substantially. And death kinetics, which Doran treats explicitly and which matters for sterilisation design in week 48 and for long fermentations where viability falls. Recognising which state a culture is in is the diagnostic skill; computing rates within a state is the easy part.

Worked anchor

Estimate parameters from two chemostat points, and then see why two is not enough.

Feed 25 g/L glucose. At D = 0.20 h⁻¹: X = 9.6 g/L, S = 0.30 g/L. At D = 0.35 h⁻¹: X = 9.1 g/L, S = 1.40 g/L.

Apparent yields: Y₁ = 9.6/(25 − 0.3) = 0.389 g/g; Y₂ = 9.1/(25 − 1.4) = 0.386 g/g.

Monod parameters from µ = D: 0.20(Ks + 0.30) = µmax(0.30) and 0.35(Ks + 1.40) = µmax(1.40). Divide one by the other to eliminate µmax: (0.20/0.35) × (Ks + 0.30)/(Ks + 1.40) = 0.30/1.40. Solving gives Ks ≈ 0.52 g/L and µmax ≈ 0.55 h⁻¹.

Now maintenance, via Pirt. 1/Y₁ = 2.571 at 1/µ = 5.00; 1/Y₂ = 2.591 at 1/µ = 2.857. Slope = (2.571 − 2.591)/(5.00 − 2.857) = −0.0093 — negative, and therefore unphysical.

That negative slope is the whole point of the exercise. The two reciprocal yields differ by less than their measurement error, so the data cannot resolve maintenance at all, and a regression through two points will always return something. Reporting a maintenance coefficient from two chemostat points is a real and common error. The correct conclusion is to state that m is not determined by this data and to specify the experiment that would determine it — four to six dilution rates, with the lowest well below 0.2 µmax where the maintenance term actually dominates.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • steady state with no wall growth and no substrate in the feed vessel
  • Monod kinetics on a single limiting substrate
  • constant yield apart from the maintenance term
  • both measured points lie exactly on the curve

Common misconceptions

  • That Ks is a physical constant of the organism. It is an empirical parameter of a whole-cell correlation, and reported values for the same organism span orders of magnitude depending on how they were obtained.
  • That a good fit means well-determined parameters. Batch data fits Monod beautifully while leaving Ks essentially unconstrained, which is why the joint confidence region matters more than the curve.
  • That the productivity-optimal dilution rate is where you should operate. It sits close to washout, so a small disturbance loses the culture — which is why industry operates well below it.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Derive the chemostat steady state and the washout condition from the balances.

A. From dX/dt = (µ − D)X = 0 with X ≠ 0, µ = D. Substituting Monod, D = µmax S/(Ks + S), so S = Ks D/(µmax − D). From dS/dt = D(S₀ − S) − µX/Y = 0 at steady state, X = Y(S₀ − S) neglecting maintenance. Washout occurs when the required S exceeds S₀, that is when D ≥ µmax S₀/(Ks + S₀), which for S₀ ≫ Ks is approximately µmax. Note the practical consequence: measuring the washout dilution rate gives you µmax directly, and is often the most reliable way to obtain it.

Q. Why does batch data poorly constrain Ks, and what experiment fixes it?

A. Because substrate sits far above Ks for nearly the whole run, holding µ at µmax and carrying no information about Ks; the region S ≈ Ks is traversed only briefly at the end, when biomass is high, sampling is sparse and low residual substrate is hardest to measure. Fitted µmax and Ks are therefore strongly correlated with a wide interval on Ks. The fix is a chemostat series at four to six dilution rates spanning roughly 0.1 to 0.8 of µmax, with a substrate assay validated near its detection limit and the number of volume changes before sampling recorded.

Q. A product follows Luedeking-Piret with α = 0.15 g/g and β = 0.02 g gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹. At what growth rate is half the product non-growth-associated, and what does that imply for the process?

A. Half non-growth-associated means αµ = β, so µ = 0.02/0.15 = 0.133 h⁻¹. Below roughly 0.13 h⁻¹ the non-growth term dominates, so a two-stage process — grow fast, then hold at low growth rate for production — captures most of the product while spending less carbon on biomass. Above it, growth-coupled operation gives higher volumetric productivity at the cost of carbon diverted to biomass. Which to choose depends on whether the economics punishes yield or productivity more, which is settled in week 52 rather than here.

Appendix — Fermi drills

Systems-biology interviews open with estimation questions. Each is answerable from numbers in these modules.

Q. Roughly how many ATP molecules does an E. coli cell consume per second at maximal growth?

A. Take maintenance at about 20 mmol ATP gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ and growth-associated demand at roughly 55 mmol ATP per gDW of biomass made. At µ = 1.0 h⁻¹ the growth term contributes about 55 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹, so total ≈ 75 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹. Per cell: 75 × 3×10⁻¹³ = 2.3×10⁻¹¹ mmol/h = 6.3×10⁻¹⁸ mol/s × 6.02×10²³ ≈ 4×10⁶ molecules/s, so of order 10⁶–10⁷ ATP per cell per second. Sanity check against the pool: ATP sits near 1–3 mM, which in 1 fL is about 10⁶ molecules, so the entire pool turns over roughly once a second — exactly the figure quoted for ATP turnover, which is the check that the estimate is self-consistent.

Q. How many ribosomes does a cell need to double in 30 minutes?

A. Protein is about 55% of 3×10⁻¹³ g, so 1.65×10⁻¹³ g, equal to 1.65×10⁻¹³/110 ≈ 1.5×10⁻¹⁵ mol of residues = 9×10⁸ residues. These must be made in 1,800 s, so 5×10⁵ residues/s. A ribosome elongates at roughly 15–20 residues/s, giving about 3×10⁴ ribosomes. The measured figure at fast growth is 5–7×10⁴, so the estimate is correct to a factor of two — the gap being ribosomes that are idle or in assembly, which is itself the content of the growth laws.

Q. What fraction of the proteome is a ten-enzyme heterologous pathway at 5 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹?

A. Per enzyme at 30 s⁻¹ and half saturation, effective rate 15 s⁻¹. Flux per cell = 5 × 3×10⁻¹³ mmol/h = 2.5×10⁵ molecules/s, so 1.7×10⁴ copies per enzyme, and 1.7×10⁵ copies across ten. At 45 kDa that is 1.3×10⁻¹⁴ g = 13 fg, against 180 fg of protein: about 7% of the proteome. Which predicts a growth penalty of roughly the same order, and explains why a ten-enzyme pathway at industrial flux is a burden problem before it is a kinetics problem.

Q. How much CO₂ does a 50 m³ fermenter vent per hour at 40 gDW/L?

A. Take a respiratory quotient near 1 and an oxygen uptake of 5 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹. Biomass = 50,000 L × 40 g/L = 2×10⁶ g. CER ≈ 5 × 2×10⁶ = 10⁷ mmol/h = 10⁴ mol/h, which is 440 kg CO₂ per hour, or about 250 m³ of gas per hour at STP. Useful for two reasons: it sizes the off-gas handling, and it tells you that dissolved CO₂ in a tall vessel is not a trace concern.

Q. How many generations separate a vial from a 50 m³ production vessel?

A. Final biomass about 2×10⁶ g from a starting inoculum of roughly 10⁻³ g, a 2×10⁹-fold increase, so log₂(2×10⁹) ≈ 31 doublings. This is the number that decides whether plasmid stability matters, whether an evolved escape mutant has time to sweep, and whether a growth-coupled design is necessary rather than merely elegant.

Q. What volume of glucose solution feeds a 50 m³ fed-batch for 24 hours?

A. At 0.3 g product per g glucose and a target of 50 g/L product in 50 m³, you need 2.5×10⁶ g of product and therefore 8.3×10⁶ g of glucose. At a 500 g/L feed that is 1.7×10⁴ L, or 17 m³ — a third of the working volume. Which is why fed-batch vessels start at half volume, and why feed concentration is itself a design variable rather than a detail.

Q. How long would it take a single cell to become one gram of biomass at µ = 0.6 h⁻¹?

A. One cell is 3×10⁻¹³ g, so ln(1/3×10⁻¹³)/0.6 = 28.8/0.6 ≈ 48 hours. Two days spans twelve orders of magnitude in mass, which is the arithmetic behind why selection screens 10⁹ variants overnight and why a plate-based screen handles 10³.

Q. What is the diffusion time of a metabolite across a cell, and why does it matter?

A. With D ≈ 5×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s for a small metabolite in cytoplasm and L = 10⁻⁶ m, t ≈ L²/2D = 10⁻¹²/10⁻⁹ = 10⁻³ s, a millisecond. Far faster than any enzymatic turnover, which is why a bacterial cell is treated as well-mixed and why intracellular gradients are ignored — and why the same calculation for a 1 mm fungal pellet, giving seconds to minutes, means the opposite conclusion there.

Q. How much heat does an aerobic fermentation generate per cubic metre?

A. Oxygen consumption releases roughly 460 kJ per mole of O₂ across most substrates. At OUR = 100 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ that is 46 kJ L⁻¹ h⁻¹ = 46 MJ m⁻³ h⁻¹, about 13 kW per cubic metre. For a 50 m³ vessel, 640 kW of cooling duty — which is why heat removal, not just oxygen supply, constrains large aerobic fermentations.

Q. What titre does a $400/kg product need before purification stops dominating cost?

A. Downstream cost scales with the water processed. At 5 g/L you handle 200 L of broth per kg of product; at 50 g/L, 20 L. If handling, concentrating and purifying costs of order $1–3 per litre of broth for a multi-step train, the first case is $200–600/kg and the second $20–60/kg. So the threshold sits near the point where downstream falls to perhaps 10–15% of price, which for most products is tens of grams per litre — the origin of the titre thresholds quoted in week 52.

Appendix — on the numbers in these notes

Every number in these modules — ribosome counts, pool sizes, half-lives, turnover times — is written from working knowledge and is an order-of-magnitude figure. Before any of them enters a notebook, a figure or a proposal, check it against BioNumbers or the primary source and cite that, not these notes. Treat the modules as a map of what matters and a scaffold for reasoning; treat the textbooks and the databases as the authority for values.

Week 19 — Genome annotation and what it is worth

A reconstruction is only as good as the annotation beneath it, and annotation is mostly inference rather than measurement. This week you learn how a genome becomes a gene list, how often that list is wrong, and how to judge the evidence behind any functional assignment you later rely on. It is the least glamorous week in the phase and it is what stops you trusting a model more than it deserves.

Core ideas

1. How a genome becomes a gene list, and where inference enters

Sequencing gives contigs; gene calling finds open reading frames by codon statistics and ribosome binding site context; then function is assigned, almost always by homology to something already annotated. That last step is where the uncertainty lives. A BLAST hit at 70% identity over most of the length is strong evidence of a shared fold and reasonable evidence of a shared reaction class; it is weak evidence of identical substrate specificity, and essentially no evidence about which cofactor the enzyme prefers. Orthologues, which arose by speciation, usually keep function; paralogues, which arose by duplication, frequently diverge — so annotation transferred along a paralogue is the single commonest source of a reaction in a model that the organism cannot actually perform.

2. Evidence codes, which you should read before any annotation

Databases record how a function was assigned, and the classes differ enormously in strength: experimental characterisation in this organism; experimental in a related organism; inferred from sequence similarity; inferred from genomic context such as operon membership or gene neighbourhood; and automatic electronic annotation with no curator involvement. In a typical bacterial genome, somewhere between a tenth and a third of metabolic genes have experimental evidence in that organism and the rest are inferred. Before you build an argument on a reaction, look at which class it sits in. A model prediction that depends on an electronically annotated transporter is a hypothesis about a transporter, not a result.

3. Orphan activities and hypothetical proteins: the two-sided gap

Two complementary problems. Orphan enzyme activities are reactions known biochemically to occur in an organism with no gene assigned — perhaps a fifth of EC numbers with characterised activity have no sequence attached anywhere. Hypothetical proteins are the reverse: genes with no assigned function, typically a quarter to a third of any genome. The two gaps are not independent, since many orphan activities are presumably carried out by some of those hypothetical proteins. For modelling, orphans are the bigger nuisance: the reaction must be in the network for the organism to work, but it has no gene, so it cannot be deleted in silico and will never appear in an essentiality prediction.

4. Why strains drift, and what that costs an engineer

Mutation rates are roughly 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻⁹ per base per generation, so a culture reaching 10¹² cells contains, for every base in the genome, many independent mutants. Any variant that grows even slightly faster is enriched, and in a producing strain the fastest-growing variant is usually the one that has lost or silenced the pathway. Add insertion sequences, which inactivate constructs at appreciable frequency, and recombination between repeated sequences, and you have the mechanism behind a strain that performs at 2 L and fails at 1 m³. This is genetics appearing as a process problem, and the defences are genetic: integrate rather than carry a plasmid, minimise burden, and couple production to growth.

5. Pangenomes and why 'the organism' is not one genome

Sequence many isolates of a species and the gene content varies substantially: a core genome present in all, and an accessory genome that differs between strains. For E. coli the core is a few thousand genes while the pangenome runs to tens of thousands. The practical consequence is that a reconstruction is of a strain, not a species, and applying an iJO1366-style model built on K-12 MG1655 to a different isolate imports assumptions that may be wrong about transporters, sugar utilisation and stress responses. Always check which strain a published model was built from and whether yours is the same.

6. The databases, and what each is for

NCBI for sequence and the submitted annotation. UniProt for protein-level information with evidence codes, which is the one to check when you want to know how a function was assigned. KEGG for pathway topology and orthology groups, useful for checking whether a route exists in your organism. MetaCyc and EcoCyc for curated, literature-backed reactions, with EcoCyc being unusually thorough for E. coli specifically. BiGG for models themselves. Learn to query each from a script once; by week 23 you will want to pull annotations and reactions programmatically rather than by hand.

Worked anchor

Judge an annotation before you build on it.

Suppose your pathway needs a dehydratase, and the organism's genome lists one. Work through the chain:

1. What is the evidence class? Open the UniProt entry. If it says 'inferred from homology' with no publication, you have a sequence similarity and nothing more. 2. To what, and how similar? A 45% identity hit over 60% of the length to a characterised enzyme of the same class tells you the fold is probably right and the specificity is unknown. 3. Orthologue or paralogue? Check whether the hit's organism has a single copy or a family. A family means divergence is likely and the specific member matters. 4. Is there genomic context? If the gene sits in an operon with other genes of the same pathway, that is independent evidence — weak individually, strong in combination with homology. 5. What does the model prediction depend on? If your conclusion changes when this reaction is removed, the annotation has become an experimental priority rather than a modelling detail.

The discipline is the point. Most published modelling work does not do this, and the difference between a prediction you can defend and one you cannot is usually whether you did.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the databases are current as of reading, with evidence codes recorded honestly
  • sequence identity is computed over a meaningful alignment length

Common misconceptions

  • That an annotated genome is a list of known functions. Most assignments are inferred from homology, and the evidence class is recorded — look at it.
  • That a model of a species applies to your strain. Reconstructions are strain-specific, and accessory gene content differs substantially within a species.
  • That scale-up failure is a process problem. A good part of it is genetics: more generations means more opportunity for a faster-growing non-producer to sweep.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Name five ways a functional annotation can be wrong, and the model error each produces.

A. Wrong EC assignment by homology to a paralogue, producing a reaction the organism cannot perform; missing annotation for a promiscuous side activity, producing a false essentiality call; wrong substrate specificity, producing the wrong product or cofactor; wrong subcellular localisation in a compartmentalised organism, producing a transport requirement that does not exist; and a transporter inferred generically for every extracellular metabolite, producing growth on substrates the organism cannot use. Each has a specific curation remedy rather than being a defect of the method.

Q. Why is an orphan reaction a particular nuisance for a deletion screen?

A. Because it must be present in the network for the organism's metabolism to balance, but it has no gene associated with it. In silico it therefore cannot be deleted, so it never appears as essential or non-essential, and any gene whose only route to a function runs through that orphan will be mispredicted. The honest treatment is to flag orphan reactions in the model and to report how many predictions depend on them.

Q. A producing strain gives 8 g/L at 2 L and 3 g/L at 1,000 L from the same protocol. What genetic explanation would you test first, and how?

A. Genetic instability. Scaling adds roughly ten doublings of inoculum build-up, so a variant that has lost or silenced the pathway and grows even a few per cent faster can become a large fraction of the population by the time the production vessel fills. Test by plating the final broth and screening colonies for production, checking plasmid retention without selection, and sequencing the construct from the end of the run rather than from the seed. If confirmed, the remedies are chromosomal integration, lower burden, or growth coupling.

Transfer prompt. If you used a genome sequence or annotation for one organism, identify a pathway claim that annotation supports and one it cannot establish without experimental evidence.

Week 20 — Network reconstruction and the stoichiometric matrix

The stoichiometric matrix is a connectivity map, a data table and a linear operator at once. Once you see that it is the mass-balance matrix you have written since second year, the rest of the phase is linear algebra with biology attached. Build one by hand this week, in a notebook, and verify that every column balances before you trust anything built on it.

Core ideas

1. What S is, concretely

Rows are metabolites, columns are reactions, and the entry Sᵢⱼ is the stoichiometric coefficient of metabolite i in reaction j — negative if consumed, positive if produced, zero if absent. A genome-scale model of E. coli has roughly 1,800 metabolites and 2,600 reactions, so S has about 4.7 million entries of which perhaps 10,000 are non-zero: it is more than 99% empty. That sparsity is not incidental. It says that each metabolite participates in only a handful of reactions, which is why metabolism has recognisable pathways at all rather than being a homogeneous soup.

2. Exchange reactions and the system boundary

A reconstruction needs a boundary. Exchange reactions are pseudo-reactions that let a metabolite enter or leave the system — written conventionally as 'A_e ⇌' with uptake as negative flux. They are not real reactions and they have no genes, which matters twice: they are where you define the medium, and they are where models most often wrongly permit growth, because a draft reconstruction that adds an exchange for every extracellular metabolite will predict utilisation of substrates the organism cannot transport. When a model grows on something it should not, check the exchanges and the transporters before anything else.

3. The six axioms, which are worth stating properly

Palsson sets out the conceptual basis as six statements. Cellular functions rest on chemistry, so they can be written as balanced equations. Annotated genomes plus experimental data permit genome-scale reconstruction. Cells operate under constraints — physico-chemical, topological, environmental and regulatory. Cells function in a context-specific way, so the expressed subset matters. Mass and energy are conserved, which gives S·v = 0 at steady state. And cells evolve under selection, which licenses optimality arguments. None is startling alone; together they are the whole justification for what follows, and the sixth is the only one that is an assumption about behaviour rather than physics.

4. Module-by-module reconstruction, and why glycolysis is taught first

You build a reconstruction by adding modules and checking each: glycolysis, then the pentose phosphate pathway, then the TCA cycle, verifying balance and recomputing the null space at each stage. Palsson teaches this on glycolysis because its matrix is small enough to read by eye and its null space is interpretable by inspection. Do the same: build your phase 2 pathway atlas as a matrix, column by column, and assert that each column balances for C, H, O, N, P and charge. The assertion is the point — a mistyped transketolase coefficient will not announce itself later.

5. Protein states can be stoichiometric too

Regulation can be represented in the same formalism. The PFK example writes each bound state of the enzyme as a species and each binding event as a reaction, so an allosteric enzyme becomes a subnetwork of twenty-odd reactions within the matrix. This is worth seeing once because it shows the formalism's reach and its cost: representing one regulated enzyme properly adds more reactions than the whole of glycolysis, which is why genome-scale models do not do it and why regulation is handled by constraints instead.

6. A reconstruction is not a model

The reconstruction is the knowledge base: reactions, genes, evidence, localisation, directionality. The model is the reconstruction plus the constraints needed to compute — bounds, a medium, an objective. One reconstruction supports many condition-specific models, and the distinction matters when you read a paper: a claim about the reconstruction is a claim about biochemical knowledge, while a claim from a model is conditional on the constraints someone chose.

Worked anchor

Build S for a three-reaction toy and read it.

Reactions: (1) A → B, (2) B → C, (3) B → D, plus exchanges for A in, C out and D out.

Metabolites A, B, C, D as rows; reactions v₁, v₂, v₃ and exchanges b_A, b_C, b_D as columns:

v₁ v₂ v₃ b_A b_C b_D A −1 0 0 +1 0 0 B +1 −1 −1 0 0 0 C 0 +1 0 0 −1 0 D 0 0 +1 0 0 −1

Four metabolites, six reactions. Rank is 4, so the null space has dimension 2: two degrees of freedom. Choose a basis and the two vectors are recognisable as the two routes — A to C and A to D — which is the simplest possible demonstration that null space basis vectors are pathways.

Now the check that matters: every column sums correctly in atoms, not just in species. If A, B and C are all C₃ compounds and D is C₂, then reaction 3 is unbalanced and no amount of linear algebra will tell you so. Assert elemental balance in code before you compute anything.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the six listed reactions are the whole network
  • rank computed over the reals, with no thermodynamic constraints yet
  • exchanges as drawn

Common misconceptions

  • That S is a model. It is a data structure; the model is S plus bounds, a medium and an objective.
  • That a balanced column means a correct reaction. Balance is necessary and not sufficient — a balanced reaction can still be one the organism does not perform.
  • That exchange reactions are reactions. They are boundary conditions with no genes, and they are where spurious growth predictions usually originate.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. What does the sparsity of S tell you about metabolism?

A. That each metabolite participates in only a handful of reactions out of thousands — typically two or three. That is the structural reason metabolism decomposes into recognisable pathways rather than being a uniformly connected network, and it is why pathway-based thinking works at all. It is also why genome-scale linear programs solve quickly despite their size: sparse matrices are cheap.

Q. A draft model predicts growth on citrate, which the strain cannot use. Where do you look first?

A. At the exchange and transport reactions, not the intracellular pathway. Draft reconstructions frequently add an exchange and a generic transporter for every extracellular metabolite, so the intracellular citrate metabolism is present and correct while the organism in fact lacks an aerobic citrate uptake system. Check whether the transport reaction has a gene associated with it; if it does not, it is a modelling artefact.

Q. Distinguish a reconstruction from a model in three sentences.

A. A reconstruction is a structured knowledge base: every reaction with its stoichiometry, gene association, evidence, directionality and localisation. A model is that reconstruction plus the constraints required to compute a flux distribution — uptake bounds, a defined medium, capacity limits and an objective function. One reconstruction therefore supports many models, and a claim made from a model is conditional on constraints a person chose, whereas a claim about the reconstruction is a claim about biochemical knowledge.

Week 21 — Curation, GPRs and gap filling

The unglamorous ninety per cent of modelling. Curation is where a draft becomes trustworthy, and knowing what it involves is what lets you judge whether a published model deserves the weight you are about to put on it. The week's practical output is your own gene-deletion implementation, which forces you to understand GPR logic rather than call a function.

Core ideas

1. The four-step process, and what each consumes

Draft reconstruction from the annotated genome, which is automatable and produces something incomplete and partly wrong. Curation against literature, which is manual, slow and the bulk of the work: checking stoichiometry, charge balance, directionality, localisation and evidence for every reaction. Conversion to a computational model by adding bounds, a medium and an objective. Validation against experimental data, which sends you back to curation. Published genome-scale reconstructions have taken person-years; the 96-step standard operating procedure exists because the work is too detailed to carry in your head.

2. GPR logic, and why AND versus OR decides essentiality

A gene-protein-reaction association maps genes to a reaction with Boolean logic. AND denotes a complex: all subunits required, so deleting any one gene removes the reaction. OR denotes isozymes or alternative complexes: either suffices, so only the double deletion removes the reaction. Real GPRs nest both — (a AND b) OR (c AND d) is a reaction catalysed by either of two heterodimers. Getting this right is what lets a model predict gene essentiality rather than merely reaction essentiality, and writing AND where the truth is OR is a leading cause of false positives. Implement the deletion logic yourself from the GPR strings this week and validate it against the library's function; the exercise takes an afternoon and removes any mystery from week 25.

3. Dead ends, blocked reactions and what they signify

A dead-end metabolite is produced but never consumed, or vice versa. At steady state it forces every reaction touching it to zero flux, so whole pathway segments go silent without complaint. Blocked reactions are those that cannot carry flux in any steady state. In a typical draft, a substantial fraction of reactions are blocked, and each blockage is a knowledge gap: a missing transporter, a missing biosynthetic step, or a reaction that genuinely should not be there. Finding them is mechanical — compute flux variability on an open medium and collect the reactions with zero range — and interpreting them is the curation work.

4. Gap filling is hypothesis generation, not evidence

Algorithmic gap filling searches a universal reaction database for the smallest set of additions that restores flux. That is a parsimony argument, and parsimony is not evidence. Before accepting a fill, look for a homologue of the candidate enzyme in the genome; if there is none, the fill is a claim that the organism does something with no known gene. Record every fill in the provenance log at the lowest confidence class, and then check whether any conclusion you draw depends on one. The specific trap to avoid is filling gaps until the model grows: that guarantees growth and destroys the model's evidential value.

5. Thermodynamic directionality, which is curation not computation

Every reaction needs bounds, and the choice of reversible or irreversible is a thermodynamic judgement made at curation time. Set too many reactions reversible and the model finds unphysical routes, including loops; set too many irreversible and you exclude flux the cell genuinely carries. Good practice is to assign directionality from ΔrG′° with physiological concentration ranges, flagging the marginal cases rather than deciding them silently. This is where week 8's conventions earn their keep, and it is the main reason two models of the same organism give different answers.

6. Quality control as a test suite

Treat a model like code. Standardised test suites check mass and charge balance on every reaction, metabolite and reaction identifiers against databases, the presence of gene associations, absence of duplicated reactions, correct exchange formulation, blocked reaction fraction, and whether the model produces energy from nothing — a stoichiometrically balanced cycle generating ATP with no substrate, which is the most embarrassing failure and still appears in published models. Run such a suite on any model before you use it, including your own.

Worked anchor

Implement gene deletion from a GPR, and find out why it matters.

Take the GPR '(b0727 and b0726) or b2910'. Two subunits forming a complex, or a single alternative gene.

Delete b2910 alone: the complex remains, so the reaction stays active. Delete b0727 alone: the complex is broken, but b2910 still provides the activity, so the reaction stays active. Delete b0727 and b2910 together: no route remains, so the reaction is knocked out.

The implementation is a Boolean evaluation with deleted genes set false. Write it, run it over every gene in the core model, and compare with the library's built-in function. They should agree exactly; where they do not, you have either a parsing bug or a GPR with syntax you did not anticipate, and both are worth finding now.

Then do the instructive variant: change the GPR to '(b0727 and b0726) and b2910' — the same genes with the wrong connective — and rerun. Every one of the three genes now reads as essential. That single character is the difference between three correct predictions and three false positives, and it is why week 25's confusion matrix is dominated by false positives rather than false negatives.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the curated GPR is correct
  • deletion means complete loss of function
  • no regulatory or expression-level compensation

Palsson Ch 3 §3.3–3.4SkimThat reconstruction is iterative and labour-intensive, and the many uses of a reconstruction. Read for perspective.

Common misconceptions

  • That gap filling completes a model. It generates hypotheses at the lowest evidence class, and a model with dozens of unflagged fills is not a reconstruction.
  • That directionality comes from the solver. It is a curation decision made from thermodynamics, and it is the main reason two models of one organism disagree.
  • That a published model is validated. Some produce ATP from nothing; run a test suite before you trust one, including your own.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Why does writing AND where the truth is OR produce a false essentiality prediction?

A. AND models a protein complex, so deleting any one listed gene removes the reaction and the model calls that gene essential. If the genes are in fact isozymes, the organism retains the activity after a single deletion and the gene is experimentally non-essential. The error produces a false positive for every gene in the mis-written rule, and because isozymes are common it is a leading contributor to the precision deficit typically seen in deletion screens.

Q. What is a blocked reaction, how do you find them, and what does a high fraction mean?

A. A reaction that cannot carry flux in any steady state, usually because it touches a dead-end metabolite. Find them by running flux variability analysis on a permissive medium and collecting reactions whose minimum and maximum flux are both zero. A high blocked fraction means the reconstruction has substantial knowledge gaps — missing transporters, missing biosynthetic steps, or reactions wrongly included — and each blockage is a curation task rather than a computational one.

Q. A model produces ATP with no substrate uptake. What has gone wrong and why does it matter?

A. A stoichiometrically balanced cycle exists that generates ATP from nothing, usually created by a reaction with the wrong directionality or an unbalanced proton or water stoichiometry. It matters because every energetic prediction the model makes is then meaningless: growth yields, maintenance fitting and any ATP-limited design all rest on the energy balance. It is a standard test in quality-control suites, and the fact that it still appears in published models is the reason you run the suite yourself.

Week 22 — The four subspaces of S

Four subspaces, each with a biological meaning. This week converts linear algebra you already have into intuition about networks, and it answers a question you will be asked in interview: how many measurements does a flux study actually need? Keep the toy networks small enough to read by eye; the point is interpretation, not computation.

Core ideas

1. The four subspaces and their dimensions

For S with m metabolites, n reactions and rank r: the column space has dimension r and lives in metabolite space; the right null space has dimension n − r and lives in flux space; the row space has dimension r in flux space; and the left null space has dimension m − r in metabolite space. The rank-nullity theorem gives these for free, and the two null spaces are where the biology is. Everything else in constraint-based modelling is a statement about restricting the right null space.

2. The right null space is the space of steady states

S·v = 0 defines the set of flux vectors consistent with mass balance, and that set is exactly the right null space. Its dimension n − r is the number of degrees of freedom: how many fluxes must be fixed, by measurement or by bounds or by an objective, before a unique solution exists. For the E. coli core model with 95 reactions and rank near 68, that is 27 degrees of freedom; at genome scale it is several hundred. This single number explains why flux balance analysis needs an objective function at all — mass balance alone leaves far too much freedom.

3. Basis vectors are pathways, with a caveat

Any basis of the null space spans the same space, and a numerically convenient basis from a singular value decomposition is not biologically interpretable. Bases chosen for interpretability — elementary flux modes, extreme pathways — consist of vectors that are themselves minimal functional routes through the network, which is why they read as pathways. The caveat is combinatorial explosion: the number of elementary modes grows faster than exponentially with network size, so they are computable for small networks and hopeless at genome scale. That limitation is why the field moved to optimisation rather than enumeration.

4. The left null space holds conserved moieties

A vector in the left null space is a linear combination of metabolite concentrations that the network cannot change: total adenylate (ATP + ADP + AMP), total nicotinamide in each pool, total coenzyme A, total quinone. These are conserved because no reaction in the network creates or destroys the moiety; it is only passed between carriers. Two practical uses. In a kinetic model these totals must be supplied as parameters, because the differential equations cannot determine them. And an unexpected extra conserved pool is a structural diagnostic — it usually means a missing exchange reaction or an unintended dead end, so checking the left null space is the fastest sanity check on any new reconstruction.

5. Singular value decomposition, used for structure rather than numbers

Writing S = UΣVᵀ gives orthonormal bases for all four subspaces at once, with the singular values ranking how strongly each mode participates. The spectrum is informative: a steep drop means a few modes dominate the network's structure. The left singular vectors group metabolites that behave together, the right singular vectors group reactions. None of this is directly biological — the vectors are orthogonal by construction, not by biology — so treat SVD as a structural probe and not as a pathway-finding method.

6. What the subspaces do not tell you

Worth stating plainly, because the formalism is seductive. The null space contains every mass-balanced flux distribution, including ones that are thermodynamically impossible, kinetically unreachable, or that require more enzyme than the cell possesses. Restricting it is the whole business of the next four weeks: bounds for capacity, directionality and loop constraints for thermodynamics, proteome constraints for enzyme cost, and an objective for the final selection. The subspaces define what is conceivable; everything else defines what is possible.

Worked anchor

Compute and read the subspaces of the toy network from week 20.

Four metabolites, six reactions, rank 4. So: column space 4, right null space 2, row space 4, left null space 0.

The right null space of dimension 2 means two independent routes, which on inspection are A→C and A→D. Fix one flux — say measure the C exchange — and with mass balance the other is determined.

The left null space is empty, which makes sense: every metabolite can enter or leave through an exchange, so nothing is trapped. Now delete the D exchange and recompute. D can now only be produced and never consumed, so it is a dead end; reaction 3 is forced to zero, the effective rank falls, and the left null space acquires a dimension corresponding to D being conserved at whatever it started with.

That is the diagnostic in miniature. When you compute the left null space of a real reconstruction and find a conserved pool you cannot name, you have almost certainly found a missing exchange rather than a new piece of biology.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the week 20 toy network, rank 4, exchanges as drawn
  • steady state, so only S·v = 0 constrains the fluxes

Common misconceptions

  • That a null space basis is the set of pathways. Any basis spans the space; only particular bases, chosen for the purpose, consist of interpretable routes.
  • That elementary modes scale. They explode combinatorially, which is precisely why the field optimises rather than enumerates at genome scale.
  • That the null space contains achievable states. It contains mass-balanced ones, including thermodynamically impossible and enzymatically unaffordable ones.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. A network has 112 reactions, 84 metabolites and rank 79. Give all four subspace dimensions and interpret two.

A. Column space 79, right null space 112 − 79 = 33, row space 79, left null space 84 − 79 = 5. The right null space of 33 means 33 independent fluxes must be fixed by measurement, bounds or an objective before a unique solution exists — which is why an objective function is needed at all. The left null space of 5 means five conserved moieties, typically total adenylate, the two nicotinamide pools, coenzyme A and quinone, which must be supplied as parameters in any kinetic model.

Q. You compute the left null space of a new reconstruction and find a conserved pool you cannot name. What is the likely cause?

A. A missing exchange reaction or an unintended dead end: some metabolite or moiety can neither enter nor leave the system, so its total is trapped and appears as a conservation relation. Occasionally it is real biology — a genuine carrier you had not thought of — but the first hypothesis should be a boundary error. Checking the left null space is therefore the fastest structural sanity check available on a new model.

Q. Why did the field move from enumerating elementary modes to optimisation?

A. Because the number of elementary flux modes grows faster than exponentially with network size, so enumeration is tractable for networks of tens of reactions and impossible for thousands. Optimisation finds one point in the null space satisfying the constraints rather than describing the whole space, which scales to genome-scale models. The cost is that you learn about one flux distribution rather than the structure of all of them, which is why flux variability analysis and sampling exist as partial substitutes.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Explain what the null space of a small network says about possible steady-state fluxes. Why can multiple flux patterns fit the same stoichiometry?

Week 23 — Flux balance analysis

The linear program you already know, with biology in the objective. The formulation takes ten minutes; the week's real content is the assumptions, the duality, and the discipline of checking the model's arithmetic against your own. Install the toolchain properly now — the environment you built in week 1 has drifted by twenty-two weeks and needs re-pinning before anything else.

Core ideas

1. The formulation, derived rather than quoted

Start from the dynamic mass balance, dx/dt = S·v, where x is metabolite concentrations. Intracellular pools turn over in seconds while growth changes over hours, so set dx/dt = 0 and you have S·v = 0. Add capacity bounds lb ≤ v ≤ ub and you have a feasible region: a convex polytope in flux space, bounded and high-dimensional. Choose a linear objective cᵀv and you have a linear program. That is all FBA is. Note the two decisions hidden in it: the bounds, which are mostly guesses, and the objective, which is an evolutionary argument rather than a physical law.

2. Sign conventions, which cost everyone a day

Exchange reactions are written as A_e ⇌ with uptake negative. So the maximum glucose uptake rate is set as the lower bound of the glucose exchange: a bound of −10 permits uptake up to 10 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹, and setting it to 0 forbids uptake while still permitting secretion. Anaerobiosis is the oxygen exchange lower bound set to zero. Getting this backwards produces a model that grows without a carbon source or cannot grow at all, and it is the single commonest beginner error in the toolchain.

3. The geometry, which is worth holding in your head

The feasible region is a convex polytope: mass balance gives hyperplanes, bounds give half-spaces. The objective is a vector, and the optimum sits where that vector is maximised over the polytope — generically at a vertex. Two consequences follow directly. If the objective vector happens to be parallel to an edge or a face, every point on that edge is optimal and the solution is degenerate, which is both common and the geometric reason flux variability analysis exists. And the optimum lies on the boundary, meaning at least some constraints are active: identifying which ones are binding tells you what is limiting, which is the dual problem.

4. Duality, read as marginal value

Every linear program has a dual, and the dual variables of the mass-balance constraints are shadow prices: the marginal change in the objective per unit change in the availability of a metabolite. A shadow price of 0.045 gDW/mmol for NADPH means one extra mmol of NADPH per gram dry weight per hour would raise growth by 0.045 h⁻¹. Reduced costs do the same job for reactions. These numbers are often more informative than the flux distribution, because they say what is scarce rather than what is flowing — and scarcity is what you engineer.

5. The assumptions, ranked by fragility

Rank them, because listing them is what everyone does and ranking them is what demonstrates understanding. Most fragile: that the cell optimises the chosen objective — an evolutionary argument that holds for a long-adapted wild type in a constant environment and fails for an engineered strain or immediately after a perturbation. Then the biomass composition, measured in one condition and applied to all. Then capacity bounds, mostly guessed. Then network completeness for the condition. Least fragile: steady state itself, which follows from the timescale separation. Note that the weakest assumption is the one that makes FBA work at all.

6. Cross-checking, which is the habit that matters

Never report a model number you have not checked against something independent. Compute ATP per glucose by hand through glycolysis, pyruvate dehydrogenase and the TCA cycle with a stated P/O, then compute it from the model with the biomass reaction bounded to zero and the maintenance reaction as objective, and resolve the discrepancy in writing. The resolution is itself informative: it will turn on which NADH dehydrogenase and oxidase the model carries and what maintenance it holds. A student who reconciles the two understands the model; a student who reports only the model's number does not.

Worked anchor

Maximum ATP yield, by hand and by model, and why they differ.

By hand, for E. coli on glucose with the efficient respiratory chain: glycolysis gives 2 ATP and 2 NADH; pyruvate dehydrogenase 2 NADH; the TCA cycle 2 GTP, 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂. With Complex I and cytochrome bo₃ at 8 charge equivalents per NADH and 4.3 H⁺ per ATP, that is 1.86 ATP per NADH and about 0.93 per FADH₂: 4 + 18.6 + 1.86 ≈ 24.5 ATP.

By model: set the glucose exchange lower bound to −10, oxygen unconstrained, the biomass reaction bounded to zero, and the ATP maintenance reaction as the objective. Divide the result by 10.

The model typically returns somewhat less than the hand value, in the low twenties. Resolve it rather than note it. Candidate explanations, each checkable: the model may use a different proton stoichiometry for its dehydrogenase or oxidase; it may carry a non-zero lower bound on maintenance that consumes part of the yield; its ATP synthase may be parameterised with a different H⁺/ATP; and it may route some flux through the less efficient NADH dehydrogenase if that is unconstrained and equivalent. Inspect the reactions, find which applies, and write the answer down.

This exercise is Brief 6's core and it is the clearest demonstration available that you can use the tool and interrogate it.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the efficient respiratory chain: Complex I and cytochrome bo₃
  • 4.3 H⁺ per ATP, GTP counted as ATP
  • biomass bounded to zero and maintenance as stated
  • the model's own stoichiometry may differ — that is the point of the comparison

Common misconceptions

  • That FBA predicts what a cell does. It predicts what a cell could do while optimising an objective you chose, under bounds you chose.
  • That setting an uptake limit means setting an upper bound. Uptake is negative flux, so the limit is the lower bound — the error that costs everyone a day.
  • That a flux distribution is the result. The shadow prices are often the result; they say what is scarce, and scarcity is what you engineer.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Write the FBA problem formally for anaerobic growth on glucose at 10 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹.

A. maximise cᵀv subject to S·v = 0 and lb ≤ v ≤ ub, with v_EX_glc_e ≥ −10, v_EX_o2_e = 0, and c selecting the biomass reaction. The sign convention matters: uptake is negative flux, so the uptake limit appears as a lower bound on the exchange reaction, and oxygen is excluded by setting its exchange lower bound to zero while leaving secretion permitted.

Q. Interpret a shadow price of 0.021 gDW/mmol for ATP and 0.045 for NADPH, and say what you would do with them.

A. One extra mmol of ATP per gDW per hour would raise growth rate by 0.021 h⁻¹; one extra mmol of NADPH by 0.045 h⁻¹. NADPH is therefore about twice as valuable per mole, so the network is more constrained by reducing power than by energy under these conditions — a warning for a reductive product, which competes with growth for the scarcer currency. To act on it, test the prediction: supply reducing power without carbon, or express a transhydrogenase, and check whether growth and yield respond in the predicted ratio. If they respond in the opposite order, the model's cofactor balance is wrong, which is itself a useful result.

Q. Rank the assumptions of FBA by fragility and justify the extremes.

A. Most fragile is optimality of the chosen objective, because it is an assumption about behaviour rather than physics and fails for engineered strains and after perturbations. Then biomass composition, measured in one condition and applied to all. Then capacity bounds, mostly guessed. Then network completeness for the condition in question. Least fragile is steady state, which follows from metabolite pools turning over in seconds while growth changes over hours. The ranking matters because the assumption doing the most work is also the least secure.

Week 24 — FBA extensions: variability, loops and alternatives

One FBA solution is a hypothesis, not a result. The extensions exist because the feasible region is large, the optimum is frequently degenerate, and mass balance alone permits flux distributions that thermodynamics forbids. This is the week that teaches scepticism about your own output, which is what an interviewer is probing when they ask what FBA assumes.

Core ideas

1. Degeneracy, and why it is the normal case

If the objective vector is parallel to an edge or face of the polytope, every point along it is optimal. In real models this happens constantly, because many reactions appear in alternative routes of identical stoichiometric cost — a redox shuttle that can run through either of two carriers, an isozyme pair, a cycle with no net exchange. The consequence is that the particular flux vector a solver returns is one arbitrary point among many, chosen by the solver's internal pivot order rather than by biology. Reporting it as the flux distribution is the commonest misuse of FBA, and flux variability analysis exists to measure how arbitrary it was.

2. Flux variability analysis, and how to read its output

FVA maximises and minimises each reaction's flux subject to holding the objective at or near its optimum, giving an interval per reaction. Read the pattern rather than individual numbers. Reactions with a zero-width interval are fixed by the constraints: those are the real conclusions. Reactions with a wide interval are degenerate, and a reaction whose interval includes zero may or may not carry flux in vivo — the model cannot say. Running FVA at 100% and again at 90% of optimum tells you how flat the landscape is; a large increase in variability for a 10% objective relaxation means the optimum is a plateau, and so is barely an optimum.

3. Parsimonious FBA and the enzyme-cost argument

pFBA selects, among all optimal solutions, the one minimising the sum of absolute fluxes. The justification is that total flux is a rough proxy for total enzyme investment, so the parsimonious solution is the one a proteome-limited cell would prefer. It is a reasonable heuristic with two useful side effects: it removes most internal loops, since a loop adds flux without objective value, and it returns a single reproducible solution rather than an arbitrary one. It is not a thermodynamic guarantee, and it should be described as a heuristic rather than as a correction.

4. Loops: why mass balance permits the impossible

A set of reactions forming a closed cycle with no net exchange satisfies S·v = 0 at any loop flux, because every metabolite is produced and consumed within the loop. It is nonetheless impossible: Gibbs energy is a state function, so the sum of ΔrG′ around a closed loop is exactly zero, and a set of strictly negative values cannot sum to zero. Therefore at least one reaction in the loop must be running against its own gradient. The remedies are loopless FBA, which adds integer constraints forcing a thermodynamically consistent set of directions at the cost of a mixed-integer program, and thermodynamics-based flux analysis, which carries concentration variables and ΔrG′ constraints explicitly at the cost of needing data that does not exist for every metabolite.

5. Flux coupling, which tells you about structure rather than state

Two reactions are fully coupled if a non-zero flux in one implies a fixed ratio in the other, directionally coupled if one implies the other is non-zero, and partially coupled if the ratio is bounded. Coupling is a property of the network and the bounds, not of a particular solution, which makes it more durable than a flux distribution. Practically it identifies correlated reaction sets, which behave as single units for engineering purposes: deleting one member of a fully coupled set has the same effect as deleting any other, and no intervention can change their ratio.

6. MOMA and ROOM: what a cell does immediately after a knockout

Growth maximisation is an evolutionary argument and applies to an organism that has had time to adapt. A freshly constructed knockout has not. MOMA instead finds the flux distribution closest, in Euclidean distance, to the wild-type one, on the argument that regulation has not been retuned; ROOM minimises the number of reactions whose flux changes significantly, on the argument that regulatory changes are discrete. Both predict knockout phenotypes better than growth maximisation for unevolved strains, and growth maximisation recovers its accuracy after adaptive evolution — a result worth knowing because it is one of the field's cleanest validations of the optimality assumption's domain.

Worked anchor

Diagnose a wide FVA interval.

FVA at 100% of optimum returns a range of 0 to 22 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ for a reaction. Work through it rather than concluding the reaction is unimportant.

First, is it a loop? Run loopless FVA. If the range collapses to a narrow interval, the variability was a thermodynamically infeasible cycle and never meant anything.

Second, is there a cheaper alternative? Run pFBA and see whether the reaction carries flux in the parsimonious solution. If it does not, an enzymatically cheaper route exists and the cell plausibly uses that one.

Third, what is it coupled to? Compute flux coupling. If the reaction is in a correlated set with an alternative, you have found the specific competing route rather than a vague alternative.

Fourth, how flat is the optimum? Rerun FVA at 90%. If the range widens substantially, the model has a plateau rather than a peak, and the objective is barely discriminating.

Fifth, and only now: resolve it experimentally. A genuinely variable split between two routes is exactly what ¹³C labelling measures, which is why week 29 follows this one. The output of this analysis should be a stated experiment, not a conclusion.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the model structure is correct and the bounds are as set
  • FVA run at 100% of the optimum
  • the objective is the one the cell is assumed to optimise
