Common misconceptions

  • That the flux distribution a solver returns is the flux distribution. It is one arbitrary point among many whenever the optimum is degenerate, which is usually.
  • That pFBA corrects loops. It removes most of them as a side effect of minimising flux; it guarantees nothing thermodynamically.
  • That a wide FVA range means a reaction is dispensable. It means the model cannot distinguish two routes of equal cost; the cell may use one exclusively.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Why does S·v = 0 permit a thermodynamically impossible loop, and what are the two principled remedies?

A. Mass balance constrains stoichiometry, not direction: a closed cycle produces and consumes each of its metabolites internally, so every row of S·v = 0 is satisfied at any loop flux. It is impossible because Gibbs energy is a state function, so ΔrG′ around a closed loop sums to exactly zero and strictly negative values cannot. The remedies are loopless FBA, adding integer constraints that force a consistent direction assignment, and thermodynamics-based flux analysis, carrying metabolite concentrations and ΔrG′ explicitly. pFBA removes most loops incidentally but guarantees nothing.

Q. When is MOMA the appropriate objective rather than growth maximisation, and what evidence supports the distinction?

A. For a freshly constructed knockout that has not had time to adapt, because growth maximisation assumes an evolutionary optimisation the strain has not undergone, whereas MOMA assumes regulation has not been retuned and the flux distribution stays close to wild type. The supporting evidence is that MOMA predicts unevolved knockout phenotypes better, while growth maximisation recovers accuracy after adaptive laboratory evolution — which both validates the optimality assumption and delimits where it applies.

Q. FVA at 100% of optimum gives a reaction a range of 0 to 20. Give the four checks before drawing any conclusion.

A. Run loopless FVA to test whether the variability is a thermodynamically infeasible cycle; run pFBA to see whether the reaction carries flux in the enzymatically cheapest solution; compute flux coupling to identify the specific competing route rather than a vague alternative; and rerun FVA at 90% of optimum to see whether the landscape is a plateau rather than a peak. If the range survives all four, the split is genuinely unresolved by the model and the next step is a ¹³C labelling experiment, not a conclusion.

Week 25 — Gene deletions, essentiality and phase planes

The first point at which your model meets experimental truth and loses. Validating against essentiality data and then explaining every disagreement is what separates a modeller from someone who has run a tutorial, and it is the single most valuable artifact you will produce in this phase.

Core ideas

1. How essentiality is predicted, and the threshold hiding inside it

Delete a gene by applying the GPR logic, constrain the affected reactions to zero, re-solve, and compare predicted growth with the wild type. Then apply a threshold: below some fraction of wild-type growth, typically 1% to 10%, the gene is called essential. That threshold is a modelling choice and it matters — a gene whose deletion leaves 5% growth is called essential at a 10% threshold and non-essential at 1%, and experimentally such a strain grows slowly rather than not at all. Report the threshold you used and show the sensitivity to it; many published screens do neither.

2. Validation, and the confusion matrix as a starting point

Compare against experimental data — the Keio single-gene deletion collection for E. coli, or equivalents for other organisms — and build the matrix: true positives are genes both call essential, false positives are predicted essential but experimentally dispensable, false negatives the reverse. Compute precision and recall. Typical genome-scale performance is precision near 0.6 to 0.8 and recall near 0.8 to 0.9, which sounds respectable until you notice that the matrix alone tells you nothing about why. The matrix is where the work starts.

3. False positives, which dominate, and their four causes

Predicted essential, experimentally dispensable. A missing isozyme or an unannotated promiscuous activity provides the reaction by another route. A missing transporter or an unrecorded medium component lets the cell bypass the blocked step by uptake — rich medium is a frequent culprit, since experiments are often done on it and models on minimal. A GPR written as AND where the biology is OR. Or the growth threshold is too strict. Each has a different remedy, and classifying them gene by gene is the actual result of a validation study; a matrix without that classification is worth perhaps a third of the marks.

4. False negatives, which are more interesting

Predicted dispensable, experimentally essential. Regulation the model does not represent, so the alternative route exists stoichiometrically but is not expressed. Accumulation of a toxic intermediate when the normal route is blocked, which stoichiometry cannot see. Moonlighting functions outside metabolism entirely. Or a gene essential for a reason the model is not about — cell division, envelope integrity. These are fewer but they point at the model's structural limits rather than at missing knowledge, which is why they are worth discussing individually in a write-up.

5. Double deletions and synthetic lethality

Run pairs and you find synthetic lethal combinations: neither single deletion is lethal, the double is. These identify redundancy — isozymes, parallel routes, alternative cofactor usage — and they are the model's most genuinely predictive output, because redundancy is hard to see by inspection. The combinatorics is manageable at genome scale for pairs, roughly 10⁶ to 10⁷ simulations, and hopeless for triples. For engineering, synthetic lethal pairs are also a warning list: they are the interventions where a single deletion appears safe and the combination is not.

6. Robustness analysis and phenotypic phase planes

Vary one bound and plot the objective: robustness analysis, which shows where a parameter matters and where it does not, and where the limiting constraint changes. Vary two — typically carbon and oxygen uptake — and you get a phenotypic phase plane: a two-dimensional map divided into regions, each with a distinct pattern of active constraints and by-product secretion, separated by lines where the limiting constraint switches. The line of optimality is the locus of maximum objective, and the empirical finding that organisms often sit near it is one of the field's more striking validations. Explain the regions from stoichiometry before reading them off the plot; the explanation is the learning.

Worked anchor

Read a confusion matrix properly.

A genome-scale screen predicts 318 essential genes; experiment reports 274, with 221 in common.

True positives 221. False positives 318 − 221 = 97. False negatives 274 − 221 = 53. Precision = 221/318 = 0.695. Recall = 221/274 = 0.807. F1 = 0.747.

Now the part that is actually the result. False positives outnumber false negatives roughly two to one, which is the usual pattern and tells you the model is over-predicting essentiality — it knows fewer alternative routes than the cell has. Classify all 97: expect a large group resolved by isozymes or promiscuous activities, a group explained by medium composition if the experiment used rich medium, a group from GPR connective errors, and a residue from the growth threshold.

Then do the sensitivity: rerun at thresholds of 1%, 5% and 10% of wild-type growth and tabulate how precision and recall move. If a tenth of your false positives disappear at a looser threshold, the disagreement was partly definitional rather than biological, and saying so is more honest than quoting one F1 score.

Finally, estimate how many disagreements are data errors rather than model errors — experimental essentiality calls are themselves threshold-dependent and condition-specific. A defensible answer here is worth more than a high F1.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the experimental essentiality set is taken as the reference
  • a single medium and condition
  • essentiality treated as binary rather than graded

Common misconceptions

  • That a confusion matrix is the result. The gene-by-gene classification of every false prediction is the result; the matrix is the summary.
  • That essentiality is binary. Both the prediction and the experiment apply a growth threshold, and genes near it are called differently by different studies.
  • That a false positive is a model failure. Most are missing knowledge — an isozyme, a transporter, a medium component — which is a curation task rather than a method defect.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. A screen gives precision 0.70 and recall 0.81. Which error class dominates, and what does it say about the reconstruction?

A. Precision below recall means false positives outnumber false negatives: the model calls genes essential that experimentally are not. That says the reconstruction knows fewer alternative routes than the cell actually has — missing isozymes, unannotated promiscuous activities, absent transporters, medium components not in the modelled medium, or GPR rules written as AND where the biology is OR. It is a knowledge gap rather than a method failure, and the remedy is curation.

Q. Give three mechanisms that produce a false negative, and say why they are more interesting than false positives.

A. Regulation the model does not represent, so a stoichiometrically available route is not expressed; accumulation of a toxic intermediate when the usual route is blocked, which stoichiometry cannot see; and moonlighting or non-metabolic essentiality, such as a role in division or envelope integrity. They are more interesting because they point at the model's structural limits rather than at missing biochemical knowledge: no amount of curation fixes them, and each identifies a class of question constraint-based models cannot answer.

Q. Explain a phenotypic phase plane's regions from stoichiometry rather than from the plot.

A. At high oxygen relative to carbon, the cell can fully oxidise the substrate and growth is carbon-limited, so the objective rises with carbon uptake and is insensitive to oxygen. At low oxygen relative to carbon, respiration cannot reoxidise all the NADH produced, so fermentation products are secreted and growth is oxygen-limited, rising with oxygen and insensitive to carbon. Between them lies the line of optimality, where both are used in the ratio that the stoichiometry makes most efficient. Each region boundary is a point where the binding constraint changes, which is why the plane is piecewise linear.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Pick a gene deletion relevant to a proposed pathway. What does model-predicted essentiality mean, and what experimental result would challenge the model?

Week 26 — Strain design and growth coupling

The payoff of the phase: turning a model into a genotype. It is also where model-driven design must be criticised honestly, because most published designs underperform their predictions and the reasons are systematic rather than accidental. Paper 3 is sat at the end of this week.

Core ideas

1. The production envelope, and how to read it

Plot product yield against growth rate by maximising product at each fixed growth rate. The resulting region's upper boundary is the maximum achievable yield at that growth rate, and the two ends tell you the most: the maximum product yield at zero growth, which is the stoichiometric ceiling, and the yield at maximum growth, which is usually near zero for an unengineered strain. The engineering goal is to deform this envelope so that high product yield is the only option at any appreciable growth rate. Reading an envelope is the first thing to do with any design, and producing one is required by Brief 8.

2. Growth coupling, stated precisely

A design is growth-coupled when product formation is stoichiometrically required for growth — when every flux distribution that produces biomass also produces product. Weak coupling means product is required above some growth rate; strong coupling means at any growth rate. The mechanism is always the same: delete every alternative sink for something growth necessarily generates, usually a reduced cofactor, so that the product pathway becomes the unique balance. The reason to want it is not elegance but population genetics — a fermentation spans roughly thirty generations from vial to production vessel, and without coupling the fastest-growing non-producer sweeps.

3. Bilevel design, and what the algorithms actually do

The design problem is naturally bilevel: choose deletions such that, when the cell subsequently maximises growth, product formation is high. The inner problem is the cell's optimisation and the outer is yours, which is formally awkward and is handled by converting the inner problem to its optimality conditions, giving a mixed-integer program. OptKnock does this for deletions; descendants add insertions, up- and down-regulation, and heuristic search for larger design spaces. What matters for you is the structure, not the solver: the algorithms assume the cell optimises growth, so every criticism of that assumption in week 23 applies to their output.

4. Why designs underperform, and the five levels to check

Systematically, not accidentally. Thermodynamic: a step that is feasible in the model is near equilibrium at real concentrations. Kinetic: the pathway enzymes cannot carry the predicted flux at achievable expression. Proteome: the required enzyme mass is a large fraction of the budget, so growth falls and volumetric productivity with it. Regulatory: the host down-regulates something the design depends on. Toxicity: the product or an intermediate inhibits at the titre required. A design document without these five, each with a measurement that would detect it, is incomplete — and writing them is what Brief 8 grades.

5. Escape routes, and checking them against your actual medium

A coupling argument is only as good as the set of alternatives you enumerated. Common escapes: transhydrogenase activity shuttling electrons between cofactor pools; hydrogen evolution via formate hydrogen lyase; an unannotated dehydrogenase; respiration on a trace electron acceptor present in the medium but not in the model; and suppressor mutations restoring a deleted activity. The first four are checkable in the model, and the medium one is the trap — check the coupling against the medium you will actually use, including its complex components, not a generic minimal one.

6. What to build first, which is a judgement rather than an output

Algorithms return many designs of similar predicted yield. Choose among them on grounds the model cannot see: how many genetic interventions are required, whether the deleted genes are essential under some other condition you will encounter, whether the predicted flux through any step exceeds a plausible enzyme capacity, whether an intermediate is known to be toxic, and whether the coupling survives the escapes above. A defended choice between two algorithmic designs is worth more in an interview than the design itself.

Worked anchor

Construct a growth-coupled design by hand, then attack it.

Target: a product requiring 2 NADH per mole, made anaerobically.

The argument. Anaerobically, ATP comes only from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis. Glycolysis necessarily produces NADH at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase. The NAD pool is conserved — it appears in the left null space from week 22 — so NADH must be reoxidised or glycolysis halts. Delete lactate dehydrogenase, alcohol dehydrogenase and the fumarate reductase route, and the product pathway is the only remaining reoxidation route. Therefore: no product, no NADH reoxidation; no reoxidation, no glycolysis; no glycolysis, no ATP; no ATP, no growth. The coupling is proved from conservation rather than asserted from an algorithm.

Now attack it. Transhydrogenase: can the cell move electrons to NADPH and dispose of them in biosynthesis? Check whether the model has one and whether the real strain does. Hydrogen: is formate hydrogen lyase present? Delete it or check its expression anaerobically. Unannotated dehydrogenases: how many genes in this genome are annotated as oxidoreductases with unknown substrate? Medium: does your medium contain nitrate, fumarate, DMSO or TMAO as a trace component — because any of them restores respiration and breaks the coupling entirely. Suppressors: at 10¹² cells, every single-base reversion exists.

The design is the easy part. The enumeration of escapes is the part that distinguishes a defensible proposal.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • anaerobic, with no trace electron acceptor in the medium
  • the model carries no unannotated oxidoreductase
  • the NAD pool is conserved, as the left null space says
  • minimal medium, so no route is rescued by a supplied nutrient

Common misconceptions

  • That growth coupling is elegance. It is population genetics: without it the fastest-growing non-producer sweeps across a thirty-generation seed train.
  • That the algorithm chooses the design. It returns many of similar predicted yield; choosing among them on grounds the model cannot see is the engineering.
  • That checking escapes in the model is enough. The commonest escape is a trace electron acceptor in a medium the model does not describe.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Prove growth coupling for an anaerobic design from conservation rather than from an algorithm.

A. Anaerobically ATP comes only from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis, and glycolysis necessarily produces NADH at GAPDH. The total NAD pool is a conserved moiety — it lies in the left null space — so NADH must be reoxidised for glycolysis to continue. With every alternative sink deleted, the product pathway is the unique reoxidation route. Hence no product means no reoxidation, no reoxidation means no glycolytic flux, no glycolysis means no ATP, and no ATP means no growth. The chain is stoichiometric throughout.

Q. Name the five levels at which a model-driven design underperforms, with a discriminating measurement for each.

A. Thermodynamic — compute ΔrG′ from measured intracellular concentrations and look for a step near equilibrium. Kinetic — measure in vitro activity in lysate and compare with the flux required. Proteome — quantify the pathway's share of total protein and compare growth against an inert-protein control at matched expression. Regulatory — measure transcript and protein for the pathway and for the host genes the design depends on. Toxicity — add the product or intermediate exogenously at the target intracellular concentration and measure growth and specific productivity.

Q. Your coupled design works in silico. Name four escape routes and say which is hardest to see.

A. Transhydrogenase activity moving electrons between the NADH and NADPH pools; hydrogen evolution through formate hydrogen lyase; an unannotated oxidoreductase providing an alternative sink; and respiration on a trace electron acceptor — nitrate, fumarate, DMSO or TMAO — present in the medium. The last is hardest to see, because it is absent from the model entirely: the coupling is checked against a minimal medium while the experiment runs on something richer. Suppressor mutations are a fifth, inevitable at 10¹² cells, and the reason coupling must be stringent rather than marginal.

Every number in these modules — ribosome counts, pool sizes, half-lives, turnover times — is written from working knowledge and is an order-of-magnitude figure. Before any of them enters a notebook, a figure or a proposal, check it against BioNumbers or the primary source and cite that, not these notes. Treat the modules as a map of what matters and a scaffold for reasoning; treat the textbooks and the databases as the authority for values.

Week 27 — Metabolomics and intracellular measurement

Every concentration you assumed in phase 2 and every bound you guessed in phase 4 is measured this week, badly and with difficulty. The content is not the instrument; it is the error budget, and the skill is knowing which term dominates and whether your conclusion survives it.

Core ideas

1. Turnover time is the design constraint, and you compute it

τ = pool / flux through the pool, and the whole protocol follows from it. Work in µmol gDW⁻¹: intracellular water is about 2 mL gDW⁻¹, so 1 mM is 2 µmol gDW⁻¹. ATP at 1.5 mM against a turnover flux of order 50 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ gives τ ≈ 0.2 s; glucose-6-phosphate at 1 mM with a glycolytic flux of 10 gives τ ≈ 0.7 s; glutamate at 60 mM drained at 1.5 gives τ ≈ 290 s. Three orders of magnitude separate the easy case from the hard one, which is why no single protocol serves a whole metabolome. Rank your metabolites by τ before choosing one.

2. Quench speed and leakage are in direct conflict

Rapid arrest and membrane integrity trade against each other, because the fastest methods work by cold shock or solvent and both perturb the membrane. How much leaks depends on the organism, the metabolite class, the solvent, the temperature, the biomass density and the contact time, so the figures are protocol-specific and must be validated rather than assumed: reported losses for cold methanol run from a few per cent for nucleotides to half the pool for some organic acids. Fast filtration is gentler, slower, and the wash itself removes metabolite. The answer is the differential method: quench whole broth, measure the filtrate separately, and take the intracellular amount as the difference, n_in = n_broth − n_extracellular. That estimates the intracellular pool only when the two measurements are commensurate — matched volumes, accounted recovery, no filtration delay — and it converts an unknown bias into a variance rather than removing it.

3. Absolute quantification needs an isotope-dilution standard

A uniformly ¹³C-labelled extract of the same organism gives many analytes a chemically identical, mass-shifted twin that tracks extraction loss, ion suppression and drift together — many rather than every, since coverage reaches only what the organism synthesises, at the labelling completeness and isotopic purity actually achieved, for species measured in a valid response range. Where it reaches, it corrects everything downstream of the point at which it was added, so spike timing decides which part of the chain is covered: added at the quench it covers extraction, added afterwards only the analysis. Without such a standard you have relative quantification, comparable to your own samples and nothing else — fine for a fold-change, not enough for a ΔrG′, which needs molar units. It matters because co-eluting compounds compete for charge in electrospray, and suppression of tens of per cent is commonly reported, so a curve built in clean solvent reads low by an amount that depends on how dirty the extract is.

4. Keep bias and variance in separate columns

Independent random errors combine in quadrature, √(Σσᵢ²), so the largest term dominates quickly and polishing a small one is wasted effort. A fifteen per cent leakage is not a random error: it is a bias, it does not shrink with replication, and it does not belong in the quadrature sum. It belongs in a correction with its own uncertainty, or in a stated direction of error. The commonest failure in published metabolomics is to propagate a bias as a variance, which converts a systematic understatement into a reassuring interval centred on the wrong value.

5. Thermodynamics needs less precision than kinetics

ΔrG′ = ΔrG′° + RT·Σᵢ νᵢ·ln aᵢ, with RT = 2.577 kJ mol⁻¹ at 37 °C. A twenty per cent error in one reactant contributes RT·ln(1.2) = 0.47 kJ mol⁻¹ and a factor of two only 1.8, while group-contribution estimates of ΔrG′° carry 3–4 kJ mol⁻¹. So for a feasibility verdict on a reaction with small stoichiometric coefficients and roughly independent errors, improving the standard-state estimate beats improving the metabolomics. Check that premise rather than assuming it: the sum runs over every reactant weighted by νᵢ, so a coefficient of two doubles that term and errors shared across metabolites — one dilution factor, one biomass normalisation — add rather than cancel. For a kinetic model the ranking reverses, because a rate law evaluates S/Kₘ directly and a factor-of-two error in concentration is a factor-of-two error in the rate of an unsaturated step. One nicety worth knowing before someone asks: Q is written in concentrations rather than activities, and the activity correction is not ignored but sits in the other term — eQuilibrator returns a transformed standard energy at a stated pH, pMg and ionic strength, so quoting ΔrG′° without those three conditions is quoting an incomplete number. Know which question you are asking before calling a measurement good enough.

6. Compartmentation, and why a eukaryotic cytosolic concentration is rarely real

A whole-cell yeast extract is a volume-weighted average over cytosol, mitochondrion and vacuole. The vacuole alone can be a fifth to a half of cell volume and concentrates amino acids by an order of magnitude, so a reported cytosolic glutamate may be wrong by a factor of several in a direction the number cannot tell you. Real compartment-specific measurement needs rapid fractionation in non-aqueous solvent or a sensor calibrated in situ, both hard enough that few data sets exist. Compartmentalised thermodynamic analysis in a eukaryote therefore rests on inferred concentrations and should say so.

Worked anchor

Turnover times, an error budget, and what both do to a thermodynamic verdict.

Intracellular water 2 mL gDW⁻¹, so 1 mM = 2 µmol gDW⁻¹.

ATP: 3 µmol gDW⁻¹ over 50,000/3600 = 13.9 µmol gDW⁻¹ s⁻¹ gives τ = 0.22 s. G6P: 2 µmol gDW⁻¹ over 2.8 µmol gDW⁻¹ s⁻¹ gives τ = 0.72 s. Glutamate: 120 µmol gDW⁻¹ over 0.42 µmol gDW⁻¹ s⁻¹ gives τ = 288 s.

A five-second protocol reports glutamate honestly, reports G6P as whatever it became during sampling, and reports ATP as a property of the quench.

Now one metabolite reported at 1.5 mM: sampling 8%, leakage 15%, extraction recovery 85 ± 10%, dilution 3%, instrument 5%. The leakage is a bias and the 85% recovery is a correction whose ±10% is its variance, so the random terms are 0.08, 0.10, 0.03, 0.05:

√(0.0064 + 0.0100 + 0.0009 + 0.0025) = √0.0198 = 0.141, about 14%.

Propagate the leakage as random instead, as most papers do, and you get √(0.0198 + 0.0225) = 0.206 — an interval of 1.5 ± 0.31 mM centred low by roughly the leakage.

Carried into ΔrG′, the 14% error contributes RT·ln(1.14) = 2.577 × 0.131 = 0.34 kJ mol⁻¹ and the 21% version 0.49. Against 4 kJ mol⁻¹ of uncertainty in ΔrG′°, both are an order of magnitude too small to matter. So for a feasibility study the metabolomics is already good enough and the standard-state estimate is not, while for week 30's kinetic model the opposite holds. Write that sentence down; it is the one that shows you know what the measurement is for.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • intracellular water 2 mL gDW⁻¹, used to convert mM to µmol gDW⁻¹
  • pools and fluxes are order-of-magnitude figures, not measurements
  • the random error terms are independent; leakage is treated as a bias
  • one reactant varies in the ΔrG′ step, with ν = 1
  • RT = 2.577 kJ mol⁻¹ at 37 °C

Common misconceptions

  • That a reported intracellular concentration is a cytosolic concentration. In a eukaryote it is an average over compartments differing by an order of magnitude.
  • That replication fixes leakage. Replication fixes variance; leakage is a bias, and averaging a hundred biased samples gives a precise wrong number.
  • That the mass spectrometer limits a thermodynamic analysis. RT·ln of a concentration error is small next to the uncertainty in ΔrG′°. It limits kinetics, where concentrations enter the rate law directly.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Your protocol quenches in five seconds. Which measurements does it support, and which does it destroy?

A. Compute τ = pool/flux. ATP at 3 µmol gDW⁻¹ over 13.9 µmol gDW⁻¹ s⁻¹ turns over in 0.2 s, so five seconds is twenty-five turnover times and the number belongs to the quench, not the cell; G6P at τ ≈ 0.7 s goes the same way. Glutamate at τ ≈ 290 s is barely perturbed and is reported honestly. The protocol must be fast relative to the shortest τ you intend to interpret, so state which subset of the metabolome your method is valid for and do not report the rest.

Q. A paper reports intracellular ATP with ±8% error bars and no mention of leakage. What do you conclude?

A. That the interval is a precision claim about replicates, not an accuracy claim about the cell. Nucleotide leakage in a methanol quench is a bias in a known direction — downward — so the true value lies above the interval rather than within it, and nothing in the stated error reflects that. The second concern is whether the quench outran a 0.2 s turnover time at all. Neither objection makes the paper wrong; both say that any conclusion resting on the absolute value rather than on a ratio between their own conditions is unsupported.

Q. When is it worth improving a measurement from 20% to 5%, and when is it not?

A. Worth it when the number enters a rate law, because an unsaturated step's rate goes as S/Kₘ and the error passes undamped into every flux and control coefficient downstream. Not worth it for a feasibility verdict, where the concentration enters only as RT·ln Q: the improvement buys about 0.3 kJ mol⁻¹ against a 3–4 kJ mol⁻¹ uncertainty in ΔrG′° that dominates regardless. Differentiate the conclusion with respect to the measurement and compare against the other error terms before spending a month on the instrument.

Week 28 — 13C metabolic flux analysis I: principles and atom mapping

Flux balance analysis tells you what a network could do; labelling tells you what it did. This week is the forward half — how carbon moves through central metabolism and how that produces a pattern a mass spectrometer sees. Build the simulator and verify it by hand, because week 29 is this model run backwards and a wrong atom map inverts to a precise, confident, wrong flux map.

Core ideas

1. What extracellular rates cannot see, stated formally

Measure every uptake and excretion rate perfectly and you have fixed S_ext·v, not v. Anything in the null space of the external stoichiometry is invisible: it can take any value with every measurable rate unchanged. Three families live there. Cycles returning carbon to their origin, of which the pentose phosphate pathway is the standard case — oxidative-branch carbon comes back as fructose-6-phosphate and triose phosphate, so the only distinct external product is CO₂, which has other sources. Bidirectional exchange, where the net flux is observable and the two magnitudes are not. And parallel routes of identical overall stoichiometry, such as Embden-Meyerhof against Entner-Doudoroff. Labelling resolves all three, because these routes rearrange skeletons differently even when they balance identically.

2. Atom mapping, and the transitions worth memorising

An atom transition network states which substrate carbon becomes which product carbon, for every reaction. Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate so C1–C3 become DHAP and C4–C6 become GAP, and triose phosphate isomerase maps DHAP C1 onto GAP C3 — so glucose C1 and C6 arrive at the same carbon and both become the methyl of pyruvate. 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase releases glucose C1 specifically as CO₂, which is the whole basis of the PPP measurement. Transketolase moves two-carbon units and transaldolase three. And fumarate and succinate are symmetric, so label entering one end is scrambled to both — the classic trap, and why a map read off a pathway chart is usually wrong somewhere in the TCA cycle.

3. Isotopomers, cumomers and EMUs: three representations of one thing

A metabolite of n carbons has 2ⁿ isotopomers, so 64 for glucose, and a full isotopomer balance over central metabolism is thousands of nonlinear equations. Cumomers are a change of variables — sums over isotopomers sharing a labelled subset — which makes the system block-triangular and solvable by cascade rather than iteration. Elementary metabolite units go further: starting from what the instrument measures and working backwards, only certain carbon subsets are ever needed, typically reducing the problem by an order of magnitude without approximation. A teaching network can afford the full balance and should use it; the reduction is a computational convenience, not a concept, and at genome scale it is what makes the method run.

4. What the instrument reports is a mass distribution vector

For a fragment of n carbons you get fractional abundances m+0 through m+n, summing to one. That is not positional information — the MDV has already summed over which carbons carry label. Position comes from measuring several overlapping fragments of the same metabolite, since GC-MS fragmentation of a derivatised amino acid gives known partial skeletons and the differences between their MDVs localise the label. So a well-chosen second fragment is worth more than a more sensitive instrument on the first. Proteinogenic amino acids are the usual target: abundant, stable, and each reporting a precursor — alanine for pyruvate, aspartate for oxaloacetate, glutamate for 2-oxoglutarate.

5. Natural abundance correction is larger than you expect

About 1.1% of carbon is ¹³C, so an unlabelled twelve-carbon fragment shows roughly 12% at m+1 before any tracer. In practice the derivative is tert-butyldimethylsilyl (TBDMS), and the two fragments ¹³C-MFA papers quote are M−57, from loss of the tert-butyl group, which retains the metabolite's full carbon skeleton, and M−159; which carbons each fragment keeps has to be taken from the derivatisation chemistry for that metabolite rather than assumed, and that mapping is not verified here. Derivatisation compounds it: a trimethylsilyl group adds three carbons and a silicon, and silicon is 4.7% ²⁹Si and 3.1% ³⁰Si, so a derivatised fragment can carry a natural m+1 above twenty per cent. The correction is linear — build the matrix from the elemental composition of the actual fragment including the derivative and apply its inverse — so you must know exactly which atoms the fragment contains. Run an unlabelled culture through the identical workup: if the correction is right, its corrected MDV is m+0 = 1 within noise.

6. Tracer choice, and why mixtures are standard

1-¹³C glucose is the classic probe of the pentose phosphate split, because the oxidative branch releases exactly that carbon as CO₂ while glycolysis retains it. U-¹³C glucose labels everything, so the signal is in which fragments stay intact and which are cleaved and recombined — the better probe of anaplerosis and the pyruvate node. 1,2-¹³C₂ glucose separates Entner-Doudoroff cleanly. Because the information is complementary, mixtures are the usual general-purpose choice and the ratio is itself a design variable for week 29 — one published recipe is 80% 1-¹³C with 20% U-¹³C, an example rather than a default, since the best mixture depends on the target flux, the network, the organism, the fragments you can measure and the cost. Select in silico against the flux you care about, not by copying the last paper in your organism.

Worked anchor

Resolving the pentose phosphate split with 1-¹³C glucose, by hand.

Let α be the fraction of glucose-6-phosphate entering the oxidative branch.

Through glycolysis: aldolase puts glucose C1–C3 into DHAP and C4–C6 into GAP, and triose phosphate isomerase maps DHAP C1 onto GAP C3, so the label becomes the methyl carbon of one pyruvate. One glucose gives two pyruvates, exactly one of which is m+1, so this route yields a pyruvate m+1 fraction of 0.5.

Through the oxidative PPP: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase releases C1 as CO₂, so the ribulose-5-phosphate is unlabelled and the carbon returning through transketolase and transaldolase carries no label either. This route contributes 0.

First order, and wrong by enough to matter: pyruvate m+1 ≈ 0.5(1 − α) assumes both routes deliver the same number of trioses, and they do not. Three G6P through the oxidative branch give 3 CO₂ + 2 F6P + 1 GAP — five trioses' worth of carbon, not six — so a glucose entering the PPP delivers 5/3 pyruvate against glycolysis's 2. Labelled pyruvate per glucose is (1 − α); total pyruvate is 2(1 − α) + (5/3)α = 2 − α/3. The relation to use is therefore m+1 = (1 − α)/(2 − α/3). Measure alanine, correct for natural abundance, and a corrected m+1 of 0.35 gives α = 0.34, where the first-order form returns 0.30 — a 13% error in the answer, which is larger than the measurement error this week's own error budget allows. Keep the first-order form only to show what neglecting the triose stoichiometry costs. Published splits for glucose-limited aerobic E. coli are of this order, but cite a primary source with its growth conditions rather than this calculation if the number is going anywhere.

Three things separate this from a publishable number. Recycling: returned carbon can go round again, so the relation is not exactly linear and the forward model must solve the cycle self-consistently. Pool mixing: malic enzyme and PEP carboxykinase return TCA carbon to pyruvate with a different pattern, from an oxaloacetate that has passed through symmetric fumarate. And the natural abundance correction is doing real work — an uncorrected 0.35 might be 0.30 corrected, which in the corrected relation gives α = 0.44 rather than 0.34.

So verify the simulator against this with recycling off, then switch it on and watch the discrepancy appear. If it appears in the wrong direction, the atom map is wrong and you have found it cheaply.

The negative half is the part to write down: no rate measurement can do this, because the branch's only distinct external product is CO₂, which pyruvate dehydrogenase and the TCA cycle also produce. It is the clearest demonstration of why labelling exists, and Brief 9's opening requirement.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • metabolic and isotopic steady state
  • no recycling of PPP carbon in the first-order version
  • no anaplerotic return of label to pyruvate
  • the atom map is exact and the MDVs are corrected for natural abundance
  • equal analytical response across isotopologues
  • alanine reports the pyruvate pool faithfully

Berg Ch 16, rereadSkipYou know glycolysis. What you need is the atom transitions, which Berg does not give; derive them from the chemistry.

Common misconceptions

  • That labelling measures flux. It measures labelling patterns; flux comes from fitting a model to them, so fluxes are only as good as the atom map — which is what week 29's chi-squared test is for.
  • That an atom map can be read off a pathway chart. Symmetric intermediates break it, and a map that misses them fits badly for reasons that look like noise.
  • That natural abundance correction is cosmetic. A silylated fragment can show over twenty per cent at m+1 with no tracer present, larger than most signals being interpreted.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Prove that extracellular rates cannot determine the oxidative PPP flux, then explain how 1-¹³C glucose resolves it.

A. Carbon entering the oxidative branch returns to glycolysis as fructose-6-phosphate and triose phosphate, so the branch has no distinct external stoichiometry except CO₂, which pyruvate dehydrogenase, the TCA cycle and biosynthetic decarboxylations also produce. The cycle flux therefore lies in the null space of the external stoichiometry and can take any value with every measurable rate unchanged, so it is unidentifiable from rates however precisely measured. 1-¹³C glucose resolves it because 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase releases precisely glucose C1 as CO₂ while glycolysis retains it and delivers it to the methyl carbon of pyruvate: to first order, pyruvate m+1 ≈ 0.5(1 − α).

Q. Why is a well-chosen second fragment worth more than better precision on the first?

A. Because the MDV has already summed over position. One fragment says how many carbons are labelled, not which, so the positional information that distinguishes flux splits comes from differences between overlapping fragments. A fragment covering a different subset of the skeleton adds independent constraints; more precision on an existing fragment only tightens constraints you already have, and in a structurally limited fit it tightens them around the wrong answer. The same logic makes a parallel labelling experiment with a second tracer the strongest available validation.

Q. You inherit a colleague's atom transition network. What do you check first, and how?

A. The symmetric molecules, because that is where maps are usually wrong: fumarate and succinate must scramble label between their halves and an inherited map often treats them as oriented. Then aldolase and triose phosphate isomerase, since mapping glucose C1 and C6 onto the same triose carbon carries most of the information in the data. Then the decarboxylations: glucose C1 at 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, pyruvate C1 at pyruvate dehydrogenase. The test is mechanical — simulate a known flux vector with a single-position tracer and check two metabolites by hand. Map errors give qualitatively impossible patterns rather than slightly wrong ones, so they are cheap to find.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Week 29 — 13C metabolic flux analysis II: estimation, statistics and design

The inverse problem. Fitting fluxes to labelling data is nonlinear estimation with an unpleasant covariance structure, and the statistics is where most published MFA is weakest. Three things separate a flux claim from a flux opinion: a multi-start optimisation, an interval from a method that does not assume local linearity, and a goodness-of-fit test you are prepared to let fail.

Core ideas

1. The objective, and why it is minimised a hundred times

Weighted least squares: minimise Σᵢ ((xᵢ,meas − xᵢ,sim(v))/σᵢ)² over the free fluxes, with x_sim from week 28's forward model. The weights are not cosmetic — unweighted, a precise fragment and a noisy one speak equally, and the σᵢ are what turn the residual sum into a statistic with a known distribution. The surface is nonlinear with local minima, so one run is not a result. Restart from random points until the best objective has been recovered repeatedly — how many that takes depends on the dimension, the bounds, the parameterisation and the optimiser, so report the strategy and the spread of objective values you obtained rather than a round number. Restarts landing on several distinct minima of similar objective value signal a genuine identifiability problem rather than a numerical one.

2. Chi-squared is the model's check on itself

At the optimum, and only if the weighted residual model is correctly specified, the objective is compared against a chi-squared distribution. Counting the degrees of freedom is where this goes wrong: it is the number of independent data constraints minus the rank of the fitted model, and MDV elements are not independent — each vector sums to one, so one element per fragment is fixed by the others, and natural abundance correction couples them further. Fitted pool sizes, scaling and other nuisance parameters, and active constraints reduce it too. With the effective count in hand, the expectation is the degrees of freedom and the standard deviation √(2·dof), which locates the acceptance region closely enough to judge a fit by eye; take the quantile from the distribution itself when the decision is marginal or formal. This is the most valuable property of the method and the one most often skipped, because it lets the data tell you the model is wrong. Note the limit: a passing test says model and data are consistent, not that the model is correct — compensating errors fit perfectly — which is why a second tracer fitted jointly is the real validation.

3. Diagnosing a failure, in order of probability

Structural error first: a missing reaction, a wrong atom mapping, an omitted by-product, a wrong biomass drain. Second, underestimated measurement errors, which inflate the statistic with nothing wrong with the model. Third, an unmodelled bidirectional exchange, which shows as systematic residuals on the metabolites whose label it scrambles. Fourth, a violated steady state. Discriminate by residual pattern rather than preference: structural errors cluster on particular fragments and mass positions, an inadequate error model inflates residuals roughly uniformly. Rescaling the errors until the test passes is the one response guaranteed to teach you nothing.

4. Confidence intervals: three methods, one of them right

Linearised covariance inverts the weighted Jacobian, (JᵀΣ⁻¹J)⁻¹, and reads intervals off the diagonal: nearly free, the usual software default, and valid only where the objective is quadratic near the optimum — true for well-determined net fluxes, false for exchange fluxes and anything near a bound, where it returns symmetric intervals that are too narrow. Parameter continuation walks one flux away from the optimum while re-optimising all the others, until the objective rise crosses a threshold: asymmetric, sometimes unbounded, one optimisation per point. It is profile likelihood proper only when the objective carries that likelihood interpretation and the nuisance parameters are re-optimised consistently, and the threshold depends on the confidence level, on how many parameters are profiled at once, and on the residual model being right. Bootstrap agrees with continuation when the problem is well-posed and is honest about the error model you assumed. Exchange fluxes are the usual case where the two part company, though not inevitably: whether one is bounded at all depends on the network topology, the tracer and the fragments measured.

5. What actually tightens an interval

Four interventions in descending value. Add extracellular rates: labelling alone fixes the map only up to its scale, so folding in well-measured uptake and secretion often halves intervals across the network. Run a parallel labelling experiment with a second tracer and fit jointly, which adds information of a different kind and tests the structure at the same time. Measure more fragments, particularly covering different subsets of a skeleton. Improving precision on fragments you already have comes last — in a structurally limited fit it tightens the interval around a biased answer, which is worse than a wide interval around the right one.

6. Design the experiment in silico, then run it

Which tracer or mixture minimises the variance of the flux you care about? Simulate data at a plausible flux vector, compute the Jacobian, invert for the covariance, read off the target variance, repeat per candidate. Optimise a scalar — one flux's variance for a specific question, the determinant or trace for a general-purpose map. The circularity is real and manageable: design against a range of plausible flux vectors and prefer a tracer whose advantage holds across it. Often two tracers differ by a few per cent and the choice is a cost decision, which costs a day to establish rather than an experiment.

7. Instationary MFA, and what it costs

Stationary MFA needs metabolic and isotopic steady state. The isotopic half can take hours with large pools or slow flux, and for an autotroph fed labelled CO₂ it may never arrive inside the metabolic steady state's lifetime. INST-MFA relaxes it: label at metabolic steady state and fit the transient. The forward model becomes ODEs over isotopomer fractions rather than an algebraic balance, one to two orders of magnitude more expensive, and pool sizes become parameters, since the transient's timescale is pool/flux — so week 27's metabolomics is an input, not an extra. The transient also constrains some fluxes the steady-state pattern cannot.

Worked anchor

A failed chi-squared, diagnosed arithmetically.

The fit returns χ² = 84 on 41 degrees of freedom. Expectation 41, standard deviation √82 = 9.06, so the observed value is (84 − 41)/9.06 = 4.7 standard deviations high: a decisive rejection. The fluxes may still be approximately right, but the intervals computed from this fit are meaningless, because they assume the residuals are what the error model says.

Test the cheapest explanation first. If every σᵢ were underestimated by a common factor k the statistic scales as 1/k², so k = √(84/41) = 1.43 would bring it to expectation. Is a 43% across-the-board underestimate plausible? From three technical replicates, entirely — three replicates estimate a standard deviation to only about 50% (the relative uncertainty on an SD is 1/√(2(n−1)); 40% would need four replicates), and replicate spread omits derivatisation and correction error anyway. From a validated error model with biological replicates, no.

Then look at residuals rather than the total. Standardise every MDV element and sort. Spread evenly across fragments and mass positions, the error model is the suspect; concentrated — the m+1 and m+2 of aspartate at five and six standard deviations while everything else sits near one — the cause is structural and touches oxaloacetate: a missing anaplerotic reaction, an unmodelled exchange on malate dehydrogenase, or a fumarate symmetry you failed to encode.

Test that properly. Add the candidate reaction and refit; one free flux costs one degree of freedom, so the gain must be much larger. Suppose χ² drops from 84 to 39 on 40 degrees of freedom: a drop of 45 for one parameter is overwhelming, since on one degree of freedom 3.84 is already the 5% threshold, so the reaction belongs. Then look at what it did to the fluxes. If the anaplerotic flux moved by a factor of two, the original map was wrong in exactly the way a passing eye never catches, because it looked plausible — which is the lesson for the critique note, and why Brief 9 asks you to omit a reaction deliberately and confirm the statistic catches it.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the weighted residual model is correctly specified
  • measurement errors independent and normally distributed
  • degrees of freedom counted as measurements minus fitted fluxes, which ignores MDV closure
  • a single structural fault rather than several compensating ones

Wolfgang Wiechert and Katharina Nöh of Forschungszentrum Jülich wrote this chapter — attribution checked against its title page, printed p73 — so it is the primary source and not a secondary one. Read it when your exchange intervals come back unbounded, which they will.

Common misconceptions

  • That a good fit validates the flux map. A passing chi-squared says model and data are consistent; compensating errors fit perfectly. Validation comes from a second tracer.
  • That the software's confidence intervals are confidence intervals. The default is linearised covariance, symmetric and too narrow wherever the objective is not locally quadratic — which includes every exchange flux.
  • That a failed chi-squared means noisy data. It means model and data disagree, and the most probable cause is a structural error in the model.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Your fit gives χ² = 96 on 44 degrees of freedom. Diagnose it, in order.

A. Rejected: on the stated degrees of freedom, expectation 44 and standard deviation √88 = 9.4, so 96 sits 5.5 standard deviations high. In order of probability: a structural error — missing reaction, wrong atom mapping, omitted by-product; underestimated measurement errors, which would need a common factor of √(96/44) = 1.48 to explain the excess, plausible from a handful of technical replicates and not otherwise; an unmodelled bidirectional exchange; and a violated steady state. Discriminate by sorting the standardised residuals, since structural errors cluster on particular fragments while an inadequate error model inflates them uniformly. Then test the leading hypothesis by adding the reaction and refitting, judged against the degree of freedom it costs.

Q. Why do exchange fluxes come back with unbounded intervals, and what should you report?

A. Because beyond a certain magnitude, raising a bidirectional exchange stops changing the labelling pattern: once the step equilibrates label across itself, further increases are invisible, the likelihood surface flattens and the upper bound runs to infinity. Linearised covariance cannot express that and returns a finite symmetric interval, which is simply wrong; continuation finds the flat direction and reports the bound honestly. Report the net flux with its interval, the exchange on the transformed scale that maps the infinite range onto a finite one, and the statement that it is bounded below but not above — a real conclusion about reversibility, not a defect.

Q. You have budget for one more experiment: a second tracer, more fragments, or better precision. Choose and justify.

A. The second tracer, almost always. It adds information of a different kind rather than more of the same, and a structural error that fits one tracer usually fails against two fitted jointly, so it validates and tightens at once. More fragments comes second, and is better when the target flux is constrained by one skeleton and the structure is not in doubt. Better precision comes last: in a structurally limited fit it tightens the interval around a biased estimate, and in a sound fit the returns are modest because the limit is the information content of the pattern, not the noise on it.

Week 30 — Kinetic models of metabolism

Where dynamics returns. A kinetic model answers questions no stoichiometric method can touch — concentrations, behaviour away from steady state, which enzyme controls the flux — at the price of parameters nobody can measure in vivo. The craft is in handling that price: thermodynamic consistency imposed as a constraint, parameters carried as ranges, and an ensemble reported instead of one fit with a false precision.

Core ideas

1. What a kinetic model buys, and when it is the wrong tool

Four things FBA cannot give: metabolite concentrations, time-dependent behaviour, the response to a change in enzyme level, and control coefficients. The cost is a rate law and several parameters per reaction, and the parameters are the problem — in vitro kcat and Kₘ come from dilute buffer at saturating substrate, while the cell is crowded, at a different pH, and working near Kₘ by design. The decision rule is scope: model the sub-pathway you have a specific dynamic question about, ten to twenty reactions anchored by measured concentrations, and use FBA for anything genome-scale. Whole-cell kinetic modelling is usually the wrong first move.

2. The reversible rate law and the Haldane relation

For one substrate and one product, v = (V_f·S/K_S − V_r·P/K_P)/(1 + S/K_S + P/K_P). Four parameters, but not four free ones: at equilibrium v = 0, giving K_eq = (V_f·K_P)/(V_r·K_S). That is the Haldane relation, and since K_eq is fixed by ΔrG′° only three of the four may be fitted. Impose it as a constraint rather than checking afterwards. A fit with all four free will return a parameter set implying an equilibrium constant that contradicts the thermodynamics, and such a model reproduces every data point while being unphysical — the worst failure mode available, because it looks like success.

3. Approximative rate laws, and when each is honest

Where the mechanism is unknown, a generic form is more honest than a mechanistic one invented to look rigorous. Convenience kinetics generalises the reversible Michaelis-Menten form to any stoichiometry, is thermodynamically consistent by construction, and needs one Kₘ per reactant plus a turnover number. Lin-log writes the rate as linear in log concentrations about a reference state, which nearly linearises the steady-state problem: excellent for control analysis near a known operating point, poor far from it. Power laws give the S-system machinery with the same local caveat. The criterion is not sophistication — mechanistic where the mechanism is established and the parameters measured, generic and thermodynamically consistent everywhere else.

4. Where the parameters come from, and what to do with the spread

BRENDA for kcat and Kₘ, read as a distribution rather than a value: entries for one enzyme commonly span an order of magnitude, reflecting real differences in assay conditions, isoforms and preparation purity rather than sloppiness. Not the mean, which corresponds to no experiment; not the most recent, since recency is not accuracy. Carry the range through and test whether the conclusion survives it — if it does not, the study's output is that the parameter must be measured, which is a legitimate result. Thermodynamics removes one parameter per reaction through the Haldane relation; the rest are fitted to the measured steady state, usually leaving the problem heavily underdetermined. Be clear about what the fitted values then are. The cytoplasm holds 300–400 g L⁻¹ of macromolecules occupying over 30% of cell volume, so excluded-volume effects raise thermodynamic activities, slow diffusion and shift apparent binding affinities: an in vivo Kₘ is an effective parameter for a crowded, non-specifically binding medium, not the buffer value. Expect to fit parameters that differ from BRENDA's by more than the BRENDA spread, and say so rather than calling the discrepancy a fitting artefact.

5. Stiffness, and verifying the steady state independently

Pools turn over in seconds while the culture changes over hours, so the eigenvalues span orders of magnitude and the ODEs are stiff. An explicit solver will crawl or go unstable; use BDF, Radau or LSODA and set tolerances deliberately rather than taking defaults. Then verify without the integrator: solve S·v(c) = 0 with a root finder from the integrator's endpoint and confirm the two agree. This catches the two commonest silent failures — a solver stopped on a slowly drifting trajectory and called it steady, and a conservation relation that makes the Jacobian singular and the steady state non-unique.

6. Sloppiness, and ensembles instead of best fits

The Hessian of the objective at the fit has an eigenvalue spectrum spanning six or more decades: a few stiff directions in which the output is highly sensitive, many sloppy ones in which parameters move by large factors with no measurable effect. So individual parameters are unidentifiable even when the model predicts well and a fitted Kₘ must not be read mechanistically; predictions along stiff directions can be trusted further than the parameters behind them; and design should target the stiff combinations, since constraining a sloppy direction buys nothing. The practical response is to stop reporting one parameter set — sample a hundred consistent with the data and the thermodynamics, and propagate the ensemble to a prediction interval.

Worked anchor

Imposing the Haldane relation, and what happens when you do not.

Take a reaction with ΔrG′° = −7.5 kJ mol⁻¹ at 37 °C, where RT = 2.577 kJ mol⁻¹. Then K_eq = exp(7.5/2.577) = exp(2.910) = 18.4.

With V_f = 10 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹, K_S = 0.2 mM and K_P = 0.5 mM from BRENDA, the reverse maximal rate is not free:

V_r = V_f·K_P/(K_S·K_eq) = 10 × 0.5/(0.2 × 18.4) = 5/3.68 = 1.36 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹.

Now suppose all four had been left free and the fit returned V_r = 6. Read the implied equilibrium constant back out:

K_eq = V_f·K_P/(V_r·K_S) = (10 × 0.5)/(6 × 0.2) = 4.17,

so the implied ΔrG′° = −2.577 × ln(4.17) = −3.68 kJ mol⁻¹. The fit has silently asserted a standard free energy 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹ from the measured one.

Be careful how much that proves. A group-contribution estimate carries 3–4 kJ mol⁻¹ of uncertainty, as week 27 established, so against an estimated value this discrepancy sits inside the noise. The argument for the constraint is structural rather than numerical: unconstrained, nothing stops the fit drifting much further, and the drift is invisible because the model still reproduces the data. Where ΔrG′° is measured rather than estimated — and for much of central metabolism it is — a discrepancy this size is a genuine contradiction and the fit must be rejected.

What the constraint does is worth seeing. Before: four free parameters per reaction, twenty for a five-step pathway, against perhaps six measured concentrations and one flux — hopelessly underdetermined. After: fifteen, still underdetermined, but every member of the solution set is at least thermodynamically possible. The Haldane relation does not identify your parameters; it removes a family of unphysical fits that would have passed every check you run.

So make the underdetermination visible. Refit from a hundred random starts, keep every set that reproduces the data, confirm the sensitivity spectrum spans decades, then propagate the ensemble through the prediction you care about — the gain from doubling the first enzyme — and set the interval beside the best fit's point estimate. That gap is this week's result and Brief 10's closing requirement.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • one substrate and one product, so the four-parameter form applies
  • RT = 2.577 kJ mol⁻¹ at 37 °C
  • BRENDA values taken to apply in vivo, which §5.3 says they do not
  • ΔrG′° read at a stated pH, pMg and ionic strength

Reading map

SourceTreatmentWhy

Lee Ch 7 §7.2.2 and §7.3Read closelyWhere K_eq comes from: estimation of standard formation energies, then the compartment-specific ionic strength and pH transform. The Haldane constraint is only as good as this number.
BRENDARead closelyAssemble parameters here and record the assay conditions with every value. The range across entries is the information; the mean is not.

Berg Ch 8 §8.4, revisitedSkimThe reversible rate law from the enzymology side. You derived this in week 5; reread only if the Haldane relation is not obvious.

Common misconceptions

  • That more data fixes unidentifiability. Sloppiness is structural: only measurements constraining the stiff combinations help, which is why the spectrum should be computed before the next experiment is designed.
  • That a fitted Kₘ can be interpreted mechanistically. Not unless it lies along a stiff direction, and most do not. Fitted parameters are coordinates in a large flat region, not estimates of physical quantities.
  • That thermodynamic consistency is a finishing check. Imposed afterwards it rejects a fit you have published a figure from; imposed as a constraint it removes the unphysical region before the optimiser enters it.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Five BRENDA entries give kcat spanning an order of magnitude. What do you do, and why not the obvious alternatives?

A. Carry the range through and test whether the conclusion survives it. Not the mean, because the spread is not noise about a true value — it reflects different assay conditions, isoforms and preparations, so the mean corresponds to no experiment. Not the most recent, because recency is not accuracy. Not the highest on the argument that the others contained inactive enzyme, which is a story rather than evidence. If the conclusion holds across the range you have a robust result; if it flips, the study's output is that the parameter must be measured for your organism and condition, which is the finding that justifies the next experiment.

Q. Your integrator reports a steady state. How do you verify it, and what two failures are you looking for?

A. Verify without the integrator: take its endpoint as a starting guess, solve S·v(c) = 0 with a root finder, and confirm the concentration vectors agree with a residual genuinely near zero rather than merely small relative to the fluxes. The first failure this catches is a solver stopped on a slowly drifting trajectory, since in a stiff system a slow mode looks flat over the integration window while still moving, making the steady state depend on how long you ran. The second is a singular Jacobian from a conservation relation: if total adenylate is conserved the steady state is fixed by the initial condition rather than unique, and the root finder says so by failing to converge.

Q. Why is a single best-fit parameter set misleading, and what should be reported instead?

A. Because these models are sloppy: output is highly sensitive to a few parameter combinations and nearly insensitive to many others, so individual parameters are unidentifiable from the available data even when the model predicts well. A single fit implies a precision that does not exist and invites mechanistic interpretation of numbers arbitrary within their unidentified directions. Report an ensemble consistent with the data and the thermodynamic constraints, propagated to a prediction interval for whatever the model is used to decide, with the sensitivity spectrum showing which combinations are determined — then target the next experiment at the stiff combinations rather than the least known parameter.

Week 31 — Metabolic control analysis and proteome-constrained models

The week that reshapes how you read every overexpression paper. Control over a flux is shared, sums to one, and redistributes the moment you act on it, so the question is never which enzyme is rate-limiting but where control will move next. The proteome constraint then supplies the budget control is spent from, and the two analyses meet. Paper 4 is sat and marked at the end of the week.

Core ideas

1. The three coefficients, with their definitions and their units

A flux control coefficient is C^J_i = (∂J/∂e_i)(e_i/J): the fractional change in steady-state flux per fractional change in enzyme i's activity, with the network re-equilibrating. A concentration control coefficient is the same with a concentration in place of the flux. An elasticity ε^i_S = (∂v_i/∂S)(S/v_i) is different in kind — a local property of one enzyme's isolated rate, everything else fixed. All three are dimensionless, which is why they compare across enzymes of different magnitudes. The distinction that matters is systemic against local: control coefficients belong to the network and are measurable only in situ, elasticities belong to one enzyme and are measurable in vitro.

2. The summation theorem, and the thing it does not say

Flux control coefficients sum to one across a pathway; concentration control coefficients sum to zero. The flux theorem follows from the fact that raising every enzyme by the same small factor raises the flux by that factor with all concentrations unchanged. So control is a shared, conserved quantity and one enzyme can have more only if others have less. What it does not say is that no enzyme has substantial control — 0.7 is entirely consistent with it. What it makes untenable is the strong rate-limiting-step picture, one enzyme at unity and the rest at zero, together with its corollary that acting on the controlling enzyme redistributes control away from it.

3. The connectivity theorem, and why a step near equilibrium has little control

For any metabolite S, Σ_i C^J_i·ε^i_S = 0 over the enzymes that see S. This links the systemic quantities to the local ones and is how control coefficients follow from network structure plus elasticities. The consequence worth holding: a step far from saturation and near equilibrium has a large elasticity, so the theorem forces its control coefficient small — the network absorbs a change in its activity through a small concentration adjustment. A saturated step far from equilibrium has a small elasticity and tends to carry control. That is the honest version of the intuition that an irreversible saturated step is rate-limiting, and it shows when the intuition fails.

4. Measuring control coefficients, and the caveat on every method

Four routes: titration with an inducible promoter series, taking the slope at the wild-type point, which assumes the promoter changes nothing else; genetic modulation by knockdown or heterozygote, assuming a small perturbation; inhibitor titration, reading the coefficient from the initial slope and assuming specificity; and double modulation, inferring elasticities from paired perturbations. All four estimate a derivative at a point, so the number holds for small perturbations only — an enzyme with a coefficient near zero may still be catastrophic to delete, because a deletion is not a small perturbation.

5. Why overexpression plateaus, with the arithmetic

A control coefficient is a logarithmic derivative, ∂lnJ/∂ln e, so read it carefully across a large perturbation. For an enzyme at C^J = 0.6 the fractional-change reading gives a 60% gain on doubling; holding the coefficient constant across the interval and integrating instead gives J₂/J₁ = 2^0.6 ≈ 1.52, about 52%. Both are sensitivity heuristics rather than predictions, and the second is the better one, since the first extrapolates a tangent to a change that is not small. Neither survives what happens next: intermediate concentrations shift, so the amplified enzyme moves towards saturation; downstream steps carry more flux and approach their capacities; and the summation theorem holds the total at one, so as its coefficient falls the others rise. The second doubling of the same gene therefore achieves much less than the first, and the first achieves well under its prediction. The correct response is coordinated amplification of the steps control has migrated to, which is why multi-gene balancing has outperformed single-gene work in many well-documented pathway optimisations.

6. The proteome as the budget: enzyme cost and allocation

An enzyme carrying flux v needs protein mass m = v·MW/kcat, so every flux has a price and total protein is finite. The budget is not an accounting convention: it is the same crowding that made week 30's parameters effective rather than measured, since a cytoplasm already at 300–400 g L⁻¹ has a finite solvent capacity for further enzyme, which is the constraint crowding-based FBA imposes directly. Coarse-grained models impose one constraint, Σ v_i·MW_i/kcat_i ≤ E, and reproduce what stoichiometric models cannot: overflow metabolism as a switch to a lower-yield but protein-cheaper route at high growth rate, a maximum growth rate at all, and the penalty of expressing anything useless. Fine-grained ME models represent transcription and translation explicitly, so the cost of the cost is accounted and the expression of the machinery itself is predicted. What they compute that an M model cannot is anything where the price of catalysis matters.

7. Where control analysis and proteome allocation meet

Maximise flux J over an allocation subject to Σe_i = E. At the optimum every enzyme's marginal flux per unit protein is equal, or protein would move to the better one, so ∂J/∂e_i = λ for all i. Substituting, C^J_i = λe_i/J, and summing with the summation theorem gives λ = J/E, hence C^J_i = e_i/E: at an optimal allocation each enzyme's control equals its share of the protein budget. That is an idealised optimal-allocation result rather than an identity that holds in a real cell. It needs a fixed total budget, activity proportional to enzyme amount, a smooth interior optimum with no expression bound active, no enzyme shared with another pathway or carrying a second function, and flux through this pathway as the only objective. Within those conditions it is a diagnostic — compute the coefficients, measure the shares by targeted proteomics, and compare. Control above share means under-allocated; below means over-allocated; and the comparison says whether the pathway is near its own optimum at all.

Worked anchor

A four-enzyme pathway, from control coefficients to a protein reallocation.

Measured flux control coefficients: 0.58, 0.27, 0.12, 0.03. They sum to 1.00, which is the first arithmetic check on the model — if they do not, the numerical derivatives are wrong or the steady state was not converged.

The naive prediction: reading C₁ as a fractional change gives 58% on doubling. Integrating instead, with the coefficient held constant across the interval, gives 2^0.58 = 1.49, about 49%. State which you are quoting and why — the first extrapolates a tangent to a perturbation that is not small, the second assumes a coefficient the summation theorem says will fall. Both are upper bounds rather than estimates.

Why the measurement comes in lower: enzyme 1's product accumulates and its substrate falls, moving it towards saturation and product inhibition; downstream steps approach their capacities; and the summation theorem forces redistribution. Recompute the steady state and the flux lands below both figures — 1.41-fold in the model behind this week's figure — while the coefficients come back as something like 0.31, 0.42, 0.21, 0.06, still summing to one, with control migrated to enzyme 2. The next intervention is therefore enzymes 1 and 2 together, not more of enzyme 1.

Now the budget. Suppose proteomics gives pathway protein shares of 0.25, 0.40, 0.25 and 0.10. At an optimal allocation C^J_i = e_i/E, so compare: enzyme 1 has control 0.58 against share 0.25, enzyme 2 has 0.27 against 0.40, enzyme 3 has 0.12 against 0.25, enzyme 4 has 0.03 against 0.10. Only enzyme 1 carries more control than protein; the other three carry more protein than control, by 0.13, 0.13 and 0.07, which is exactly the 0.33 enzyme 1 lacks — necessarily so, since both sets sum to one. The remedy is specific: take protein from enzymes 2, 3 and 4 and give it to enzyme 1. Control analysis alone says amplify enzyme 1; the budget comparison says you can do it without spending additional protein, which is a different and better experiment because it avoids the burden.

The burden itself, and it is larger than the protein share rather than equal to it. In the growth-law framework of Scott, Gunderson, Mateescu, Zhang and Hwa (Science 2010, 330:1099–1102), protein the cell cannot use takes its mass out of the adjustable part of the proteome — the ribosomal and metabolic sectors together, φmax, estimated for E. coli at roughly 0.45 to 0.55 — and growth falls in proportion, Δµ/µ ≈ φpathway/φmax. At 14% of cell protein that is a 25 to 31% penalty, about 29% at φmax = 0.48, from protein mass alone and before any carbon or cofactor drain. The tuning-library anchor in phase 6 runs the same argument against the metabolic sector alone at 40% and gets 37% for a 15% pathway, which is the more pessimistic divisor; quote whichever you use and say which sector you divided by, because that choice is most of the answer. What the penalty is not is the 10 to 20% a reader expects when they assume it tracks the protein share one for one. Measuring it needs the right control, and this is where most published burden claims fail — an empty vector conflates the cost of synthesising any protein at that level with the pathway's metabolic drain. The correct comparison is an equivalent mass of catalytically inert protein from the same promoter and plasmid, with the mass verified; the residual difference is the metabolic cost and nothing else.

Finally, close the loop with week 30. Every coefficient above came from a model whose parameters are unidentifiable in most directions, so propagate the ensemble: if the hundred sets agree that enzyme 1 carries the most control, the conclusion is a model result; if a third put it on enzyme 2, the honest output is that a titration is needed before any construct is built.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the coefficients come from the week 30 model and inherit its parameter uncertainty
  • a fixed total protein budget for the pathway
  • enzyme activity proportional to enzyme amount
  • a smooth interior optimum with no expression bound active
  • no enzyme shared with another pathway or carrying a second function
  • flux through this pathway as the only objective

Common misconceptions

  • That a flux control coefficient near zero means the enzyme does not matter. It means amplifying it slightly changes little. Deleting it may still be catastrophic, because a deletion is not a small perturbation.
  • That the summation theorem rules out a controlling step. It rules out the strong rate-limiting-step picture and forces redistribution after an intervention. A single coefficient of 0.7 is consistent with it.
  • That an empty-vector control measures burden. It conflates synthesis cost with metabolic drain. The control is an equivalent mass of inert protein from the same promoter and plasmid, with the mass verified.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. A flux control coefficient of 0.1: what does it predict for a two-fold overexpression, and why will the measured gain be smaller still?

A. Read as a fractional change, about 10%; integrated with the coefficient held constant, 2^0.1 = 1.07, about 7%. Both are local sensitivity heuristics rather than predictions, since the coefficient is a derivative at the wild-type point and a doubling is not small. The recomputed gain is smaller still, for three compounding reasons: the amplified enzyme moves towards saturation as its substrate is drawn down; downstream steps approach their capacities; and the summation theorem forces its coefficient down as the others rise. There is also a cost the analysis omits — the extra protein comes from the same budget as everything else, so at a coefficient of 0.1 the burden may exceed the benefit, which is the argument against amplifying a low-control step at all.

Q. Derive the relationship between control coefficients and protein shares at an optimal allocation, and say what you would do with it.

A. Maximise J subject to Σe_i = E. At the optimum the marginal flux per unit protein is equal across enzymes, ∂J/∂e_i = λ, since otherwise protein could be moved to a higher-return enzyme. Substituting into C^J_i = (∂J/∂e_i)(e_i/J) gives C^J_i = λe_i/J, and summing with ΣC^J_i = 1 gives λ = J/E, hence C^J_i = e_i/E, under the conditions listed with the worked anchor. Use it as a diagnostic: measure the shares by targeted proteomics, compute the coefficients from the model, and compare. Control above share means the enzyme should receive protein, below means it can give protein up, and that reallocation costs no additional protein so carries no additional burden — a better first experiment than amplification.

Q. What does a proteome-constrained model predict that a stoichiometric one cannot, with two examples?

A. Anything in which the protein price of catalysis matters rather than only the mass and electron balance. Overflow metabolism first: acetate secretion at high growth rate has no stoichiometric explanation, since respiration has the higher ATP yield and the network can perform it, but under a proteome constraint it follows directly, because fermentative ATP production is cheaper in protein per ATP, so above a threshold growth rate the cheaper route is optimal despite the lower yield. Second, the penalty of a useless protein: a stoichiometric model sees only the amino acids diverted, while a proteome-constrained one sees catalytic capacity displaced from the budget.
