Week 32 — DNA manipulation: PCR, cloning and assembly

The build step, and the only week whose deliverable is a protocol rather than a model. The content is not the enzymology of any one method but the arithmetic that chooses between them — error rate against construct length, overlap design against repeat content, hands-on days against calendar days against money — and the verification cascade, which is best written as what each check excludes and what remains possible afterwards.

Core ideas

1. Polymerase fidelity sets how many colonies you sequence

Errors accumulate per base per duplication, so expected substitutions in a finished amplicon are roughly e·L·d, with d about 20 effective duplications for a 25–30 cycle reaction from nanograms. Reported fidelities run from about 10⁻⁵ errors per base per duplication for Taq to about 10⁻⁷ for proofreading enzymes; take the supplier's figure, not a remembered one. For a 3 kb insert at 10⁻⁷, e·L·d = 0.006 and 99% of clones are clean. At 10⁻⁵ the same build expects 0.6 errors, so only e⁻⁰·⁶ = 55% are clean. The clean fraction falls exponentially with length.

2. Primer design is three constraints, not one

Annealing temperature, specificity and secondary structure. Use nearest-neighbour Tm above about 14 nt; the 2(A+T)+4(G+C) rule drifts badly past 20 nt and ignores salt. Anneal a few degrees below the lower Tm and keep the pair within about 2 °C, since the hotter primer otherwise dominates the first cycles. Specificity lives at the 3′ end: a mismatched 5′ tail still extends, which is how overhangs are added, while a 3′ mismatch mostly does not. Hairpins and dimers compete with template for primer, and a 3′-end dimer is amplified preferentially because it is its own substrate.

3. Restriction-ligation fails on uniqueness, not chemistry

The method needs sites that cut at the junctions and nowhere else, so its limit is the chance of an internal site. For a 6-cutter at roughly uniform base composition the expected count in a 1 kb fragment is 2 × 1000/4096 = 0.49 across both strands, so about 39% of kilobase fragments carry one; across five fragments all are clean with probability 0.61⁵ = 8%. That, plus the surviving scar in the junction — translated if it lands in frame — is why multi-fragment work moved on.

4. Gibson trades uniqueness for overlap, and repeats punish it

Chew-back, anneal, fill and ligate in one isothermal reaction, with 15–40 bp of designed overlap and no site requirement at all. The failure mode moves to sequence similarity: two junctions sharing homology anneal to each other, so a construct using one terminator twice assembles in the wrong order at a rate set by that similarity. The design rules follow — every overlap unique, junctions placed away from repeated parts, and a synonymous or alternative version used at one copy where a part must repeat. Efficiency falls with fragment count, so five-way assemblies are routine and ten-way are a project.

5. Golden Gate cuts outside its own site, which is what makes it scarless and one-pot

Type IIS enzymes such as BsaI recognise an asymmetric site and cut a fixed distance away, so the four-base overhang is yours to choose and the recognition site is destroyed by the cut. Digestion and ligation run together: correct joins are stable, re-ligated parents are re-cut, and the reaction is driven towards the assembly. The cost is domestication — internal sites removed by one synonymous codon each, needed for a kilobase coding sequence about 39% of the time by the arithmetic above. Overhangs are picked from characterised high-fidelity sets rather than invented, because some combinations mis-ligate.

6. Synthesis and yeast assembly are the two ends of the same spectrum

Ordering a domesticated, codon-adjusted, verified fragment removes the cloning and adds lead time: the trade is calendar against hands-on time more than money. Yeast homologous recombination takes many fragments at once, on overlaps of tens to hundreds of base pairs and the host's own machinery, which keeps it the method for very large or repetitive assemblies even when the eventual host is bacterial.

7. Every verification step is blind to something

Colony PCR says a junction of roughly the right size exists; it cannot see point mutations and reports happily on a construct carrying a second, wrong insert. A diagnostic digest gives size and orientation and catches gross rearrangement, nothing below its resolution. Sanger reads the insert for about 700–900 informative bases per primer and says nothing about the backbone — where a Gibson misassembly or an origin mutation hides. Whole-plasmid sequencing catches all of it and is now the cheapest of the four per construct actually verified.

Worked anchor

Cost a five-gene build, in hands-on days, calendar days and money. Five coding sequences averaging 1.2 kb into a 4 kb backbone, 10 kb final.

Restriction-ligation is excluded on arithmetic: all five fragments are clean of a given 6-cutter with probability 0.61⁵ = 0.08, and five compatible unique sites would be needed in the backbone besides.

Golden Gate. Domestication of about two of the five genes at a 39% chance each, one primer pair apiece. Amplify five inserts plus backbone with overhang primers (1 day), one-pot assembly and transformation (1 day), colony PCR on 8 and whole-plasmid sequencing on 2 (2 days). Hands-on 4 days, calendar 7 with sequencing turnaround.

Gibson. No domestication, but six junctions needing unique 25 bp overlaps, and a terminator shared between two genes must be swapped. Same days, same cost. Synthesis: no construction days, 10–15 working days of lead time, 6 kb of coding sequence as the dominant line item.

So the choice is not cost but which constraint your parts violate: repeats without internal sites, Golden Gate; internal sites without repeats, Gibson; both, or a deadline longer than the lead time, buy the fragments. The one fact that moves the answer is the sequence of the parts, which is why domestication and repeat screening come first, not last.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • expected errors per molecule taken as e·L·d, with about 20 effective duplications
  • errors independent and Poisson-distributed along the amplicon
  • restriction site frequency estimated as 2L/4⁶ at uniform base composition
  • internal site presence independent between the five fragments
  • sequencing and consumable prices as quoted at the time of writing

Reading map

SourceTreatmentWhy

Addgene molecular biology reference and Plasmids 101Read closelyThe practical layer the textbooks skip: real maps, feature-by-feature annotation, current assembly protocols. Annotate one map completely.

Alberts Ch 7 — Recombinant DNA TechnologySkimThe 1994 third edition, named sections not numbers: read DNA Cloning and DNA Engineering for principles. It predates Gibson, Golden Gate and whole-plasmid sequencing, so none of its method comparisons are current.

Common misconceptions

  • That a high-fidelity polymerase makes sequencing optional. It changes the expected error count by two orders of magnitude, not to zero, and the count scales with length: 6 kb at 10⁻⁷ still leaves one clone in eight wrong.
  • That Golden Gate is scarless and Gibson is not. Both are scarless if designed so; the Golden Gate overhang is four bases of your choosing, usually placed at a codon boundary.
  • That sequencing the insert verifies the construct. It verifies the insert. Misassemblies and origin mutations sit in the backbone, which is where a cheap read does not go.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. You must assemble five genes once. Which method, and what single fact would change your answer?

A. Golden Gate by default — one pot, directional, scarless, and five fragments is well inside its range. The fact that changes it is the sequence of the parts: internal type IIS sites at about 39% per kilobase mean domestication, and enough of them push you to Gibson, while a repeated promoter or terminator is a Gibson misassembly risk and argues back. With both problems, or a deadline longer than the synthesis lead time, buy the fragments domesticated.

Q. Colony PCR gives the expected band and the insert sequences perfectly. What can still be wrong?

A. Everything outside the two windows you looked through. The backbone is unread, so a junction formed at a second homologous site, or a mutation in the origin or marker, would not show. The colony may carry two plasmids with the PCR reporting the correct one. And a long insert verified from one end is only partly verified, since each read covers 700–900 informative bases. Whole-plasmid sequencing closes all three.

Q. Why does an eleven-fragment Gibson usually fail where a five-fragment one works?

A. Two compounding reasons. Every junction must find its partner, so success scales as roughly pⁿ and ten junctions punish a per-junction efficiency that five tolerate; and the number of overlap pairs that could cross-anneal grows as n², so misassembly competes harder in the same tube. The remedies are hierarchical assembly or yeast recombination.

Week 33 — Vectors, expression systems and chassis preparation

Where the construct lives decides how it behaves, and the decisions are quantitative: an origin fixes copy number and so both dosage and segregational stability, a marker commits you to a recurring cost at production scale, a promoter choice sets an inducer bill per cubic metre. The arithmetic most often skipped is the one this week insists on — how many generations a seed train actually takes, and what fraction still carries the plasmid when it gets there.

Core ideas

1. Copy number is a property of the origin's control circuit

Initiation is negatively regulated by a plasmid-encoded antisense RNA or iteron, so copy number is set by a feedback loop and mutations in it move the set point. The usable grades are high (pUC-type, hundreds), medium (p15A and pBR322-type, tens), low (pSC101-type, a handful) and broad-host-range (pBBR1-type, modest and transferable across proteobacteria). Treat published numbers as ranges that depend on host, growth rate and temperature, and note that output saturates in dose: Shuler’s §14.5 rule of thumb is that 25 to 50 copies roughly doubles protein while 50 to 100 gives less than a doubling, because transcription, translation and folding capacity are shared. Two plasmids sharing a control circuit are incompatible, which is why multi-plasmid designs take origins from different families.

2. Segregational loss is set by the copy-number distribution, not the mean

For random partition the probability of a plasmid-free daughter is P = 2^(1−Z) with Z the number of independent replicative units. Shuler's Example 14.1 makes the point: 40 single copies give P = 1.8 × 10⁻¹²; if half the DNA is dimers and a fifth tetramers the units fall to 12 + 10 + 2 = 24 and P = 1.2 × 10⁻⁷; and a population split half at 10 copies and half at 70 — the same mean of 40 — gives P = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴, some 5 × 10⁸ times worse. Multimerisation and copy-number variance decide stability, and a recombination-deficient host suppresses the first.

3. What kills a culture is the growth-rate difference, amplified over generations

Plasmid-free cells appear at R = P·μ⁺ and then outgrow the producers at Δμ = μ⁻ − μ⁺. Shuler's two-population model (eqs. 14.7–14.22) reduces, when Δμ dominates R, to f⁻ ≈ (f⁻₀ + R/Δμ)e^(Δμ·t): the generation rate sets the seed, the growth differential sets the exponent. So reducing burden usually beats reducing loss probability, because Δμ sits in an exponent and P does not, and delaying induction to the last doublings is the cheapest way to hold Δμ near zero for most of a run.

4. Selection costs money at scale and is often not permitted

Selection is free in a flask and not in a vessel: 50 mg L⁻¹ over 50 m³ is 2.5 kg of kanamycin per batch, and the antibiotic is destroyed by the very enzyme you selected for, so maintenance is not guaranteed either. Food and therapeutic products add a residue objection outright. The alternatives — auxotrophic or essential-gene complementation, antitoxin against a chromosomal toxin, operator-repressor titration — convert a consumable into a one-off construction cost.

5. Integration trades tunability for stability

A chromosomal copy segregates with the chromosome, needs no selection and no replication capacity, and removes both failure modes above — at one or a few copies, and with re-engineering now an edit rather than a plasmid prep. The routes are site-specific recombination into attB, homologous recombination at a chosen locus, transposon delivery, and engineered landing pads at characterised sites. Dosage is recovered by integrating at several loci; the honest comparison is dosage and iteration speed against stability and operating cost.

6. Inducible systems are chosen on leakiness, range and inducer economics

lac/IPTG is strong, leaky and expensive in bulk; the ara system is tighter but catabolite-repressed and, with its native transporter, all-or-none across the population at intermediate inducer, so a reported average hides a bimodal culture; tet systems are tight and tunable but the inducer is an antibiotic; rhamnose is graded and cheap. Autoinduction by phosphate depletion, acetoin or quorum sensing removes the inducer cost and the addition step, at the price of tying the switch to a process variable you also care about.

Worked anchor

Generations in a real seed train, and what the loss model predicts.

1 mL at OD 1 to 50 m³ at OD 50: biomass ratio = 5 × 10⁷ in volume × 50 in density = 2.5 × 10⁹, so n = log₂(2.5 × 10⁹) = 31.2 doublings. Thirty-one, where people guess ten.

Segregation alone, for a burdened, partly multimerised plasmid at P = 10⁻⁴ per division: the producing fraction is (1 − 10⁻⁴)³¹ = 0.9969, so 0.3% plasmid-free. Negligible on its own.

Add the growth difference. μ⁺ = 0.60 h⁻¹, μ⁻ = 0.75 h⁻¹, so Δμ = 0.15 h⁻¹ and the 31 doublings take t = 31 × ln2/0.60 = 35.8 h. Then R = P·μ⁺ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ h⁻¹, R/Δμ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴, and with f⁻₀ = 0 the Case 1 solution gives

f⁻ ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ × e^(0.15 × 35.8) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 215 = 0.086.

Nine per cent of the harvest is plasmid-free — thirty times the segregation-only answer from the same P. Halving the burden to Δμ = 0.075 h⁻¹ gives f⁻ ≈ 0.012, a sevenfold improvement that costs nothing per batch, while cutting P tenfold gives only 0.0086: P enters linearly and Δμ enters the exponent.

The inducer line, for comparison: IPTG at 0.1 mM in 50 m³ is 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ × 5 × 10⁷ L × 238 g mol⁻¹ ≈ 1.2 kg per batch. Induction at the last two doublings is a process decision, not a preference.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • 1 mL at OD 1 to 50 m³ at OD 50, so a biomass ratio of 2.5×10⁹
  • every doubling productive, no lag and no death
  • P = 2^(1−Z) with Z the same in every cell
  • Δμ and R constant over the whole train
  • the Case 1 approximation, Δμ ≫ R, with f⁻₀ = 0
  • IPTG at 0.1 mM throughout the final vessel volume

Common misconceptions

  • That a high-copy origin means high product. Output saturates above roughly 50 copies, and the extra copies cost replication capacity and segregational margin.
  • That antibiotic selection holds a plasmid in a production vessel. The resistance gene destroys or modifies the antibiotic, so pressure falls during the run — and 2.5 kg of kanamycin per 50 m³ batch is a cost, not a control.
  • That mean copy number predicts stability. P = 2^(1−Z) is set by replicative units in individual cells, so multimers and a broad distribution can worsen loss by eight orders of magnitude at constant mean.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. How many generations does a 50 m³ seed train take, and what does your loss model predict for an unselected plasmid?

A. From 1 mL at OD 1 to 50 m³ at OD 50 the biomass ratio is 2.5 × 10⁹, so 31 doublings. At P = 10⁻⁴, segregation alone leaves 0.3% plasmid-free; add a 0.15 h⁻¹ growth advantage over the 35.8 h the train takes and Case 1 gives about 9%. The asymmetry is the lesson: P enters linearly and Δμ enters an exponent, so burden reduction and late induction beat stability engineering.

Q. Your product is a food ingredient and the host is a Lactobacillus. Argue the vector decision.

A. Antibiotic markers are out on residue and resistance grounds, which removes the easiest selection and most off-the-shelf shuttle vectors with it, and transformation efficiency is binding. That leaves a food-grade shuttle vector with auxotrophic or essential-gene complementation, or integration with the marker excised, which also removes the plasmid-free population from a long fermentation. The cost is iteration speed: screen week 34's library on a plasmid and integrate only the winner.

Q. Two plasmids, the same mean copy number, and one culture collapses. What do you measure?

A. The distribution and the multimer fraction, not the mean: single-cell copy number by quantitative PCR on sorted cells, and undigested plasmid on a gel for dimers and higher multimers. Both cut the number of independent replicative units, and P = 2^(1−Z) is exponential in Z. Then measure Δμ directly, by competing plasmid-bearing against plasmid-free cells in one vessel.

Week 34 — Tuning expression: promoters, RBS, copy number and burden

Pathway flux is set less by which genes you add than by how much of each enzyme you make, and week 31 already said the optimum allocates protein so that control coefficients match protein shares. This week turns that into construction: how far each dial really moves expression, how large the resulting library is, whether the screen can cover it, and how to measure the cost of the extra protein without fooling yourself with the wrong control.

Core ideas

1. The dials are unequal, and they multiply

Between a gene and a working catalyst sit copy number (roughly 1–50× across usable origins), promoter strength (about three orders of magnitude across a characterised library), translation initiation set by the ribosome binding site and 5′ UTR structure (two to three orders), codon usage (a few fold), and folding and proteolysis (0–100% of what was translated). The ranges multiply, so promoter and ribosome binding site together already cover more range than any pathway needs: the problem is resolution within it, not reach. Resolution is where prediction runs out — initiation depends on Shine-Dalgarno spacing, 5′ UTR folding energy and the gene’s first codons, which fold into the same structure, so calculators rank variants usefully but predict absolute rate only to about an order of magnitude. They build a spread to measure rather than specify a level.

2. Architecture carries information the parts list does not

In an operon, position matters: transcripts are degraded from the 5′ end and polymerase falls off, so downstream genes are expressed less and gene order is itself a dial. Insulating with a ribozyme or strong terminator removes the coupling, and terminators are graded rather than binary, so read-through into a downstream module is a common reason a part behaves differently in context. Lee §13.5 engineers this layer explicitly: about 12,000 synthetic expression modules combining the UP element, the −35/−10 spacing, the transcription start site and the Shine-Dalgarno-to-start spacer, yielding variants up to 13-fold above an already strong housekeeping promoter.

3. Combinatorial design is arithmetic before it is biology

A library of m modules at v variants has vᵐ members and needs more clones than members: a given variant is absent from N random picks with probability about e^(−N/L), so N = 3L covers 95% of variants in expectation and N = L covers 63%. Four modules at five variants is 625 members and 1,875 clones — past a hand-picked microtitre screen and inside a plate-based colorimetric one. Published practice agrees: Ajikumar's taxadiene work split the pathway into two modules at the IPP node and screened 16 strains, precisely because no high-throughput taxadiene screen existed.

4. The screen, not the library, sets the ceiling

Order-of-magnitude throughputs: hand-picked microtitre cultures 10²–10³ a week; plate colour or halo screens 10⁴–10⁵; flow cytometry on a fluorescent proxy 10⁷–10⁸; droplet microfluidics 10⁶–10⁸; mass-spectrometry screening 10³–10⁴, with the advantage of measuring the actual product. The proxy is the catch: fluorescence is not titre. Match format to library size, then ask what the readout omits and design the confirmation assay for the winners.

5. Burden has four mechanisms and they are distinguishable

Ribosome competition from heterologous translation; precursor and cofactor drain; folding and chaperone load, including inclusion bodies; and the replication cost of the plasmid. They respond to different interventions, so a titre that falls with the strongest promoter diagnoses nothing until they are separated — by growth rate, a ribosome-fraction reporter, labelled-precursor fate and an inert-protein comparison. The strongest promoter often lowers titre because two of these rise faster than flux does, and because the amplified step's control coefficient falls as it saturates.

6. The burden control is inert protein at matched mass, not an empty vector

An empty vector measures replication cost alone and so charges all synthesis cost to the pathway. The comparison is an equivalent mass of a protein that does nothing, from the same promoter, ribosome binding site and plasmid, with the mass verified rather than inferred from the promoter's reputation. Pathway strain minus that control is the metabolic drain; control minus plasmid-free strain is the synthesis and replication cost.

Worked anchor

Size a tuning library to a real screen, then price its burden.

Four modules — precursor supply, the committed step, the downstream branch, cofactor regeneration — at five promoter-RBS variants each: L = 5⁴ = 625, and 95% expected coverage needs N = 3L = 1,875 clones.

The screen: the product is colourless with no sensor yet, so detection is LC-MS on supernatant. At 6 minutes a sample, 20 hours a day, that is 1,000 a working week. Covering 1,875 takes two weeks with no room for repeats; a one-week budget allows about 1,000 picks, N/L = 1.6, which finds 1 − e^(−1.6) = 80% of variants.

Redesign. Fix cofactor regeneration at the level week 31's allocation analysis implies and drop to three modules at four variants: L = 4³ = 64, N = 192 clones. One day of instrument time, room for triplicate controls, and the winner can be re-screened rather than believed once.

Which module gets the widest variation comes from the control coefficients: in the week 31 model the committed step carried C = 0.58 against a protein share of 0.21, the largest gap in the set.

The burden. Say the winner expresses the pathway at 15% of total protein against a metabolic sector of about 40%. If catalytic capacity scales with allocated protein and the drain comes from that sector, remaining capacity is (40 − 15)/40 = 0.63, which at a wild-type 0.60 h⁻¹ predicts about 0.38 h⁻¹: a 37% growth penalty, and the dominant cost where productivity is biomass times specific rate. Treat it as a bound, and test it with the inert-protein control at the same 15%.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • library members equiprobable and picks independent, so coverage is 1 − e^(−N/L)
  • one LC-MS instrument at 6 minutes per sample, 20 h a day
  • pathway at 15% of total protein and the metabolic sector at 40%
  • catalytic capacity proportional to the protein allocated to it
  • the whole pathway drain taken from the metabolic sector
  • control coefficients and protein shares carried over from the week 31 model

Common misconceptions

  • That the strongest promoter gives the most product. Above the allocation optimum the extra protein buys saturated enzyme at rising burden, and the amplified step's control coefficient falls as its substrate is drawn down.
  • That a ribosome binding site calculator sets the expression level. It ranks variants and predicts absolute rate to about an order of magnitude; it is a tool for building a spread that is then measured.
  • That an empty-vector control measures burden. It measures replication cost. The control is an equivalent, verified mass of inert protein from the same construct.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Why does the strongest promoter often lower titre, and which four mechanisms would you distinguish experimentally?

A. Because flux stops responding while cost keeps rising: the enzyme saturates, its control coefficient falls, and the protein comes from a fixed budget. The four are ribosome competition, precursor or cofactor drain, folding load and plasmid replication cost. Separate them with inert protein at matched verified mass from the same construct, a ribosome reporter, labelled precursor fate into product against biomass, and the soluble-versus-inclusion-body split; a plasmid-free strain isolates replication.

Q. Your library is 625 members and your screen does 1,000 assays a week. What do you do?

A. Recognise 1,000 picks as 1.6-fold coverage, finding 80% of variants with no replicates. Either enlarge the screen — a fluorescent or growth-coupled proxy moves throughput by orders of magnitude, at the price of measuring a proxy — or shrink the library, usually the right answer: fix the modules allocation analysis says are near optimum, keep three at four variants for 64 members and 192 picks, and spend the recovered capacity on replicates.

Q. Which module should carry the widest variation, and how do you decide before building anything?

A. The one whose flux control coefficient most exceeds its share of the pathway protein budget, since the two are equal at the optimum and a gap marks mis-allocation. Compute both from the week 31 model and the proteomics: control above share means amplification should pay, below means protein can be given up. Decide this first, because vᵐ makes every extra varied module expensive.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. For a proposed expression change, predict both the intended flux effect and the burden risk. Which measurements would tell whether more transcript produced more active enzyme?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 35 — Genome editing: recombineering, CRISPR and multiplexing

Chromosomal engineering at scale. Every editing method persuades a repair pathway to do something useful, so knowing which repair biology each depends on predicts which will work in a host nobody has edited before — and predicts, correctly, that most published protocols do not transfer. The week ends in an editing plan, which means a biosafety section as much as guides.

Core ideas

1. The repair pathway available decides the method

A break is repaired by homologous recombination, which uses a donor and is precise, by non-homologous end joining, which is error-prone and needs none, or by microhomology-mediated end joining in between (Lee §10.1). Most bacteria have little or no end joining, so an unrepaired break is lethal — which is why Cas9 in a bacterium is a counter-selection against unedited cells rather than a mutagen, and why a donor must be supplied. Eukaryotes have the opposite problem: end joining dominates and competes with the donor, so knockouts come easily and precise edits do not; Lee §10.1 puts homologous integration in mammalian cells at about 1 in 1,000 transfected cells.

2. Recombineering makes a bacterium recombinogenic, and counter-selection makes the edit markerless

Gam blocks the exonuclease that would destroy linear DNA, Exo resects one strand, Beta anneals it at the replication fork. Datsenko and Wanner (PNAS 97:6640, 2000) showed PCR products carrying only 36–50 nt of homology suffice, and that the cassette can then be removed by FLP acting on flanking FRT sites; oligonucleotide recombineering needs Beta alone and no selection, so its limit is detection. Without a nuclease the markerless route is two selected events: the cassette integrates under positive selection, then excises under a counter-selection — sacB on sucrose, rpsL in a streptomycin-resistant host, upp on 5-fluorouracil, manP on mannose, or an I-SceI site. Lee §13.4.1 reports deletions up to 78 kb this way, and the catch: each system needs its own host background.

3. CRISPR-Cas9 is guide design plus a repair template, and its efficiency is published

Cas9 is targeted by a 20-nt spacer to a protospacer adjacent to an NGG motif, and the PAM is a hard requirement: a target without one nearby needs an orthologue with a different PAM. Lee's Bacillus survey (§13.4.2–13.4.3) gives the realistic range — 33–53% in the first report, 90–97% once promoters and delivery were optimised, 80% for a 38 kb deletion, 69% for point mutations, 49–65% for three loci at once. The nickase appears there at both 93–97% and 53%: efficiency belongs to the whole system, not the nuclease.

4. For an essential gene, knockdown beats knockout and can be graded

Deleting an essential gene gives no colony or a suppressor, and either way carries little information; dCas9 blocking transcription gives a dial. In the genome-wide B. subtilis essential-gene CRISPRi library (Lee §13.4.3.2) repression of a chromosomal reporter was titratable with xylose from 3-fold to 150-fold, and eight genes were knocked down together at 140-fold or more in exponential growth. That is what week 25's essentiality analysis wants: a dose-response through the essential range, not a binary verdict.

5. Base and prime editing avoid the break; MAGE embraces the numbers

A deaminase fused to dCas9 or a nickase converts C to T or A to G in a small window with no donor and no break, at up to 100% in Lee §13.4.3.3. Prime editing writes a templated edit from a reverse transcriptase primed by the guide itself, at 20–50% efficiency with 1–10% indels in human cells (Anzalone et al., Nature 576:149, 2019), with no established bacterial workhorse. MAGE goes the other way, cycling oligonucleotide recombineering across many loci at once: over 4 × 10⁹ variants a day (Wang et al., Nature 460, 2009, doi:10.1038/nature08187).

6. Tool transfer fails on homology length, transformation efficiency and mismatch repair

The sharpest number in the week's reading: λ-Red needs about 50 bp of homology in E. coli and roughly 800–1,000 bp in Lactococcus lactis (Lee §15.2.3.3), which alone turns a primer-tail protocol into a cloning project. Lactic acid bacteria are also not natively recombinogenic, so a Beta homologue such as RecT must be expressed and its best variant found empirically, and mismatch repair differs between strains. Transformation efficiency is usually binding, which is why week 33's chassis work comes first.

Worked anchor

The same 1.2 kb deletion, two ways, then the multiplex arithmetic.

Recombineering with counter-selection. Two 70-mers with 50 nt arms amplify the cassette; the λ-Red plasmid is induced and the cells electroporated; transformants are selected and checked by colony PCR; then the plasmid is cured, FLP expressed, the excision counter-selected and the junction sequenced. Hands-on about 5 days, calendar 7–10, a small screening burden because the first step is positively selected, and an FRT scar in the product.

CRISPR-Cas9. A PAM check, three guides cloned by Golden Gate and a donor with two 500–1,000 bp arms; transform and induce; screen 8 colonies, which suffices at Lee's 80–97% for a deletion of this kind. Calendar 5–7 days, scarless. The difference is the donor — 1–2 kb of arms to build against 100 nt of primer tail, traded for no marker, no curing and no scar.

So the decision is iteration count. One deletion: either. Three interventions in sequence: CRISPR, because marker and scar do not accumulate. A host with poor transformation: recombineering, because positive selection finds a rare event and screening does not.

MAGE diversity. Twenty-four sites at 0.30 replacement per cycle: a site is converted with probability 1 − 0.70ⁿ, so 0.76 at four cycles and 0.97 at ten, over a space of 2²⁴ = 1.7 × 10⁷ genotypes. Ten cycles put the expected conversions per cell at 23.3, piling the population into the fully converted corner, while four put the mean at 18.2 with a spread of about ±2.1 and sample the interior. At 10⁹ cells the space is covered many times over either way, so the design variable is where in it the library sits, not how large it is.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • per-site allelic replacement of 0.30 per MAGE cycle, equal at every site
  • sites independent and treated as binary, converted or not
  • editing efficiencies taken from Lee's Bacillus survey and assumed to transfer to this target
  • homology arm lengths as published for the host in question
  • hands-on and calendar days exclude ordering and queueing time

Common misconceptions

  • That CRISPR edits a bacterial genome. In most bacteria it kills the cells whose genome was not edited, because they cannot repair the cut; the donor and homologous recombination do the editing.
  • That a knockout tells you what an essential gene does. It tells you the cell dies or finds a suppressor. The informative experiment is a graded CRISPRi series through the essential range.
  • That a protocol working in E. coli needs only optimisation elsewhere. λ-Red needs about 50 bp of homology in E. coli and 800–1,000 bp in Lactococcus lactis: a different experiment, not a tuned one.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. When would you replace a native promoter rather than knock down with CRISPRi, and what do you lose?

A. When the change must be permanent and heritable without an inducer, in a production strain where a dCas9 cassette and its inducer are liabilities; replacement also avoids polar effects across an operon. What you lose is the dial: CRISPRi gives a dose-response from one construct, 3- to 150-fold in the Bacillus library, whereas each replacement is one point on it. So CRISPRi to find the level, replacement to fix it.

Q. A published CRISPR protocol gives 90% editing in E. coli and nothing in your host. Name the four things you check, in order.

A. Transformation efficiency first, since everything downstream is conditional on delivery. Then homology arm length against the host's own requirement, 50 bp in E. coli against 800–1,000 bp elsewhere. Then Cas9 expression and toxicity. Then repair capacity: any end joining, and what mismatch repair does to a single-stranded donor.

Q. Design the verification for a markerless deletion and say what each step cannot catch.

A. Colony PCR with primers outside both arms gives a size shift and excludes the wild-type allele, but shows a mixed population only if both products amplify comparably. Sequencing the junction catches scars and indels there and nothing elsewhere; a PCR against the delivery plasmid confirms curing. Only whole-genome sequencing catches off-target cuts, secondary recombination and suppressors picked up during selection.

Transfer prompt. Plan a targeted edit or knockdown to test a pathway hypothesis. How would you distinguish the intended edit effect from off-target, polar, or growth effects?

Week 36 — Dynamic regulation and biosensors

Feedback control applied to a pathway, which is the clearest place in the course where a chemical engineer arrives already equipped. The content is not the molecular biology of any one sensor but the arithmetic that chooses between them and that places the operating point: a sensor is four numbers — specificity, detection range, sensitivity and reporter dynamic range — and a loop is a gain and a delay. The week's hardest idea is that a 110-fold sensor placed at the wrong concentration resolves nothing, so the design decision is where on the transfer curve you sit, not which reporter you fuse.

Core ideas

1. Static tuning sets one operating point for a process that has several

Week 34 chose a promoter and a copy number, and those choices are fixed for the run. A fed-batch run is not: substrate falls from 20 g L⁻¹ to near zero, biomass rises two orders of magnitude, oxygen transfer saturates, and a toxic intermediate accumulates only after the pathway is carrying flux. A tuning optimal at inoculation is wrong at harvest, and the growth-production trade-off makes the error systematic rather than random — the expression level that maximises product per cell is below the level that maximises product per litre, because the latter needs the biomass that the former suppresses. Dynamic regulation does not improve on the best static tuning at any single instant; it improves on the fact that no single instant is representative.

2. There are four sensor classes and they fail differently

Protein Engineering Ch 2 divides them by what does the sensing. RNA-type riboswitches put an aptamer upstream of an expression platform, so ligand binding changes a secondary structure and the ribosome or terminator reads the consequence; they need no protein and so impose almost no burden, but the aptamer must be selected for each new ligand. DNA-type sensors act through a DNA-binding event rather than a conformational switch. Transcription-factor sensors hand the problem to an evolved allosteric protein, which is why they amplify — a small change in ligand is converted through gene expression into a large change in phenotype — and why they are confined to metabolites some organism already had a reason to sense. Enzyme-type sensors convert the analyte chemically into something visible, as DOPA dioxygenase turns DOPA into the fluorescent pigment betaxanthin; they work on intermediates no regulator recognises, at the cost of consuming the thing being measured.

3. A sensor is characterised by four numbers, and three of them are not the dynamic range

§2.4 names specificity, detection range, sensitivity and reporter dynamic range, and they answer different questions. Specificity sets the false-positive rate: the theophylline aptamer binds theophylline about 10,000-fold more tightly than caffeine, which is why a screen built on it returned no false positives across a large library, whereas a transcription factor with a broad effector profile returns hits that respond to something else in the medium. Detection range is the span of analyte concentrations that produce any response at all. Sensitivity is the derivative — the change in output per change in analyte — and it is what decides whether a 30% improvement is visible. Reporter dynamic range is the output span between off and full on, reported as 110-fold for the DOPA sensor. Note that response time is not in this list; §2.4 does not treat it, and a loop analysis needs it, so it has to come from the promoter and maturation literature rather than from this chapter.

4. Where you place the operating point decides what the sensor can resolve

Model the response as a Hill curve, output = R_min + (R_max − R_min)·sᵃ/(Kᵃ + sᵃ). The useful quantity is the local logarithmic gain, d ln(output)/d ln(s), which for a Hill form peaks near s = K and falls to zero at both ends. With K placed at the wild-type concentration the sensor is maximally sensitive to the improvements you are looking for; with K placed three-fold above it, a candidate sitting at 1.3× wild type moves almost nowhere on the curve, and the 110-fold dynamic range is spent on concentrations no variant in the library reaches. This is why sensor engineering is mostly promoter and operator engineering: moving K, by changing operator affinity or sensor expression level, is the design variable, and widening R_max/R_min is secondary.

5. Architecture: feedback, feedforward, and the two-stage switch that is neither

Negative feedback from an accumulating intermediate onto the enzyme that makes it holds the intermediate near a set point and is the architecture the control course predicts. Feedforward from the substrate anticipates rather than corrects, which matters when the lag between sensing and actuation is comparable to the disturbance. The architecture most often actually implemented is neither: a two-stage switch that runs growth to a threshold and then redirects carbon. Lee §18.2.5.3 is the worked case — flux to farnesyl diphosphate is raised while the downstream squalene synthase Erg9 is throttled, so the native ERG9 promoter is replaced with a copper- or methionine-inducible promoter or the glucose-dependent P<i>HXT1</i>, giving enough Erg9 for biomass in the growth phase and little in the production phase. Alternatives named there are deleting the promoter's upstream activation sequence or adding a degradation tag, which move the switch from transcription to protein turnover and change its speed accordingly.

6. Quorum sensing buys timing without an inducer, and pays in tunability

An inducible promoter needs someone to add the inducer at the right optical density, which is a manual step in the laboratory and a cost line plus a validation problem at scale. A quorum-sensing circuit makes the switch a function of cell density itself, so the timing is set at design time by the synthase and receptor strengths rather than at run time by an operator. The cost is that the set point is now a property of the construct: changing when the switch fires means rebuilding, and the same circuit fires at a different time in a different medium or vessel because the autoinducer concentration depends on dilution rate and on whether the molecule is stable at the run's pH.

7. Gain and delay, which is the part no assigned text supplies

A genetic loop oscillates when the loop gain exceeds one at the frequency where the phase lag reaches 180°. Both terms are estimable. The gain is the product of the local logarithmic sensitivities around the loop — sensor gain times promoter gain times the elasticity of the controlled step — and a Hill coefficient of 2 contributes at most 2 to it, which is why cooperativity is what makes a genetic circuit capable of oscillating at all. The delay is the sum of transcription, translation, folding and reporter maturation, tens of minutes in total, against a dilution time set by the growth rate: at μ = 0.6 h⁻¹ the protein half-life by dilution is about 70 minutes, so the delay is a substantial fraction of the loop's own time constant. The practical reading is that a high-gain loop with a slow reporter is the configuration that rings, and that lowering the gain — a weaker operator, a less cooperative sensor — is the first fix.

8. Converting a screen into a selection, and the escape problem

A screen measures every clone; a selection makes the clone measure itself, which is the only way to reach 10⁸ and above. Coupling titre to growth — the sensor driving an antibiotic resistance gene, or complementing an auxotrophy — converts throughput from a cost into a non-issue, and Protein Engineering Ch 2 notes that resistance markers used in tandem widen the effective dynamic range in units of growth rate and tighten stringency. The failure is specific and predictable: any mutation that produces signal without producing product is selected harder than the phenotype you want, because it is cheaper. Reporter mutation, operator mutation that makes the promoter constitutive, and loss of the sensor's repression are all escapes, and all are more probable per cell than the improvement being selected for. The countermeasures are a second orthogonal reporter, periodic reversion of the selection, and sequencing the sensor rather than only the target in every hit.

Worked anchor

Can a biosensor screen resolve a 30% improvement? Take a transcription-factor sensor for the pathway intermediate, driving GFP, characterised as in §2.4: reporter dynamic range R_max/R_min = 110, Hill coefficient n = 2, and K tunable by operator choice. The wild-type strain sits at s₀. Flow cytometry on 10⁴ events per clone has a coefficient of variation of about 15% on the population mean fluorescence, dominated by expression noise rather than by counting statistics.

First, the gain at the operating point. For a Hill form the logarithmic gain is d ln R / d ln s = n·Kⁿ/(Kⁿ + sⁿ). At s = K it is n/2 = 1.0; at s = 3K it is 2/(1+9) = 0.2; at s = K/3 it is 2·9/10 = 1.8.

Now the signal. A 1.3-fold improvement is Δln s = ln 1.3 = 0.262. Placed at K, the output moves by 1.0 × 0.262 = 0.262 in ln units, a 30% rise in fluorescence. Taking the 15% CV as 0.15 in ln units, that is 0.262/0.15 = 1.7 sigma — detectable, marginally, and only with replicates. Placed at 3K the output moves by 0.2 × 0.262 = 0.052, a 5% rise, which is 0.35 sigma and invisible. Placed at K/3 it moves 1.8 × 0.262 = 0.47, a 60% rise and 3.1 sigma, which is comfortable.

So the sensor does not have a resolution; the sensor plus its operating point does, and the same 110-fold reporter gives either a four-sigma or an undetectable readout depending on a choice about operator affinity. Note also that the 110-fold dynamic range never entered the arithmetic, because the question was a derivative and the dynamic range is a range.

Second, how many clones. If the improvement sought is present at 1 in 10³ of the library, a plate-based screen of 10³ clones finds about one of them. At the operating point K, a one-tailed threshold set at 1.7 sigma lets through about 4% of unimproved clones, so the same 10³ clones also yield roughly 40 false positives for that one true hit — a confirmation assay on 41 candidates. At K/3 and 3.1 sigma the pass rate is about 0.1%, so the expected false-positive count across the whole plate set is one. The screen's real output is therefore not a hit rate but a confirmation workload, and moving K is what sets it.

Note what did not help. Widening the reporter from 110-fold to 2,000-fold changes nothing at all here, because the logarithmic gain of a Hill form is independent of the amplitude R_max − R_min — the amplitude cancels when the derivative is taken in log units. The only two levers on resolution are K, through operator affinity or sensor expression, and the Hill coefficient n, which sets the maximum gain at n/2. A three-fold shift in K is one round of operator mutagenesis; a change in n means a different sensor protein.

The stopping decision follows: if no operator variant puts K within about three-fold of the wild-type concentration, the sensor cannot support a screen at this library size and the money belongs in a growth-coupled selection instead, where throughput buys back what resolution cannot.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • sensor response modelled as a Hill curve with n = 2, so the logarithmic gain is n·Kⁿ/(Kⁿ + sⁿ)
  • the 110-fold reporter dynamic range and the Hill coefficient taken as independent of where K sits
  • assay coefficient of variation 15% on the population mean of 10⁴ events, dominated by expression noise rather than counting statistics
  • output noise taken as multiplicative, so a CV in linear units is a standard deviation in ln units
  • fluorescence proportional to the reporter protein and the reporter protein to promoter output, with no maturation lag inside the measurement
  • the improvement sought present at 1 in 10³ of the library, which is an assumption about the library and not a measurement
  • false-positive rates read off a normal distribution at 1.7 and 3.1 sigma, one-tailed
  • K movable by operator mutagenesis over at least a three-fold range, which is the premise the stopping decision tests

Zhang, Carothers & Keasling, Nat. Biotechnol. 30(4):354–359 (2012)SkimThe primary source behind Lee's one line, and the clearest published example of a metabolite sensor closing a loop on its own pathway. Cited here because the assigned chapters carry the result without the design.
Elowitz & Leibler, Nature 403:335–338 (2000); Gardner, Cantor & Collins, Nature 403:339–342 (2000)SkimThe repressilator and the toggle switch. Needed because no assigned text covers engineered oscillators or bistability at all, and the week's objective on stability and gain has no other source.

Common misconceptions

  • That a wide dynamic range makes a sensor sensitive. Dynamic range is the span between off and full on; sensitivity is the slope at the concentration you are actually at. A 110-fold reporter with K three-fold above the operating point resolves a 30% improvement as a 5% signal, which is invisible against a 15% assay CV. Move K, not R_max.
  • That negative feedback always stabilises. It stabilises when the loop gain is low and the delay is short. A genetic loop has a delay of tens of minutes from transcription, translation and maturation, and cooperativity raises the gain, so a tightly tuned negative loop is exactly the configuration that oscillates. The chemical engineering intuition transfers, including the part about overshoot.
  • That a growth-coupled selection removes the screening problem. It removes the throughput problem and creates an escape problem. Any mutation that produces signal without product is selected harder than the phenotype you want, because it is cheaper to acquire; reporter and operator mutations are more probable per cell than the improvement. A selection without a counter-check is a device for enriching cheats.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. What determines whether a genetic feedback loop oscillates, and how would you detect it experimentally?

A. Loop gain above one at the frequency where the phase lag reaches 180°. The gain is the product of the logarithmic sensitivities around the loop — sensor, promoter, and the elasticity of the controlled step — with cooperativity contributing up to its Hill coefficient; the lag is transcription plus translation plus folding plus reporter maturation, tens of minutes, against a dilution time of about 70 minutes at μ = 0.6 h⁻¹. Detection needs time-resolved single-cell measurement, because a population average of cells oscillating out of phase is flat: either a microfluidic device with per-cell traces, or synchronisation followed by sampling at intervals short compared with the suspected period. A flat bulk fluorescence trace is not evidence of a settled loop.

Q. Your sensor has a 110-fold dynamic range and your best variant gives no measurable signal increase. List the explanations in order of how cheaply you can test them.

A. Cheapest first: the operating point is wrong, so test by titrating exogenous analyte across three orders of magnitude and finding where the response curve actually sits relative to the strain's concentration. Next, the analyte is not reaching the sensor — compartmentalisation, export, or degradation — tested by measuring the intracellular pool directly. Next, the reporter is saturated at the top rather than the bottom, tested by the same titration read for a plateau. Next, the variant does not in fact make more product, tested by the confirmation assay the screen was supposed to replace. Last and most expensive, the sensor has mutated or the promoter has gone constitutive, tested by sequencing the sensor cassette in the clone. The ordering matters because the first explanation is both the most likely and the only one fixed without new biology.

Q. Why would you choose a quorum-sensing switch over an inducible promoter, and what do you give up?

A. You give up run-time control and gain process simplicity. An inducible promoter needs an operator to add inducer at the right density, which is a manual step, a cost line and a validation burden at scale, and in a food or pharmaceutical process the inducer may be unacceptable in the product. Quorum sensing makes the switch a function of cell density, so the timing is fixed at design time by synthase and receptor strengths. What you give up is tunability: moving the set point means rebuilding the circuit, and the same construct fires at a different time in a different medium, vessel or dilution rate, because the autoinducer concentration depends on both accumulation and the molecule's stability at the run's pH. The right question is whether the set point needs to change more often than the construct does.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Imagine a fermentation where product formation should turn on after growth. What signal could a biosensor detect, and how would you check that reporter output tracks the actual intracellular signal?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 37 — Enzyme engineering: rational design and directed evolution

Sometimes the pathway is right and the catalyst is wrong. This week is library arithmetic, and the arithmetic is unusually unforgiving: the number of transformants needed to see 95% of a saturation library rises so fast with the number of randomised positions that the design decision is made before any enzymology is considered. The content is how positions are grouped and which codon alphabet is used, because those two choices move the requirement by six orders of magnitude, and they are made from structure and consensus data rather than from intuition.

Core ideas

1. Three strategies differ in what they require you to know, not in what they achieve

Rational design needs a structure, a mechanism and a hypothesis about which residue does what; it tests a handful of variants and is cheap when the hypothesis is right and worthless when it is wrong. Directed evolution needs only a screen and makes no claim about mechanism, which is why it works on properties nobody can predict — expression, solubility, tolerance of a cosolvent — and why it costs library-sized effort. Semi-rational design uses structure to choose where to randomise and evolution to decide what to put there, which is the dominant mode in practice because structural information is now cheap and screening still is not. Protein Engineering Ch 5 formalises this as CAST: residues lining the binding pocket are identified from a structure or a docked substrate, then saturated.

2. Oversampling for 95% coverage is the number that decides the campaign

A saturation library of L distinct members needs roughly 3L clones screened before 95% of it has been seen, because sampling with replacement leaves e⁻ᴺ/ᴸ unsampled. Protein Engineering Table 5.1 tabulates this through the Patrick–Firth algorithm for the two standard codon schemes. With NNK degeneracy — 32 codons covering all 20 amino acids — one position needs 94 transformants, two need 3,066, three need 98,163, four more than 3.1 × 10⁶, six more than 3.2 × 10⁹, and ten more than 3.4 × 10¹⁵. The growth is 32-fold per position at the DNA level, so each additional randomised residue costs a factor of about 30 in screening, and the fourth one is where the campaign stops being a plate experiment.

3. A reduced codon alphabet buys back orders of magnitude and pays in diversity

NDT degeneracy uses 12 codons encoding 12 amino acids — Phe, Leu, Ile, Val, Tyr, His, Asn, Cys, Arg, Ser, Asp and Gly — chosen so the set still spans hydrophobic and hydrophilic, polar and non-polar, aromatic and aliphatic, small and large. The same table gives 34 transformants for one position, 430 for two, 5,175 for three, 62,118 for four, 745,433 for five and more than 8.9 × 10⁶ for six. At six positions that is a 360-fold reduction against NNK; at four it is a 50-fold reduction. What is given up is eight amino acids, including alanine, methionine, tryptophan, proline, threonine, lysine, glutamate and glutamine — so no proline-driven backbone change and no new salt bridge from lysine or glutamate. The chapter's own conclusion is that high coverage of a reduced alphabet beats low coverage of NNK, and notes that this still needs generalising.

4. Grouping positions beats reducing their number

The limonene epoxide hydrolase campaign is the arithmetic made concrete. Ten residues were identified by docking cyclohexene oxide into the crystal structure. NNK saturation at all ten requires more than 3 × 10¹⁵ transformants for 95% coverage, which is not a number; a triple-code alphabet over all ten brings it to about 10⁶, which is still a year. The residues were instead grouped into three randomisation sites — four, three and three residues — and, because docking showed the pocket residues to be hydrophobic and a consensus analysis over 100 related epoxide hydrolases agreed, the building blocks were restricted to valine, phenylalanine and tyrosine. The three libraries then needed 576, 192 and 192 transformants for 95% coverage. Wild-type enantioselectivity of 4% ee became 97–99% ee for the (S,S) product, and one iterative step gave 97% ee for (R,R). The reduction from 10¹⁵ to 10³ came from two structural inferences, not from a better screen.

5. Iterative saturation multiplies calendar, not library size

Having grouped into sites, the order in which they are visited is itself a choice, and the number of upward pathways through the sites is factorial: two sites give two pathways, three give six, four give twenty-four. Each pathway is a sequence of rounds, each round is a library and a screen, and the best variant from one site becomes the parent for the next. This is where a campaign's duration actually lives. The practical consequence is that site count is capped by calendar rather than by screening capacity — four sites at even two weeks per round is two years if the pathways are explored exhaustively, so a real campaign commits to one pathway and justifies the choice, usually by taking the site with the largest single-site effect first.

6. Screening format is a throughput ladder with a resolution penalty at every rung

Agar plates with a colorimetric readout reach 10³–10⁴ per week and measure a crude proxy. Microtitre plates with a real assay reach 10³–10⁴ and measure the property you care about, but each well costs reagent. Flow cytometry reaches 10⁷–10⁸ per day and requires the property to be fluorescent and cell-associated, which is the condition week 36's biosensors exist to manufacture. Droplet microfluidics reaches comparable numbers while keeping the enzyme and its product in the same compartment, which is what lets a secreted or diffusible product be screened at all. Growth coupling is effectively unlimited and measures only whether the cell lived. Every rung up trades the directness of the measurement for throughput, and the campaign is designed from both ends at once: the library size the format can cover, and the property the format can see.

7. Continuous evolution is bounded by the error threshold, and its cost is targeting

Ch 1 derives why in-vivo continuous evolution is hard. Organisms sit near a mutational error threshold of order 1/L: with a genome of 5 × 10⁶ bases, E. coli's measured rate is about 5 × 10⁻⁸ substitutions per base, and yeast at 1.2 × 10⁷ bases sits near 10⁻¹⁰. A 1 kb gene of interest, being three to four orders of magnitude shorter, can tolerate about 10⁻³ per base and needs that much to generate comparable total diversity. So the whole engineering problem is targeting: mutating the gene at 10⁻³ while leaving the genome at 10⁻⁸ demands on-target against off-target discrimination of about 10⁶-fold in E. coli and 10⁷-fold in yeast and human cells, far beyond the 10- to 1,000-fold selectivity typical of molecular recognition problems. The reported systems land at various points — orthogonal replication near 10⁻⁵ per base, error-prone polymerase I systems at 10⁻³ and up to 10⁻² adjacent to a nicked site, a 7.7-million-fold local elevation, with off-target rates rising too, in one case 40-fold over a 10 kb window.

8. Stability is spent, not preserved, and has to be bought in advance

Activity-improving substitutions are disproportionately destabilising, because the active site is already strained and the residues that tune it are the ones holding the fold together. A campaign that gains four-fold activity over four rounds and loses 8 kJ mol⁻¹ of folding free energy has produced an enzyme that is better on the bench and worse in a 48-hour fermentation at 37 °C. The buffers are known and cheap relative to the campaign: consensus substitutions, where the most common residue across a large homologue alignment is adopted; ancestral sequence reconstruction, which tends to yield more thermostable parents; and B-FIT, which saturates the positions with the highest crystallographic B-factors on the argument that the most mobile residues are where rigidification pays. All three are applied before the activity campaign, not after it, because the stability margin is what the activity campaign then spends.

Worked anchor

Design the campaign for the weakest enzyme in the pathway. Week 31's control analysis put a flux control coefficient of 0.58 on one step; the enzyme is characterised, there is a crystal structure, and docking identifies six first-shell residues. The screen available is a microtitre assay at 10⁴ wells per week, and a biosensor-based sort is possible at 10⁷ per day if the week 36 sensor can be made to work.

Option A, NNK at all six. Table 5.1 gives more than 3.2 × 10⁹ transformants for 95% coverage. At 10⁴ per week that is 6,100 years, and even at 10⁷ per day by sorting it is 320 days of continuous sorting. Excluded.

Option B, NDT at all six. More than 8.9 × 10⁶ transformants. At 10⁴ per week, 17 years — excluded for the plate assay. At 10⁷ per day it is a single day's sort, so this option exists if and only if the sensor exists. That is the decision the two weeks are linked by: the sensor is not a convenience, it is what makes a six-position library legal.

Option C, two sites of three with NDT. Each site needs 5,175 transformants for 95% coverage, so one round is half a week of microtitre screening and both sites are one week. Two sites give two iterative pathways; committing to one, the campaign is two rounds, with build and assay turnaround putting each round at about three weeks. Total nine weeks including the confirmation assay.

Option D, three sites of two with a reduced three-amino-acid code, if docking and a consensus alignment support restricting the alphabet as the limonene epoxide hydrolase case did. Each site then needs a few hundred transformants, so a round is a day of screening, but three sites give six pathways and the calendar, not the screening, becomes the constraint.

Choose C. The arithmetic says so: it is the largest search that the available screen can actually cover without depending on a sensor that does not yet exist, and it keeps the pathway count at two so the commitment to one ordering costs at most a factor of two in explored space.

Expected gain and stopping. Published semi-rational campaigns on selectivity report wild-type values moving most of the way to the achievable limit in one to two rounds — 4% to 97–99% ee in the limonene case. For activity rather than selectivity the usual observation is two- to five-fold per round for the first two rounds, flattening after. So the campaign is specified as: two rounds, target a four-fold improvement in kcat/KM against the wild type, measured by the confirmation assay on purified protein rather than by the screen, with a stability check of ΔTm no worse than −3 °C. Stopping criterion as a result and a date: if round one does not deliver two-fold by week six, stop and reconsider the target, because the second round's expected gain is conditional on the first. The alternative if it is not met is to spend the remaining budget on consensus and B-FIT stabilisation of the wild type and accept the wild-type activity, on the grounds that an enzyme that survives the run is worth more than one that is faster for six hours.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • transformant counts for 95% coverage taken from Protein Engineering Table 5.1 as printed, computed there by the Patrick–Firth algorithm
  • sampling treated as with replacement, so coverage is 1 − e⁻ᴺᐟL and N ≈ 3L at 95%
  • microtitre screening capacity 10⁴ wells per week and sorting capacity 10⁷ per day, both taken as sustained rather than peak
  • transformation efficiency not limiting, so the number of transformants needed equals the number obtainable
  • each campaign round taken as three weeks from library build to confirmed hit, including assay turnaround
  • one iterative pathway committed to, so the explored space is a factor of two below the two-site exhaustive set
  • expected gain of two- to five-fold per round taken from reported semi-rational campaigns on other enzymes, not from this target
  • the week 31 flux control coefficient of 0.58 assumed still to hold at the improved activity, which is a tangent and not a prediction
