Common misconceptions

  • That more randomised positions means a better search. Each position multiplies the library by about 32 under NNK and 12 under NDT, so the sixth position costs three orders of magnitude and buys coverage of a space you cannot screen. Real campaigns search less space more completely: the limonene case went from 3 × 10¹⁵ to 576 transformants by grouping and alphabet reduction and got 99% ee out of it.
  • That NNK is the safe default because it covers all 20 amino acids. It covers them at a coverage you cannot afford past three positions. The chapter's own position is that high coverage of a reduced alphabet beats low coverage of the full one — and a library screened at 5% coverage is a random sample dressed as a saturation experiment, with no basis for concluding that an absent substitution was tested.
  • That raising the mutation rate speeds up evolution. Above about 1/L it destroys the population: the genome is near its error threshold already, which is why E. coli sits at 5 × 10⁻⁸ per base. Continuous evolution systems do not raise the mutation rate, they relocate it, and their whole engineering difficulty is the 10⁶- to 10⁷-fold on-target to off-target discrimination that relocation requires.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Saturation at six positions needs how many transformants for 95% coverage, and which screening formats can deliver that?

A. Under NNK degeneracy, more than 3.2 × 10⁹ — no format reaches that at 95% coverage except growth coupling, which only reports survival. Under NDT, more than 8.9 × 10⁶, which flow cytometry at 10⁷–10⁸ per day or droplet microfluidics can cover in about a day, provided the property is fluorescent and cell-associated; plate and microtitre formats at 10³–10⁴ per week cannot. The correct answer to the question as posed in a campaign is to not randomise six positions at once: two NDT sites of three need 5,175 transformants each, which is half a week of microtitre screening and keeps a direct assay instead of a proxy.

Q. A collaborator proposes continuous evolution instead of your two-round campaign. What do you ask before agreeing?

A. Three things. What is the selection, since continuous evolution selects continuously and therefore needs the phenotype linked to host fitness at every generation — it cannot select for a property measured in a plate reader, nor for anything requiring purified protein, nor for stability at a temperature the host will not grow at. What is the off-target rate, because a system driving the target at 10⁻³ per base while raising the genome 40-fold over a 10 kb window accumulates host mutations that confound every subsequent measurement, so the endpoint needs resequencing. And what happens to the parent: continuous systems have no round structure, so there is no intermediate to retreat to and no record of the trajectory unless frozen stocks are banked deliberately. If the property is growth-coupled and the campaign would otherwise take a year, it is the right tool; if the property needs an assay, it is not.

Q. Your campaign gains four-fold in kcat/KM and the enzyme now denatures in eight hours at the process temperature. What went wrong, and at what point in the plan should it have been prevented?

A. Nothing went wrong in the screen; the screen measured what it was asked to. Activity-improving substitutions are disproportionately destabilising because the residues tuning the active site are the ones holding the fold, so a campaign that does not measure stability spends the stability margin without recording it. The prevention is upstream of round one, not after it: consensus substitutions from a large homologue alignment, ancestral reconstruction, or B-FIT saturation at the highest-B-factor positions, applied to the wild type to build margin that the activity campaign can then consume. Retrofitting afterwards means re-screening every stabilising candidate against the new active site, since the mutations now interact. The procedural fix is a stability gate in the round criteria — ΔTm no worse than some stated figure — so the trade is visible at each round instead of discovered at the end.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Pick a candidate enzyme in a cassava-related pathway. Would rational redesign or directed evolution be the better first move, and what assay makes the choice practical?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 38 — Data-driven protein design and high-throughput screening

The part of the field that changed most recently, and the week where the discipline is epistemic rather than arithmetic. The governing fact is an asymmetry in the data: there are over 100 million protein sequences and over 100,000 structures, and almost no sequence-to-function measurements. Everything these models can and cannot do follows from that, and so does the only honest way to test them — which is not a random split.

Core ideas

1. The data asymmetry is the whole explanation

Protein Engineering Ch 6 states the position plainly: UniProt holds more than 100 million unique sequences and the Protein Data Bank more than 100,000 experimentally determined structures, both growing exponentially, while data mapping sequence to function remains scarce. The chapter's further observation matters more than the counts — function data is hard to standardise because it depends on assay conditions and even on who ran the assay, so statistical models are most useful on data generated by one group under one protocol. Two consequences follow. Models trained on sequences alone can only have learned what evolution constrained, because that is the only signal in the training set. And a supervised model of your enzyme's activity has to be trained on your measurements, which means the campaign generates its own training data and the cost of the first batch is unavoidable.

2. A sequence model predicts likelihood under evolutionary constraint, not activity

Trained to reconstruct masked or next residues across a large sequence database, a protein language model learns the statistics of what has survived selection. Its per-position output is therefore a statement about how constrained a site has been across the family, which correlates with being important for something — folding, binding, catalysis, regulation, or an interaction with a partner the engineering project does not care about. It does not distinguish between these, and it cannot: nothing in the training signal separates a residue conserved because it is catalytic from one conserved because it contacts a chaperone. Zero-shot variant effect prediction works as well as it does because most substitutions at highly constrained positions are bad, which is a statement about the base rate and not about the variant.

3. Conservation and the active site agree in the middle and disagree at the edges

Mapping per-position conservation onto the structural active site from week 3 produces three categories, and the third is the useful one. Conserved and in the first shell: catalytic or substrate-contacting, and not to be randomised. Variable and remote: free, and where a stability campaign can work. Conserved and remote is the interesting class — these are folding nuclei, allosteric paths, interface residues and sites under constraint for reasons outside the assay, and they are exactly where a model's confidence is high and its relevance to the engineering objective is unknown. The converse class, variable and in the first shell, is where directed evolution has historically found its gains, because evolution had no reason to optimise for the non-natural substrate.

4. Supervised fitness models fail on combinations because epistasis is not in the training set

A model trained on single mutants learns a sum of independent effects, because that is all single-mutant data can identify. Epistasis — the dependence of one substitution's effect on another's presence — is by construction unmeasured, so the model extrapolates additively into a space where additivity is the thing being violated. This is the specific reason that a model with excellent held-out accuracy on singles predicts double and triple mutants badly, and it is also why the limonene epoxide hydrolase result is informative: Protein Engineering notes that CAST/ISM produces strong cooperative effects beyond additivity, which is exactly the regime a single-mutant model cannot see. Deep mutational scanning supplies millions of variants, but of one property, in one assay, usually at low mutational depth.

5. A predicted structure supports a pocket and not an energy

Structure prediction is reliable enough for fold assignment, domain boundaries and the approximate shape and lining of a binding pocket, which is sufficient for choosing CAST positions — and choosing CAST positions is what week 37 needed a structure for. It does not deliver the conformational ensemble, the transition state geometry, or folding free energy differences at the few kJ mol⁻¹ resolution that a stability prediction needs. Docking into a predicted structure inherits both limits and adds its own scoring-function error. The practical rule is that a predicted structure is admissible for deciding where to randomise and inadmissible as evidence for a mechanism, which is also the rule for a crystal structure, only more so.

6. Active learning converts a model into a campaign, and the arithmetic is cost per improvement

The loop is: measure a batch, fit, propose the next batch, repeat. Three parameters decide it. Batch size is set by what the assay runs at once, not by the algorithm. Acquisition strategy sets the exploration-exploitation balance — proposing only the predicted best exploits a model that is wrong off-distribution, while proposing only the most uncertain learns fast and delivers nothing. The stopping rule is the same kind of object as week 37's: a measurable result by a date. The comparison that matters is total measurements per unit improvement, and it has a break-even, because the first batch of a model-guided campaign buys no improvement at all.

7. Screening technology is matched to the property, and the numbers are published

Lee §9.5.1 gives the throughput ladder for metabolite measurement explicitly. With a chromatographic separation it is difficult to go below five minutes per sample, and resolving similar compounds in a complex matrix reduces throughput to 200–400 samples per day. Omitting separation and relying on high-resolution or tandem mass spectrometry with flow injection or direct infusion gives about one sample per minute, so 1,000–2,000 per day, and makes untargeted profiling of up to 10,000 samples in a few weeks possible — the approach used to profile whole single-knockout collections. The trade is the one every rung on every ladder in this phase has: throughput against the ability to resolve isomers and suppress matrix effects. A screen that cannot separate the product from its isomer has a false-positive rate, not a throughput.

8. Structures are becoming an omics layer, which is the same integration problem in a new coordinate

Lee §2.6.3 reports that complete structural proteomes have been assembled for the current E. coli and human reconstructions, and that the GEM-PRO workflow evaluates a genome-scale model down to tertiary structure. The three stated uses are worth holding onto because they are claims about what structures buy: physicochemical properties of the structural proteome become an omics data source supporting residue-level analysis; structure-based functional assignment improves the model's proteome allocation predictions; and fold and family distributions across a network allow comparison between strains and species. This is the same move as every integration in week 39 — a measurement layer mapped onto a mechanistic network so that correlations can become causes — and it inherits the same risks.

Worked anchor

Cost per improvement: classical directed evolution against a machine-learning-guided loop, on the same target as week 37. The assay is the microtitre screen at 10⁴ wells per week; take the fully loaded cost per well as the unit, so the answer is in wells rather than currency and survives a change of reagent price.

Classical, as designed in week 37. Two NDT sites of three residues, 5,175 transformants per site for 95% coverage, two rounds. Total measurements 10,350 wells, plus about 50 confirmation assays. Expected outcome, from the published base rate for semi-rational campaigns, is a two- to five-fold improvement, so take four-fold. Cost per fold of improvement: 10,400/4 = 2,600 wells per fold.

Machine-learning-guided. The first batch has to be measured before the model exists. Ch 6's framing says the useful training data is your own, under one protocol, so take a design-of-experiment batch of 500 variants sampled across the same six positions — one week of screening — to fit a sequence-function model. Then run active learning in batches of 96, the plate size, at one batch per round. Suppose six rounds. Total measurements 500 + 6 × 96 = 1,076 wells, about an eighth of the classical campaign.

The comparison turns entirely on the expected improvement, which is where honesty is required. If the model-guided loop achieves the same four-fold, the cost is 269 wells per fold, a factor of ten better. If epistasis defeats it and it achieves two-fold, it is 538 wells per fold, still better. If it achieves nothing because 500 training variants are too few to identify interactions among six positions — and the number of pairwise interactions among six NDT positions is 15 pairs times 144 combinations, which is 2,160 parameters against 500 observations — it costs 1,076 wells and returns zero.

That last line is the actual result of the calculation. The model is underdetermined at the batch size the assay permits, so the honest design is not a choice between the two but a hybrid: run site one classically at 5,175 wells to get a dense, high-coverage data set at one site, use it to fit a model that is identifiable because it only has to cover 12³ = 1,728 combinations at one site, and use the model to propose site two's 96 variants rather than screening its 5,175. Total 5,175 + 500 + 96 = 5,771 wells against 10,400, with the first round's result in hand before the model is trusted with anything.

The break-even condition, stated generally: the model-guided arm wins when the measurements saved on later rounds exceed the measurements spent on training, which requires the training set to be large relative to the number of interaction parameters at the positions being modelled. That ratio, not the model class, is what to compute before committing.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • cost measured in assay wells rather than currency, so reagent price changes do not move the comparison
  • the classical arm as designed in week 37: two NDT sites of three residues, 5,175 transformants each, two rounds
  • a four-fold improvement assumed for the classical arm, taken as the midpoint of reported two- to five-fold outcomes
  • active-learning batch size fixed at 96 by the plate rather than chosen by the algorithm, and six rounds assumed
  • a 500-variant training set taken as the largest affordable first batch at one week of screening
  • pairwise interaction parameters counted as 15 position pairs × 144 amino acid combinations = 2,160 under NDT, with higher-order terms ignored
  • identifiability judged by parameters against observations alone, with no regularisation or prior credited
  • throughput figures for separation-based and flow-injection metabolite screening taken from Lee §9.5.1 as reported

The second is how a campaign produces model-grade training data as a by-product.

Common misconceptions

  • That a protein language model knows which residues are catalytic. It knows which residues have been constrained across the family, and nothing in its training signal distinguishes catalysis from folding, allostery, or a contact with a partner irrelevant to your assay. The informative class after mapping conservation onto structure is conserved-and-remote, precisely because the model is confident there and its reason is unknown.
  • That a model with good held-out accuracy on single mutants will rank double mutants well. Single-mutant data cannot identify interaction terms, so the fit is additive by construction and extrapolates additively into the regime where additivity fails. The number to check is parameters against observations: six NDT positions have 2,160 pairwise interaction parameters, which a 500-variant training set cannot determine.
  • That a predicted structure is weaker evidence than a crystal structure for the same claim. It is weaker, but the error that matters is the same one: both are a single static model standing in for an ensemble, and neither supports a transition state or a folding free energy at the resolution a stability prediction needs. A predicted structure is admissible for choosing where to randomise, which is what it is used for here.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. What can a protein language model not extrapolate to, and why does that follow from how it was trained?

A. It cannot extrapolate to anything evolution had no occasion to constrain: activity on a non-natural substrate, stability at a temperature the family never experienced, expression in a non-native host, or tolerance of a process solvent. The training objective is reconstruction of residues from sequence context across a database of sequences that exist, so the only signal available is which residues selection preserved. It therefore scores a variant by how typical it is of the family, and a variant that is atypical because it is bad and one that is atypical because it does something new are indistinguishable to it. This is also why its predictions degrade as mutational distance from the family grows, which is the direction every engineering campaign travels.

Q. You are given a published ML-guided design paper reporting a 20-fold improvement. Name three claims it probably does not support.

A. First, that the model caused the improvement, unless there is a matched arm in which the same number of variants was chosen at random or by a baseline additive model — without it, the result is confounded with the library design and the number of variants measured. Second, that the reported accuracy generalises, if the train-test split was random over variants rather than held out by position or by mutational depth: a random split leaks, because a double mutant in the test set shares both of its substitutions with singles in the training set. Third, that the method transfers, if the training data came from one assay in one laboratory — which Ch 6 argues is the condition under which such data is usable at all, and which therefore also bounds its transferability. A fourth worth checking is whether the 20-fold is in the screen's units or in the confirmation assay on purified protein, since proxies inflate.

Q. Your assay runs 96 wells a week and you want a model of six positions. What do you do?

A. Not fit the model of six positions. The interaction terms alone are 15 pairs by 144 amino acid combinations, about 2,160 parameters under NDT, and at 96 wells a week a training set large enough to determine them is years of assay. The three available moves are: reduce the positions modelled, fitting one site of three at 12³ = 1,728 combinations, which a dense classical round at that site already samples; reduce the alphabet, since a three-amino-acid code at six positions is 3⁶ = 729 combinations and a few hundred measurements become meaningful; or raise the throughput by changing format, which means making the property fluorescent and cell-associated and so returns to week 36's biosensor. The general rule is to compute parameters against achievable observations before choosing a model class, because the assay's throughput, not the algorithm, determines what is identifiable.

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Week 39 — Omics, the design-build-test-learn cycle and adaptive evolution

The learn step, and the end of the phase. Data is cheap and a model revision is not: the scarce skill is turning a measurement into a changed assumption rather than into a figure. Two ideas carry the week. A genome-scale model is a context for omic data rather than a consumer of it, which is what separates integration from curve-fitting; and the circularity risk is real — a model constrained by expression data and then validated against expression data has been told what to say. The week also sits and marks Paper 5, so the artifact has to be scoped to ten sessions, not twelve.

Core ideas

1. Networks as context for content, and the two kinds of network this contrasts

Palsson Ch 24 opens on the distinction and Table 24.1 tabulates it. Inference-based networks are built from correlation and recurring pattern in the data itself: they need no prior knowledge, apply wherever there is data, relate directly to the omic measurement, and rewire substantially when more data arrives. Knowledge-based reconstructions are built from biochemistry: they are directly mechanistic, require that the biochemistry be known, obey mass and charge conservation and thermodynamics, relate more closely to phenotype through fluxes, and do not rewire once reconstructed. The consequence that matters is stated directly — statistical correlation between omic variables does not confer causality, whereas contextualising the same variables in a mechanistic network can establish it, because the network says which measurements are allowed to co-vary.

2. The GPR is where the integration is actually done, and it is where it is usually done wrong

Mapping expression onto reactions runs through the gene-protein-reaction rules, and the logic is not decoration. A complex is an AND: the reaction's capacity is set by the least-expressed subunit, so the correct aggregate is a minimum, and averaging across subunits silently invents capacity that the limiting subunit denies. Isozymes are an OR: capacity is the sum, and taking a minimum there silently removes the redundancy that makes the gene non-essential. Week 21 built these rules; this week is where getting them wrong changes a prediction. Palsson's statement of the advantage is exactly this — reconstructions capture the relationship between genes and enzyme activities explicitly, with the chain from genomic location through mRNA, protein and complex to activity providing the route by which a transcript measurement reaches a flux bound.

3. Omics as constraints and omics as validation are different experiments, and only one of them is a test

Using expression to set flux bounds — favouring reactions whose genes are up and penalising those whose genes are down — produces a prediction of differential reaction use between conditions, and §24.3 reports the method doing real work: a focused prediction of active pathways in a pathogen, confirmed by conditional knockouts, implicating branched-chain amino acid limitation and the regulator CodY in virulence. Using expression to check an unconstrained model's prediction is the opposite operation, and §24.4 is its exemplar: across wild-type and adaptively evolved E. coli, more than 98% of the active reactions in the optimal growth solutions are supported by transcriptomic and proteomic data, with evolved strains up-regulating genes inside the optimal solution and down-regulating those outside it. The discipline is to decide which of the two you are doing before you run it. A model constrained by a data set cannot then be validated by that data set, and the before-and-after comparison the artifact requires is only meaningful if the comparison's test case was withheld.

4. What a fold change is, and the three decisions upstream of it

A fold change is a ratio of normalised counts, and three choices made before it exists decide its value. Library preparation sets what was counted — total RNA against poly-A selection against ribosomal depletion changes which transcripts are present at all. Normalisation sets the denominator, and the standard methods assume most genes do not change, an assumption that fails exactly in the comparisons strain engineering produces, where a heterologous pathway at high expression consumes a measurable fraction of transcription. The significance threshold sets the error trade, and with tens of thousands of tests the multiple-testing correction is not a formality. Lee §9.4.1 makes the parallel point for metabolomics: peak picking, retention-time alignment, missing-value treatment and normalisation each change which features are called, and missing values in particular are not missing at random — they are missing where the analyte was lowest, which is systematically the condition of interest.

5. Independent component analysis recovers structure that differential expression cannot

Lee §2.6.2 sets out the method and its interpretation. Differential expression asks which genes changed between two conditions; ICA applied to a compendium of transcriptomes decomposes the expression matrix into independently modulated gene sets — iModulons — and their condition-specific activities. The structure matrix is the outcome of evolution and so represents distal causation; the activity matrix is the condition's own state and so represents proximal causation. The number to hold is the interpretive one in §2.6.2.2: because iModulons are mechanistic rather than merely statistical, the variance they explain is the fraction of the transcriptome explained by underlying regulatory mechanism, so iModulons accounting for 67% of the variance in the data explain 67% of the function of the transcriptional regulatory network — a claim principal component analysis cannot make about its components. Lee also notes the public bacterial transcriptome count has been doubling roughly every two years, which is what makes the method available at all, and that iModulons have been applied to the central metabolic engineering problem of how a host responds to heterologous expression, finding five classes of stress response activated.

6. Adaptive evolution produces a small number of mutations and a large deconvolution problem

Palsson Ch 26 gives the empirical shape. Significant adaptation occurs within the first 500 to 2,000 generations, though growth rate continues improving over tens of thousands, so an endpoint is wherever the experiment was stopped rather than an optimum. An endpoint clone often carries only two to six mutations, with the same genes hit in replicate experiments — unless a mutator arose, in which case there are many and they are uninformative. Most changes are point mutations, but up to a third are small insertions or deletions between 1 and 80 base pairs, and large duplications or rearrangements occur occasionally, which matters because a variant-calling pipeline tuned for substitutions will miss a third of the answer. Causality is established by reconstruction in the parent — one mutation, then pairs, then triples — and the cost is concrete: an allelic replacement in E. coli takes up to three weeks, serial introduction of up to six mutations has been done, and doing all the reconstructions of interest can take more than half a year.

7. The population frequency trajectory is the cheap substitute for reconstruction

Because known mutations can be screened for in frozen stocks from intermediate time points, the order and dynamics of fixation can be recovered from the archive without building anything. Palsson's observation is that the most causal mutations tend to fix first, and that endpoints sometimes show 100% allelic frequency for the causal ones, so the fixation order ranks candidates by likely contribution. That ranking is what makes a reduced reconstruction defensible: build the singles, and build only the pairs involving the two earliest fixers. The method's limit is also clear — the ordering is expected to hold if the mutations are relatively independent, so a reconstruction set that finds the singles do not sum is itself the evidence of epistasis, and that is a result rather than a failure.

8. A learning step is falsifiable or it is a figure

The DBTL cycle's weak joint is the L. The test for whether a measurement is doing work is written before the measurement: name the model assumption each possible outcome would reject. If the expression data show the pathway genes at the intended level and flux is still low, that rejects the transcription-limitation assumption and promotes translation, enzyme folding, cofactor supply or thermodynamic infeasibility. If the metabolite upstream of the bottleneck accumulates, that rejects the hypothesis that the bottleneck is upstream of itself. If neither changes, the measurement had no power and the next round should spend differently. Written in advance, this is an experiment; written afterwards, it is an interpretation, and the difference is whether any outcome could have been surprising.

Worked anchor

Budget the post-ALE analysis before running the evolution. The selection scheme is to be run for about 1,000 generations on the production phenotype, and the planning question is what the analysis costs if it works.

Take the common case: six mutations in the endpoint clone. Full deconvolution means every subset, which is 2⁶ − 1 = 63 strains. By size that is 6 singles, 15 pairs, 20 triples, 15 quadruples, 6 quintuples and the sextuple. At up to three weeks per allelic replacement, and reckoning the strains of size k as k serial replacements, the total replacement work is the sum over subsets of their size, which is 6 × 2⁵ = 192 replacements. At three weeks each that is 576 weeks of replacement work, which is Palsson's "more than half a year" only if a great deal runs in parallel — about twenty-five constructions at once to finish in a year. This is the number that makes full deconvolution a non-plan.

Now cut it with what Ch 26 says. Most causal mutations fix first, and frozen stocks from intermediate time points can be sequenced for known mutations without any construction at all. So: sequence six archived time points for the six known mutations — one sequencing run, days, no strain building — and obtain the fixation order. Build the six singles in parallel: six replacements, three weeks of calendar, one round of work. Build only the pairs involving the two earliest fixers: that is 1 pair between them plus 4 pairs of each with the remaining four, so 9 pairs, 18 replacements, a second three-week round. Total 24 replacements across two parallel rounds, roughly six to eight weeks of calendar against 192 replacements and a year.

What the cut costs is explicit. It tests all six single effects, so no causal mutation is missed outright. It tests nine of fifteen pairwise interactions, so six pairwise interactions are untested, all of them among the four later-fixing mutations. And it tests no higher-order interaction at all. The defence is that the untested interactions are between mutations that fixed late, which under the independence assumption contribute least — and that assumption is checkable from the results already obtained, because if the six single effects sum to the endpoint phenotype within measurement error then epistasis is small and the untested terms are small with it. If they do not sum, the shortfall is a measurement of total epistasis and buys the argument for spending on the remaining 39 strains.

One more line, because it changes the sequencing plan rather than the strain plan: up to a third of endpoint differences are indels of 1 to 80 base pairs and some are large duplications or rearrangements. A pipeline calling substitutions only would return four of the six mutations, and the deconvolution above would then be a tidy and confident answer to the wrong question. The variant calling has to include indel and copy-number detection before any of this arithmetic is worth doing.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • six mutations in the ALE endpoint, which is the upper end of Palsson's reported two-to-six range rather than a measurement
  • full deconvolution counted as every non-empty subset, 2⁶ − 1 = 63 strains, and the replacement work as the sum of subset sizes, 6 × 2⁵ = 192
  • an allelic replacement taken at Palsson's stated three weeks, treated as the same for every locus
  • reconstructions of the same size assumed to run in parallel and those within one strain serially
  • mutations assumed relatively independent, which is the condition under which fixation order ranks causality
  • frozen intermediate time points assumed to exist and to be sequenceable for known mutations without new construction
  • single effects assumed additive when tested against the endpoint phenotype, so a shortfall is read as total epistasis
  • up to a third of endpoint differences taken as indels of 1–80 bp, from Palsson §26.2, when judging what a substitution-only pipeline returns

Common misconceptions

  • That constraining a model with expression data and then finding it predicts the expression state is a validation. It is a restatement. The >98% agreement in §24.4 is evidence precisely because those optimal growth solutions were computed without the expression data; the same number obtained after constraining with it would mean nothing. Decide whether you are constraining or validating before running, and withhold the test case either way.
  • That a high transcript means a high flux. Four things break the chain, and the week's check question is built on them: translation and folding, so protein may not follow mRNA; post-translational regulation and allostery, so active enzyme may not follow protein; thermodynamics, so a reaction near equilibrium carries little net flux at any capacity; and substrate or cofactor supply, so capacity may exceed what arrives. Expression sets an upper bound on capacity and says nothing about which bound is binding.
  • That averaging expression across the genes of a reaction is a reasonable aggregation. It is wrong in opposite directions for the two GPR operators. A complex is an AND and is limited by its least-expressed subunit, so averaging invents capacity; isozymes are an OR and their capacities add, so taking a minimum deletes the redundancy that makes the gene non-essential. The logic in the GPR is doing arithmetic, not documentation.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Transcript high, flux low. Four explanations, and the one measurement that discriminates between them?

A. The transcript may not become protein, through translation initiation, folding or degradation. The protein may not be active, through post-translational modification, allosteric inhibition by a downstream product, or lack of a cofactor or metal. The reaction may be thermodynamically constrained, sitting near equilibrium so that net flux is small whatever the capacity. Or substrate may not be arriving, because the limitation is upstream and this enzyme is waiting. The single measurement that cuts across all four is ¹³C flux analysis, which reports the flux itself and so settles whether the premise is even true. If the question is instead which of the four, the most informative single measurement is targeted proteomics with the metabolite pool on either side of the step: protein present with substrate accumulating and product low points to activity or thermodynamics, protein present with substrate low points upstream, and protein absent points to translation. The mass action ratio against the equilibrium constant then separates thermodynamics from regulation.

Q. You have 1,000 generations of ALE and six mutations in the endpoint. Design the analysis within one quarter.

A. Start with the archive, not the bench. Sequence six frozen intermediate time points for the six known mutations, which takes days and no construction, and recover the fixation order; the most causal mutations tend to fix first and the endpoint may show them at 100% frequency. Then one parallel round of six single reconstructions in the parent, three weeks, phenotyped against parent and endpoint. Then one parallel round of the nine pairs involving the two earliest fixers, three weeks. That is about eight weeks and 24 allelic replacements against 63 strains and 192 replacements for the full set. State what is untested: six pairwise interactions among the late fixers and all higher-order terms. Test the assumption that licenses the cut by checking whether the six single effects sum to the endpoint phenotype — a shortfall is a quantitative measurement of total epistasis and is the argument for funding the rest. Before any of it, confirm the variant calling detected indels of 1 to 80 base pairs and copy-number changes, since up to a third of endpoint differences are not substitutions.

Q. Your reviewer says the before-and-after comparison in your omics-constrained model is circular. Is it, and what would make it not?

A. It is circular if the quantity compared is one the constraint determined. Constraining fluxes from expression and then reporting that the model's predicted reaction use matches the expression pattern is a restatement of the constraint. It stops being circular when the prediction is in a different observable from the constraint and was not available to it — growth rate on a substrate not in the training conditions, the identity of a gene the constrained model now calls essential, a by-product secretion rate, or a flux measured by labelling. The structural requirement is a withheld condition: constrain on a subset of conditions, predict the held-out one, and report the error there. This is the same discipline as week 38's held-out split, and it fails the same way for the same reason, which is that the easiest split to perform is the one that leaks.

Before any of them enters a notebook, a figure or a proposal, check it against BioNumbers or the primary source and cite that, not these notes. Treat the modules as a map of what matters and a scaffold for reasoning; treat the textbooks and the databases as the authority for values.

Week 40 — Escherichia coli as a platform

The reference host, and the week where four decades of published strain engineering are available to check your understanding against. The content divides cleanly: what the knowledge base actually buys, what acetate overflow costs and why it happens, and how to read a published titre. The week's hardest habit is the last one — every number in Lee's Ch 11 tables is a titre, a yield or a productivity measured under conditions the table does not state, and the first thing to do with any of them is recompute it as a fraction of the theoretical maximum you derive yourself. One of them comes out above 100%, which is the most useful thing in the chapter.

Core ideas

1. What "reference host" buys, stated as capability rather than reputation

Shuler §14.3.2 is the honest inventory: E. coli is chosen first when post-translational modification is unnecessary, because the knowledge base, host backgrounds, vectors and promoters are deeper than for any other organism. The quantities behind that are high growth rate, growth to over 50 g dry weight per litre, expression from strong vector–promoter combinations at roughly 25–50% or more of total protein, and cheap defined media — which multiply into volumetric productivity. Table 14.2 rates five hosts across growth rate, genetic systems, expression level, media cost, folding, glycosylation, proteolysis, secretion and safety; it is the skeleton of Artifact 24 and the matrix should keep its columns. Modelling depth is part of the same inventory: Lee §2.4 traces the E. coli genome-scale model from iJE660 through iJR904, iAF1260 and iJO1366 to iML1515, whose reconstruction covers 1,515 genes. No other organism has that lineage, which is exactly why every model you have built in phases 4 and 5 was built here.

2. The same inventory read as liabilities

Shuler §14.3.2 continues into what E. coli does badly, and the list is specific. It does not normally secrete protein: about 20% of its protein is translocated across the inner membrane, and excretion into the medium is the exception. High-level cytoplasmic expression triggers the heat-shock regulon, one response of which is increased proteolysis, in some cases fast enough to degrade product as quickly as it is made. More often the product forms an inclusion body of misfolded, inactive protein, recoverable by resolubilisation at a cost that varies enormously between proteins — and advantageous when resolubilisation is easy, because it simplifies the first purification steps. The cytoplasm may not form disulfide bridges, the product usually retains an N-terminal methionine, and lysing the cells releases lipopolysaccharide endotoxin, which is a purification problem rather than a nuisance when the product is injectable.

3. Acetate overflow is four mechanisms, and the assigned chapter does not contain any of them

This has to be said plainly because the week's curriculum points at Lee Ch 11 for it: the chapter mentions acetate six times, all incidentally, and has no section on overflow. The mechanisms, from the primary literature, are (i) flux imbalance — glucose uptake exceeding what the acetyl-CoA node, TCA cycle and respiratory chain can process, the classical account of el-Mansi and Holms, J Gen Microbiol 135:2875–2883 (1989); (ii) proteome allocation — fermentation is a cheaper way to make ATP per gram of protein invested than respiration, so at high growth rate excreting acetate maximises growth, which is Basan et al., Nature 528(7580):99–104 (2015), doi:10.1038/nature15765, and which predicts the threshold-linear rise of acetate with growth rate; (iii) loss of the scavenging route — acetyl-CoA synthetase is under carbon catabolite repression, so the cell stops reassimilating what it excretes, per Valgepea et al., BMC Syst Biol 4:166 (2010), doi:10.1186/1752-0509-4-166; and (iv) redox state — a high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio inhibits TCA flux and shifts transcription, per Vemuri et al., Appl Environ Microbiol 72(5):3653–3661 (2006). They are not alternatives. A fast-growing fed-batch culture has all four acting at once.

4. One countermeasure per mechanism, and they are not interchangeable

Against flux imbalance: controlled glucose feeding so that glucose never accumulates, which Shuler §14.3.2 names as the engineering contribution that made high-cell-density E. coli possible, coupled to consumption rate where that can be estimated on-line; or weakening uptake itself by moving from the PTS to a permease-plus-kinase route. Against proteome allocation: grow slower in the production phase, because the threshold is in growth rate — which is why a two-phase process with induction late is both a burden and an overflow decision. Against the repressed scavenging route: de-repress or overexpress acs so the excreted acetate is taken back. Against redox: raise respiratory or NADH-oxidising capacity, or aerate harder. Deleting pta and ackA removes the main excretion route and appears in Lee Ch 11 doing exactly that, in the 3-hydroxypropionate strain that reached 72 g L⁻¹ from glycerol at 1.8 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ — but it is a blunt instrument: it does not remove the cause, and the carbon reappears as pyruvate, lactate or formate unless something downstream takes it.

5. Ch 11 is organised by what the carbon becomes, and the tables are the chapter

§11.2 fuels, §11.3 chemicals, §11.4 materials, with no methods sections at all — tools, expression and genome engineering are elsewhere in the book, as week 33 to 35 already found. Tables 11.1 onward give product, titre, yield, productivity, carbon source, culture style, strategy and reference, and the spread within one product is as instructive as the differences between products: ethanol at 34.6 g L⁻¹ in flask from overexpressed Zymomonas mobilis pdc and adhII, then 54.4 g L⁻¹ at 0.57 g g⁻¹ in batch once the operon was integrated into pflB and frd deleted, then 63.2 g L⁻¹ from xylose in a tolerance-evolved derivative. 1-butanol runs from 0.552 g L⁻¹ in flask to 30 g L⁻¹ at 0.287 g g⁻¹ and 0.18 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ in fed-batch with in situ product removal. Isopropanol reaches 143 g L⁻¹ — in 240 hours, so 0.60 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹. Caprolactam sits at 79.6 µg L⁻¹. A titre without its culture style and duration is not a number you can use.

6. Recompute every reported yield against a ceiling you derived

Take the degree of reduction of substrate and product, divide, and you have the electron-limited ceiling; compare with the carbon-limited one and the smaller binds. Ethanol from glucose: both limits give 0.511 g g⁻¹. Table 11.1 reports 0.57 g g⁻¹ for the integrated KO11 strain on glucose — 112% of the maximum. The number is not wrong, it is differently based: the extra carbon comes from somewhere the yield definition excludes, almost always the complex medium, and occasionally from a yield taken on sugar consumed for product rather than on sugar consumed. This is the single most transferable skill in the week. A yield above its own ceiling means the basis is undeclared, and a yield of 0.45 g g⁻¹ from xylose in the same table — 88% of theoretical, which is excellent and plausible — tells you the chapter's numbers are not systematically inflated, just inconsistently defined.

7. Yim et al. 2011, criticised with the tools you now have

The 1,4-butanediol paper (Nat Chem Biol 7(7):445–452, cited in Lee Ch 11 as reference 63 for the 18 g L⁻¹ fed-batch result) was read in week 26 as a strain-design success. Three criticisms are available now and were not then. First, the algorithm did the pathway enumeration and the growth coupling, but the enzyme assignment, the expression tuning and the host background were hand work, so the paper demonstrates less about algorithmic design than its framing suggests — week 26's own distinction between a pathway and a strain. Second, 18 g L⁻¹ is a titre against an electron-limited ceiling of about 1.09 mol BDO per mol glucose, 0.55 g g⁻¹: the gap to be closed is in yield and rate, which the paper does not report in a form that lets you close it. Third, growth coupling is a property of a model under an objective, and the week 25 and 26 caveats apply — a coupled design is only coupled while the constraints it was computed under hold, and a seed train is not that environment.

8. Three situations in which E. coli is the wrong choice

When the product needs post-translational modification: Shuler §14.3.1 makes this the first branch in the decision, and no amount of E. coli engineering moves it. When the product is a secreted enzyme sold by the kilogram: a host that secretes natively removes the lysis, the inclusion-body and the endotoxin problems at once, which is week 42's argument for Bacillus. When the process environment itself is hostile — a low-pH acid fermentation, a solvent-containing broth, a feedstock of lignin aromatics — the tolerance of the host matters more than its tool stack, which is weeks 42 and 43. A fourth, weaker case is regulatory: for a food product the question is not what E. coli can express but whether an engineered Gram-negative with an endotoxin problem is a sensible thing to put in the process at all.

Worked anchor

What acetate costs, in carbon and in money, at a stated flux.

Basis: aerobic fed-batch on glucose, product of molar mass 90.1 (take 1,4-butanediol), 15% of consumed carbon leaving as acetate. Glucose 180.16 g mol⁻¹, six carbons; acetic acid 60.05 g mol⁻¹, two.

Carbon first. Per 100 mol of substrate carbon — 16.67 mol glucose, 3,003 g — 15 mol C leaves as acetate, which is 7.5 mol of acetate, 450 g. Nothing has been made from it.

Yield. If the diverted carbon would otherwise have gone to product at the same efficiency, a reported yield of 0.30 g g⁻¹ becomes 0.30/0.85 = 0.353 g g⁻¹ once the leak is closed. Against the electron-limited ceiling of 0.55 g g⁻¹ that is a move from 55% to 64% of theoretical.

Money. Glucose at $400 per tonne: at 0.30 g g⁻¹ the substrate cost is 1/0.30 = 3.33 kg glucose per kg of product, $1.33 kg⁻¹. At 0.353 g g⁻¹ it is 2.83 kg, $1.13 kg⁻¹. The saving is $0.20 per kg, $200 per tonne. For a bulk chemical selling near $1,800 per tonne that is 11% of revenue, and plausibly the whole margin; for a $20,000-per-tonne specialty it is noise. Acetate is a bulk-product problem.

What the arithmetic leaves out, and why it understates the penalty: acetate also inhibits growth. Shuler §14.3.2 says so without giving a threshold, and no number in the assigned reading supplies one, so the honest statement is mechanistic rather than numeric — acetic acid has pKₐ 4.76, so at the pH of a controlled fermentation most of it is dissociated, and the undissociated fraction that crosses the membrane and acidifies the cytoplasm is the week 2 derivation applied to a different acid. The real cost is the carbon above plus a growth-rate term and a titre ceiling that have to be measured in your own strain.

So the rank order of countermeasures follows from where your flux sits, not from a list: if glucose is accumulating, feed control is free and immediate; if it is not, and the culture is fast, the overflow is the proteome-allocation kind and only a slower production phase or more respiratory capacity touches it.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • 15% of consumed carbon leaving as acetate, and that carbon available to product at the same efficiency if the leak were closed
  • product taken as 1,4-butanediol, 90.1 g mol⁻¹, with an electron-limited ceiling of 0.55 g g⁻¹
  • glucose at $400 per tonne and a bulk selling price near $1,800 per tonne
  • no growth-rate or titre penalty from acetate included in the money figure
  • yields compared on grams per gram of glucose consumed, which is the basis Lee's tables do not state

Common misconceptions

  • That acetate overflow means the cell has run out of oxygen. It happens in fully aerated cultures with dissolved oxygen in excess, because the limit is the processing capacity downstream of acetyl-CoA and the proteome cost of respiration, not oxygen availability. Oxygen limitation is a fifth, separate cause with a different signature.
  • That deleting pta and ackA solves it. It removes the main excretion route, not the imbalance that fills it: the carbon re-emerges as pyruvate, lactate or formate, and the strain often grows worse, because acetate excretion was doing something for it.
  • That a published yield can be compared with a theoretical one without checking its basis. Lee's Table 11.1 reports 0.57 g ethanol per g glucose against a ceiling of 0.511 — 112% of theoretical. The yield is on an undeclared basis, almost certainly complex medium carbon; find the basis before you use any number from a table.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Name the four causes of acetate overflow and the specific countermeasure for each.

A. Flux imbalance at the acetyl-CoA node, where uptake outruns TCA and respiratory capacity — countered by controlled glucose feeding, or by weakening uptake itself. Proteome allocation, where fermentation is the cheaper ATP route per gram of protein at high growth rate — countered only by lowering growth rate in the production phase or by buying more respiratory capacity. Carbon catabolite repression of acetyl-CoA synthetase, which switches off reassimilation — countered by de-repressing or overexpressing acs. A high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio inhibiting TCA flux — countered by raising NADH oxidation or aeration. Deleting pta and ackA is not a fifth cause's countermeasure; it blocks the exit, and only helps if something downstream can take the carbon.

Q. A table reports 0.57 g ethanol per g glucose. What do you do?

A. Compute the ceiling before anything else: glucose to ethanol is limited at 0.511 g g⁻¹ by both carbon and electrons, so 0.57 exceeds it and the basis must be undeclared. The usual explanation is carbon from a complex medium counted into product but not into substrate; a second is a yield taken only over the sugar routed to product. Neither makes the strain bad — KO11 is a real strain — but the number cannot enter a comparison with a yield computed on total sugar, and nothing in the matrix should be populated from it without the basis stated beside it.

Q. You are asked to justify E. coli for a secreted industrial enzyme. What is the strongest argument against you, and what would you need to win?

A. That the host does not secrete: about 20% of E. coli protein crosses the inner membrane and excretion to the medium is the exception, so the process acquires lysis, inclusion-body recovery and endotoxin clearance — three unit operations a natively secreting host does not need, for a product whose price cannot carry them. To win you would need either a demonstrated excretion titre in your own hands in the same vessel, or a product that folds only in the cytoplasm, or a downstream train already built and paid for. Expression level alone does not win it, because the 25–50% of total protein that E. coli can reach is intracellular protein.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Ask whether E. coli is a sensible chassis for a cassava-derived product. Compare its pathway, transport, tolerance, and process fit with the organism(s) you already know.

Week 41 — Yeasts: Saccharomyces and the non-conventional species

The eukaryotic chassis, and the week where the host's advantages and its complications are the same fact. Compartments give yeast the membrane surface and the redox environment that cytochrome P450 chemistry needs, and they also mean every heterologous enzyme has an address that must be specified and can be wrong. The quantitative spine of the week is not in the assigned chapter: Lee Ch 18 contains no section on physiology or tools and does not mention the Crabtree effect once, so the respiratory-capacity arithmetic that governs every aerobic yeast process is taken from Shuler and derived here from first principles.

Core ideas

1. The Crabtree effect, stated as a capacity constraint rather than an effect

Shuler §5.1 gives it in one sentence: S. cerevisiae makes ethanol anaerobically and biomass aerobically, but even aerobically, at high glucose concentration, some ethanol forms — regulation by glucose as well as by oxygen. The engineering content is the consequence. Respiratory capacity per litre of broth is bounded by oxygen transfer, so sugar delivered faster than that capacity is fermented whatever the dissolved oxygen reads. Shuler's appendix on bakers' yeast draws the conclusion explicitly: production is run fed-batch to avoid the Crabtree effect, with feeding rates adjusted to maximise growth, and ethanol is reported as inhibitory to growth and as reducing biomass yield. The same appendix gives the numbers the calculation needs — about 0.5 g cells per g substrate, 1 g cells per g oxygen, µmax 0.6 h⁻¹, 30 °C, pH 6–7, dissolved oxygen above 2 mg L⁻¹, vessels of 50–350 m³ at a height-to-diameter ratio of 3.

2. Yeast against E. coli, on the properties that actually decide

Shuler's Table 14.2 is the only like-for-like comparison in the uploaded texts and it is blunt: E. coli excellent on growth rate, genetic systems, expression level and media cost; S. cerevisiae very good to excellent on the same, better on protein folding, capable of simple glycosylation and not complex, very good on secretion where E. coli is poor, and excellent on safety where E. coli is very good. Shuler §14.3.1 adds the decision rule: post-translational modification sends you to animal cells, simple glycosylation permits yeast or fungi, and food use favours a GRAS-listed organism such as S. cerevisiae because it simplifies regulatory approval. Neither claim is about elegance. The second is about calendar time and the first about whether the product works at all.

3. Compartments are addresses, and an address has a cost

Alberts Ch 12 — third edition, sections named rather than numbered — is the mechanism. Signal peptides are typically 15 to 60 residues and often cleaved; ER-destined proteins carry an N-terminal peptide including about 5 to 10 hydrophobic residues, mitochondrial ones a peptide alternating positive and hydrophobic residues, peroxisomal ones a three-residue signal at the carboxyl terminus, and nuclear ones an internal cluster of positive residues. Proteins without any of these stay in the cytosol by default. The chapter's import sections carry the cost that pathway engineering keeps rediscovering: translocation into the mitochondrial matrix requires both the electrochemical gradient across the inner membrane and ATP hydrolysis, and proteins enter in an unfolded state, drawn through by sequential binding to mitochondrial hsp70 and hsp60. An enzyme that will not unfold, or that needs a cofactor bound before it folds, is not a candidate for matrix targeting however good its signal sequence is.

4. Where to put a pathway, as a decision with four inputs

Lee Ch 18 shows the choice being made rather than theorised. Medium-chain fatty acyl-CoAs were hijacked from β-oxidation by compartmentalising the pathway in peroxisomes, setting a physical barrier against competing cytosolic alcohol and aldehyde reductase activity; elsewhere the chapter notes a pathway complicated by subcellular compartmentalisation because its upstream half sits in one compartment and its downstream half in another. The inputs are therefore: where the precursor already is, what competing enzymes are present there, whether the organelle's redox and pH suit the chemistry, and whether the enzymes can be delivered — which Alberts answers. Transport of intermediates across the membrane is the fifth input and the one most often assumed away.

5. Why yeast suits P450 chemistry, and what it costs in oxygen

Cytochromes P450 are membrane-bound and need a reductase partner and a supply of NADPH and molecular oxygen; the ER membrane provides the environment and S. cerevisiae provides the native machinery. Lee §18.2.5 is specific about the cost: when expressing heterologous P450s it is common practice to overexpress the reductase from the same organism, but poor coupling between reductase and P450 consumes NADPH and causes toxicity, as seen in artemisinic-acid-producing strains, which was improved by reducing reductase expression while overexpressing the plant cytochrome b5. Overexpressed P450s can also deplete heme and iron. So the advantage is real and the failure mode is cofactor drain, not catalysis — which makes it a week 31 control problem with an oxygen demand attached, since every P450 turnover consumes O₂ in a vessel whose oxygen transfer already caps the sugar feed.

6. The terpenoid numbers, and what the industrial one proves

Lee §18.2.5.3 gives the lineage: truncating HMG1 to its catalytic domain raised amorphadiene titres fivefold; an improved strain carrying three copies of tHMG1 reached over 40 g L⁻¹ in an ethanol pulse-feed process; Erg20 is the second rate-limiting step, and squalene synthase Erg9 is the competing drain, dynamically repressed by swapping its promoter for a copper-, methionine- or glucose-responsive one so the process runs growth-first and production-second. The β-farnesene strain is the one to study: a synthetic route to cytosolic acetyl-CoA with reduced ATP cost, balanced cofactor supply and increased flux to FPP raised production while requiring 75% less oxygen, reaching 130 g L⁻¹. That last clause is the lesson — at industrial scale the binding constraint was oxygen transfer, and the pathway was redesigned to need less of it.

7. The artemisinin case is about ten years, not about titre

The science in Ro et al., Nature 440:940–943 (2006) was artemisinic acid in engineered yeast; what followed was a decade of process and chemistry work before material reached the market, and then a market that did not need it at the price offered because agricultural supply recovered. Lee Ch 18 supplies the technical half of why: the CYP–CPR–cytochrome b5 coupling problem, heme and iron depletion, and the gap between a flask titre and the 40–130 g L⁻¹ class of strain that an industrial process needs. The non-technical half — semi-synthesis chemistry, regulatory qualification, and the price of the botanical route — is not in the assigned reading and should be cited from elsewhere when you write the case note, not inferred from the chapter.

8. The non-conventional yeasts, and where the week's reading runs out

Yarrowia lipolytica has a chapter of its own and it is the most quantitative in the book. Lee Ch 19 reports intracellular protein at about 50% of dry cell weight when lipid is below 10%, lipid bodies exceeding 50% of dry weight in engineered strains, and states a theoretical yield beside each product: citrate at 1.07 g g⁻¹ against 49 g L⁻¹ from 60 g L⁻¹ glucose under nitrogen limitation, 76% of theoretical; succinate at 110 g L⁻¹ and 0.53 g g⁻¹, 83% of theoretical; triacylglycerol at 61.7% of dry weight, an overall process yield of 0.195 g g⁻¹ and 0.143 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹. That is a storage organism with an electron sink, which is what a hydrophobic product wants. Pichia pastoris appears only in Shuler Table 14.2 — very good growth rate, excellent expression, low-cost media, simple glycosylation, very good secretion — and Kluyveromyces has no treatment anywhere in the uploaded texts beyond a line noting K. fragilis as an option when the substrate is lactose or pentose. The week's fourth objective cannot be met from the week's reading, and the matrix entry should say so rather than be filled from memory.

Worked anchor

The respiratory capacity limit, and the feed rate it implies.

Basis: Shuler's bakers' yeast appendix. Yield on oxygen 1 g cells per g O₂; yield on substrate about 0.5 g cells per g substrate; working volume in the 50–350 m³ class; dissolved oxygen held above 2 mg L⁻¹.

Step 1, the oxygen ceiling. The appendix reports kLa = 600 h⁻¹ for these vessels. With a driving force of about 7 mg L⁻¹ — air-saturated broth at 30 °C less the 2 mg L⁻¹ held in solution — the transfer rate is

OTR = kLa (C* − C) = 600 × 7 = 4,200 mg L⁻¹ h⁻¹ = 4.2 g O₂ L⁻¹ h⁻¹, which is 131 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹.

The same appendix also prints an oxygen transfer rate of 1 mole O₂ per litre per hour. That is 32 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹, about eight times what its own kLa and driving force give, and five to ten times the 100–250 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ that large stirred vessels are usually credited with. The two numbers in one paragraph cannot both be right; the kLa-derived one is the one consistent with everything else, and the printed molar figure should be treated as an error until checked against a second source.

Step 2, from oxygen to biomass. At 1 g cells per g O₂, 4.2 g O₂ L⁻¹ h⁻¹ supports 4.2 g cells L⁻¹ h⁻¹ of purely respiratory growth.

Step 3, the growth rate that permits. At X = 30 g L⁻¹, µ_max,resp = 4.2/30 = 0.14 h⁻¹ — against a µmax of 0.6 h⁻¹. The organism is capable of four times the growth rate the vessel can oxygenate, and the difference is exactly the room in which the Crabtree effect operates.

Step 4, the feed. At 0.5 g cells per g substrate, 4.2 g cells L⁻¹ h⁻¹ needs 8.4 g sugar L⁻¹ h⁻¹. In a 100 m³ working volume that is 840 kg h⁻¹ of sugar; as 50% w/w molasses, about 1.7 m³ h⁻¹ of feed. Any sugar delivered above that is fermented to ethanol, lost from the biomass yield and inhibitory at the titre it reaches.

Step 5, what it costs to get it wrong. Suppose 20% of the sugar overflows. At the respiratory yield of 0.5 g g⁻¹, that fifth would have made 0.1 g cells per g of total sugar; routed to ethanol at roughly 0.48 g g⁻¹ it makes ethanol that is not the product and that suppresses the yield of the rest. The biomass yield falls from 0.5 to about 0.4 g g⁻¹ — a 20% increase in sugar bill per tonne of yeast, from a feed pump setting.

The decision this supports: in any aerobic yeast process the feed rate is set by oxygen transfer, not by the strain's appetite, and the engineering options are to raise kLa, lower the biomass concentration, or lower the demand — which is what the β-farnesene strain did when it was rebuilt to need 75% less oxygen.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • Shuler's bakers' yeast appendix values: 1 g cells per g O₂, about 0.5 g cells per g substrate, μmax 0.6 h⁻¹, kLa 600 h⁻¹
  • an oxygen driving force of 7 mg L⁻¹, air-saturated broth at 30 °C less 2 mg L⁻¹ held in solution
  • oxygen transfer taken from kLa rather than from the 1 mol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ the same appendix prints, which its own kLa contradicts
  • biomass at 30 g L⁻¹ when the respiratory growth rate is computed
  • overflowed sugar routed to ethanol at about 0.48 g g⁻¹ with no further oxidation
  • molasses feed taken as 50% w/w fermentable sugar

Common misconceptions

  • That the Crabtree effect is a fermentation that happens when oxygen runs out. It happens with oxygen in excess and is triggered by glucose: the constraint is respiratory capacity per litre, set by oxygen transfer and by the cell's own respiratory proteome, so a culture at 30% dissolved oxygen can overflow to ethanol while the probe reads comfortable.
  • That compartmentalising a pathway is a matter of adding a targeting sequence. The enzyme must also reach the compartment in a form the import machinery accepts — mitochondrial import runs on the membrane potential plus ATP and takes proteins unfolded — and the intermediates must cross a membrane that may have no transporter for them.
  • That yeast's advantage over E. coli is genetic. Shuler rates E. coli higher or equal on growth rate, genetic systems, expression level and media cost. Yeast's advantages are folding, secretion, simple glycosylation, the membrane environment for P450s, GRAS status and a century of industrial familiarity — none of which is a genetic feature.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Why does yeast suit P450-dependent chemistry, and what does that cost you in oxygen demand?

A. P450s are membrane-bound heme enzymes needing a reductase partner, NADPH and molecular oxygen; the ER membrane and the native reductase and b5 machinery are present in S. cerevisiae and absent in E. coli, so the enzyme folds and couples where it would otherwise be inactive or inclusion-bodied. The cost is twofold. Each turnover consumes O₂ in a vessel whose oxygen transfer already caps the sugar feed — at kLa 600 h⁻¹ and a 7 mg L⁻¹ driving force that ceiling is about 4.2 g O₂ L⁻¹ h⁻¹ — and poor coupling between reductase and P450 burns NADPH without product and is toxic, which Lee reports for artemisinic acid strains and which was fixed by lowering reductase expression and raising cytochrome b5.

Q. Your feed pump is set from the strain's µmax. What happens, and what should it have been set from?

A. The strain will take the sugar and ferment what it cannot respire. At 30 g L⁻¹ biomass the vessel supports about 0.14 h⁻¹ of respiratory growth against a µmax of 0.6 h⁻¹, so a feed sized for the organism overshoots the vessel fourfold: ethanol accumulates, biomass yield falls from roughly 0.5 toward 0.4 g g⁻¹ at a fifth overflowing, and the ethanol inhibits what is left. The feed should be set from oxygen transfer — OTR divided by the yield on oxygen gives the respirable biomass rate, and dividing by the yield on substrate gives the sugar the vessel can actually oxidise, about 8.4 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ here.

Q. You want a heterologous three-enzyme pathway in the mitochondrial matrix. What do you check before designing the constructs?

A. Whether each enzyme can be imported at all: matrix import requires the electrochemical gradient and ATP, and the chain enters unfolded through hsp70 and hsp60, so an enzyme that needs a bound cofactor to fold, or that assembles as an obligate multimer before import, will not arrive functional. Then whether the precursor is in the matrix or has a transporter into it, whether the product can leave, and what competing matrix enzymes will do to the intermediates. Then the redox and pH of the compartment against the chemistry. Only after those four does the choice of targeting peptide matter, and that part is the easy part.

Week 42 — Corynebacterium, Bacillus and Pseudomonas

Three industrial workhorses, chosen for three unrelated reasons: an anaplerotic node and a tolerance that make C. glutamicum the amino acid organism, a secretion apparatus that makes Bacillus the enzyme organism, and a sugar catabolism that makes Pseudomonas putida an NADPH and robustness organism. The habit to build this week is product-host matching as an argument rather than a table — for each pairing, the one property of the host that the product needs, and the thing you give up by choosing it. The lysine arithmetic is the week's anchor because it is the one case where a published strain can be compared with a ceiling you derive in five lines.

Core ideas

1. C. glutamicum's case is a node, not a toolbox

Lysine carbon leaves central metabolism at oxaloacetate, so the anaplerotic reactions that refill it are the design target, and Lee §12.4.1.2 reports them being worked systematically: pyruvate carboxylase was identified as the major bottleneck, PEP carboxylase was engineered into a feedback-resistant variant to remove its allosteric regulation, and attenuating the competing TCA cycle helped — shown for strains with downregulated isocitrate dehydrogenase, pyruvate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase. One pathway-spanning design coupled the TCA cycle to lysine biosynthesis and used the high cycle flux to drive product formation. Connect this to the week 11 node map: the same three reactions you drew as anaplerosis there are the ones being tuned here, and the tuning is bidirectional — more flux into oxaloacetate, less flux around the cycle.

2. The redox half of the same strain, and why it is the harder half

Lysine costs 4 NADPH per molecule, which Lee states explicitly, and the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway emerged from ¹³C flux analysis as the major route supplying it. The interventions follow: amplified fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, overexpressed PP pathway enzymes, modified kinetics of the flux-controlling ones, and interruption of the competing EMP pathway. More recently an NADPH-forming glycolysis was built by installing an NADP⁺-dependent glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase — GapN from Streptococcus mutans, GapC from Clostridium acetobutylicum, or an engineered C. glutamicum GapA variant — and with GapN the strain produced lysine independently of the PP pathway altogether. That is the clearest example in the phase of a cofactor constraint being engineered away rather than optimised around.

3. LYS-12, and what 55% of substrate means against a ceiling

Lee §12.4.1.2 reports systems metabolic engineering taking the wild type to C. glutamicum LYS-12, producing 120 g L⁻¹ of lysine in 30 hours at a yield of 55%, against a world market of about 2.5 million tonnes a year. Those three numbers do different work: 120 g L⁻¹ over 30 h is 4.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹, which is a productivity a downstream train can be designed around; 55% is a yield whose basis — grams per gram of glucose — must be checked against a derived ceiling before it means anything, which the worked anchor does; and 2.5 Mt a year is why a yield point is worth a research programme at all. The chapter also lists lysine made from starch, xylose, arabinose, cellobiose, glycerol and mannitol, which is the substrate-flexibility argument for the host rather than a performance claim.

4. Bacillus is chosen for secretion and punished by differentiation

Lee §13.7 puts the benefit plainly — a natural efficiency at secreting large amounts of extracellular enzyme — and names the bottleneck as the versatile extracellular proteases that degrade most heterologous proteins, largely solved by multi-protease-deficient hosts carrying six or eight protease deletions, and by the genome-reduced strain PG10, which lacks 1,553 genes of wild-type 168 including eight major extracellular proteases, with enhanced translation credited for part of its advantage with difficult proteins. Against that sits §13.2: Bacillus responds to starvation by differentiating — motility, competence, biofilm, then the sporulation cascade, with early sporulation accompanied by the killing of sibling cells to delay commitment. Cells that have entered the cascade cannot resume vegetative growth quickly, and the SigB general stress regulon alone can exceed 150 genes, which is a metabolic burden that reduces productivity. That is the real argument for disabling sporulation: not spores in the product, but a subpopulation that has stopped making it.

5. The Bacillus species choice is a bioenergetic one

Lee §13.2 reports maintenance energy coefficients differing markedly between Bacillus species, and concludes that B. subtilis may not be the optimal cell factory bioenergetically, while the sporulation-deficient B. licheniformis T380B had the lowest maintenance coefficient of those compared, with more robust growth and weaker acetate overflow. The proposed explanation is mechanistic and testable: B. subtilis lacks the glyoxylate shunt, so it cannot reuse its own overflow metabolites, whereas B. licheniformis has it and grows on acetate, acetoin and 2,3-butanediol; introducing B. licheniformis isocitrate lyase and malate synthase into B. subtilis let it use acetate. Note what this costs you — the tools, the knowledge base and the genome-reduction work are all deepest in B. subtilis, so this is a tooling-against-physiology trade of exactly the kind the matrix is for.

6. Pseudomonas putida: the EDEMP cycle is the whole argument

Lee §14.2.2 describes glucose entering through oxidation to gluconate or 2-ketogluconate or by direct phosphorylation, converging at 6-phosphogluconate and feeding the Entner–Doudoroff route to pyruvate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. The distinctive feature is the EDEMP cycle — ED, pentose phosphate and an incomplete EMP route operating together, recycling triose phosphates back to hexose phosphates — which gives high NADPH regeneration rates, modulated by oxidative stress, and variable ATP and NADPH formation rates depending on how much is recycled. The stoichiometric basis: ED yields half the ATP per glucose that EMP does, but produces one NADH and one NADPH; net NADPH formation rises linearly with the recycling flux from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate upward. KT2440 lacks 6-phosphofructo-1-kinase, so linear glycolysis is interrupted — and a synthetic EMP glycolysis has been installed to restore ATP yield, which supported higher carotenoid content and yield than the native route.

7. What else P. putida brings, and what the chapter does not supply

Lee §14.2.1 gives a 6,181,873 bp genome with 5,592 coding sequences, no conspicuous virulence factors, biosafety level 1, remarkable resistance to oxidative stress, and the latest annotation listing 1,256 degradation reactions covering 32 carbon, 28 nitrogen and 29 phosphorus sources. Solvent tolerance is named — strains DOT-T1E and S12 are said to have effective defence mechanisms and enhanced robustness against organic solvents — but the mechanisms are not described in the chapter, so the week's session asking you to write them cannot be done from the assigned reading. Genome-reduced variants are reported with a NADPH/NADP⁺ ratio about 1.2-fold above wild type, which helped them overcome oxidative stress as well as raising anabolic capacity: a quantified robustness claim, and the kind of number the matrix should carry.

8. Product-host matching, written as reasons

Amino acids to C. glutamicum: the oxaloacetate node, the NADPH machinery, GRAS status and a 2.5 Mt market with incumbent processes. Secreted industrial enzymes to Bacillus: native secretion at scale removes lysis, refolding and endotoxin, at the price of proteases and differentiation. Aromatics, lignin-derived substrates and oxidative or solvent-stressed chemistry to P. putida: ED-driven NADPH, BSL-1 status and a degradation repertoire in the hundreds of reactions. Anything needing the deepest tool stack and the densest literature to E. coli. Anything needing compartments, folding or GRAS eukaryotic status to yeast. The matching rule that survives contact with a real project is negative: name the one host property the product cannot do without, then eliminate every host that lacks it, and only then compare the survivors on tools.

Worked anchor

Lysine's theoretical yield, derived, and LYS-12 measured against it.

Step 1, the carbon ceiling. Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ has six carbons, lysine C₆H₁₄N₂O₂ has six. Carbon alone permits 1 mol per mol, which is 146.19/180.16 = 0.81 g g⁻¹.

Step 2, the electron ceiling. Degrees of reduction, counting nitrogen as ammonia at −3: glucose γ = 6(4) + 12(1) − 6(2) = 24. Lysine γ = 6(4) + 14(1) − 2(2) + 2(−3) = 24 + 14 − 4 − 6 = 28. Electrons permit 24/28 = 0.857 mol per mol, which is 0.857 × 146.19/180.16 = 0.695 g g⁻¹.

The electron ceiling is the lower of the two, so lysine is an electron-limited product: its 28 electrons per molecule against glucose's 24 are why the strain needs 4 NADPH per lysine, and why NADPH supply is the recurring intervention in the chapter rather than carbon routing.

Step 3, the comparison. LYS-12 is reported at 55%, that is 0.55 g g⁻¹. Against the electron ceiling, 0.55/0.695 = 79%. Against the carbon ceiling, 68%. In molar terms 0.55 g g⁻¹ is 0.678 mol per mol.

Step 4, what the remaining 21% is. Not one thing. Biomass carbon, which a growth-associated product cannot avoid entirely; maintenance; the CO₂ released by the oxidative PP pathway in the act of making the NADPH — which is the specific loss that installing GapN removes, since an NADP⁺-dependent glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase makes NADPH in glycolysis without a decarboxylation; and residual by-product formation. A design that recovered even half of it would be worth, at 2.5 Mt a year, more than most of the pathway engineering in the chapter put together.

Step 5, the productivity check, because yield alone does not size a plant. 120 g L⁻¹ in 30 hours is 4.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹. For 50,000 t a year at 8,000 operating hours, that is 6.25 t h⁻¹, needing 1,560 m³ of instantaneous fermenter capacity at that productivity — before downtime, turnaround and seed trains, so perhaps 3,000–4,000 m³ installed. Doubling the productivity halves the vessel count; adding a yield point changes the sugar bill. Which of the two to chase is a question about where the money is, and for a feed amino acid at commodity price it is usually the yield.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • nitrogen supplied as ammonia, so lysine's degree of reduction is 28 and glucose's 24
  • no ATP limitation and no maintenance term in either ceiling
  • LYS-12's reported 55% read as grams of lysine per gram of glucose consumed
  • 8,000 operating hours a year and productivity sustained at the batch average of 4.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹
  • vessel sizing ignores turnaround, sterilisation, seed trains and downstream holdup
