Common misconceptions

  • That C. glutamicum beats E. coli for lysine because it is a better amino acid producer by nature. It wins on a combination the matrix has to state: an anaplerotic node whose flux can be raised, tolerance of high product and salt concentrations, GRAS status for a feed product, and seventy years of process and downstream investment. Its genetic tools are the weaker half of the comparison, which is the point of the question.
  • That sporulation must be disabled because spores contaminate the product. The process reason is prior: cells that enter the cascade stop producing and cannot resume vegetative growth quickly, and the stress regulons they switch on — over 150 genes for SigB alone — are a burden on the ones that have not.
  • That the Entner–Doudoroff pathway is simply a less efficient glycolysis. It yields half the ATP per glucose, which is a real cost, but produces NADPH where EMP does not, and in P. putida it runs as the EDEMP cycle whose recycling flux sets the NADPH-to-ATP ratio. The trade is adjustable, which is why KT2440 can be given a synthetic EMP glycolysis when ATP is what the application needs.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Why does C. glutamicum beat E. coli for lysine despite weaker genetic tools?

A. Because the properties lysine needs are physiological and regulatory, not genetic. The product leaves at oxaloacetate, and the anaplerotic node — pyruvate carboxylase as the identified bottleneck, PEP carboxylase made feedback-resistant, the competing TCA cycle attenuated — is tractable in this organism; the 4 NADPH per lysine are supplied by an oxidative PP pathway that has been systematically amplified and latterly bypassed with GapN; the organism tolerates the titres (120 g L⁻¹ in LYS-12) and is GRAS for a feed product; and the existing industrial base is enormous at 2.5 Mt a year. Weaker tools cost iteration speed, which matters most when the design space is unexplored — and for lysine it is the most explored space in the field.

Q. Quantify the NADPH advantage of the ED route and name a product class that benefits.

A. Per glucose, ED gives half the ATP that EMP gives but yields one NADH and one NADPH, and in the EDEMP cycle the net NADPH formation rises linearly with the recycling flux from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate upward, so the NADPH-to-ATP ratio is a tunable rather than a constant. The beneficiaries are NADPH-hungry chemistries: oxidative transformations driven by P450s and monooxygenases, aromatics from lignin-derived substrates, and anything run under oxidative stress — which is also why genome-reduced P. putida variants with a 1.2-fold higher NADPH/NADP⁺ ratio were better at withstanding it. The cost is ATP, which is why an ATP-hungry whole-cell biocatalysis argues for the synthetic EMP glycolysis instead.

Q. A client wants a secreted enzyme at 20 g L⁻¹ in Bacillus. What do you tell them, and what do you not know from the reading?

A. That the host choice is right for the reason that matters — native secretion removes lysis, refolding and endotoxin from the downstream train — and that the two things that will decide the project are proteolysis and population heterogeneity: use a multi-protease-deficient background, six or eight deletions or a reduced-genome strain such as PG10, and disable sporulation so that a starving subpopulation does not stop producing. What the assigned reading does not supply is the titre itself: Lee Ch 13 gives no secretion-capacity figure, so 20 g L⁻¹ can be neither confirmed nor refuted from it, and that number has to come from a vendor datasheet or a primary paper on a comparable protein, stated with its protein and its host.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Compare B. subtilis with another host relevant to cassava fermentation for a target product. What native physiology favors each, and what single experiment would make the comparison fair?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 43 — Lactic acid bacteria and food-grade hosts

The host group where regulatory status outweighs genetic convenience, and the one where the Lactobacillus volume gives depth most applicants will not have. Two threads run through the week and they pull against each other: genome reduction has made these organisms nutritionally fastidious, so the medium is expensive and is usually the largest line in the cost of goods for a low-value product; and food-grade status is worth enough, in market access and regulatory calendar, to pay for that medium anyway. Everything else — the expression toolbox, the acid-tolerance engineering, the surface layer — is downstream of those two facts.

Core ideas

1. Genome reduction is the organism's defining fact, and it is quantified

The Lactobacillus volume's Ch 1 gives the numbers: genomes range from 1.23 Mbp in L. sanfranciscensis to 4.91 Mbp in L. parakefiri; across 213 analysed genomes of lactobacilli and related LAB the pangenome holds about 45,000 gene families while only 73 genes, mostly for growth and replication, are shared by every strain analysed. The evolutionary pattern is loss of ancestral genes and metabolic simplification on moving into nutritionally rich environments, with horizontal acquisition on top. Larger genomes belong to free-living and nomadic species and smaller ones to host-adapted specialists, with both genome size and GC content lower in the specialists. Dairy isolates carry a very limited carbohydrate-utilisation repertoire — fewer PTS cassettes, and in L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus a high pseudogene count — because lactose is the only sugar that matters in milk.

2. What that costs you is a medium, not a capability

The same chapter states the consequence directly: the move to nutritionally rich environments lost the ability to biosynthesise many cofactors, vitamins and amino acids. Whatever the organism cannot make, you buy — as peptone, yeast extract, beef extract, corn steep or a defined amino acid blend — and you buy it per litre of broth, not per kilogram of product. That is why the medium cost per kilogram of product is the first calculation in any LAB process and the content of the worked anchor. It is also why the engineering question in this host is often subtractive in reverse: restoring a biosynthetic pathway to drop a medium component can be worth more than raising a titre.

3. Homolactic and heterolactic, stated quantitatively

Lee §15.1.2 is the reference: LAB have a simple central metabolism with a high glycolytic flux and a fermentative metabolism relying on substrate-level phosphorylation. Homofermentative strains — lactococci, streptococci, some lactobacilli — run the EMP pathway and produce almost exclusively lactic acid from readily fermentable sugars; heterofermentative ones — Leuconostoc, most pediococci, some lactobacilli — rely on the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway with a phosphoketolase and produce a mixture of lactate, acetate, ethanol and CO₂, with obligate heterofermenters lacking glycolytic enzymes entirely. On pentoses some strains use the non-oxidative PP pathway instead. And on slowly fermentable sugars the metabolism can shift to mixed-acid mode, giving lactate, formate, acetate, ethanol and CO₂. Connect this to the week 13 ledger: the homolactic route is 2 ATP and 2 lactate per glucose with no net redox imbalance, the heterolactic route is 1 ATP, 1 lactate, 1 CO₂ and one two-carbon product — so the yield difference is a third of the carbon and half the ATP, and which route the strain runs is not a detail.

4. Acid tolerance is where the process and the organism meet

Lee §15.3.2.2 states the process preference first: for lactic acid fermentations a pH below about 3.8 is wanted, because the acid is then in its free form and removable by electrodialysis or ultrafiltration, whereas neutralisation raises osmotic stress during the run and leaves a salt to be recovered from. Lactobacilli are naturally rather acid-tolerant and still need improving. The reported routes are all evolutionary rather than rational: genome shuffling of two mutagenised populations gave roughly a fivefold increase in tolerance to protonated lactic acid at pH 3.8 and a doubling of production at pH 4.0 without any prior genomic knowledge; L. delbrueckii Uc-3 reached 50 g L⁻¹ with no pH adjustment after UV mutagenesis, protoplast fusion and adaptive evolution; an adapted Leuconostoc mesenteroides tolerated 70 g L⁻¹ and made 76.8 g L⁻¹ under pH control, though by salt tolerance rather than acid tolerance proper. A hypermutator mutS background accelerated the evolution and gave better endpoints than wild-type parents.

5. The expression toolbox exists and its dynamic range is modest

The Lactobacillus volume's Ch 9 surveys it: low-copy replicons p256 and pWV01 and the high-copy pSH71 underlie most vectors; nisin-controlled expression, the NICE system built on PnisA induced by sub-inhibitory nisin, is the best-known inducible system, and pSIP, built on the sakacin promoters including PsppA, is its main alternative and avoids NICE's regulation problems in Lactobacillus species. Carbohydrate-responsive systems are reported with their ranges — a xylA promoter gave 60- to 80-fold induction by xylose where a second promoter gave only 3- to 10-fold — and FOS-, lac- and tre-based vectors are inducible by their sugar and repressed by glucose. Temperature-inducible and copper-inducible options exist. For constitutive expression, the Rud et al. library built by randomising the spacer between consensus −10 and −35 elements gave stable expression from low levels up to as high as or higher than induced PorfX in both L. plantarum and L. sakei, which makes it the practical choice for metabolic engineering. One cautionary result: differences in reporter output between constructs traced back to mRNA stability driven by unfavourable codons in the 5′ portion of the gene, which is week 34's lesson arriving in a new host.

6. The surface layer is both a tool and a proteome line item

The volume's Ch 5 covers envelope remodelling under osmotic stress and Ch 6 the S-layer proteins themselves: two-dimensional crystalline arrays of self-assembling subunits attached non-covalently to the cell wall, generally 40–200 kDa across bacteria and 25–71 kDa in lactobacilli, glycosylated in some species, and accounting for 10–15% of total cellular protein — among the most abundant proteins the cell makes. Two consequences. As a display platform it is unmatched: a strong native promoter, a secretion and anchoring route the cell already runs at high flux, and a surface presentation suited to mucosal delivery and whole-cell biocatalysis. As a burden it is a tenth of the proteome already committed, which is the week 31 allocation argument applied to a host where the budget is smaller to begin with.

7. Food-grade status is a regulatory argument with a technical tail

GRAS in the United States and the EFSA Qualified Presumption of Safety in Europe attach to organisms, and neither transfers automatically to an engineered derivative: the status shortens the path for the species, while the construct brings its own assessment, and an antibiotic-resistance marker or a heterologous sequence of uncertain provenance is exactly what that assessment looks for. Hence the food-grade toolbox — Ch 9 notes systems designed to meet self-cloning criteria with no antibiotic resistance genes — and hence the preference for chromosomal integration and complementation markers that week 33 costed. Note the honest limit: the assigned reading describes the tools, not the regulatory process, so the regulatory note the week asks for should be written from primary regulatory sources and flagged as outside the reading.

8. When a lactobacillus is the right answer, and when it is not

It is the right answer when the product goes into food or into a human as a live organism, when the organism's own acidification is part of the process's contamination control, when the substrate is a dairy or plant side-stream the host is already adapted to, or when surface display is the product. It is the wrong answer when the chemistry needs NADPH or oxygen, when the economics cannot carry a complex medium, when the product needs high-density aerobic fed-batch, or when the engineering programme needs fast iteration — transformation efficiency and marker availability in this group are week 33's constraint, not a formality. The matrix's LAB page is the one that needs a column the others do not: regulatory status, with the distinction between the species and the construct written into it.

Worked anchor

Medium cost per kilogram of lactate, complex against defined, with the prices flagged as the weakest part of the calculation.

Basis: a complex LAB medium with 20 g L⁻¹ of complex nitrogen source — peptone plus yeast or beef extract, as MRS-type media use — at an assumed food-grade price of $4 kg⁻¹; glucose at $400 t⁻¹; salts and buffer at $0.01 L⁻¹. Product at 50 g L⁻¹, which is the titre Lee §15.3.2.2 reports for an acid-tolerant L. delbrueckii strain fermenting without pH adjustment. Yield on sugar 0.90 g g⁻¹, within the range the Lactobacillus volume's Ch 4 reports for homolactic strains.

Per litre of broth: complex nitrogen 20 g × $4 kg⁻¹ = $0.080 glucose 55.6 g × $0.40 kg⁻¹ = $0.022 salts and buffer = $0.010 total = $0.112 per litre

Per kilogram of lactate, at 50 g L⁻¹, that is 20 litres of broth: $2.24 kg⁻¹, of which $1.60 is the complex nitrogen source — 71% of the medium cost, and 3.6 times the sugar bill.

Against a lactic acid price in the $1.5–2.0 kg⁻¹ range, the medium alone exceeds the revenue. The process as costed does not close, and no titre improvement available in the chapter closes it: at 76.8 g L⁻¹, the best pH-controlled titre reported, the medium cost falls to $1.46 kg⁻¹ only if the complex component is unchanged per litre — which it is not, since a higher titre needs more nitrogen.

The defined-medium comparison. A host that makes its own amino acids and vitamins — E. coli on glucose and salts, at roughly $0.05 L⁻¹ including trace elements and vitamins — at the same 0.90 g g⁻¹ and 50 g L⁻¹ pays about $0.05 + $0.022 = $0.072 per litre, $1.44 per kilogram, of which the sugar is now a third. Note that this salts line is five times the complex medium's, and deliberately so: in the complex medium the extract is supplying the trace metals and vitamins, so they are already paid for inside the $4 kg⁻¹ nitrogen source and must not be counted twice. The gap is $0.80 per kilogram, and it is the price of the 73-gene core and the lost biosynthetic pathways.

So the trade, stated as a decision rather than a lament: the complex medium costs roughly $800 per tonne of product more than a defined one. A food-grade organism is worth that if the product cannot be made in a non-food-grade host at all, or if the regulatory calendar it shortens is worth more than $800 a tonne — which for a food ingredient at modest volume it often is, and for commodity lactic acid it is not, which is why commodity lactic acid is made by organisms selected for acid tolerance and cheap media rather than for food-grade status.

The honest caveat is the prices: all three are assumptions at order-of-magnitude accuracy, and the conclusion is sensitive to the complex nitrogen price in a way it is not sensitive to anything else. Before this number enters a proposal, quote the actual components.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • complex nitrogen source at 20 g L⁻¹ and an assumed food-grade price of $4 kg⁻¹
  • glucose at $400 per tonne, salts and buffer at $0.01 L⁻¹
  • lactate at 50 g L⁻¹ and a yield on sugar of 0.90 g g⁻¹
  • medium composition unchanged per litre when the titre changes
  • defined medium for the comparison host at about $0.05 L⁻¹ including trace elements
  • no credit for the regulatory or market value that the food-grade status itself carries
  • all three prices are order-of-magnitude assumptions and the conclusion is sensitive to the first

Common misconceptions

  • That food-grade status transfers to an engineered strain. GRAS and QPS attach to the organism; the construct is assessed on its own, and markers, vectors and heterologous sequences are exactly what is assessed. The status buys a shorter path for the species, not an exemption, which is why the food-grade toolbox is built around self-cloning criteria and the absence of antibiotic resistance genes.
  • That LAB are nutritionally demanding because they are delicate. They are demanding because they have discarded biosynthetic pathways they did not need in a rich niche — a 73-gene core across 213 genomes, with cofactor, vitamin and amino acid biosynthesis among the first losses. It is an adaptation, and it is why the medium, not the strain, is the cost centre.
  • That a low-pH fermentation is simply harder. It is harder for the organism and much cheaper downstream: below about pH 3.8 the acid is protonated and can be recovered by electrodialysis or ultrafiltration, where a neutralised fermentation adds osmotic stress during the run and leaves a salt to be split afterwards. The pH is a downstream decision made in the fermenter.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Name two reasons to choose a lactobacillus despite weaker tools, and the cost each choice carries.

A. First, food-grade status: for a product going into food or into a person as a live organism, a GRAS or QPS species shortens the regulatory path in a way no amount of engineering in a non-food-grade host can. The cost is that the status covers the species and not the construct, so the toolbox narrows to self-cloning, marker-free, integration-based designs — the slowest tools available. Second, niche fit: the organism is already adapted to the substrate and to the acidified, anaerobic process, and its own acidification is part of the contamination control. The cost is nutritional, and it is quantified — a complex medium runs roughly $2.2 per kilogram of lactate against $1.4 on a defined medium, most of it the complex nitrogen source, which for a commodity acid is the whole margin.

Q. A strain is reported making lactate at 0.93 g per g of sugar. What do you check before putting it in the matrix?

A. That the basis is sugar consumed and not sugar supplied, since conversion and yield are reported interchangeably in this literature; that the medium is not contributing carbon, which it does whenever whey, yeast extract or stillage is in it — the homolactic ceiling is 1.0 g g⁻¹ and a complex medium can push an apparent yield towards it or past it; whether the strain is homofermentative, because a heterofermentative route caps the yield near 0.5 g g⁻¹ and a mixed-acid shift lower still; and whether the number is for one isomer or for total lactate, which decides whether the product is polymer-grade at all.

Q. You are asked to display an antigen on the surface of L. plantarum. What does the reading support, and what does it not?

A. It supports the route: Ch 9 covers secretory expression and surface display, and Ch 6 gives the S-layer as a self-assembling array that is already 10–15% of total cellular protein, so the promoter, the secretion machinery and the anchoring chemistry are all running at high flux natively. It supports the expression choice too — the Rud constitutive library reaches induced-PorfX levels and avoids an inducer that a live product cannot carry, where NICE needs nisin and pSIP needs a peptide. What it does not support is any claim about immunogenicity, dose or persistence in vivo, and it gives no display density; those come from the therapeutic literature, and the matrix entry should carry the capability without the efficacy.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. For L. plantarum or another lactic acid bacterium in your work, connect acid formation and pH control to carbon balance and product tolerance. Which process change could alter physiology as well as pH?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 44 — Clostridia, actinomycetes, fungi and photosynthetic hosts

The specialists, and the week where the matrix has to stop being a list of organisms and start being a comparison on one basis. Four host classes, each of which exists in industry because it does one thing no model host can: clostridia ferment gases and make four-carbon solvents anaerobically, actinomycetes carry the assembly-line enzymes that make most of the antibiotics in the pharmacopoeia, filamentous fungi secrete protein at concentrations nothing else approaches, and photosynthetic cells fix their own carbon. Each carries a correspondingly specific difficulty, and in three of the four cases the difficulty is a transport problem rather than a genetic one — gas into liquid, oxygen into a viscous broth, photons into a volume. The week's quantitative task is to put all four on the same productivity axis as the hosts of weeks 40 to 43, which requires deriving the photosynthetic ceiling, because no assigned chapter contains it.

Core ideas

1. The specialist bargain, and two session pointers that do not resolve

Say the bargain plainly before the detail: you accept a worse tool stack, a harder vessel, or a lower rate in exchange for a capability the model hosts do not have, and the trade is only worth making when that capability is the thing the product cannot do without — the negative matching rule from week 42. Two of this week's sessions cannot be run as written. Lee Ch 16 has four sections — §16.1 introduction, §16.2 aims of metabolic engineering in Clostridium, §16.3 genomic editing, §16.4 genetic parts — and there is no section on clostridial metabolism and none on gas fermentation, so the ABE stoichiometry and the acetogenesis energetics have no source in the chapter and are derived below. Lee Ch 21 contains no areal or volumetric productivity figure anywhere, so the session asking you to extract them cannot be run either; the ceiling is derived in the anchor instead. Both gaps are recorded in the README.

2. Clostridia: the record, and the two paradigms that frame it

Lee §16.1 gives the history — acetone first, for cordite in the First World War, by the Weizmann process on potato starch with C. acetobutylicum, and butanol second, as the better fuel. §16.2 gives the numbers, and they are organised around a comparison worth keeping. Import the clostridial butanol pathway into E. coli and the first attempts gave under 1 g L⁻¹; subsequent engineering reached 15–20 g L⁻¹ in batch and 30 g L⁻¹ with in situ product removal. The native host, unengineered, makes about 15 g L⁻¹ in batch; a chemically mutagenised strain makes 19 g L⁻¹, or 30 g L⁻¹ with in situ recovery; and a rationally engineered strain in continuous fermentation reaches 14 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹. That is the clearest statement in the phase of the two competing design paradigms — move the trait to a tractable chassis, or make the native producer tractable — and after two decades the chassis route has pulled level on titre and not on rate.

3. ABE stoichiometry and its ceiling, derived because the chapter has none

n-Butanol is C₄H₁₀O: degree of reduction 4(4) + 10(1) − 1(2) = 24, exactly glucose's 24. Carbon permits 6/4 = 1.5 mol per mol; electrons permit 24/24 = 1.00. Electrons bind, so the ceiling is 1 mol per mol, 74.12/180.16 = 0.411 g g⁻¹, and the two carbons that cannot come along leave as CO₂ — which is the carbon escape §16.2 names as limiting biofuel viability. Against that ceiling the native 15 g L⁻¹ titre is a titre, not a yield, and the chapter gives no yield beside it, so the matrix entry must carry the gap. The redox reason the route is tight: two acetyl-CoA condense to acetoacetyl-CoA and four reducing equivalents are needed to reach butanol, while clostridial pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase disposes of electrons as H₂. Every mole of H₂ evolved is electrons that could have been butanol, which is why solvent yields rise when hydrogenase flux falls and why §16.2's quintuple deletion of the hydrogen, acetate, lactate and formate routes in C. thermocellum doubled the ethanol yield.

4. Gas fermentation: the bookkeeping is clean, the transfer is the problem

The Wood–Ljungdahl pathway is named in §16.2 and not described, so do the bookkeeping yourself; it is exact. Acetate, as acetic acid C₂H₄O₂, has degree of reduction 8. Carbon monoxide has 2, so four CO carry exactly the eight electrons an acetate needs, and the carbon balances as four CO giving two carbons in acetate and two as CO₂. Hydrogen has 2 per molecule, so four H₂ plus two CO₂ give the same acetate with no carbon lost. Ethanol has 12, so six CO, or six H₂ plus two CO₂. Nothing here is limiting. What is limiting is mass: four H₂ is 8 g of gas per 60 g of acetate, and hydrogen is about fifty times less soluble in water than oxygen, so a gas fermenter is a gas–liquid transfer device before it is a reactor, and the week 41 oxygen ceiling returns in a harder form. The thermodynamics is the other half and no assigned chapter supplies it: take standard formation energies from Lee Ch 7 §7.2.2 rather than from memory. Note the energetic position qualitatively — acetogens conserve so little energy per acetate that they live on a chemiosmotic gradient rather than on substrate-level phosphorylation, which is why titres in this group are low and why §16.2 reports that installing solventogenesis in C1 fermenters and the WLP in solventogens have both proved difficult.

5. Actinomycetes: clusters, assembly lines, and the 10% number

Lee Ch 17 §17.1 is the case for the host: Streptomyces and relatives gave erythromycin, tetracycline, nystatin, ivermectin, bleomycin, doxorubicin, lovastatin, tacrolimus, rapamycin and spinosyn, most between 1940 and the late 1960s. §17.3 is the mechanism, in three steps. Precursors first, usually primary metabolites — glucose, proteinogenic amino acids, malonyl-CoA — with the enzymes for unusual building blocks carried inside the cluster itself. Assembly second: a multimodular polyketide synthase condenses (methyl)malonyl-CoA extender units by chemistry that closely resembles fatty acid biosynthesis, as for the erythromycin skeleton in Saccharopolyspora erythraea, while nonribosomal peptide synthetases do the equivalent for peptides such as vancomycin. Tailoring third — oxidations, reductions, halogenations, methylations, ring formations. The kirromycin example in §17.3 shows all three at once, with the cluster carrying kirD for β-alanine and kirN for ethylmalonyl-CoA because primary metabolism does not supply enough of either. The whole of this is why the host is chosen: the precursor pools, the phosphopantetheinylation machinery and the GC-rich expression context are already there.

6. Why a cluster does not simply move, with the four reasons the chapter gives

§17.5.1 states the success rate for heterologous expression as about 10% for non-Streptomyces clusters and 30% for Streptomyces clusters in a Streptomyces host, and attributes the failures to incompatible regulatory systems, missing triggering signals or their receptors, insufficient precursor supply and product toxicity. §17.5.2 and §17.4.3 add the mechanics: most clusters exceed 20 kb and some exceed 100 kb — the pristinamycin cluster is 210 kb — actinobacterial DNA is 65–75% GC, which defeats long-range PCR, so clusters are cloned by cosmid or fosmid libraries to 45 kb, BAC libraries to 200 kb, or by TAR, LLHR and CATCH, all three of which handle over 100 kb; and rule-based genome mining cannot find a pathway whose chemistry has not been described before. §17.5.1 also gives the host-selection criteria as a list to lift straight into the matrix: transformability, absence of native restriction systems, fast disperse growth, small genome, detectable product levels and an existing tool set, improved further by deleting the host's own clusters to clean the chemical background — S. coelicolor M145 with four clusters removed, S. albus Del14, S. chattanoogensis L321. Non-actinomycete hosts have expressed actinobacterial clusters, E. coli for erythromycin among them, but §17.5.1 is explicit that the GC mismatch and the missing precursor machinery have to be engineered in first.

7. Filamentous fungi secrete at a scale nothing else reaches

This is the single most decisive number in the phase. Lee §20.5.5 reports Trichoderma reesei cellulase at 30 g L⁻¹ for the Rutgers strain Rut-C30 in the 1980s and 100 g L⁻¹ from hypersecreting strains obtained by directed evolution — the highest protein secretion titres ever reported, exceeding what bacterial, yeast or mammalian factories achieve by 10- to 10,000-fold, those sitting at milligrams per litre to a few grams per litre. That last clause also fills the gap week 42 left open: Lee Ch 13 gives no Bacillus secretion figure, and this is the comparison that bounds it. The rest of §20.5 is equally quantitative: Aspergillus niger makes about 80% of world citric acid by submerged fermentation at 0.95 g g⁻¹ glucose against a stated theoretical 1.067 g g⁻¹; A. terreus reaches 140 g L⁻¹ itaconate but only about 1 g L⁻¹ lovastatin from adjacent clusters in the same genome; Penicillium chrysogenum production strains carry up to 50 copies of the penicillin cluster and make up to 55 g L⁻¹; A. oryzae reaches 127 g L⁻¹ malate and an engineered Thermothelomyces thermophilus 200 g L⁻¹ from crystalline cellulose; monacolin J reaches 5.5 g L⁻¹ in A. terreus against 75 mg L⁻¹ in S. cerevisiae and 600 mg L⁻¹ in P. pastoris. Recompute the citric acid figure before anything else: 0.95/1.067 is 89% of theoretical, the highest ratio anywhere in this phase, and it is why strain programmes on that product are now about uncoupling production from growth rather than about flux.

8. Morphology is the fungal process variable, and rheology is why

Lee §20.7 and Doran §7.7–7.8 are the same subject from two directions. Pellets resist shear and keep the liquid phase at low viscosity, but oxygen and substrate transport into the core is limited by the hyphal network; dispersed mycelia grow fast and transport well but raise viscosity, cut volumetric gas–liquid mass transfer and are shear-sensitive. §20.7 is honest that no canonical coupling of morphology to product formation exists and that the literature contradicts itself, while noting the pattern for A. niger that a low morphology number — a dispersed form, on a scale where 0 is a line and 1 a perfect circle — correlates with protein production and a high one with citric acid. Doran supplies the physics: mycelial suspensions are modelled as pseudoplastic or, with a yield stress, Bingham or Casson plastic, while dilute broths, yeast and non-chain-forming bacteria are Newtonian; in a batch of Endomyces the flow behaviour index starts at 1 and falls while the consistency index rises throughout, so apparent viscosity climbs as the culture does the thing you want. §7.8 gives the levers — the Vand equation holds for yeast and spores only to about 14 vol% solids, a doubling of plant-cell concentration can raise apparent viscosity up to 90-fold, a pullulan broth can reach 24 000 cP at 1 s⁻¹, and raising medium osmotic pressure lowers turgor and makes hyphae more flexible and the broth thinner. The engineering results in §20.7 follow the same logic: downregulating chitin synthase raised citric acid and penicillin titres by 40%, upregulating cell-cycle genes raised malate by about 50%, and a hyperbranching A. niger with glucoamylase under a Tet-on switch secreted 400% more enzyme, all four with smaller pellets or smaller dispersed mycelia than their parents.

9. Photosynthetic hosts, and where Ch 21 actually stands

Lee Ch 21 is a plant and algal metabolic engineering chapter, not a productivity chapter, and the honest matrix entry says so. What it gives: Rubisco carboxylates at only 2–10 CO₂ molecules per second and nevertheless fixes some 250 billion tonnes of CO₂ a year; photorespiration costs C3 crops a 20–50% yield penalty; engineering the whole photorespiratory bypass into the chloroplast of field-grown tobacco raised postharvest dry mass by 24% over two seasons, and accelerating non-photochemical quenching raised it by 15%, against a global breeding trend under 2% a year. Those are agronomic yield increases on a mass-of-crop basis, not reactor productivities, and nothing in §21.6 on microalgae supplies the latter. So the like-for-like comparison the artifact needs has to be derived from the photon flux, which the anchor does, and the answer is not close. Lee Ch 22 sits in the same position for environmental applications: §22.5's bottlenecks are real and specific — construct portability between genetic backgrounds, expression parts that work across hosts, genetic stability against mutation and loss, and the absence of any reliable model of how an engineered organism or its DNA propagates, which makes environmental risk assessment unanswerable — but there is no economics anywhere in the chapter, so the session asking where the economics closes today cannot be answered from it.

Worked anchor

The photosynthetic productivity ceiling, derived from photons, against heterotrophic fermentation.

No assigned chapter gives an areal or volumetric productivity for photosynthetic production, so derive the ceiling from the only quantity that cannot be engineered: the photon flux onto the ground.

Step 1, photons available. Take a good site at an annual-average total irradiance of 200 W m⁻², which is 17.3 MJ m⁻² d⁻¹. Photosynthetically active radiation is about 43% of that, 86 W m⁻². A mole of photons at a 550 nm mean carries hc/λ × N_A = (6.626×10⁻³⁴ × 3.00×10⁸ / 550×10⁻⁹) × 6.022×10²³ = 218 kJ. So the PAR flux is 86/218 000 = 3.95×10⁻⁴ mol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, which over a full day is 34.1 mol photons m⁻² d⁻¹.

Step 2, carbon fixed. At a quantum requirement of 10 photons per CO₂ — the usual minimum is 8, and 10 is the generous end of what is measured — that is 3.41 mol CO₂ m⁻² d⁻¹. Biomass as CH₁.₈O₀.₅N₀.₂ weighs 24.6 g per C-mol, so the ceiling is 3.41 × 24.6 = 84 g dry biomass m⁻² d⁻¹.

Step 3, the sanity check, which matters more than the number. At roughly 20 kJ g⁻¹ of biomass that is 1 680 kJ m⁻² d⁻¹ out of 17 300 in, or 9.7% of incident solar energy. No crop and no algal culture has ever been measured near 10%, and Ch 21's own 20–50% photorespiration penalty for C3 plants is one reason. So 84 g m⁻² d⁻¹ is a floor on the cost, not a target: apply the photorespiration penalty and a respiration term and the realisable figure is of order 30–40 g m⁻² d⁻¹, and the best measured outdoor values are lower still and are not in the assigned reading.

Step 4, convert to the axis the matrix uses. An open pond 0.30 m deep holds 300 L m⁻², so 84 g m⁻² d⁻¹ is 0.28 g L⁻¹ d⁻¹, or 0.012 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹; at the realisable 30 g m⁻² d⁻¹ it is 0.004 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹. A tubular photobioreactor with a 0.05 m light path holds 50 L m⁻² and reaches 1.7 g L⁻¹ d⁻¹, 0.070 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹, at the ceiling.

Step 5, the comparison. C. glutamicum LYS-12 runs at 4.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ (week 42, Lee §12.4.1.2) and a continuous clostridial butanol process at 14 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ (Lee §16.2). Against the open-pond ceiling that is a factor of 340; against the realisable pond, about 1 000; against the thin photobioreactor at its own ceiling, 57. Two to three orders of magnitude, and the direction of the error is known, since the fermentation numbers are measured and the photosynthetic ones are ceilings.

Step 6, what sets the gap, which is the examinable part. Photon flux is capped per unit area at 34 mol m⁻² d⁻¹ by the sun; substrate flux into a fermenter is capped per unit volume only by what the pumps and the oxygen transfer allow. Light therefore makes the reactor a surface and sugar makes it a volume, and the only way to close the gap is to buy more illuminated surface per unit volume — which is what a photobioreactor is and what it costs. Scale it once to see the shape: at 30 g m⁻² d⁻¹ a hectare yields about 110 t of dry biomass a year, so matching the 50 000 t a year of product that needed roughly 1 560 m³ of instantaneous fermenter capacity in week 42 would take of order 900 hectares even if half the biomass were product.

So the honest matrix entry for photosynthetic hosts is: unique capability, since nothing else makes product from CO₂ and light with no sugar bill at all; volumetric productivity two to three orders below heterotrophic fermentation for reasons that are physical and not genetic; and therefore viable where the product is high-value per hectare or where the sugar that a heterotroph would need is itself the binding cost.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • annual-average total irradiance 200 W m⁻² (17.3 MJ m⁻² d⁻¹), PAR taken as 43% of it
  • a 550 nm mean photon wavelength, so 218 kJ per mole of photons
  • all incident PAR absorbed by the culture, with no reflection, transmission or saturation loss
  • 10 photons per CO₂ fixed, against a usual minimum of 8
  • biomass as CH₁.₈O₀.₅N₀.₂ at 24.6 g per C-mol and about 20 kJ g⁻¹
  • pond depth 0.30 m and photobioreactor light path 0.05 m, with the whole volume illuminated
  • the 30-40 g m⁻² d⁻¹ realisable figure is the photon ceiling less Ch 21's stated C3 photorespiration penalty and a respiration term, not a measured value
  • heterotrophic comparators taken as measured: 4.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ for LYS-12 and 14 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ for continuous clostridial butanol
  • the 900-hectare figure assumes half of the dry biomass is product

See the misconception below and the README.

Common misconceptions

  • That gas fermentation is limited by carbon. The electron and carbon bookkeeping closes exactly — four CO, or four H₂ plus two CO₂, per acetate — and what binds is transfer and energy: hydrogen is roughly fifty times less soluble than oxygen, so the reactor is a gas–liquid contactor first, and acetogens conserve so little energy per acetate that they depend on a chemiosmotic gradient rather than substrate-level phosphorylation. Treat a syngas process as a mass-transfer design with a thermodynamic constraint, not as a pathway problem.
  • That fungal pellets are the better morphology, or that dispersed growth is. Lee §20.7 states that no canonical coupling of macromorphology to product formation exists and that reports contradict each other; the only consistent pattern reported for A. niger is that a dispersed form correlates with protein secretion and a pelleted one with citric acid. Pellets trade transport into the core against low broth viscosity, and which side of that trade is right depends on whether the product is oxygen-hungry or shear-sensitive.
  • That cyanobacterial and algal productivity is low because the organisms are under-engineered. The ceiling is set by photon flux per unit ground area — about 34 mol photons m⁻² d⁻¹ at a good site — which no genetic intervention raises. Engineering can raise the fraction of those photons that reach product, which is what Ch 21's 24% and 15% field gains are, but the two-to-three-order gap to heterotrophic volumetric productivity is geometric: light makes the reactor a surface and sugar makes it a volume.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. How far below heterotrophic fermentation is cyanobacterial volumetric productivity, and what sets that gap?

A. Two to three orders of magnitude. From 34 mol photons m⁻² d⁻¹ at a good site and 10 photons per CO₂, the ceiling is about 84 g dry biomass m⁻² d⁻¹, which in a 0.30 m pond is 0.012 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ and in a 0.05 m photobioreactor 0.070 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹; realisable figures are several-fold lower, since 84 g m⁻² d⁻¹ corresponds to about 10% of incident solar energy and nothing has been measured there. Against 4.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ for LYS-12 and 14 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ for continuous clostridial butanol, that is a factor of 340 to 1 000 for a pond and about 57 for a thin reactor at its ceiling. What sets it is geometry, not genetics: the photon flux is capped per unit area, so the illuminated surface per unit volume is the only lever, and buying more of it is what a photobioreactor costs money for.

Q. A collaborator has a 90 kb biosynthetic gene cluster from a Nonomuraea isolate and proposes to express it in E. coli. What do you tell them?

A. That the base rate is against them: Lee §17.5.1 puts heterologous expression success at about 10% for non-Streptomyces clusters even in a Streptomyces host, and attributes failures to incompatible regulatory systems, absent triggering signals, insufficient precursor supply and toxicity. In E. coli they take on two further problems the chapter names explicitly — the GC mismatch, since actinobacterial DNA is 65–75% GC, and the absence of the full secondary-metabolite machinery, so precursor supply has to be engineered in first. At 90 kb the cluster is beyond reliable long-range PCR and needs a BAC library, TAR, LLHR or CATCH, all of which handle over 100 kb. The sensible counter-proposal is a genome-minimised Streptomyces chassis such as S. albus Del14 with its own clusters deleted for a clean background, with E. coli reserved for the cloning and editing steps.

Q. You are asked to justify a filamentous fungus for a secreted industrial enzyme against Bacillus. What is your strongest number, and what does the choice cost you?

A. The strongest number is Lee §20.5.5: T. reesei cellulase at 100 g L⁻¹, described as the highest protein secretion titre ever reported and 10- to 10 000-fold above bacterial, yeast and mammalian factories, which sit between milligrams per litre and a few grams per litre — and since Lee Ch 13 gives no Bacillus secretion figure at all, this is the only bound either side of that comparison has. What it costs is the vessel. A secreting fungus grows as a mycelium, so the broth becomes pseudoplastic as the culture does the thing you want: the flow behaviour index falls from 1 and the consistency index rises through the batch, apparent viscosity rises with it, volumetric gas–liquid mass transfer falls, and the published kLa correlations do not apply, being derived for non-viscous Newtonian media and already overestimating transfer in large vessels by about 100%. You are buying titre with agitator power, oxygen transfer and a morphology control problem that Lee §20.7 says is not yet reducible to a rule.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Choose a non-model host or consortium member from your experience. What evidence is needed before transferring a pathway or model assumption from a standard chassis?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 45 — Product classes I: bulk chemicals, organic acids and alcohols

Where yield is everything and the margin is thin, and therefore the week in which strain design becomes arithmetic about money. The habit from weeks 40 to 44 — derive the ceiling, then read the published number as a fraction of it — is necessary here but no longer sufficient, because a bulk product can sit at 90% of theoretical and still lose money. Three further terms decide it: the substrate bill at the achieved yield, the utilities bill that aerobic operation adds, and the allowance left for recovery once the first two are paid. Stanbury Ch 12 is where those come from, and it is a 1999 text whose prices are historical, so use its structure and ratios and quote your own prices into them.

Core ideas

1. Compute the ceiling for all six products first, and note which constraint binds

Degrees of reduction, nitrogen-free: glucose 24 per mole, six carbons. Ethanol C₂H₆O has 12, so electrons permit 2 mol per mol and carbon permits 3; electrons bind at 2 × 46.07/180.16 = 0.511 g g⁻¹ — the week 40 figure. n-Butanol and isobutanol C₄H₁₀O both have 24, so electrons permit 1.00 and carbon 1.5; electrons bind at 0.411 g g⁻¹. Lactate and 3-hydroxypropionate are both C₃H₆O₃ with 12, so carbon and electrons both permit 2 mol per mol and the ceiling is 1.000 g g⁻¹ with neither binding — which is why a homolactic fermentation is the cleanest stoichiometry in industrial biology. Succinate C₄H₆O₄ has 14: carbon permits 1.5 mol per mol and electrons 24/14 = 1.714, so carbon binds at 0.983 g g⁻¹. That last case is the one to understand, because carbon binding is a constraint you can buy out of.

2. Where CO₂ fixation raises the ceiling, and where it cannot

If carbon binds and electrons are in surplus, supplying carbon from somewhere other than the sugar lifts the ceiling to the electron limit. Succinate is the standard case: route carbon through the reductive branch with PEP or pyruvate carboxylase and each succinate takes one CO₂, so the ceiling rises from 0.983 to 24/14 × 118.09/180.16 = 1.124 g g⁻¹, more than a gram of product per gram of sugar. Nothing of the kind is available for ethanol or butanol, where electrons already bind and the limit is reducing power; adding CO₂ there makes the problem worse, not better. Lactate and 3-HP sit exactly on the boundary with both constraints tight, so neither CO₂ fixation nor extra reductant moves them. Test every bulk target this way before any strain work: identify the binding constraint, then ask whether it is the kind that can be bought out of.

3. The recurring design pattern is a redox ledger with an ATP clause

Every product in this class is made in a reaction network that must balance NADH and pay for its own maintenance. The patterns repeat. Alcohols and solvents are more reduced than sugar per carbon, so they consume the reductant glycolysis makes and the route competes with anything else that disposes of electrons — which is why deleting the hydrogen, acetate, lactate and formate routes in C. thermocellum doubled the ethanol yield (Lee §16.2) and why butanol's four reducing equivalents per molecule put it against hydrogenase. Reduced acids via the reductive TCA branch need two NADH per succinate and return ATP at the carboxykinase step, so the route can be made ATP-positive and growth-coupled. Fully oxidised three-carbon acids need neither net reductant nor CO₂, which is why they reach unit yield and why their problem is downstream rather than metabolic. The ATP clause is what usually decides anaerobic feasibility: a route that balances electrons but makes no net ATP cannot support the cell that runs it.

4. Reported strains against those ceilings

Lee §12.4.2 Organic Acids and Alcohols is the most useful table for this week, because the host is held constant. Itaconate in C. glutamicum reaches 7.8 g L⁻¹ at 0.4 mol mol⁻¹, which the chapter itself calls modest; 3-HP reaches 39 g L⁻¹ in batch and 63 g L⁻¹ in fed-batch; 2,3-butanediol 18.9 g L⁻¹ from 80 g L⁻¹ glucose, and a two-stage process 6.3 g L⁻¹ at 0.3 g g⁻¹; ethanol 106 g L⁻¹; cis,cis-muconate 4.5 g L⁻¹; glutarate 7 and 12 g L⁻¹ as a by-product. Set those beside week 40's E. coli figures from Lee Ch 11 — ethanol 54.4 g L⁻¹ at a reported 0.57 g g⁻¹, isopropanol 143 g L⁻¹ over 240 h for 0.60 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹, 1-butanol 30 g L⁻¹ at 0.287 g g⁻¹ and 0.18 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹, 3-HP 72 g L⁻¹ at 1.8 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ — and beside week 44's clostridial 15 g L⁻¹ butanol and 14 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ continuous. The pattern across all three is consistent and worth stating in the dossier: three-carbon acids reach high titres and high fractions of theoretical, four-carbon alcohols do not, and nothing in the class is rate-limited in the way the amino acid processes are.

5. Acid tolerance, and the pH decision made in the fermenter

Week 43 established the process preference from Lee §15.3.2.2: for a lactic acid fermentation a pH below about 3.8 is wanted, because the acid is then protonated and removable by electrodialysis or ultrafiltration, where neutralisation adds osmotic stress during the run and leaves a salt to split afterwards. The mechanism is the week 2 derivation applied to the product: only the undissociated acid crosses the membrane, it dissociates in a cytoplasm held near neutrality, and the proton load scales with the external undissociated concentration, so inhibition rises steeply as pH falls below the pKₐ — 3.86 for lactic acid, 4.76 for acetic. That is also why the tolerance work Lee §15.3.2.2 reports is evolutionary rather than rational: genome shuffling gave roughly a fivefold increase in tolerance to protonated lactic acid at pH 3.8, L. delbrueckii Uc-3 reached 50 g L⁻¹ without pH adjustment, and an adapted Leuconostoc made 76.8 g L⁻¹ under pH control. Treat fermentation pH as a downstream decision taken in the fermenter, and cost both sides of it.

6. The cost skeleton, from Stanbury Ch 12

Stanbury's Ch 12 is titled Fermentation Economics and its sections are named rather than numbered. The structural claims are the durable part. Across a range of processes the cost components rank in decreasing order as raw materials, fixed costs, utilities and labour, which is why media and strain improvement earn development effort and why work on a component contributing little cannot be justified. Capital scales as the sixth to three-quarter power of size — reported scale factors of 0.6 for brewing, 0.7–0.8 for single-cell protein, 0.6 for antibody production, 0.75 for fermentation processes generally — and the relative cost per unit of output falls steeply with scale, the chapter's Table 12.4 giving 30.0 at 1 unit of volume against 1.0 at 100 and 0.3 at 1 000. Containment inverts that: basic fermenter cost rises 10–30% per containment level, only about 30% of a containment building is usable space, and a 3 m³ recombinant facility can cost as much to build as a 2 000 m³ antibiotic plant. Energy for a stirred aerobic fermentation, covering agitation, air compression and chilled water, is about 8.2 kW m⁻³. Turnaround between batches is 15–25 h, and the batch cycle is t = (1/μₘ)ln(X_f/X₀) + t_T + t_L + t_D, so productivity over the cycle and not over the fermentation is what sizes a plant.

7. What is left for recovery, which is the number most proposals omit

Stanbury quotes Atkinson and Mavituna's estimates of the allowance a bulk process can afford for recovery, and they are the most transferable figures in the chapter because they are stated as a limit per tonne against a selling price and a broth concentration: about £40 per tonne for ethanol selling at £220 per tonne at 7% w/v from a local carbohydrate; about £100 per tonne for single-cell protein selling at £300 per tonne at 3% w/v; about £300 per tonne for organic acids or glycol selling at £700 per tonne at 10% concentration. The pattern is the one week 46 generalises: the allowance rises with both price and broth concentration, and a dilute cheap product has almost nothing to spend. Two further numbers from the same section: recovery and purification lose 8% of citric acid and 4% of penicillin G before salt formation, so a yield quoted at the fermenter is not the yield at the drum; and filter aid used economically still adds about £9 per tonne for a product at 10% concentration in broth. Keep the currency as printed — these are 1990s sterling figures and converting them silently would hide both the vintage and the exchange assumption.

8. Why most announced bio-based chemicals never scaled, stated as four checks

Run them in this order on any announcement. First, the substrate check: at the reported yield, what fraction of the selling price is sugar? Above about 40% a bulk process has no room for anything else, and the anchor puts the breakeven for a product at $1.80 per kilogram at 0.222 g g⁻¹. Second, the aeration check: is the route aerobic? At 8.2 kW m⁻³ the utilities term alone can approach a third of a bulk selling price, which is why the bulk products that scaled — ethanol, lactate, 1,3-propanediol — are fermentative and the aerobic ones mostly did not. Third, the concentration check: what is the titre, and what does the recovery allowance at that concentration permit? A 20 g L⁻¹ broth selling at commodity price cannot pay for a distillation train. Fourth, the incumbent check: the competing petrochemical price is not a fixed target, and a process designed against a high oil price meets a low one. None of these four is a strain property, which is the week's uncomfortable lesson: most of the failures were not strain failures.

Worked anchor

The cost skeleton for a bulk product selling at $1.80 per kilogram, and the yield it demands.

Basis: glucose at $400 per tonne, that is $0.40 per kilogram; electricity at $0.07 per kWh, as Stanbury's own example uses; product selling at $1.80 per kilogram, which is roughly where lactic acid sits.

Step 1, the substrate line as a function of yield. Substrate cost per kilogram of product is 0.40/Y. Setting that equal to the selling price gives the point at which the process loses money on sugar alone: Y = 0.40/1.80 = 0.222 g g⁻¹. That is the answer to the week's check question, and it is a very low bar — every product in the class can clear it.

Step 2, the bar that matters. A bulk process needs the substrate line at roughly 30% of revenue, because the other 70% has to carry utilities, medium, labour, capital recovery and downstream. At 30% of $1.80, that is $0.54 per kilogram, so Y ≥ 0.40/0.54 = 0.741 g g⁻¹.

Step 3, which products can reach it. Against the ceilings derived above: lactate and 3-HP at 1.000 g g⁻¹ can, and at a realistic 0.90 g g⁻¹ the sugar costs $0.44 per kilogram, 25% of revenue. Succinate at 1.124 g g⁻¹ with CO₂ fixation can, and at 0.85 g g⁻¹ pays $0.47. Ethanol cannot: its ceiling is 0.511 g g⁻¹, so even at 90% of theoretical the sugar costs 0.40/0.46 = $0.87 per kilogram, 48% of revenue — which is why fuel ethanol is made from sugar at a fraction of $400 per tonne and carries co-product credits. Butanol at a reported 0.287 g g⁻¹ pays $1.39 per kilogram, 77% of revenue, before anything else is bought. The yield ceiling is not the obstacle for the three-carbon acids; it is decisive for the four-carbon alcohols.

Step 4, the utilities line, which is where aerobic routes die. Take a 48-hour aerobic batch at 8.2 kW m⁻³: 8.2 × 48 = 394 kWh m⁻³, which at $0.07 is $27.6 per cubic metre of broth. At a 50 g L⁻¹ titre one tonne of product needs 20 m³, so that is $552 per tonne, $0.55 per kilogram — 31% of the $1.80 selling price, on top of the sugar. The same calculation for a fermentative route, where Stanbury places aeration and agitation among the minor costs, gives a line that nearly vanishes. Doubling the titre to 100 g L⁻¹ halves it, which is the clearest statement of why titre earns engineering effort even when yield does not change.

Step 5, the neutralisation line, for the acid case. One tonne of lactic acid is 11.1 kmol of acid. Neutralised with lime, 0.5 mol of Ca(OH)₂ per mol, that is 5.55 kmol, 411 kg; at an assumed $120 per tonne, $49 per tonne of product, $0.05 per kilogram, which is small. The salt is not: springing the acid with sulfuric acid precipitates 5.55 kmol of gypsum at 172.17 g mol⁻¹, which is 956 kg of CaSO₄·2H₂O per tonne of lactic acid — very nearly a tonne of solid waste per tonne of product, to be filtered, washed and disposed of. That burden, not the lime, is the reason a low-pH fermentation is worth the tolerance engineering of week 43.

Step 6, the total, and the conclusion. Fermentative, at 0.90 g g⁻¹ and 50 g L⁻¹: sugar $0.44, utilities small, neutralisation $0.05, leaving roughly $1.30 of the $1.80 for medium, labour, capital and recovery. Stanbury's recovery allowance for organic acids at 10% concentration is about £300 per tonne against a £700 per tonne price, that is 43% of revenue, which at $1.80 would be $0.77 — so the skeleton closes, but only just, and only because the route is anaerobic and the yield is near unity. Change any one of those three and it does not. Note what has not been costed: the complex nitrogen source, which week 43 showed can be $1.60 per kilogram on its own and would close this process on its own.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • glucose at $400 per tonne, electricity at $0.07 per kWh, product selling at $1.80 per kilogram
  • nitrogen supplied as ammonia, so all degrees of reduction are taken nitrogen-free
  • a viable bulk process needs the substrate line at about 30% of revenue; the figure is a rule of thumb, not a derived threshold
  • a 48-hour aerobic batch at Stanbury's 8.2 kW m⁻¹ — agitation, air compression and chilled water — with no credit for heat recovery
  • titre 50 g L⁻¹ when broth volume per tonne of product is computed
  • lime at an assumed $120 per tonne, and the acid sprung with sulfuric acid so the salt is gypsum
  • no medium, labour, capital or downstream cost in the skeleton beyond the lines named
  • Stanbury's and Atkinson and Mavituna's figures left in the currency and vintage as printed, with no indexing to the present

Common misconceptions

  • That a high fraction of theoretical yield means a viable process. Citric acid runs at 89% of its stated ceiling and lactate can approach 90%, and both can still lose money: the substrate line is only one of four, and an aerobic route at 8.2 kW m⁻³ can add a third of a bulk selling price in utilities while a dilute broth leaves nothing for recovery. Viability is a cost skeleton, not a ratio.
  • That CO₂ fixation can raise any yield ceiling. It raises the ceiling only where carbon binds and electrons are in surplus, which among these products means succinate and the other reduced four-carbon acids — 0.983 to 1.124 g g⁻¹. For ethanol and butanol electrons already bind, so supplying more carbon does nothing; identify the binding constraint before proposing a carboxylation.
  • That neutralised fermentation is simply the easy option. It costs little in base — about $0.05 per kilogram of lactic acid at an assumed lime price — and a great deal in solid: springing the acid again precipitates about 956 kg of gypsum per tonne of product, to be filtered, washed and disposed of, besides the osmotic stress on the culture during the run. The pH decision is a downstream capital decision taken in the fermenter.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. At what yield does a product selling at $1.80/kg stop losing money on substrate alone?

A. At 0.222 g g⁻¹, with glucose at $400 per tonne: substrate cost is 0.40/Y per kilogram of product, and setting that equal to $1.80 gives Y = 0.222. That is the floor, not the target. A bulk process needs the substrate line near 30% of revenue, which is $0.54 per kilogram and therefore Y ≥ 0.741 g g⁻¹ — a bar the three-carbon acids clear at their ceiling of 1.000 g g⁻¹ and ethanol, at 0.511, cannot clear at any yield from sugar at that price. The useful form of the answer is the inversion: given a price and a substrate cost, the required yield follows, and it can be compared with the ceiling before any strain work begins.

Q. A paper reports succinate at 1.05 g per g of glucose. Is the number credible, and what do you check?

A. Credible, and that is the point of knowing which constraint binds. Succinate's carbon ceiling is 1.5 mol per mol, 0.983 g g⁻¹, so 1.05 exceeds it — but succinate's electron ceiling is 1.714 mol per mol, 1.124 g g⁻¹, and the gap between the two is exactly what one CO₂ per succinate fixed through the reductive branch buys. So check first that the route is reductive and carboxylating, and that CO₂ or bicarbonate was supplied; then check the basis, as always, that the yield is on sugar consumed rather than supplied and that no complex medium is contributing carbon. A reported 1.05 g g⁻¹ from an oxidative route, by contrast, would be impossible and the basis would be wrong.

Q. Two routes to the same bulk acid are offered: aerobic at 80 g L⁻¹ and 0.80 g g⁻¹, or anaerobic at 40 g L⁻¹ and 0.90 g g⁻¹. Which do you take?

A. Cost both skeletons rather than comparing yields. Sugar at $400 per tonne: $0.50 per kilogram aerobic against $0.44 anaerobic, a difference of $0.06 that favours the anaerobic route slightly. Utilities reverse the size of the question: a 48-hour aerobic batch at 8.2 kW m⁻³ and $0.07 per kWh costs $27.6 per cubic metre, which at 80 g L⁻¹ is $0.35 per kilogram, against a fermentative route where Stanbury puts aeration among the minor costs. Recovery pulls the other way, since the allowance rises with broth concentration and 40 g L⁻¹ gives half the concentration to work from — Atkinson and Mavituna's organic acid limit of about £300 per tonne is quoted at 10% in broth. So the decision is anaerobic unless the downstream train is concentration-limited, and the way to settle it is to carry both skeletons to a cost per kilogram rather than to argue the yields.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Select a bulk product class compatible with your interests. Estimate whether titre, productivity, or yield is most likely to dominate feasibility, and state the process assumptions behind that choice.

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 46 — Product classes II: amino acids, natural products and proteins

Where the economics inverts. For the products of week 45 the sugar bill decided everything; here the sugar is almost free and purification decides everything, and the strain parameter that matters is the one that makes the broth easier to work up. Shuler §11.1 states the relationship in a single comparison that is worth memorising: citric acid enters recovery at around 100 g L⁻¹ and sells for order 1 to 2 dollars a kilogram, while a therapeutic protein can enter at 0.00001 g L⁻¹ and sell for order 100 million dollars a kilogram — seven orders of magnitude in price against seven in dilution. Everything in this week follows from that line, including the phase synthesis at the end of it, because the host you defend in Artifact 26 is the one whose failure modes your product's price can absorb.

Core ideas

1. The economics of a high-value product, stated as two ratios

Shuler §11.1 gives the first: recovery and purification often exceed 50% of total manufacturing cost, especially for an intracellular product, and the difficulty of recovery is tightly coupled to how dilute the product is when it leaves the fermenter. Stanbury's recovery costs section gives the second, and it is the sharper one: cost analyses of older fermentation processes split roughly 1:1 between fermentation and isolation, but the shift to recombinant organisms making exotic compounds at extremely low titres has moved that split to 1:8 or 1:10 — the fermentation becoming 10% of the cost and the recovery 90%. Read those two together and the design consequence is immediate. A yield point is worth almost nothing here. A titre point is worth a great deal, because it shortens the concentration train. A change that moves the product from inside the cell to outside it is worth more than either, because it deletes unit operations rather than shrinking them.

2. Amino acids are the bridge case, and they behave like bulk

Keep them in the matrix as the calibration point. Lysine is a 2.5 million tonne a year market at commodity price, made by C. glutamicum LYS-12 at 120 g L⁻¹ in 30 hours and 55% yield — 4.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ and 79% of the electron ceiling derived in week 42 — with glutamate in §12.4.1.1 at a comparable industrial scale. At that price and that titre every term in the week 45 skeleton still applies: the sugar bill is the largest line, the recovery allowance is generous because the broth is concentrated, and yield earns research. Lee §12.4.1 also lists the specialty amino acids where the economics has already inverted — pipecolic acid, trans-4-hydroxyproline, shinorine, ectoine, theanine, 4-hydroxyisoleucine — at titres orders below lysine and prices orders above it. The same organism, the same tools, and a completely different set of design priorities: that contrast is the cleanest teaching device in the week.

3. Terpenoids: the mevalonate route as Lee gives it

Lee §18.2.5.3 is precise and worth following step by step, because the anchor needs it. More than 68 000 terpenoids are known, more than the flavonoids, polyketides and alkaloids combined, and all of them come from the C5 units isopentenyl pyrophosphate and its isomer dimethylallyl pyrophosphate. In S. cerevisiae those come from the cytosolic mevalonate pathway: Erg10 and Erg13 condense three acetyl-CoA, Hmg1 or Hmg2 reduces, Erg12 and Erg8 add two phosphates, Erg19 decarboxylates to give IPP, and Idi1 isomerises. Erg20 then condenses IPP with DMAPP to geranyl pyrophosphate and adds a second IPP to give the C15 farnesyl pyrophosphate, with Bts1 extending to C20 and Erg9 drawing FPP off to squalene and ergosterol. The chapter's five engineering targets for sesquiterpenoids follow from that map: cytosolic acetyl-CoA supply, flux to FPP, preventing FPP drainage to ergosterol, efficient turnover by the heterologous enzyme, and sufficient NADPH. And it states the host argument in one sentence — yeast harbours native cytochrome P450s and their redox partners, which is why artemisinic acid, originally planned for E. coli, moved to yeast when a P450 oxidation proved difficult in the bacterium.

4. The MEP route is not in the chapter, and the difference is a yield

Lee Ch 18 is a yeast chapter and describes only the mevalonate route; the methylerythritol phosphate route of bacteria and plastids appears nowhere in it, and the session asking for both routes with their cofactor demands cannot be answered from the assigned reading alone. What can be done exactly, and is done in the anchor, is the carbon bookkeeping, which is fixed by the precursors each route takes. Mevalonate starts from three acetyl-CoA, and every acetyl-CoA costs a pyruvate decarboxylation before the pathway begins, so four CO₂ are lost per C5 unit. MEP starts from one pyruvate and one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, exactly what one glucose yields, and loses one CO₂ per C5. That single difference is worth about 29% in mass yield. The cofactor demands differ too — the mevalonate route needs two NADPH and three ATP per C5, while MEP needs of order three reducing equivalents and two nucleotide triphosphates, with its last two steps requiring reduced ferredoxin in bacteria — but take those from a pathway database rather than from these notes before they enter a proposal, and note that the ferredoxin requirement is itself a reason the MEP route is hard to move into yeast.

5. Polyketides and nonribosomal peptides: the four obstacles, now as a product problem

Week 44 read Lee Ch 17 as a host question; read it here as a product question and the four obstacles §17.5.1 names become a design checklist. Regulatory incompatibility: the cluster's own promoters and regulators may not function in the new host, which is what full pathway refactoring in §17.5.4.4 exists to solve and what the bottromycin work did by replacing every native promoter with synthetic constitutive ones, for a 5- to 50-fold titre increase. Missing triggering signals or receptors: a silent cluster in its native host often stays silent elsewhere. Precursor supply: the extender units are malonyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA and the carrier proteins need phosphopantetheinylation, so a host without the full machinery has to be given it. Toxicity. Over those sits the base rate — about 10% success for non-Streptomyces clusters and 30% for Streptomyces ones in a Streptomyces host — and the mechanics of 20 to 210 kb of 65–75% GC DNA. The titres that result are modest in absolute terms: pristinamycin II at 2.2 g L⁻¹ in flask and 2 g L⁻¹ in batch is reported as the highest for that compound. A product class where a gram per litre is a result is a product class whose price must be high.

6. Malonyl-CoA is the recurring precursor limit, and the numbers show it

Lee §18.2.5.1 gives the flavonoid case with enough detail to generalise. Chalcone synthase is a type III polyketide synthase that takes p-coumaroyl-CoA as the starter and runs three malonyl-CoA-dependent elongations to a tetraketide, which becomes a chalcone and then, through chalcone isomerase, the flavanone naringenin — the core from which almost all flavonoids derive. So three malonyl-CoA per molecule, before any decoration. The titres: naringenin at about 55 mg L⁻¹ from an Arabidopsis pathway in an optimised chassis in shake flasks, raised to 90 mg L⁻¹ by dividing the pathway into three modules — tyrosine supply, malonyl-CoA supply, and naringenin formation — and balancing them stepwise; then kaempferol at 26.6 mg L⁻¹ and quercetin at 20.4 mg L⁻¹ downstream. Set those milligrams beside the 140 g L⁻¹ itaconate and 100 g L⁻¹ cellulase of week 44 and the gap is four orders of magnitude, with the same organism types and better tools. The cause is that malonyl-CoA is a tightly regulated node feeding fatty acid synthesis, so pulling flux from it fights the cell's own control; Lee §18.2.4.1 reports the same problem for 3-HP made from malonyl-CoA, solved by upregulating pyruvate to malonyl-CoA flux and by swapping in enzymes with better kinetics. The chapter gives no intracellular malonyl-CoA concentration, so quantify the pool from a measurement database rather than from the chapter if the dossier needs it.

7. Modular balance, in week 31's language

Ajikumar et al. 2010 and the naringenin result above are the same experiment done twice in different organisms, and week 31 gives the vocabulary for why the approach works. Partition a long pathway into an upstream module supplying precursor and a downstream module consuming it, vary the expression of each over a grid, and measure product. In control-analysis terms the grid is a direct search for where the flux control coefficient sits, without having to measure elasticities: if raising upstream expression alone accumulates intermediate and does not raise product, control is downstream; if it raises product proportionally, control is upstream; and the characteristic result in these papers — that the optimum is an interior point and that overexpressing both modules is worse than balancing them — is the summation theorem made visible, control being shared and the sum fixed. The practical rule to carry into the dossier is that the intermediate pool is the readout, and a pathway that accumulates its intermediate is telling you which module to tune.

8. When the product is a protein, the design question moves downstream

Shuler §11.1 reduces recovery to four functions — separate insoluble solids, concentrate and remove most of the water, remove contaminating chemicals, and prepare the product — and insists the water comes out early so that everything after it is smaller equipment. Apply that to the three locations a protein can be made in. Intracellular: lysis, debris removal, and for E. coli the inclusion-body and endotoxin problems of week 40, with 25–50% of total protein as product but every gram of it behind a cell wall. Periplasmic: an osmotic-shock step releases a fraction of the proteome rather than all of it, so the first purification begins far cleaner, at the cost of the translocation capacity — about 20% of E. coli protein crosses the inner membrane. Secreted: no lysis, no debris, no endotoxin from the cytoplasm, and the fungal numbers of week 44 show how far that can go at 100 g L⁻¹ cellulase against the milligrams-to-grams per litre of bacterial, yeast and mammalian hosts. The downstream consequence is not marginal: it is the difference between Stanbury's 1:1 split and its 1:8. Then the branch Shuler §14.3.1 puts first still binds — if the product needs post-translational modification, none of this is available in a bacterium at all.

9. Defending a choice, which is what Artifact 26 is

The defence has a shape, and it is the negative rule of week 42 followed by the arithmetic of weeks 45 and 46. Name the one property the product cannot do without and eliminate every host lacking it — modification, secretion, tolerance, anaerobiosis, food-grade status, a P450 redox partner. Among the survivors, compute the ceiling, place the best published strain against it as a fraction, and state the basis of that number. Then cost the skeleton: substrate at the achievable yield, utilities at 8.2 kW m⁻³ if the route is aerobic, and the recovery allowance implied by the titre and the price. Then state the failure mode you are accepting and what it costs. Finally, and this is the part that makes it a defence rather than a preference, state the result that would reverse it: a measured secretion titre, a solvent tolerance figure, a sugar price, a modification requirement discovered in assay. A choice with no such condition attached has not been defended, it has been asserted — and the three places in this phase where the assigned reading could not supply a number (Bacillus secretion capacity, Pseudomonas solvent-tolerance mechanisms, the regulatory path for an engineered food-grade strain) are exactly the conditions most likely to decide a real project.

Worked anchor

The theoretical yield of a C15 terpenoid by each route, computed, and the gap between them explained.

Take β-farnesene, C₁₅H₂₄, 204.36 g mol⁻¹, degree of reduction 15(4) + 24(1) = 84. Glucose is 180.16 g mol⁻¹, six carbons, degree of reduction 24.

Step 1, the two absolute ceilings, before any pathway is named. Carbon permits 15/6 = 2.5 glucose per farnesene, that is 204.36/(2.5 × 180.16) = 0.454 g g⁻¹. Electrons permit 84/24 = 3.5 glucose per farnesene, that is 204.36/(3.5 × 180.16) = 0.324 g g⁻¹. Electrons bind, as they do for every terpene, because a terpene is a hydrocarbon and carries 5.6 electrons per carbon against glucose's 4.

Step 2, the mevalonate route's own carbon bookkeeping. Per C5 unit the route condenses three acetyl-CoA. Each acetyl-CoA comes from a pyruvate, losing one CO₂, so three acetyl-CoA consume 1.5 glucose and release 3 CO₂. The pathway then decarboxylates once more at Erg19, C6 mevalonate pyrophosphate to C5 IPP, for a fourth CO₂. So 9 carbons in, 5 carbons out, 4 lost. Farnesene is three C5 units: 4.5 glucose, 27 carbons in, 15 out, 12 CO₂ released. Yield = 204.36/(4.5 × 180.16) = 204.36/810.7 = 0.252 g g⁻¹.

Step 3, the MEP route's bookkeeping. Per C5 unit the route takes one pyruvate and one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and loses one CO₂ in forming 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate. One glucose yields exactly two trioses, one of which becomes the pyruvate and one of which is the GAP, so one glucose supplies one C5 unit: 6 carbons in, 5 out, 1 lost. Farnesene: 3 glucose, 18 carbons in, 15 out, 3 CO₂. Carbon-wise that is 204.36/(3 × 180.16) = 0.378 g g⁻¹.

Step 4, the comparison, with the constraint check that matters. MEP's carbon figure of 0.378 g g⁻¹ exceeds the electron ceiling of 0.324, which means carbon is no longer what binds the MEP route — electrons are, and the route's real ceiling is 0.324 g g⁻¹, reached by spending some of the surplus carbon on reducing power. The mevalonate route's 0.252 g g⁻¹ is below the electron ceiling, so carbon still binds there, and the strain can never reach 0.324 no matter how much NADPH it is given. In fractions of the absolute limit: MEP 100%, mevalonate 78%. In mass terms MEP is worth 0.324/0.252 = 1.29, about 29% more product per tonne of sugar.

Step 5, where the difference comes from, in one sentence. Three pyruvate decarboxylations paid before the mevalonate pathway even starts — 3 of the 12 CO₂ per farnesene, with a fourth from Erg19 — against one decarboxylation in MEP, because MEP builds its C5 from a C3 and a C3 rather than from three C2 units that each cost a C1.

Step 6, why yeast is nonetheless the host that made the product. Lee §18.2.5.3 is explicit: S. cerevisiae carries native cytochrome P450s and their redox partners, and artemisinic acid moved to yeast from E. coli precisely because a P450 oxidation was difficult in the bacterium. A 29% yield advantage is decisive for a bulk chemical and secondary for a product whose cost is dominated by purification — and the reported performance confirms it, with amorphadiene above 40 g L⁻¹ and β-farnesene at 130 g L⁻¹ in yeast, the latter also reported as needing 75% less oxygen than the alternative. Against the 0.324 g g⁻¹ ceiling, 130 g L⁻¹ is a titre and not a yield, and the chapter does not give the sugar consumed, so the matrix entry carries the titre and marks the yield as unstated.

So the answer to the session is not that one route is better. It is that MEP has the higher ceiling by a calculable 29%, that the ceiling is irrelevant to whether a terpenoid programme succeeds, and that the host was chosen for a cofactor partner rather than for carbon efficiency — which is the whole week in one example.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • β-farnesene as the C15 terpenoid, C₁₅H₂₄ at 204.36 g mol⁻¹ and degree of reduction 84
  • all acetyl-CoA for the mevalonate route derived from pyruvate, so one CO₂ per acetyl-CoA before the pathway starts
  • one glucose supplying exactly one pyruvate and one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate for the MEP route
  • no carbon to biomass, maintenance or by-product in either route's bookkeeping
  • no ATP or cofactor limitation imposed; both ceilings are carbon and electron balances only
  • the MEP cofactor demand quoted as approximate and not taken from any assigned chapter
  • reported amorphadiene and β-farnesene figures are titres; the sugar consumed is not stated in the chapter, so no yield is inferred from them
