Common misconceptions

  • That a high-value product forgives a bad strain. It forgives a bad yield, which is a different thing. Titre it does not forgive, because the recovery allowance scales with broth concentration — Stanbury's limits are quoted per tonne at a stated w/v — and a dilute broth multiplies the size of every unit operation downstream of it. Nor does it forgive a product locked inside the cell, since that adds lysis, debris removal and, in a Gram-negative, endotoxin clearance to a train that may already be 90% of the cost.
  • That the mevalonate and MEP routes differ mainly in cofactor demand. They differ first in carbon: mevalonate pays three pyruvate decarboxylations to make its three acetyl-CoA and a fourth at Erg19, losing four CO₂ per C5 unit, where MEP builds a C5 from a C3 and a C3 and loses one. That is 0.252 against 0.324 g g⁻¹ for a C15 terpenoid, a 29% difference, and it is fixed by stoichiometry rather than by expression.
  • That a flavonoid or polyketide titre in the milligram range means the pathway is badly expressed. More often the precursor node is the constraint: three malonyl-CoA per naringenin, drawn from a pool the cell regulates tightly for fatty acid synthesis. The naringenin results make the point — 55 mg L⁻¹ from an optimised chassis, 90 mg L⁻¹ once the pathway was split into tyrosine, malonyl-CoA and naringenin modules and balanced. The intermediate pool, not the enzyme level, is the diagnostic.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. For a high-value product, which strain parameter does the economics punish most, and why not yield?

A. Titre, because the recovery allowance scales with how concentrated the product is when it leaves the fermenter. Shuler §11.1 states the correlation directly — citric acid enters recovery near 100 g L⁻¹ and sells for 1 to 2 dollars a kilogram, a therapeutic protein can enter at 0.00001 g L⁻¹ and sell for order 100 million — and puts recovery above 50% of manufacturing cost, especially for intracellular products, while Stanbury reports the fermentation-to-isolation split moving from about 1:1 in older processes to 1:8 or 1:10 for recombinant products made at very low titre, which is to say the fermentation becomes 10% of the cost. Yield is punished least because the substrate is a negligible line: at 0.40 dollars a kilogram of glucose, even a tenfold worse yield is invisible against a product selling in the thousands. The ranking that follows is titre first, then product location — secreted beats periplasmic beats intracellular, because each step deletes unit operations rather than shrinking them — and then yield.

Q. Your flavonoid strain makes 90 mg L⁻¹ and accumulates p-coumaric acid. What does that tell you, and what do you do?

A. That control sits downstream of the starter unit, not upstream: the cell is making p-coumaroyl-CoA's precursor faster than chalcone synthase can consume it, and since CHS runs three malonyl-CoA-dependent elongations per naringenin, the usual cause is malonyl-CoA supply rather than CHS expression. In week 31's terms the accumulating intermediate is the readout that the flux control coefficient has moved, and the summation theorem says raising upstream expression further can only make it worse. So do what the modular work did: treat tyrosine supply, malonyl-CoA supply and naringenin formation as three modules and vary them against each other rather than in series — that is the step that took the reported titre from 55 to 90 mg L⁻¹. Then, before proposing a malonyl-CoA intervention, get an actual pool measurement from a metabolomics database, because Lee Ch 18 gives no concentration for it.

Q. Defend a product and host choice for the capstone in the form the artifact requires. What must be in it, and what makes it a defence rather than a preference?

A. Five things. The eliminating property first — the one requirement the product cannot do without, used to remove hosts rather than to rank them, which is week 42's negative rule. Then the ceiling, derived from degrees of reduction, with the best published strain placed against it as a fraction and the basis of that published number stated, since weeks 40 and 43 both found yields reported above their own ceilings on undeclared bases. Then the cost skeleton: substrate at the achievable yield, utilities at about 8.2 kW m⁻³ if the route is aerobic, and the recovery allowance the titre and the price imply. Then the failure mode being accepted — proteases and sporulation for Bacillus, the Crabtree effect and compartment targeting for yeast, medium cost for a lactobacillus, transfer limitation for a gas or photosynthetic process, morphology for a fungus. What makes it a defence is the fifth: a stated result that would reverse it. For most of the hosts in this matrix that result is one of the three numbers this phase could not find in the reading — a measured secretion titre, a solvent tolerance mechanism, or the regulatory path for an engineered food-grade strain — and saying so is stronger than filling the gap from memory.

Every number in these modules — ribosome counts, pool sizes, half-lives, turnover times — is written from working knowledge and is an order-of-magnitude figure. Before any of them enters a notebook, a figure or a proposal, check it against BioNumbers or the primary source and cite that, not these notes. Treat the modules as a map of what matters and a scaffold for reasoning; treat the textbooks and the databases as the authority for values.

Week 47 — Media, sterilisation and inoculum development

The half of a fermentation that no paper reports and every plant lives with. Three decisions sit in this week — what the medium is made of, how it is sterilised, and how the inoculum gets to the vessel — and each is a cost against a risk rather than a yield against a ceiling. The habit from weeks 44-46 carries over unchanged: cost every option against what it buys. What is different here is that the arithmetic is unusually clean, because sterilisation kinetics are first order with an Arrhenius constant and the numbers are published. The single most useful thing in the week is that the del factor delivered during heat-up and cool-down is usually larger than the del factor the holding period was designed for, which means most hand-computed cycles are over-specified and destroy nutrients for nothing.

Core ideas

1. What the medium is for, and the four things that decide it

Stanbury Ch 4 lists the medium's duties and they are worth stating as a specification rather than a recipe: supply every element in the biomass, supply the carbon and electrons for the product, supply the energy for maintenance, and buffer the pH excursion the process creates. The elemental demand is not a judgement call — it comes straight out of the biomass formula you built in week 16 and Shuler §7.3.1 is the method: write CH1.8O0.5N0.2 (or your own measured formula), multiply by the target biomass, and that is the nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur bill before anything else is decided. Stanbury's chapter is organised by component — water, energy sources, carbon sources, nitrogen sources, minerals with chelators, growth factors, nutrient recycle, buffers, precursors and regulators, oxygen requirements, antifoams, medium optimization — and the four decisions that actually move cost are: complex against defined, the carbon source, whether anything must be fed rather than batched, and how much of the nitrogen is there for biomass you do not want. On that last point the arithmetic is brutal and is done in the anchor of week 52: nitrogen in the medium that produces biomass rather than product is a cost twice, once as the nitrogen and once as the oxygen to burn the carbon that went with it.

2. Complex against defined, costed rather than argued

The argument is usually had on grounds of reproducibility and that is the wrong axis to start on, because the difference in cost per kilogram of product is often larger than the difference in yield. Take Stanbury's own framing — factors influencing the choice of carbon source, and the examples under carbohydrates, oils and fats, hydrocarbons — and convert it. A defined medium on glucose at the week 45 price of $400 per tonne, at a biomass yield of 0.45 g g⁻¹ and a product yield of 0.30 g g⁻¹, costs 3.33 kg of glucose per kilogram of product, $1.33. A complex medium replacing part of the nitrogen with corn steep liquor or yeast extract typically raises titre and rate but adds a nitrogen line costing dollars rather than cents per kilogram, and the test is whether the productivity gain pays for it. The second axis is variability: Stanbury is explicit that complex sources are batch-variable, which is a validation cost in a regulated product and a control cost in any product, because every analytical method you built in phase 5 now has a matrix that changes between deliveries. The third is downstream, and it is the one most often forgotten — a complex medium puts colour, protein and particulates into the broth that week 51's train has to remove, and the clarification burden is a real line in the cost of goods rather than an inconvenience.

3. Thermal death is first order, and that is the whole of the design

Stanbury Ch 5 sets it out: −dN/dt = kN, integrating to ln(N₀/N_t) = kt, with N the total number of viable organisms in the batch rather than a concentration, because the minimum number needed to spoil a batch is one regardless of volume. Deindoerfer and Humphrey's design criterion is the del factor, ∇ = ln(N₀/N_t), and the temperature dependence is Arrhenius: k = A e^(−E/RT), so ln k against 1/T is a straight line. Two consequences follow immediately and both are stated in the chapter. First, sterility is unattainable in finite time, so the target is a probability — the fermentation industry's usual figure, which Stanbury attributes to Deindoerfer and Humphrey, Richards, Banks and Corbett, is one contaminated batch in a thousand, so N_t = 10⁻³. Second, the del factor is scale-dependent: N₀ is proportional to volume, so going from 1,000 to 10,000 dm³ at fixed risk raises the required del from 34.5 to 36.8. That is a rise of exactly ln 10, which is the whole of the scale effect and is worth seeing as such — the del factor grows as the logarithm of volume, so a thousand-fold scale-up costs only 6.9 more del.

4. Verified kinetics, and what they say about 121 °C

Doran's Example 13.8 supplies parameters you can use rather than assume: for bacterial spores, E_d = 283 kJ gmol⁻¹ and A = 5.7 × 10³⁹ h⁻¹. Put those through k_d = A e^(−E_d/RT) and the temperature ladder falls out, with D (the time for a one-log reduction, 2.303/k_d) beside it: 100 °C gives k_d = 1.38 h⁻¹ and D = 100 min; 110 °C gives 15.0 h⁻¹ and 9.2 min; 115 °C gives 47.0 h⁻¹ and 2.9 min; 121 °C gives 179 h⁻¹ and 0.77 min; 130 °C gives 1,228 h⁻¹ and 0.11 min; 140 °C gives 9,474 h⁻¹ and 0.015 min. Two things are worth reading off that ladder. The activation energy is high, so the rate rises by roughly a factor of ten for every 10 °C — which is why 121 °C is the autoclave temperature and why nothing useful happens at 100 °C. And Doran says plainly that cell death below about 100 °C is minimal, which is the licence to start the heat-up integral at 100 °C rather than at ambient. Doran also records, for direct steam sparging, that condensate typically adds 10-20% to the liquid volume; if you size the vessel from the medium volume and sterilise by injection, the fill is 10-20% larger than you planned.

5. Heat-up and cool-down are not a correction, they are usually most of the cycle

Doran §13.6.1 is explicit that cell death occurs at all times during the cycle, that holding periods are of the order of minutes while heating and cooling of large volumes take hours, and that t_hd can be minimised by accounting for the ramps. Stanbury's Ch 5 names the same calculation — 'calculation of the Del factor during heating and cooling' is its own named subsection, ahead of the holding-time one. The integral is ∫k_d dt over the ramp, and it cannot be done until the temperature profile is known; Deindoerfer and Humphrey's generalised profiles, reproduced in Doran's Table 13.3, give the form — hyperbolic for direct steam sparging, linear for electrical heating, exponential for heat transfer from isothermal steam through a coil — and linear cooling against a constant-temperature coolant. The anchor does the integral numerically for a linear ramp, and the result is the point of the week: a 60-minute heat-up from 100 to 121 °C delivers del 37.7 on its own, and a 45-minute cool-down delivers 28.3, against a requirement of 40.1 for 50 m³. The ramps over-deliver by a factor of e²⁶. Every minute of holding time computed without them is a minute of nutrient destruction bought for nothing.

6. The thing you are trading against is the medium, and it has its own Arrhenius constant

Deindoerfer and Humphrey's second criterion, which Stanbury gives as equation (5.11) onward, is the Nutrient Quality Criterion Q = ln(x₀/x_t) = k·t, built on exactly the same first-order-with-Arrhenius logic as the del factor, with the nutrient's own activation energy. Superimpose the two families of lines on ln t against 1/T and you have the continuous sterilisation performance chart of their 1961 paper, reproduced as Stanbury's Fig. 5.12: lines of constant del, lines of constant Q, and a safe operating region between the nutrient-in-excess bound and the nutrient-exhausted bound. The reason the chart slopes the way it does is the only thing you need to remember from it. Spore destruction has an activation energy around 283 kJ mol⁻¹; nutrient destruction is far lower, of the order of 100 kJ mol⁻¹ for vitamins and sugars, which is not a figure from the assigned reading and is flagged as an assumption in the anchor. Because the spore reaction is the more temperature-sensitive of the two, hotter and shorter always buys more sterility per unit of nutrient destroyed. That single inequality is the entire case for high-temperature short-time continuous sterilisation, and the anchor puts a number on it. Stanbury's own caveat is worth keeping: the approach only works if the limiting heat-labile nutrient has been identified and its Arrhenius parameters measured, which Banks points out is rarely true of a complex medium — so in practice the chart tells you which direction to move, not where to stop.

7. What has to be sterilised separately, and why the list is short but non-negotiable

Three mechanisms, and they are chemical rather than kinetic, so no temperature-time regime avoids them. Maillard reaction between reducing sugars and amino groups browns the medium, destroys lysine and arginine preferentially, and generates compounds that inhibit growth — which is why glucose and the nitrogen source are routinely sterilised apart and combined cold. Phosphate precipitates with calcium and magnesium at sterilisation temperature, removing both the phosphate and the divalent cations from solution, which is why phosphate is a separate addition and why chelators appear in Stanbury's component list at all. Vitamins and some amino acids are simply destroyed, which is why they are filter-sterilised; Stanbury notes that filtration is the method of choice for animal-cell media precisely because they are completely soluble and heat-labile, and Ch 5's filter-sterilization section covers media as well as air. The decision rule is not 'sterilise everything separately' — every separate stream is another vessel, another transfer and another aseptic connection, which is a contamination risk of its own. It is: separate the reducing sugar from the amino nitrogen, separate the phosphate from the divalent cations, filter what heat destroys, and heat the rest together.

8. The seed train is a generation count, and the generation count is a stability calculation

Stanbury Ch 6 gives the structure — criteria for the transfer of inoculum, then the development of inocula for yeast, bacterial and mycelial processes, then the aseptic inoculation of plant fermenters — and the criterion matters more than the stages. The usual inoculum ratio is 5 to 10% v/v, so each stage multiplies volume by 10 to 20 and the train from a 1 mL vial to 50 m³ is about seven to eight transfers. The number that actually matters is not the number of stages but the number of generations, because that is what week 33's plasmid-stability model takes as its argument. Volume from 1 mL to 50,000 L is a factor of 5 × 10⁷, which is log₂(5 × 10⁷) = 25.6 generations of net growth, plus whatever is spent re-entering exponential phase after each transfer. Twenty-six generations is a long time for an unselected plasmid: at a segregational loss rate per generation of 1%, the plasmid-free fraction at inoculation is 1 − 0.99²⁶ = 23%, and the production vessel is seeded with a population that is already nearly a quarter wrong. Stanbury's transfer criterion — transfer in late exponential phase, on a defined physiological state rather than a clock — is what keeps the lag short and therefore keeps the generation count near its theoretical minimum, and it is the only lever in the train that does not cost a vessel.

9. The contamination risk you accept, stated as a number rather than a posture

The week's fourth objective asks you to state the risk you accept and why, and the honest version of that is an expected-cost calculation rather than a safety factor. One batch in a thousand is the industry figure; the question is whether it is right for your process. A contaminated batch costs the medium, the utilities, the vessel time, the clean-down, and the downstream capacity that was reserved for it — for the 50 m³ aerobic process costed in week 52 that is of the order of tens of thousands of dollars. Moving from 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁶ risk costs 6.9 more del, which at 121 °C is 2.3 more minutes of holding, which costs a little nutrient and nothing else. Moving the other way, to 10⁻², saves 2.3 minutes and buys a ten-fold higher failure rate. The asymmetry is the point: sterility is cheap at the margin and failure is expensive, so the usual error is not over-sterilising the broth but under-specifying everything else — the seals, the valves, the sample ports and the exhaust filter, which Stanbury Ch 7 covers at length and which is where contamination actually comes from. A del factor is a statement about the medium, not about the plant.

Worked anchor

A batch sterilisation cycle for 50 m³, with the ramps integrated, and what ignoring them would have cost.

Step 1 — the del factor required. Doran's Example 13.8 basis: spores at 5 × 10¹² m⁻³. In 50 m³, N₀ = 2.5 × 10¹⁴. Accepting one contaminated batch in a thousand, N_t = 10⁻³. So ∇ = ln(2.5 × 10¹⁴ / 10⁻³) = ln(2.5 × 10¹⁷) = 40.1.

Sanity check against Stanbury: their 1,000 dm³ figure of 34.5 corresponds to ln(10¹²/10⁻³) = 34.54, i.e. 10⁹ organisms per dm³. Doran's 5 × 10⁹ per dm³ is the same order, and the two sources agree to within one del factor on the same basis. Good.

Step 2 — the rate constant. k_d = A e^(−E_d/RT) with E_d = 283 kJ gmol⁻¹, A = 5.7 × 10³⁹ h⁻¹, E_d/R = 34,036 K. At 121 °C (394.15 K): E_d/RT = 86.35, k_d = 179 h⁻¹ = 2.98 min⁻¹, D = 0.77 min.

Step 3 — the naive answer. Ignoring the ramps, t_hd = 40.1 / 2.98 = 13.5 min at 121 °C.

Step 4 — the ramps, for a fast cycle. Direct steam injection to 121 °C in 20 min from 100 °C, flash cooling back to 100 °C in 15 min, both taken as linear in temperature, death below 100 °C neglected per Doran. Numerical integration of ∫k_d dt over each ramp gives ∇_heat = 12.6 and ∇_cool = 9.4. Together 22.0, which is 55% of the requirement.

The holding period therefore needs only 40.1 − 22.0 = 18.1 del, i.e. t_hd = 18.1 / 2.98 = 6.1 min. Accounting for the ramps more than halves the holding time: 6.1 min against the naive 13.5.

Step 5 — the ramps, for a slow cycle, which is the usual case at this scale. A 50 m³ vessel heated through a jacket does not reach 121 °C in 20 minutes. Take 60 min up and 45 min down: ∇_heat = 37.7, ∇_cool = 28.3, total 66.0 against a requirement of 40.1. The holding time required is negative. The cycle is already sterile before the hold begins, by a margin of e^(66.0−40.1) = e^25.9, which is a factor of 1.8 × 10¹¹.

Step 6 — what that over-delivery costs, in nutrient. Compare two regimes delivering the same del of 40.1: a 121 °C hold for 13.5 min, and a 140 °C continuous steriliser for 40.1/157.9 = 0.254 min = 15.2 s. Take the nutrient's activation energy as 100 kJ mol⁻¹ — this figure is not from the assigned reading and is the one assumption carrying the result. The ratio of nutrient destruction is Q₁₄₀/Q₁₂₁ = [k_n(140)/k_n(121)] × (t₁₄₀/t₁₂₁) = 4.07 × 0.0189 = 0.077. The hotter, shorter regime destroys about one-thirteenth as much nutrient for the same sterility.

Step 7 — what the arithmetic chooses. Three options, costed:

(i) Batch, slow ramps, no holding time. Free. Delivers del 66 against 40 needed, so the nutrient damage is whatever a 105-minute excursion above 100 °C does. This is what most plants actually run, and the reason it survives is that the damage is absorbed into the medium recipe during development rather than measured.

(ii) Batch, fast ramps by direct steam injection and flash cooling, 6.1 min hold. Costs clean steam and 10-20% condensate dilution, and Stanbury warns of foaming on heating and the need for steam free of anticorrosion additives. Cuts the above-100 °C excursion from 105 min to 41 min.

(iii) Continuous, 140 °C, 15 s hold. Costs a spiral or plate exchanger and its capital, and Stanbury notes plate exchangers cannot handle suspended solids while spirals can and are self-cleaning. Buys the factor of thirteen on nutrient destruction, and buys back the vessel time — 105 minutes of a 50 m³ vessel per batch, which at a 48-hour cycle is 3.6% of capacity.

The order of magnitude of the decision is set by option (iii)'s two credits, and the larger of them is not the nutrient. It is the vessel time, because vessel time is what week 52 will show carries the capital charge. The nutrient argument is the one in the textbooks; the capacity argument is the one that gets funded.

One caveat the arithmetic cannot carry: Stanbury, following Armenante and Li (1993), records that particles in the medium heat far more slowly than the bulk, that their cores may not reach temperature before leaving a continuous steriliser, and that the conclusion is to overdesign the steriliser and the first cooling exchanger rather than lengthen the holding coil — and that direct steam injection is unwise for a particulate medium for the same reason. A hydrolysate or a starch slurry is a particulate medium. The 15-second answer above is for a soluble one.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • spore load 5 × 10¹² m⁻³ of raw medium, from Doran's Example 13.8 rather than from a measurement on this medium
  • E_d = 283 kJ gmol⁻¹ and A = 5.7 × 10³⁹ h⁻¹ for the contaminating spores, also from Doran's Example 13.8 and treated as applying to the whole population
  • one contaminated batch in a thousand accepted, which is the figure Stanbury attributes to the fermentation industry and not a derivation
  • cell death below 100 °C neglected, so the ramp integrals start and finish there, per Doran §13.6.1
  • heat-up and cool-down taken as linear in temperature, which is Deindoerfer and Humphrey's electrical-heating profile rather than the jacket profile this vessel would actually have
  • nutrient destruction activation energy of 100 kJ mol⁻¹ — this figure is not from any assigned reading and is the single assumption carrying the hot-and-short conclusion
  • medium taken as fully soluble, so Armenante and Li's particle-core lag does not apply; a hydrolysate or starch slurry would invalidate the 15-second continuous answer
  • the seed train's generation count taken as the volume ratio alone, with no allowance for growth spent re-entering exponential phase after each transfer
  • segregational loss of 1% per generation assumed when converting the generation count into a plasmid-free fraction

Common misconceptions

  • That the holding time is the sterilisation cycle. For a vessel of this size it is usually the smallest of the three contributions: a 60-minute heat-up to 121 °C delivers del 37.7 on its own against a requirement of 40.1. Compute the ramps first and the hold last, which is the order Stanbury's own subsection headings use.
  • That higher temperature is harder on the medium. It is harder per minute and much easier per unit of sterility, because spore destruction has roughly three times the activation energy of nutrient destruction. At fixed del, 140 °C for 15 seconds destroys about a thirteenth of the nutrient that 121 °C for 13.5 minutes does. The whole of high-temperature short-time processing is that inequality.
  • That separate sterilisation is a precaution. It is a reaction-avoidance measure with named chemistry: Maillard between reducing sugars and amino groups, and phosphate precipitating with calcium and magnesium. No time-temperature regime prevents either, because neither is a thermal-death problem. Conversely, every extra stream is an extra aseptic connection, so the list of what to separate should be short and justified rather than long and cautious.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Why must heat-up and cool-down be integrated into the del calculation, and what happens if you ignore them?

A. Because cell death is first order with an Arrhenius rate constant and therefore proceeds at every temperature, not only at the holding temperature, and because at production scale the time spent above 100 °C during the ramps is in hours while the hold is in minutes. Ignoring them means solving ∇ = k_d·t_hd for the whole requirement and getting a holding time that is too long — in the worked case 13.5 min instead of 6.1 min with fast ramps, and with slow ramps a positive holding time where the correct answer is zero, because the ramps alone deliver del 66 against a requirement of 40. The cost is not safety, it is the medium: every surplus minute at 121 °C destroys nutrient, browns the broth and consumes vessel time, and none of it buys sterility that was not already there. The ramps have to be integrated numerically because k_d varies by two orders of magnitude over the ramp, so an average temperature does not work.

Q. Your seed train takes a 1 mL vial to a 50 m³ vessel. How many generations is that, and what do you do with the answer?

A. A volume ratio of 5 × 10⁷, so log₂(5 × 10⁷) = 25.6 generations of net growth as a floor, plus the growth spent re-entering exponential phase after each of the seven or eight transfers. Feed 26 generations into the week 33 segregational-loss model: at 1% loss per generation the production vessel is inoculated with 23% plasmid-free cells before the fermentation starts, and the loss continues through it. Three things follow. Use a chromosomally integrated construct if the product allows, because the arithmetic does not improve with vessel design. If a plasmid is unavoidable, keep selection on through the train and know what the selection costs in the production vessel, where antibiotic is usually not permitted. And transfer on Stanbury's criterion — a defined physiological state in late exponential phase — rather than on a clock, because that minimises the lag and therefore the generations spent outside net growth, which is the only part of the count that vessel design can touch.

Q. A reviewer says your decision to sterilise glucose separately is over-engineering. Answer them quantitatively.

A. The mechanism is not thermal death, so no cycle avoids it: reducing sugars condense with free amino groups in a Maillard reaction whose products brown the medium, consume lysine and arginine preferentially, and inhibit growth. The quantitative part is the excursion — with jacket heating, this medium spends about 105 minutes above 100 °C, and Maillard rate rises steeply through that range, so the exposure is not a few minutes at peak but most of two hours. The cost of separating is one extra vessel, one extra transfer and one extra aseptic connection, which raises contamination risk against the 10⁻³ target; the cost of not separating is a yield loss that has to be measured rather than argued, and a broth that is harder to clarify in week 51. The right answer is to run both and compare titres, and to say which way the comparison came out — and if it came out neutral, combine them, because the connection is a real risk and the chemistry is only a real cost when it is large.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Revisit your inoculum and medium choices. Which variation could be biological versus process-driven, and how would blocking or randomization help separate them?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 48 — Heterogeneous reaction, immobilisation and reactor choice

The week where a chemical engineering degree needs no translation at all, and the one place in this course where the biology is the easy part. A catalyst you can retain is a catalyst you can starve, and the whole content is the arithmetic that decides how big the particle may be. Three texts give the same problem three different ways and it is worth seeing why: Doran's generalised Thiele modulus divides by three for a sphere, Plawsky's divides by three inside the square root, and Shuler's does not divide at all, so the same bead can have a modulus of 0.7, 0.7 or 2.1 depending on whose definition you picked up. The number that matters is not the modulus but the effectiveness factor, and the safe route — the one that works when you do not know the intrinsic kinetics, which is almost always — is Weisz's observable modulus, which is built from the rate you measured rather than the rate you assumed.

Core ideas

1. Immobilisation is five chemistries and one trade, stated as what each costs

Shuler §3.4.1 lists the methods and Doran §12.1 the reasons; put them in the order of what they do to activity. Adsorption is cheap, reversible and leaks — the enzyme comes off with ionic strength or shear, so the catalyst has a half-life rather than a lifetime. Covalent attachment does not leak but reacts with residues that may be in the active site, so activity retention is typically a fraction rather than all of it, and the fraction has to be measured per enzyme. Entrapment in a gel — alginate, carrageenan, polyacrylamide — retains activity well because the protein is never chemically touched, and introduces the diffusion problem that is the rest of this week; it also leaks anything smaller than the mesh, which for an enzyme means slow loss and for a whole cell means none. Encapsulation behind a membrane is entrapment with a harder cut-off and a worse mass-transfer coefficient. Cross-linked enzyme aggregates dispense with the carrier entirely, so the catalyst is all catalyst rather than 95% support, which is the single largest gain available on a cost-per-kilogram basis and the reason they exist. Whole-cell flocculation and biofilm are the free versions, and the biofilm in particular is immobilisation you get whether you designed it or not. The trade across all five is the same one: everything that makes the catalyst easier to retain makes the substrate harder to deliver.

2. The shell balance, done once, in the geometry that matters

Take a sphere of radius R, effective diffusivity 𝒟_Ae, and a reaction consuming A at rate r_A per unit catalyst volume. A balance on a shell between r and r + Δr at steady state gives 𝒟_Ae (d²C_A/dr² + (2/r) dC_A/dr) = r_A, with dC_A/dr = 0 at r = 0 by symmetry and C_A = C_As at r = R. Doran §12.3 carries this through analytically for first and zero order; Plawsky §5.5.1 does the same balance in slab geometry for a first-order reaction, with the coupled energy balance alongside it, which is the better place to see the method because nothing is hidden in the Laplacian. For first order and a sphere the solution is the familiar hyperbolic-sine profile; the substitution u = r·C_A turns the equation into a constant-coefficient one and that is the whole trick. Do it by hand once. The reason to do it by hand is that the boundary condition at r = R is the one every real system breaks — C_As is not the bulk concentration, it is the surface concentration, and Doran says plainly that surface concentrations are very difficult to measure accurately, which is why §12.5 exists and why the external film cannot be dismissed as a refinement.

3. Three Thiele moduli for one bead, reconciled

Doran's generalised modulus is φ = (V_p/S_x)·r_A|C_As / √(2∫𝒟_Ae r_A dC_A), with V_p/S_x = R/3 for a sphere and b for a flat plate, which for first order collapses to φ₁ = (R/3)√(k₁/𝒟_Ae). Plawsky's Table 8.1 gives the spherical pellet modulus as √(k″r_o²/9𝒟_eff), which is the same number written differently — √(r_o²/9) is r_o/3 — and the planar one as √(k″L²/𝒟_eff) with L = V_p/A, also the same. The two books agree exactly. Shuler §3.4.2 defines it as φ = R√(V_m″/K_m 𝒟_e), with no division by three, so Shuler's modulus is three times Doran's and Plawsky's for the same sphere; Shuler's effectiveness-factor expression, η = (3/φ)(1/tanh φ − 1/φ), carries the compensating factor of three, so the physics is identical and only the bookkeeping differs. This is worth stating because the two conventions produce different-looking rules of thumb for the same bead: 'limitation begins above φ = 0.3' in Doran's convention is 'above φ ≈ 1' in Shuler's. Plawsky's Eq. (8.74) as printed in this PDF reads φ_p = k″L²/𝒟_eff, which would be the square of the modulus; the radical does not extract from the file, and Table 8.1 shows it, so take the table.

4. The effectiveness factor, and how much of the curve you actually need

η_i is the observed rate over the rate that would occur at C_As everywhere, so η_i = 1 means no internal limitation and η_i < 1 measures it. For first order and a sphere, η_i1 = (1/φ₁²)(3φ₁ coth 3φ₁ − 1); for a flat plate, tanh φ₁/φ₁; Plawsky's cylindrical case is I₁(2φ)/[φ I₀(2φ)]. Doran's Figure 12.8 and Plawsky's Figure 8.17 plot all three and they coincide exactly in both asymptotes and fall within 10-15% between, which is the practical result: geometry barely matters once you use V_p/S_x as the length scale. Two asymptotes carry most of the engineering. Below φ₁ = 0.3, η_i1 = 1 and the catalyst is working at full rate. Above φ₁ = 10, η_i1 ≈ 1/φ₁ for all geometries, which means the observed rate scales as 1/R — halve the bead and you double the rate, exactly, with no curve-reading required. Zero order is different in kind rather than degree: η_i0 = 1 for all φ₀ ≤ 0.577 in a sphere and ≤ 1 in a flat plate, because the rate does not depend on concentration until the concentration hits zero, at which point part of the particle switches off entirely. Doran's own warning is worth carrying: because of the errors in estimating the parameters that define φ, the effectiveness-factor curves should be viewed as diffuse bands rather than precise functions.

5. Weisz's observable modulus, which is the one to reach for first

The problem with everything above is that φ needs k₀, k₁ or V_max and K_m, and Doran §12.9 is explicit that those are hard to get for biological systems — and that an immobilised catalyst reports apparent values, not intrinsic ones, so measuring them on the bead is circular. Weisz's modulus removes the circularity: Φ = (V_p/S_x)²·r_A,obs/(𝒟_Ae C_As), which for a sphere is (R/3)²·r_A,obs/(𝒟_Ae C_As), and every quantity in it is measured. The criteria are flat and apply to all geometries and all kinetics: below Φ = 0.3, η_i = 1 and internal limitation is insignificant; above Φ = 3, η_i is substantially below 1; between 0.3 and 3 you have to look closer. The relation back to the conventional modulus is Φ = φ₁²η_i1 for first order and Φ = 2φ₀²η_i0 for zero order, which is how Doran's Figure 12.11 is constructed. What Φ cannot do is decide a Michaelis-Menten case cleanly, because the curve depends on β = K_m/C_As and that needs K_m — but the first- and zero-order curves bracket it, so you can always bound η_im from above and below without knowing K_m at all. That bracketing is the single most useful operational fact in the chapter.

6. The external film, which adds as a resistance and is checked the same way

Doran §12.5 defines the matching observable modulus for the film, Ω = (V_p/S_x)·r_A,obs/(k_s C_Ab), sphere (R/3)·r_A,obs/(k_s C_Ab), and the result that makes it usable: C_As/C_Ab = 1 − Ω. So Ω is literally the fractional drop across the boundary layer, Ω ≪ 1 means the film is irrelevant, and Ω approaching 1 means the film is delivering nothing. External and internal effectiveness multiply, η_T = η_i η_e, with η_e1 = C_As/C_Ab for first order and η_e0 = 1 for zero order — the zero-order case being the trap, because η_e0 = 1 does not mean there is no gradient across the film, only that the rate does not care about it until the surface concentration reaches zero. Plawsky §8.4.1 gives the same physics in series-resistance form, 1/η_g = 1/η_p + φ_p²/Bi_m, with the mass-transfer Biot number Bi_m = k_c λ_v/𝒟_eff, which is the more transferable way to see it: internal and external resistances add as reciprocals, so the larger one dominates and improving the smaller one does nothing. The order of operations in practice is therefore Ω first, then C_As, then Φ, then η_i — which is exactly the sequence of Doran's Example 12.5 and of this week's anchor.

7. Apparent kinetics: why the bead reports a K_m that is not its K_m

Shuler §3.4.2 states it plainly: under internal diffusion limitation, V_m,app and K_m,app are not true intrinsic constants. The mechanism is the shape of the curve rather than any change to the enzyme. At low bulk substrate the interior is depleted and the reaction is close to first order, so the observed rate is depressed by η_i; at high bulk substrate the interior is saturated, η_i rises toward 1, and the observed rate approaches the intrinsic V_max. Fitting Michaelis-Menten to that titration therefore returns a K_m larger than the true one — the apparent half-saturation point moves right because low concentrations are penalised more than high ones — with V_m,app roughly unchanged if saturation is reached. The same mechanism explains why diffusion masks substrate inhibition: if the interior never sees the bulk concentration, it never sees the inhibitory concentration either, so an immobilised preparation can look well-behaved over a range where the free enzyme is inhibited. That is a real process advantage and it is routinely mistaken for the immobilisation having stabilised the enzyme. Shuler's remedy is the right one and the only one: to get intrinsic constants, eliminate the resistances — small particles, high turbulence, high substrate — and measure there.

8. Oxygen in a pellet, and the √3 result

The fungal pellet is the same problem with the substrate changed to oxygen, and the numbers come out somewhere surprising. For zero-order consumption, the slab penetration depth before the concentration reaches zero is δ = √(2𝒟_Ae C_As/k₀). For a sphere, Doran's zero-order criterion says the core first goes anaerobic when the observable modulus reaches 0.667, i.e. at R_crit = 3√(0.667 𝒟_Ae C_As/k₀). Divide one by the other and the kinetics cancel completely: R_crit = √3 · δ. The critical radius of a sphere is 1.73 times the penetration depth of a slab, for any diffusivity, any surface concentration and any zero-order rate. That is worth having because it means one slab calculation sizes any pellet. Put numbers on it with Doran's measured alginate figure 𝒟_Ae = 1.88 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹, air-saturated water at 7.0 g O₂ m⁻³, a specific uptake of 3 mmol O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ and 100 kg dry weight per m³ of pellet: δ = 99 µm and R_crit = 172 µm. Lee §20.7's 600 µm A. niger pellet has a radius of 300 µm, so it is already well past the threshold — its core is anaerobic, and that is not a defect of that pellet but a property of every pellet anyone has ever grown. Which reframes §20.7's morphology engineering: chitin-synthase downregulation raising citric acid and penicillin titres 40%, cell-cycle genes raising malate about 50%, and a hyperbranching Tet-on glaA strain secreting 400% more glucoamylase are not fixes for the diffusion problem. They are ways of changing the ratio of active shell to dead core, which is the only variable the organism offers.

9. Reactor configuration follows from the particle, not the other way round

Doran §13.2 is the chapter's configuration section and §13.5 the comparison of ideal operation; the choice is decided by three numbers you now have. Retention: a stirred tank with a settler or screen retains the catalyst but subjects it to the full impeller shear, and gel beads attrit; a packed bed retains perfectly and shears not at all, but the pressure drop goes as 1/d_p² in the Blake-Kozeny regime, so the bead size that the effectiveness factor wants is the one the pump bill does not. A fluidised bed splits the difference and buys back the channelling risk. A membrane reactor retains the catalyst absolutely and gives you the worst mass-transfer coefficient of the four. Oxygen: a packed bed cannot be aerated along its length, so an aerobic immobilised system in a packed bed is a sequence of progressively more anoxic zones — which is why aerobic immobilised processes are either fluidised, trickle beds, or not immobilised. Compressibility: Stanbury's filtration chapter makes the point for filter cakes and it applies identically here — a soft particle under its own bed weight closes the voidage it needs, so the pressure drop of a tall gel-bead column is not the one the correlation predicts at zero load.

Worked anchor

How big may the bead be, and what does immobilisation cost at that size? An oxygen-limited whole-cell system, costed in the order Ω → C_As → Φ → η → loading → productivity.

Basis. Spherical gel beads of immobilised aerobic cells. Effective diffusivity of oxygen 𝒟_Ae = 1.88 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹, which is Doran's measured value for alginate. Bulk dissolved oxygen at air saturation and 30 °C, C_Ab = 7.0 g m⁻³. Liquid-solid mass-transfer coefficient k_s = 1 × 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹, Doran's value for a stirred vessel with neutrally buoyant beads. Specific oxygen uptake 3 mmol O₂ per g dry weight per hour, which is 0.096 g O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹.

Step 1 — the design as stated fails, and the failure is in the film. Try a 1 mm radius bead at the free-suspension cell density of 100 kg dry weight per m³. The volumetric uptake is k₀ = 0.096 × 100,000 / 3600 / 1000 = 2.67 × 10⁻³ kg O₂ m⁻³ s⁻¹. Then Ω = (R/3)·k₀/(k_s C_Ab) = (3.33 × 10⁻⁴)(2.67 × 10⁻³)/((1 × 10⁻⁵)(7 × 10⁻³)) = 12.7.

Ω = 12.7 means C_As/C_Ab = 1 − 12.7, which is negative, which means the film cannot deliver the oxygen at all. The bead cannot consume at that rate, so 'r_A,obs' was never an observable — the design is not slow, it is impossible. Setting Ω = 1 gives the radius at which the film saturates: R = 3 k_s C_Ab/k₀ = 3(1 × 10⁻⁵)(7 × 10⁻³)/(2.67 × 10⁻³) = 7.9 × 10⁻⁵ m, i.e. 79 µm. At full cell density the film alone caps the bead at 80 µm of radius, before any internal gradient is considered.

Step 2 — so fix the bead size and solve for the loading instead. Take R = 1.5 mm, a bead you can actually make, screen and retain. Require that the core stay aerobic: Doran's zero-order sphere criterion is Φ ≤ 0.667, so

k₀ ≤ 0.667 𝒟_Ae C_As/(R/3)² = 0.667(1.88 × 10⁻⁹)(7.0 × 10⁻³)/(5 × 10⁻⁴)² = 3.51 × 10⁻⁵ kg m⁻³ s⁻¹ = 126 g O₂ m⁻³ h⁻¹.

At 0.096 g O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ that is a loading of 126/0.096 = 1,320 g dry weight per m³ of bead, i.e. 1.3 g L⁻¹.

Step 3 — the film takes another quarter. Check Ω at that loading: Ω = (5 × 10⁻⁴)(3.51 × 10⁻⁵)/((1 × 10⁻⁵)(7 × 10⁻³)) = 0.25. So C_As = 0.75 C_Ab = 5.25 g m⁻³, not 7.0. Repeat step 2 with the correct surface concentration and the allowable loading falls to 0.99 g L⁻¹. Call it 1 g per litre of bead.

Step 4 — what that costs, stated as the comparison the week asks for. A free-cell fed-batch of the same organism runs at 30 to 50 g dry weight per litre. The immobilised bead at 1.5 mm runs at 1 g per litre of bead, and the bed is at best 60% beads, so 0.6 g per litre of reactor. That is a factor of 50 to 80 in catalyst density, paid for one thing: retention.

Step 5 — does retention pay it back? Retention buys dilution rates above µ_max, because the catalyst does not wash out. Compare volumetric rates. A chemostat at D = 0.4 h⁻¹ and 30 g L⁻¹ gives a biomass-hour product of 12 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹. A packed or fluidised bed at D = 5 h⁻¹ and 0.6 g L⁻¹ gives 3.0 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹. The ratio is 0.25. Retention does not pay it back — it recovers a quarter.

Step 6 — which is the answer, and it is a negative one with three named exceptions. For an aerobic whole-cell conversion, immobilisation in beads of a size you can handle loses a factor of four on volumetric productivity, and the loss is caused by oxygen, not by the substrate. It becomes the right answer when any of three things is true. (i) The reaction is anaerobic or the acceptor is not oxygen, in which case C_As is the substrate concentration — grams per litre rather than milligrams — and the same arithmetic with C_As = 10 g m⁻³ × 1,000 allows a loading three orders higher and the whole objection evaporates. This is why immobilised-cell processes in industry are overwhelmingly anaerobic. (ii) The catalyst is expensive and the retention is about catalyst cost rather than productivity, which is the enzyme case and the reason Artifact 31 is scoped around an enzyme. (iii) The product inhibits and continuous removal at high dilution is worth more than volumetric rate, which is the week 51 argument arriving early.

Step 7 — the sensitivity that decides whether to believe any of it. Every number above moves with 𝒟_Ae, which appears linearly in the loading limit, and 𝒟_Ae in a gel is the least well known quantity in the calculation. A liquid correlation from Plawsky §3.8 gives the free-solution diffusivity; the gel value is that multiplied by porosity and divided by tortuosity, and for alginate the published ratio ranges from about 0.5 to nearly 1. Taking the extremes, the allowable loading at R = 1.5 mm is between 0.5 and 1.0 g L⁻¹ — a factor of two, which is smaller than the factor of 50 the comparison turns on, so the conclusion survives the uncertainty. That is the right way round for a design calculation, and it is worth checking explicitly rather than assuming: the honest version of this anchor is not '1 g per litre' but 'between 0.5 and 1, and the decision does not depend on which'.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • effective diffusivity of oxygen in the gel taken as Doran's measured alginate value, 1.88 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹, for a gel that is not necessarily alginate
  • bulk dissolved oxygen 7.0 g m⁻³, water under air at 30 °C, with no correction for medium solutes
  • liquid-solid mass-transfer coefficient 1 × 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹, Doran's Example 12.5 value, with the chapter's own caveat that k_s is hard to determine for neutrally buoyant particles
  • specific oxygen uptake 3 mmol O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹, taken as independent of position inside the bead and of local oxygen concentration down to zero
  • oxygen consumption treated as strictly zero order, which is what makes Doran's Φ = 0.667 the anaerobic-core criterion; a Michaelis–Menten treatment would give a softer threshold
  • beads taken as uniform spheres of uniform cell loading, with no cell growth, no gradient in loading and no bead-size distribution
  • bed voidage 40%, so 60% of reactor volume is bead, when the volumetric comparison is made
  • the retention comparison assumes a packed or fluidised bed can be run at D = 5 h⁻¹ without channelling or attrition, which is the optimistic case for the immobilised side
  • porosity-and-tortuosity correction on 𝒟_Ae taken as between 0.5 and 1.0 of the free-solution value, which is the range the sensitivity step uses

Common misconceptions

  • That the Thiele modulus is a defined quantity. Three of the texts on this reading list define it three ways for the same sphere — Doran and Plawsky as (R/3)√(k/𝒟), Shuler as R√(V_m/K_m𝒟) — so a modulus quoted without its convention is a number without units. Quote the effectiveness factor instead, or quote Weisz's observable modulus, whose criteria (0.3 and 3) hold for every geometry and every kinetic order.
  • That a diffusion-limited bead reports a damaged enzyme. It reports a shifted curve: low bulk concentrations are penalised more than high ones, so the fitted K_m rises while V_max is roughly unchanged. The enzyme is intact. The same mechanism makes an immobilised preparation look resistant to substrate inhibition, because the interior never reaches the inhibitory concentration — a real process benefit routinely misattributed to stabilisation.
  • That zero-order kinetics means diffusion does not matter. It means the effectiveness factor is exactly 1 right up to the point where the concentration hits zero somewhere inside, and then part of the particle switches off completely — η_i0 = 1 for φ₀ ≤ 0.577 in a sphere and falls steeply after. For oxygen in a cell-loaded bead that threshold is at a radius of under 200 µm, which is smaller than any pellet or bead anyone works with, so the zero-order case is the one where the limitation is total rather than absent.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. At what bead radius does your system cross from reaction-limited to diffusion-limited, and which criterion did you use to decide?

A. Use Weisz's observable modulus, because it needs only measured quantities: Φ = (R/3)²r_A,obs/(𝒟_Ae C_As) for a sphere, with the crossing taken at Φ = 0.3 for the onset and Φ = 3 for substantial limitation, criteria that hold for all geometries and all kinetic orders. Solving for R at Φ = 0.3 gives R = 3√(0.3 𝒟_Ae C_As/r_A,obs). For the anchor's oxygen case — 𝒟_Ae = 1.88 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹, C_As = 7 g m⁻³, r_A,obs at 100 g dry weight per litre of bead — that is about 115 µm, and the stricter zero-order criterion for an anaerobic core, Φ = 0.667, gives 172 µm. Do not use the conventional Thiele modulus for this unless you have intrinsic kinetics measured on a particle small enough to be unlimited, because the constants fitted on a limited particle are apparent, not intrinsic, and using them is circular. And check Ω = (R/3)r_A,obs/(k_s C_Ab) before any of it: if Ω is not small, C_As is not C_Ab and the Φ you computed is wrong in the direction that flatters the design.

Q. Your immobilised preparation shows a K_m four times the free enzyme's and no substrate inhibition where the free enzyme is strongly inhibited. Two reviewers give two explanations. Which is right and how would you settle it?

A. Both observations have the same cause and it is not a change in the protein. Internal diffusion depresses the observed rate most at low bulk concentration, where the interior is most depleted relative to the surface, and least at high bulk concentration, where the interior saturates and η_i approaches 1; fitting Michaelis-Menten to that titration moves the apparent half-saturation point to the right. The same gradient means the interior never experiences the bulk concentration, so it never experiences the inhibitory concentration either, which is why the inhibition disappears. Settle it as Shuler §3.4.2 says: remove the resistances and measure again — crush or make much smaller particles, raise the turbulence to collapse the film, and work at high substrate — and if K_m returns to the free value, it was diffusion. A second and cheaper check is to vary only the particle radius: an intrinsic change in K_m is independent of R, an apparent one scales with it, and the direction of that dependence is unambiguous.

Q. A proposal immobilises an aerobic organism in 2 mm alginate beads at 30 g dry weight per litre of bead, to run a packed bed at high dilution. Give the quantitative objection.

A. Three numbers, in order. First the film: at 30 g L⁻¹ and 3 mmol O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ the volumetric demand is 8 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻³ s⁻¹, so Ω = (R/3)r/(k_s C_Ab) = (3.3 × 10⁻⁴)(8 × 10⁻⁴)/(10⁻⁵ × 7 × 10⁻³) = 3.8, which exceeds 1, so the boundary layer cannot deliver the stated rate at all and the design is not slow but impossible. Second the core: even if the film were removed, Φ for the interior at that loading is three orders above the 0.667 threshold, so all but an outer shell of about 100 µm is anaerobic — a 2 mm bead is 90% dead volume by that measure. Third the bed: a packed bed cannot be aerated along its length, so the oxygen that does arrive is consumed in the first centimetres and the rest of the column is an anoxic plug. The constructive version of the objection is to ask what the loading could be: at R = 1 mm, the aerobic-core criterion allows about 3 g per litre of bead, so the proposal is a factor of ten out, and the honest options are an anaerobic conversion, a fluidised or trickle bed, or free cells.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. If an enzyme or cell-associated catalyst converts a cassava-derived substrate, estimate whether mass transfer could limit the observed rate. What experiment would separate diffusion from intrinsic kinetics?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 49 — Fermenter design, aeration and mixing

Sizing a vessel is one calculation run until it closes, and the week's content is which constraint stops it. The chain is short — strain physiology gives an oxygen uptake rate, the uptake rate gives a required k_L a, the required k_L a gives a power input, the power input gives a heat load, and the heat load gives a cooling duty — and at production scale it does not close on air at atmospheric pressure. The honest part of this week is the uncertainty: Doran's own k_L a correlation states that it was derived in vessels up to 4.4 m³, agrees to within 20-40%, and overestimates transfer in vessels up to 25 m³ by about 100%, so a 50 m³ design is outside the correlation's range altogether. The right response is not a better correlation. It is to notice that the uncertainty in k_L a is larger than the difference between the design options, and to choose on the things that are certain — the oxygen balance, the heat balance, and Shuler's Table 10.2, which is arithmetic rather than correlation.

Core ideas

1. The vessel's geometry is mostly fixed, and the ratios are the specification

Shuler §10.2.4 states the convention: fermenters maintain a height-to-diameter ratio of 2:1 or 3:1. Stanbury Ch 7 fills in the rest under its named sections — basic functions of a fermenter for microbial or animal cell culture, aseptic operation and containment, body construction, aeration and agitation, the achievement and maintenance of aseptic conditions, valves and steam traps, other fermentation vessels, animal cell culture. The agitator subsection and the sparger subsections are the design content: impeller diameter typically a third of the tank diameter, four baffles at a tenth of the diameter to break solid-body rotation, and spargers in four kinds — porous, orifice, nozzle, combined sparger-agitator — whose difference is bubble size at source and therefore interfacial area before the impeller touches it. Two things in that chapter are easy to skip and should not be. The valves-and-steam-traps section is twenty pages because aseptic failure is a valve problem; week 47's contamination risk is spent here rather than in the autoclave. And the H:D ratio has a consequence Shuler draws out explicitly — if H:D is held constant, surface-to-volume falls steeply on scale-up, so surface aeration, which is irrelevant for a bacterial fermentation, becomes critical for shear-sensitive cultures where stirring and sparging are both restricted.

2. Power input: ungassed first, because that is the larger number

Rushton's result as Stanbury gives it: in the turbulent regime P = c ρ N³ D⁵, and in the viscous regime P = c µ N² D³. The turbulent form is the one that matters and its exponents are the whole of the scale-up problem — power goes as the cube of speed and the fifth power of diameter, so nothing about power scales with anything else about the vessel. Aeration reduces the draw, because an aerated liquid is less dense and the gas cavities behind the blades cut hydrodynamic resistance; Stanbury gives Michel and Miller's widely used correlation P_g = k(P²ND³/Q^0.56)^0.45 and Hughmark's later one, fitted to 248 published data sets, as P_g/P = 0.1(Q/NV)^−0.25(N²D⁴/gW V^0.67)^−0.2. The operational point Stanbury draws from this is the one that gets forgotten in design and bites in commissioning: in non-mycelial fermentations the greatest power demand occurs when the system is not gassed — during in-situ sterilisation of the medium, or if the air supply fails — so the motor must be sized for the ungassed draw and, for a fixed-speed motor, the operating speed specified against it. Gassed power is what you pay for; ungassed power is what you buy.

3. Non-Newtonian broths break the correlations, and Metzner-Otto is the patch

Stanbury is explicit that the power correlations apply to Newtonian fluids and are not directly applicable to non-Newtonian systems, because viscosity is not constant and therefore the impeller Reynolds number cannot be evaluated. If the agitation can hold fully turbulent conditions the problem disappears, since power is then independent of Reynolds number — but the chapter says plainly that the high viscosities of most mycelial broths make fully turbulent conditions impossible or extremely difficult, so those fermentations sit in the transitional regime and need a full power curve rather than an exponent. Metzner and Otto's 1957 device is to define an average shear rate proportional to the shaft speed, γ = kN, with k determined as 13 for pseudoplastic fluids in baffled reactors with single turbines; later work puts k between about 10 and 13 and Metzner et al. (1961) suggest 11 as a compromise with little loss of accuracy. With k you get an apparent viscosity, hence a Reynolds number, hence a point on the power curve. The reason to know this is not to use it — Stanbury notes the approach has not been widely applied — but to recognise when a quoted k_L a cannot mean what it says. Stanbury's own example makes it concrete: a Streptomyces aureofaciens broth on starch began as a Bingham plastic at about 18 pseudopoise, fell to a few pseudopoise and became Newtonian by 22 hours as the starch was degraded, then rose to about 90 pseudopoise and increasingly pseudoplastic as the mycelium developed. One number for one broth describes none of that.

4. k_L a against OUR, and the two concentrations that set the driving force

The balance is OTR = k_L a(C − C_L) and it has to equal OUR = q_O2 X at steady state. Both concentrations deserve a number rather than a symbol. C is the saturation concentration at the operating temperature and oxygen partial pressure, about 7.0 g m⁻³ for water under air at 30 °C, and Doran §9.8 is the section on estimating it with solute corrections. C_L is a setpoint, and the floor under it is Stanbury's Table 9.3 of critical dissolved oxygen concentrations: Azotobacter 0.018, E. coli 0.008, Saccharomyces 0.004 and Penicillium chrysogenum 0.022 mmol dm⁻³ at their stated temperatures — for E. coli that is 0.26 g m⁻³, under 4% of saturation. The gap between the critical concentration and a typical 20-30% setpoint is the whole of the margin, and the margin exists because the measured bulk concentration is not the concentration at the cell in a vessel with mixing time in the tens of seconds. Stanbury also carries the more interesting case, Hirose and Shibai's work on Brevibacterium flavum, where oxygen satisfaction below 1.0 harmed the glutamate and aspartate families but phenylalanine, valine and leucine peaked at satisfaction of 0.55, 0.60 and 0.85 — because the former come from TCA intermediates and the latter from pyruvate and PEP, so partial oxygen limitation moves carbon from one to the other. The critical dissolved oxygen for product formation is not the critical concentration for growth, and for some products it is below 1.

5. Mixing time and circulation time, and the comparison that matters

Doran §7.9 and §7.10 cover mixing and its power requirement, §7.11 the scale-up of mixing systems, §7.12 improving mixing in fermenters, §7.13 the effect of rheological properties on mixing and §7.14 the role of shear. The number to extract is the circulation time, the mean time for a parcel of liquid to make one pass through the impeller zone and back, and the comparison to make is against the strain's metabolic response time rather than against another vessel. In a 50 m³ vessel the circulation time is of the order of 20-60 s. Glucose uptake and the acetate overflow response, from weeks 40 and 42, operate on timescales of seconds. So a cell in a fed-batch vessel sees a glucose concentration that oscillates over its own response time — high near the feed point, depleted at the far wall — and responds to each excursion. That is the physical content of the scale-down experiment week 50 designs, and it is why the question 'what is the mixing time' is only interesting relative to 'what does the strain do in that long'. Doran §7.14's shear treatment gives the complementary comparison: tip speed πND, which is the quantity cells actually experience, against the host class's tolerance — filamentous fungi fragment, plant and animal cells lyse, bacteria mostly do not care.

6. Scale-up: four criteria, and Shuler's table proves they cannot be reconciled

Shuler Table 10.2 is the single most useful page in the week, and it is arithmetic rather than correlation, so it carries no uncertainty at all. Take a stirred tank from 80 L to 10,000 L — diameter up by 5, volume up by 125, H:D constant — and hold one of four things constant. Holding P₀/V constant: power rises 125-fold, impeller speed falls to 0.34, pumping rate per volume falls to 0.34, tip speed rises 1.7-fold, Reynolds number rises 8.5-fold. Holding impeller speed N constant: power rises 3,125-fold, P/V rises 25-fold, tip speed rises 5-fold, Re rises 25-fold. Holding tip speed ND_i constant: power rises 25-fold, P/V falls to 0.2, Re rises 5-fold. Holding Reynolds number constant: power falls to 0.2, P/V falls to 0.0016, tip speed falls to 0.2. Shuler's framing of what each criterion is for is the part to memorise: constant P/V implies constant oxygen transfer rate, constant Re implies geometrically similar flow patterns, constant N gives constant mixing time, and constant tip speed gives constant shear. Since power goes as N³D⁵ and volume as D³, the dependencies differ and no change of scale can hold more than one. Shuler's conclusion is stated as a theorem rather than a caution: the physical conditions in a large fermenter can never exactly duplicate those in a smaller one if geometric similarity is maintained.

7. Which criterion to hold, decided by which limitation you are in

The table does not choose; the oxygen balance does. If the process is oxygen-limited — which an aerobic fed-batch above about 20 g L⁻¹ always is — then constant P/V is the only criterion that preserves the thing the process is limited by, and the price is listed in the same column: mixing time gets worse, because N falls to a third, so the glucose gradients that the scale-down experiment is about get longer relative to the strain's response time. If the process is shear-limited — filamentous fungi, plant cells, animal cells — constant tip speed is the criterion, and the price is that P/V falls to a fifth, so the oxygen transfer must be bought some other way: enrichment, pressure, or a different vessel geometry altogether. If the process is mixing-limited — a very fast-responding strain, a pH-sensitive product, a feed that must be distributed — constant N is the criterion and the price is a 25-fold rise in P/V, which is a heat load and a shear load and usually unaffordable. Constant Reynolds number is in the table for completeness and is almost never the right answer in a fermenter, because it drops P/V by nearly three orders and oxygen transfer with it. The deliverable for this week is not a criterion; it is a sentence naming the criterion, the limitation it protects, and the quantity you have accepted will degrade, with the factor from Shuler's table beside it.

8. Heat is not a detail, and the arithmetic is one line

Doran §5.9 gives the result the whole week leans on, in its subsection 5.9.2, Heat of Reaction With Oxygen as Electron Acceptor: about 115 kJ per gmol of electrons transferred, four electrons per O₂, so approximately 460 kJ per gmol of oxygen consumed for aerobic metabolism — a figure Doran notes is verified against Cooney et al.'s experimental data. That makes the metabolic heat load a direct read-off from the oxygen demand, with no fermentation-specific data required. Doran's own Example 8.2 is the template: a 150 m³ vessel at 1.5 kg O₂ m⁻³ h⁻¹ generates 898 kW of metabolic heat, against 150 kW from an agitator at 1 kW m⁻³. The ratio is the point — metabolic heat is six times agitation heat in that case, so a vessel sized for the oxygen demand is heat-limited before it is power-limited, and the cooling surface is what actually constrains large aerobic vessels. Doran Ch 8 is the design side: §8.5 design equations for heat-transfer systems and §8.6 their application, which is where the log-mean temperature difference, the overall coefficient and the jacket-against-coil decision live. At 50 m³ an external jacket cannot carry a megawatt, which is why production vessels have internal coils, which is why they are harder to clean, which is week 47's contamination risk reappearing as a heat-transfer decision.

9. What the correlation can and cannot tell you, stated as a range

Doran §9.9 gives Eq. (9.46) as the mass-transfer correlation and is unusually honest about its own validity, and the surrounding prose is more useful than the equation — which is fortunate, since the equation is an image in this PDF and its exponent on P/V does not extract, so it is not quoted anywhere in these notes. The stated conditions: derived for non-coalescing, non-viscous media, between 500 and 10,000 W m⁻³, in vessels of 2 × 10⁻³ to 4.4 m³; agrees with data to within 20-40%; overestimates transfer in vessels up to 25 m³ by about 100%; and explicitly does not account for non-Newtonian behaviour, added sugars, antifoam, or the presence of cells. A fermentation broth at 50 m³ violates every one of those: it is larger than the largest vessel in the fit by an order of magnitude, it contains sugars, antifoam and cells by construction, and if the host is filamentous it is non-Newtonian as well. So the correct use of the correlation is to get an order of magnitude and a scaling exponent, not a number — and then to put a measured k_L a from §9.10's methods into the design as soon as a pilot vessel exists. Stanbury's parallel statement for the gassed power correlations is the same: provided it is remembered that these expressions are not particularly accurate, they may be used to predict power consumption in gassed systems where turbulent flow is known to be operating. Both books say the same thing, which is that at this scale the correlation is a prior and the measurement is the answer.

Worked anchor

Sizing a 50 m³ vessel from the strain's oxygen demand, until it fails, and then the three ways to make it close.

Basis. Working volume 50 m³, E. coli fed-batch, production phase at 40 g dry weight per litre and µ = 0.12 h⁻¹. Specific oxygen uptake taken as q_O2 = µ/Y_XO + m_O with Y_XO = 1.0 g DW per g O₂ and m_O = 0.01 g O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹, giving 0.13 g O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹, which is 4.1 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ — the figure used below is 4 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹, i.e. 0.128 g g⁻¹ h⁻¹.

Step 1 — the oxygen uptake rate. OUR = 40 g L⁻¹ × 0.128 g g⁻¹ h⁻¹ = 5.12 g O₂ L⁻¹ h⁻¹ = 5.12 kg m⁻³ h⁻¹. Over 50 m³ that is 256 kg of oxygen per hour, which is 8.0 kmol h⁻¹.

Step 2 — the required k_L a, on air. Hold dissolved oxygen at 30% of air saturation: C* = 7.0 g m⁻³, C_L = 2.1 g m⁻³, driving force 4.9 g m⁻³. k_L a = 5,120/4.9 = 1,045 h⁻¹ = 0.29 s⁻¹.

That is the end of the design. Stirred tanks at this scale reach a few hundred per hour; 1,045 h⁻¹ is not available on air at atmospheric pressure, and no choice of impeller fixes it, because the deficit is in the driving force rather than in the coefficient.

Check the margin before changing anything: Stanbury's Table 9.3 puts the critical dissolved oxygen for E. coli at 0.008 mmol dm⁻³, which is 0.26 g m⁻³. The 2.1 g m⁻³ setpoint is eight times critical. Lowering the setpoint to 1.0 g m⁻³ — still four times critical — raises the driving force to 6.0 and drops the requirement to 853 h⁻¹. Not enough, and it spends the whole mixing margin to buy 18%.

Step 3 — three ways to make it close, each costed against what it buys.

(i) Head pressure. At 2 bar absolute, C* doubles to 14.0 g m⁻³. Holding C_L at 2.1 g m⁻³ gives a driving force of 11.9 and k_L a = 5,120/11.9 = 430 h⁻¹, which is achievable. Cost: a vessel rated for 2 bar rather than 1, which Stanbury Ch 7's body-construction section prices as a wall-thickness and code question, plus compressor duty on the inlet air. Side effect: dissolved CO₂ doubles too, which for a strain sensitive to it is a real penalty and is why pressure is not free.

(ii) Oxygen enrichment to 40% v/v. C* = 7.0 × 0.40/0.2095 = 13.4 g m⁻³, driving force 11.3, k_L a = 454 h⁻¹. Cost: liquid oxygen, which is a per-kilogram operating cost rather than a capital one, and at 256 kg O₂ h⁻¹ the consumption is not small. Advantage over pressure: it is a dial rather than a design, so it can be turned up only in the production phase.

(iii) Lower the target. At 25 g L⁻¹ instead of 40, OUR falls to 3.2 kg m⁻³ h⁻¹ and the air requirement to 653 h⁻¹ — still high. At 20 g L⁻¹ it is 522 h⁻¹. So on air the vessel supports roughly 20 g L⁻¹ at this specific uptake rate, which is half the target. The cost is titre, and whether that is acceptable is week 52's question rather than this week's.

The arithmetic chooses (i) or (ii) over (iii) unless the product is cheap, and between (i) and (ii) on CO₂ sensitivity and on whether the capital is already spent. State which and why; that sentence is the deliverable.

Step 4 — the heat load, which is independent of all three choices. Oxygen consumption is 8.0 kmol h⁻¹ regardless of how it got there. At Doran's 460 kJ per gmol O₂, metabolic heat is 8,000 × 460/3,600 = 1,022 kW. Agitation at 2 kW m⁻³ adds 100 kW. Total about 1.12 MW to remove from a 50 m³ vessel.

Cooling water at a 20 °C rise: 1,122 kW / (4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 20 K) = 13.4 kg s⁻¹ = 48 m³ h⁻¹. That is a river's worth per vessel, and it is the number that decides jacket against coils: 50 m³ of broth has roughly 70 m² of jacketed surface, so a jacket would need an overall coefficient near 800 W m⁻² K⁻¹ across a log-mean ΔT of 20 K to carry 1.12 MW, which is optimistic for a jacket on a viscous broth. Internal coils, which can supply several hundred m², are the answer, and the consequence is the cleaning and sterilisation problem Stanbury Ch 7 devotes a section to.

Step 5 — how much of this to believe. The oxygen balance in steps 1 and 2 is stoichiometry and solubility: good to perhaps 10%, the error being mostly in q_O2. The heat balance in step 4 is also stoichiometry, through 460 kJ per gmol O₂: good to the same. The k_L a figures in step 3 are the weak link, because converting 430 h⁻¹ into a power input needs a correlation and Doran §9.9's correlation states it overestimates in vessels up to 25 m³ by about 100% and was never fitted above 4.4 m³. A factor of two on the power input is a factor of two on 100 kW of agitation, which is 9% of the heat load and does not change step 4, and it is a factor of two on an operating cost that week 52 will show is small beside raw materials. So the uncertainty that looks worst matters least. The number to get right is q_O2, because it drives the oxygen bill, the heat bill, the vessel rating and the cell density simultaneously — and it is a strain measurement from phase 3, not a correlation.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • working volume 50 m³ with height-to-diameter 2:1 or 3:1 and geometric similarity preserved on scale-up, per Shuler §10.2.4
  • q_O2 = μ/Y_XO + m_O with Y_XO = 1.0 g DW per g O₂ and m_O = 0.01 g O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹, giving 4 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at μ = 0.12 h⁻¹ — a correlation, not a measurement on this strain
  • C* = 7.0 g O₂ m⁻³ for water under air at 30 °C, scaling linearly with absolute pressure and with oxygen mole fraction
  • dissolved oxygen held at 2.1 g m⁻³, which is 30% of air saturation and eight times Stanbury's critical concentration for E. coli
  • the vessel treated as well mixed for the oxygen balance, which the same week's circulation time of 20–60 s contradicts
  • agitation at 2 kW m⁻³ when the heat load is computed, and 460 kJ per gmol O₂ of metabolic heat from Doran §5.9.2
  • cooling water available with a 20 K rise and a heat capacity of 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
  • an achievable k_L a of a few hundred per hour at this scale, which is an engineering judgement rather than a figure from the reading — Doran §9.9's correlation is explicitly invalid above 4.4 m³
  • no credit taken for surface aeration, which Shuler §10.2.4 says is unimportant for bacterial fermentations at this scale
