Common misconceptions

  • That a k_L a requirement that cannot be met means the impeller is wrong. It usually means the driving force is wrong. On air at 1 bar the maximum driving force is about 7 g m⁻³ minus the setpoint, and no agitator changes that ceiling — pressure and enrichment do, by raising C. Check which of the two factors in k_L a(C − C_L) is binding before redesigning the one that is not.
  • That holding P/V constant is the scale-up rule. It is one of four and it is the right one only when the process is oxygen-limited. Shuler's Table 10.2 shows what it costs: impeller speed and pumping rate per volume both fall to about a third, so mixing time gets substantially worse at the same time as oxygen transfer is preserved. Naming the criterion without naming the quantity you have let degrade is half an answer.
  • That agitation heat is the cooling problem. Metabolic heat is the cooling problem: at 460 kJ per gmol of oxygen consumed, Doran's own 150 m³ example generates 898 kW of metabolic heat against 150 kW from a 1 kW m⁻³ agitator. Sizing the cooling from the power input alone understates the duty by most of it, and the error grows with cell density, which is the direction every process is being pushed.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Holding P/V constant on scale-up, what happens to mixing time and to k_L a, and which fails first?

A. k_L a is approximately preserved, which is the reason the criterion is chosen: Shuler states constant P/V as implying constant oxygen transfer rate, and the correlations have k_L a as a power of P/V with a positive exponent and of superficial gas velocity, so fixing both roughly fixes k_L a. Mixing time gets worse, and Table 10.2 says by how much: going from 80 L to 10,000 L at constant P₀/V, impeller speed falls to 0.34 of the small-scale value and pumping rate per unit volume falls to 0.34 with it, while tip speed rises 1.7-fold. Since mixing time scales roughly as 1/N for a geometrically similar vessel, it lengthens by about a factor of three on top of the lengthening that comes from the vessel simply being bigger. Which fails first depends on the strain, and the comparison is circulation time against metabolic response time rather than mixing time against any absolute number: a fed-batch E. coli responding to glucose and oxygen in seconds fails on mixing, because it experiences the gradients as real excursions; a slow-growing fungus with a 40-minute response does not notice a 60-second circulation time and fails instead on shear, since tip speed went up 1.7-fold. The general answer is that at constant P/V oxygen is protected and homogeneity is sacrificed, and whether that is the right trade is a property of the organism, not of the vessel.

Q. Your design needs k_L a = 1,045 h⁻¹ on air and the vessel can deliver 450 h⁻¹. Give three options with their costs, and say which you would reject first.

A. Raise C by head pressure: at 2 bar absolute the saturation concentration doubles to about 14 g m⁻³, the driving force goes from 4.9 to 11.9 g m⁻³ and the requirement falls to 430 h⁻¹. Cost is a vessel rated to 2 bar and compressor duty, and the side effect is that dissolved CO₂ doubles as well, which inhibits some strains. Raise C by oxygen enrichment to 40%: C* = 13.4 g m⁻³, requirement 454 h⁻¹, cost is liquid oxygen as an operating line, advantage is that it is a dial rather than a design and can be used only in the production phase. Lower the demand: at 20 g L⁻¹ instead of 40 the requirement is about 520 h⁻¹, cost is half the titre and therefore, by week 51's sensitivity, substantially more than half the downstream cost per kilogram. Reject first the option of lowering the dissolved-oxygen setpoint toward the critical concentration — it looks free, but E. coli's critical concentration is 0.26 g m⁻³ against a 2.1 g m⁻³ setpoint, and that eight-fold margin is not conservatism, it is the allowance for the fact that the probe reads a bulk average in a vessel whose circulation time is tens of seconds. Spending it buys 18% of driving force and removes the protection against the gradients that week 50's scale-down experiment exists to characterise.

Q. Why is Doran's k_L a correlation of limited use for this vessel, and what do you do instead?

A. Because the vessel is outside every condition of the fit. §9.9 states that the correlation was derived for non-coalescing, non-viscous media, at 500 to 10,000 W m⁻³, in vessels from 2 × 10⁻³ to 4.4 m³, that it agrees with data to within 20-40%, that it overestimates transfer in vessels up to 25 m³ by about 100%, and that it does not account for non-Newtonian behaviour, added sugars, antifoam or the presence of cells. A 50 m³ fermentation broth is an order of magnitude beyond the largest vessel in the fit and contains sugars, antifoam and cells by definition. What you do is three things. Use the correlation for its exponents rather than its value, to get the scaling of k_L a with P/V and gas velocity, since the exponents are more robust than the prefactor. Design the oxygen supply from the balance instead, which is stoichiometry and solubility and carries about 10% error — the 460 kJ per gmol O₂ heat figure and the 7 g m⁻³ saturation figure are not correlations. And measure k_L a as soon as a pilot vessel exists, by §9.10's methods, since Stanbury makes the same point about the gassed-power correlations: they may be used provided it is remembered that they are not particularly accurate. The constructive conclusion is that the uncertainty in k_L a is larger than the difference between the design options, so the decision should be made on the quantities that are certain.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Relate oxygen transfer and mixing to one fermentation outcome from your work. Which scale-up parameter should be preserved, and what limitation does that choice create?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 50 — Instrumentation, control and feeding strategies

Control applied to a catalyst that adapts to the control action, which is the one sentence that makes this week different from a process-control course. The content divides into what can be measured, what has to be inferred, and what the feed rate is actually allowed to be — and the third of those is where the arithmetic lives. The result that organises the week is that the feed profile is not set by the strain's maximum growth rate, nor by the overflow threshold, but by the vessel's oxygen transfer capacity from week 49: once cell density is high enough, the exponential feed has to stop being exponential, and the correct policy becomes constant oxygen uptake rate with a growth rate that falls as the reciprocal of biomass. Every feeding strategy in the textbooks is a way of implementing that without saying so.

Core ideas

1. What is measured, and what each measurement's failure mode is

Stanbury Ch 8 is organised as a catalogue and it should be read as one, with a failure mode written beside each entry, because that column is what the control philosophy document needs and no book supplies it. The chapter's named sections: methods of measuring process variables, covering temperature (mercury-in-glass, electrical resistance, thermistors, and temperature control), flow measurement and control for gases and liquids, pressure measurement and control, safety valves, agitator shaft power, rate of stirring, foam sensing and control, weight, microbial biomass, measurement and control of dissolved oxygen, inlet and exit-gas analysis, pH measurement and control, redox, carbon dioxide electrodes; then on-line analysis of other chemical factors — ion-specific sensors, enzyme and microbial electrodes, near infra-red spectroscopy, mass spectrometers; then control systems, from manual through two-position, proportional, integral and derivative and their combinations; then computer applications, with data logging, data analysis and process control. The failure modes worth writing in: a dissolved-oxygen probe drifts and fouls and reads a bulk average in a vessel with gradients; a pH probe drifts and cannot be recalibrated in situ; a weight signal is the most reliable measurement on the vessel and is usually ignored; exit-gas analysis is the most informative and has the longest dead time, because it includes the headspace residence time. That last one is the reason the off-gas soft sensor is a diagnostic rather than a control input.

2. The DO cascade, and why it is a cascade rather than a loop

Dissolved oxygen has four actuators and they must be ordered, because they differ by two orders of magnitude in cost per unit of transfer. Agitation first: cheapest, fastest, and bounded above by shear tolerance and by the motor. Aeration rate second: cheap, but bounded by flooding of the impeller at high gas rate and by foam, and with a side effect — raising the gas rate strips CO₂, which changes pH control. Head pressure third: raises C* in proportion to absolute pressure, which is the week 49 design decision reappearing as a control action, and bounded by the vessel rating and by dissolved CO₂ rising in the same proportion. Oxygen enrichment last: unbounded in effect and the only one with a significant per-kilogram operating cost. The reason for the order is that each step should be exhausted before the next begins, and the reason it is a cascade rather than four independent loops is that they interact — more air both raises k_L a and strips CO₂ and increases foam, so a controller allowed to use them in parallel will hunt. Write the setpoints and the handover points explicitly, including what happens on reverse: coming down from enrichment should be the first thing to go, not the last.

3. The exponential feed, derived rather than quoted

Fed-batch at constant specific growth rate is the one control strategy in biology that has a closed-form answer, and it is worth deriving because every term in it is a decision. If the feed is the only source of the limiting substrate and the substrate concentration in the vessel is negligible — the defining assumption of a fed-batch, and the one that fails first — then the substrate consumed equals the substrate fed, so F·S_F = (µ/Y_XS)·X·V. With X·V = X₀V₀e^(µt) the feed rate is F(t) = (µ/Y_XS)·(X₀V₀/S_F)·e^(µt), which is an exponential ramp with the same exponent as the growth it is driving. The cumulative volume added is F(0)(e^(µt) − 1)/µ, which is why the vessel's headspace sets the run length as firmly as the strain does. Stanbury Ch 2's named section on fed-batch culture gives the taxonomy around it — variable volume, fixed volume, cyclic fed-batch, applications and examples — and the distinction that matters for control is variable against fixed volume, because a fixed-volume fed-batch with a concentrated feed keeps the vessel constant and therefore keeps k_L a constant, which the variable-volume version does not. Shuler §9.3.3 is the quantitative treatment of fed-batch operation and §9.3.1 the chemostat-with-recycle case that is its continuous cousin.

4. The setpoint comes from physiology, and there are two candidate ceilings

Having derived the profile, the only free parameter is µ, and there are two different arguments for where it goes. The overflow argument, from week 40: acetate excretion is threshold-linear in growth rate, so the setpoint should sit below the threshold with a margin, and the threshold is a strain measurement from phase 3 rather than a literature value. The oxygen argument, from week 49: q_O2 = µ/Y_XO + m_O, so the oxygen demand per gram rises linearly with µ and the total demand rises as X·q_O2, which means the vessel's transfer capacity sets a combined ceiling on the product of biomass and growth rate rather than on either alone. These two ceilings are not the same and they bind at different times in the run. Early, when X is low, oxygen is abundant and the overflow threshold binds. Later, when X is high, the oxygen ceiling binds at a growth rate well below the overflow threshold, so the overflow constraint stops being active and the strain's own metabolic preference stops being the issue. The anchor computes where the crossover is. The practical consequence is that a feed profile set once, at the start, from the overflow threshold, will violate the oxygen ceiling in the second half of every high-density run — which is exactly what a DO crash at hour ten is.

5. DO-stat and pH-stat: feedback on a consequence rather than on a model

The exponential profile is open-loop: it assumes Y_XS, X₀ and µ and corrects for none of them, so an error in any of the three compounds over the run. The alternative is to feed on a signal that the substrate's exhaustion produces. DO-stat exploits the fact that when the carbon source runs out, respiration stops and dissolved oxygen spikes; the controller adds feed on a rising-DO event. Its advantage is that it is self-correcting with respect to every parameter in the open-loop model. Its instability risk is specific and worth stating: the loop has a dead time set by the circulation time plus the probe response, and the plant gain changes through the run as biomass rises, so a controller tuned at 10 g L⁻¹ oscillates at 50 g L⁻¹, and the oscillation is in substrate concentration, which means the culture is cycling between starvation and excess — the exact condition the strategy was adopted to avoid. pH-stat works the same way on a different consequence: with ammonia as both nitrogen source and base, consumption of the carbon source acidifies and the base addition tracks growth, so base flow is a feed signal. Its failure mode is that anything else which changes pH — acetate excretion above all — corrupts the signal, so pH-stat is least reliable exactly in the overflow condition it would be most useful for.

6. The off-gas soft sensor, which is the best instrument on the vessel

From inlet and exit gas composition and the gas flow rate, a nitrogen balance gives the exit flow, and the oxygen and carbon dioxide balances then give OUR and CER directly, with no assumption about the culture at all. That makes OUR and CER the only two rates on a production fermenter that are measured rather than inferred, and their ratio RQ = CER/OUR is the single most informative number available in real time. RQ has a value for each metabolic state and the table is the deliverable: on glucose with full respiration, RQ ≈ 1.0; growing on glycerol or another more-reduced substrate, below 1; producing a reduced product such as a lipid or an alcohol, below 1; oxidising a partially-oxidised substrate such as an organic acid, above 1; fermenting — ethanol or acetate overflow — distinctly above 1, because CO₂ is produced without a matching oxygen consumption; and consuming a previously-excreted acid after the carbon source is exhausted, below 1 and falling with OUR. The diagnostic value is in the deviations rather than the value: RQ rising from 1.0 to 1.3 mid-fermentation means fermentative metabolism has started, which means either the feed has outrun the oxygen supply or the oxygen supply has fallen, and the two are distinguished by whether OUR rose or fell at the same moment. Doran §13.4's monitoring-and-control section covers this under state estimation and indirect metabolic control, which is where the soft-sensor idea is treated as a control architecture rather than an instrument.

7. The mass balance as an observer, and what it can and cannot reconstruct

Doran §13.4.5 state estimation and §13.4.4 process modelling are the formal version of what the off-gas sensor does informally: with a stoichiometric model and a subset of measured rates, the unmeasured rates can be reconstructed, and the reconciliation machinery from week 17 is exactly the tool. The useful framing is degrees of freedom. A carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and electron balance over the vessel gives four equations; the measured quantities on a production fermenter are typically OUR, CER, base addition, feed rate and weight, which is five; the unknowns are biomass, product, each by-product and the residual substrate. Count them and the system is usually underdetermined by one or two, which is why on-line biomass estimation by capacitance or optical probe is worth its drift problems — it closes the system. When the system is overdetermined, the redundancy is a consistency check rather than a bonus, and the week 17 habit applies: an inconsistency is information about which measurement is wrong, and the usual answer is the one nobody calibrated. What the observer cannot reconstruct is anything with no elemental signature distinct from biomass, which includes most intracellular product — so for an intracellular product the soft sensor tracks the process but not the thing you are selling.

8. The scale-down experiment, which is the only honest test of a scale-up decision

Shuler §10.2.5 is the scale-down section and its logic is the inverse of §10.2.4's: since the large vessel cannot reproduce the small one, reproduce the large vessel's heterogeneity in a small one and see what the strain does. The standard construction is two compartments — a stirred vessel representing the well-mixed bulk, connected to a plug-flow loop representing the poorly-mixed zone, with the loop's residence time set to the large vessel's circulation time from week 49 and the feed introduced into the loop so that the cells see the same concentration excursion they would see at the feed point. The design parameters are therefore not free: the cycling timescale comes from the circulation time, the amplitude from the feed concentration and the loop's residence time, and the only genuine choices are what to measure and for how long. What to measure is the thing the gradients are supposed to cost — by-product formation, yield, and the plasmid or construct stability from week 33 — and the comparison is against the same strain in a single well-mixed vessel at the same average conditions. A strain that performs identically in both is a strain whose scale-up is a transport problem only. A strain that loses 20% of yield in the two-compartment system has told you the number to put in week 52's model, and that number cannot be obtained any other way.

9. The control philosophy document, which is the week's actual deliverable

Every loop, setpoint, alarm and the response to each alarm, which sounds like documentation and is actually a design review. Three things make it worth writing. It forces the handover points in the DO cascade to be numbers, which they otherwise never are. It forces an alarm to have a response, which exposes the alarms that exist because the signal exists rather than because anything would be done — and an alarm with no response trains operators to ignore alarms, which is the mechanism by which real failures are missed. And it forces the distinction between a control variable and a diagnostic: RQ is a diagnostic, because closing a loop on a quantity with the off-gas dead time produces oscillation, whereas dissolved oxygen is a control variable despite being the less informative of the two. Writing which is which, and why, is the part of this week that transfers directly into the capstone dossier, because it is the part a reviewer can check without rerunning anything.

Worked anchor

Where the exponential feed has to stop, and what replaces it.

Basis. The week 49 vessel: 50 m³ working volume, starting the feed at V₀ = 30 m³ and X₀ = 20 g L⁻¹, so X₀V₀ = 600 kg dry weight. Feed of 600 g L⁻¹ glucose. Biomass yield Y_XS = 0.45 g g⁻¹. Oxygen demand q_O2 = µ/Y_XO + m_O with Y_XO = 1.0 g DW per g O₂ and m_O = 0.01 g O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹.

Step 1 — the open-loop profile at the overflow-based setpoint. Phase 3 put the acetate threshold at about 0.2 h⁻¹; take µ = 0.12 h⁻¹, a 40% margin below it. F(0) = (µ/Y_XS)(X₀V₀/S_F) = (0.12/0.45)(600,000 g)/(600 g L⁻¹) = 267 L h⁻¹.

The profile: at 4 h, 431 L h⁻¹ with 1.37 m³ added and 970 kg of biomass; at 8 h, 696 L h⁻¹ with 3.58 m³ added and 1,567 kg; at 12 h, 1,126 L h⁻¹ with 7.16 m³ added and 2,532 kg. At 12 h the volume is 37.2 m³ and the cell density 68 g L⁻¹. The vessel has headspace for about 20 more hours at this rate before it reaches 50 m³, so volume is not the binding constraint.

Step 2 — the oxygen ceiling, which is. At 12 h, q_O2 = 0.12 + 0.01 = 0.13 g O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ and X = 68 g L⁻¹, so OUR = 8.8 kg O₂ m⁻³ h⁻¹.

Week 49's vessel delivers, at 2 bar absolute and k_L a = 500 h⁻¹ with C_L held at 2.1 g m⁻³, an OTR of 500 × (14.0 − 2.1) = 5,950 g m⁻³ h⁻¹ = 5.95 kg m⁻³ h⁻¹.

So the demand at 12 h is 1.5 times the supply. The run does not reach 12 hours at µ = 0.12.

Step 3 — where it actually stops. The ceiling is X(µ + 0.01) ≤ 5,950 g m⁻³ h⁻¹ with X in g m⁻³, i.e. X ≤ 5,950/(µ + m_O) in g m⁻³. At µ = 0.12 that is X ≤ 45.8 g L⁻¹. Working back through X·V = 600e^(0.12t) and V = 30 + 0.267(e^(0.12t) − 1)/0.12: solving X(t) = 45.8 gives t ≈ 8.9 h, with V = 34.2 m³ and X·V = 1,750 kg. So the exponential phase lasts just under nine hours and delivers 46 g L⁻¹, not the 68 g L⁻¹ the profile would reach at twelve.

Step 4 — what replaces it. Past the ceiling the correct policy is constant OUR: feed at whatever rate holds OTR = OUR, which means the total oxygen consumption is pinned at 5.95 kg m⁻³ h⁻¹ × V and the growth rate falls as biomass rises. Explicitly, µ(t) = OTR_max/X(t) − m_O, so at 60 g L⁻¹, µ = 5,950/60,000 − 0.01 = 0.089 h⁻¹; at 80 g L⁻¹, 0.064 h⁻¹; at 100 g L⁻¹, 0.0495 h⁻¹. Biomass then grows almost linearly rather than exponentially, because X·µ is constant, which is the signature of an oxygen-transfer-limited fed-batch and is what the biomass curve of nearly every high-density process actually looks like.

Time to 80 g L⁻¹: integrating dX·V/dt = (OTR_max/Y_XO)·V with V rising slowly, the biomass increment from 46 to 80 g L⁻¹ in roughly 36 m³ is about 1,200 kg, at a production rate of about 5.95 × 36 = 214 kg O₂ h⁻¹ and therefore about 214 kg DW h⁻¹, giving about 5.6 h. So 80 g L⁻¹ is reached at roughly 14.5 h against the 11 h the pure exponential would have predicted — a 30% longer run for the same endpoint, and the difference is entirely oxygen.

Step 5 — the three ways to implement constant OUR, costed. (i) Compute it open-loop from the model above and program the pump. Free, and wrong by however much Y_XO, m_O and X₀ are wrong, with the errors compounding. (ii) Close the loop on dissolved oxygen: feed down when DO falls below setpoint. Self-correcting with respect to every parameter, and this is the only version that is actually robust, because DO is the variable the ceiling is expressed in. Its instability risk is the dead time — circulation time plus probe response, tens of seconds at this scale — against a plant gain that rises with biomass, so the loop must be retuned or gain-scheduled through the run. (iii) Close the loop on off-gas OUR directly, which is the physically correct variable. Rejected: the off-gas dead time includes headspace residence, which at this scale is minutes, so a feed loop closed on OUR will oscillate. Use OUR as the diagnostic that tells you whether the DO loop is doing what you think.

Step 6 — the arithmetic that chooses the setpoint, stated once. Before the ceiling, µ is chosen from overflow: as high as the acetate threshold allows, because a higher µ gets to the ceiling sooner and the time before the ceiling is the only time the vessel is not oxygen-limited. After the ceiling, µ is not chosen at all — it is the quotient of a fixed oxygen supply and a rising biomass, and the only lever is the oxygen supply. Which means the single most valuable control action in a high-density fed-batch is not in the feed loop. It is the head pressure and the enrichment valve, which is to say it is week 49's design decision, exercised. A control philosophy that treats the feed as the primary manipulated variable and enrichment as a last resort has the hierarchy upside down for the second half of the run.

What this leaves out, and it matters: the whole calculation treats the vessel as well mixed, and week 49 put the circulation time at 20-60 s. The cells near the feed point see glucose at far above the vessel average for a few seconds per pass, and that is precisely the condition that triggers overflow regardless of the average growth rate. So the margin below the acetate threshold in step 1 is not conservatism about µ, it is an allowance for a gradient the model does not contain, and the only way to size it is the two-compartment scale-down experiment.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the week 49 vessel and its oxygen supply carried forward unchanged, including the 2 bar absolute decision
  • feed is the only source of the limiting substrate and its concentration in the vessel is negligible, which is what makes the exponential profile exact
  • Y_XS = 0.45 g g⁻¹ and Y_XO = 1.0 g DW per g O₂ both constant through the run, when maintenance makes both fall at low μ
  • feed glucose at 600 g L⁻¹ and no volume change on mixing
  • the acetate overflow threshold at about 0.2 h⁻¹, from phase 3 for this strain, with μ set 40% below it
  • k_L a held at 500 h⁻¹ through the run, which a variable-volume fed-batch does not do as the liquid height rises
  • the vessel treated as well mixed, so the computed μ ceiling ignores the local excursion at the feed point — the margin below the overflow threshold is the allowance for it and is not derived
  • product formation neglected in the biomass and oxygen balances, so the figures are for a growth phase rather than a production phase
  • no evaporative loss and no change in broth density as cell density rises

Common misconceptions

  • That the feed profile is set by the strain. It is set by the strain only until the oxygen ceiling binds, which in a high-density aerobic process happens in the first half of the run. After that, growth rate is the quotient of a fixed oxygen supply and a rising biomass, falling as 1/X, and no feed-controller tuning changes it — only pressure or enrichment does. A DO crash at hour ten is this arithmetic arriving on schedule, not a control fault.
  • That RQ is a control variable. It is the most informative number on the vessel and the worst one to close a loop on, because the off-gas measurement carries a dead time that includes headspace residence — minutes at production scale. Close the feed loop on dissolved oxygen, which has a dead time of tens of seconds, and use RQ to check that the DO loop is doing what you intended.
  • That DO-stat is self-correcting and therefore safe. It is self-correcting with respect to the parameters of the open-loop model, which is its real advantage, and it is not safe, because its plant gain rises with biomass through the run while its dead time stays fixed. A loop tuned at 10 g L⁻¹ oscillates at 50, and the oscillation is in substrate concentration — cycling the culture between starvation and excess, which is the condition the strategy was adopted to avoid.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Your RQ rises from 1.0 to 1.3 mid-fermentation. What happened, and what is your control response?

A. CO₂ is being produced without a matching oxygen consumption, which means fermentative metabolism has started — on glucose that is acetate or ethanol overflow. Two causes produce the same RQ signature and the discriminator is what OUR did at the same moment. If OUR fell while CER held or rose, the oxygen supply failed: a blocked sparger, impeller flooding, a foam-over onto the exhaust filter, or a drop in head pressure. If OUR held at its ceiling while CER rose, the demand outran the supply: the feed is now driving a growth rate the vessel cannot oxygenate, which is the anchor's step 3 arriving. Response differs accordingly. For a supply failure, restore the supply and do not touch the feed until you know why it fell, because cutting the feed masks the fault. For a demand overrun, cut the feed to the rate that holds OUR at the transfer ceiling and, if the product phase needs the biomass, buy supply with head pressure and then enrichment in that order. In both cases check the dissolved oxygen trace against the RQ trace: if DO fell before RQ rose, it is supply; if RQ rose while DO was already at setpoint and the controller was saturated, it is demand. And record the acetate, because overflow carbon does not come back and the yield loss goes into week 52's model as a number rather than a worry.

Q. Derive the exponential feed rate for a target specific growth rate, and state the assumption that fails first.

A. Take the limiting substrate as supplied only by the feed and consumed with a constant biomass yield, and take its concentration in the vessel as negligible, which is what makes the culture substrate-limited rather than substrate-sufficient. Then the substrate fed equals the substrate consumed: F·S_F = (µ/Y_XS)·X·V. Biomass at constant µ is X·V = X₀V₀e^(µt), so F(t) = (µ/Y_XS)(X₀V₀/S_F)e^(µt), with cumulative volume F(0)(e^(µt) − 1)/µ. For the worked basis — X₀V₀ = 600 kg, S_F = 600 g L⁻¹, Y_XS = 0.45, µ = 0.12 h⁻¹ — F(0) = 267 L h⁻¹, doubling every 5.8 h. The assumption that fails first is not the yield and not the negligible residual substrate; it is that the vessel is well mixed. The derivation prices the feed against the vessel average, while the cells passing the feed point see a concentration far above it for a few seconds per circulation, and overflow responds to the local concentration rather than the average. That is why the µ setpoint carries a margin below the measured acetate threshold and why the margin can only be sized by a two-compartment scale-down experiment. The second assumption to fail is constancy of Y_XS, which falls as maintenance becomes a larger fraction at low µ — so the open-loop profile systematically over-feeds late in the run, which is a second reason to close the loop on dissolved oxygen rather than trust the ramp.

Q. Design the two-compartment scale-down experiment for this process, and say what result would change your scale-up decision.

A. A well-mixed stirred vessel representing the bulk, connected to a plug-flow loop representing the feed zone, with the feed introduced into the loop. Set the loop residence time to the large vessel's circulation time from week 49 — 20 to 60 s for 50 m³ — and set the loop's glucose concentration from the feed rate and loop volume so the excursion amplitude matches what a cell passing the feed point would see. Run the same strain in a single well-mixed vessel at the same average dilution, temperature, pH and dissolved oxygen as the control. Measure three things over a full fed-batch: acetate or by-product accumulation, biomass and product yield on substrate, and construct stability by the week 33 assay. The result that changes the decision is a yield or stability gap between the two vessels. If the two-compartment system matches the control, the scale-up is a transport problem only and constant P/V with its degraded mixing time is acceptable. If it loses yield, the choice between Shuler's four criteria changes — constant impeller speed protects mixing time at a 25-fold cost in P/V, which then has to be weighed against the measured yield loss rather than guessed at — and the feed point itself becomes a design variable, since multiple feed points or a feed into the impeller discharge reduce the amplitude of the excursion without touching the criterion. If it loses construct stability, the answer is upstream of the vessel entirely and is week 33's: integrate the construct, because no mixing regime fixes segregational loss.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Choose a feeding or control strategy for a substrate-limited fermentation. What signal would trigger the control action, and how could sensor lag or model error cause a poor feed?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 51 — Downstream processing

For most products the majority of the cost, and the week where the strain engineering of the previous fifty weeks gets priced. The content is a selection problem — a train of unit operations chosen from the product's physical properties — and the thing that makes it a quantitative week rather than a catalogue is that stage yields multiply while stage costs add. Ten stages at 95% each give 59.9% overall, which is the arithmetic every proposal with a long purification train has not done. The second organising number is Shuler's: recovery and purification exceed 50% of manufacturing cost, especially for intracellular products, and the fraction rises as titre falls, from roughly half at a citric-acid titre to roughly nine-tenths at a therapeutic-protein titre. That is why titre and product location outrank yield in this week, and why the strain decisions that look like downstream decisions — secrete or not, excrete or not — are the expensive ones.

Core ideas

1. The train is selected from four physical properties, not from a flowsheet

Size, solubility, volatility and charge, in that order of coarseness, and each one maps to a family of operations. Size separates cells from broth and, at the other end of the scale, separates the product from everything bigger or smaller than it: filtration and centrifugation at the micron scale, micro- and ultrafiltration at the sub-micron, nanofiltration and reverse osmosis at the molecular. Solubility decides between extraction, precipitation and crystallisation. Volatility decides whether distillation is available, which for ethanol is the whole process and for a protein is never. Charge decides ion exchange and electrodialysis, and in combination with solubility it decides isoelectric precipitation. Belter, Cussler and Hu organise the book exactly this way — Part I Removal of Insolubles, Part II Isolation, Part III Product Purification, Part IV Polishing — and the ordering principle behind those four parts is the one to carry: remove the largest contaminant first, then concentrate, then purify, then finish, because every operation's cost scales with the volume entering it and the cheapest way to make a later stage cheap is to make it smaller.

2. Cell separation, and the driving force that is capped

Stanbury Ch 10's filtration treatment starts from Darcy's law, its Eq. (10.1): dV/dt = KAΔP/(µL), rate proportional to area and pressure drop and inversely proportional to viscosity and cake depth. Everything about industrial filtration follows from the L in the denominator — the cake grows, so at constant pressure the rate decays and at constant rate the pressure must rise, and when the solids are compressible raising the pressure closes the voids and makes things worse. Hence filter aid, which Stanbury's economics chapter prices at about £9 per tonne at 10% product in broth, and hence precoating. The number that decides the equipment is the ceiling on ΔP: a rotary vacuum filter's driving force is limited to one atmosphere, 100 kN m⁻², and in practice significantly less, whereas a pressure filter runs at many atmospheres. The discharge mechanism is then chosen by what the cake is — string discharge for fibrous fungal mycelium, scraper for yeast, scraper with a 2 to 10 cm precoat for bacteria and actinomycete mycelia, because those blind the cloth. Centrifugation is the alternative and its selection rule is a particle size: Stanbury's economics chapter states centrifugation is more economical than ultrafiltration above 1 to 2 µm particle size, which is a cleaner criterion than any amount of equipment comparison.

3. Centrifuge scale-up, and the two ways Belter does it

Belter §3.3 is explicit that there are two approaches and that they do different jobs. The first is the equivalent time, Gt, the product of centrifugal acceleration and time, Eq. (3.3-1) with a characteristic radius usually taken as the maximum; Belter calls it qualitative but the best starting point, and tabulates typical Gt values for a variety of biomass in Table 3.3-1. Its merit is that a bottle centrifuge in the laboratory gives it directly, which is usually the only data available. The second is the Σ factor, taken from the bracketed groups in Belter's Eqs (3.2-7) and (3.2-17), which makes quantitative use of the geometric analysis — for a disc stack, capacity scales with the number of discs, the square of the angular velocity, the difference of the cubes of the outer and inner radii, and the cotangent of the disc angle. The point of Σ is that it separates the machine from the suspension: the settling velocity is a property of the cells and Σ is a property of the centrifuge, so a measured settling velocity plus a manufacturer's Σ gives a capacity without a trial. Belter's warning is the one to keep: a bottle centrifuge gives an idealised separation with a clear supernatant and a packed paste that is removed manually, and that ideal is never reached in a continuous-flow machine, so the laboratory result is an upper bound rather than a prediction.

4. Disruption, and the reason intracellular is expensive

Shuler §11.3 splits it into mechanical (§11.3.1) and non-mechanical (§11.3.2) methods, Stanbury Ch 10 into physical-mechanical — liquid shear, solid shear, agitation with abrasives, freezing-thawing, ultrasonication — and chemical, with detergents, osmotic shock, alkali and enzyme treatment, and Belter gives it a chapter of its own after cell membranes. The cost of disruption is not the disruption. It is three consequences. The debris is finer than the cells were, so the clarification that follows is harder than the one that preceded it, and Stanbury's own note that centrifugation beats ultrafiltration above 1 to 2 µm now cuts the other way, because disrupted debris is below that. The entire intracellular contents are released, so the purification that follows begins with every host protein and nucleic acid rather than with a handful of secreted ones, and nucleic acid raises viscosity enough to change the filtration arithmetic by itself. And the product is now in contact with every host protease simultaneously, so there is a clock on everything downstream of the homogeniser. The contrast with a secreted product is therefore not one unit operation but a change in the starting purity of the whole train, and that is the quantitative content of the secrete-or-not decision from weeks 40 to 43.

5. Chromatography, and when it is affordable

Shuler §11.4.9 and Stanbury Ch 10's chromatography section give the modes — adsorption, ion exchange, gel permeation, affinity, reverse phase, HPLC, continuous — and Belter Ch 7 gives the design equations, with §7.3 discrete stage analysis and §7.4 kinetic analysis as the two framings and §7.5 scaling-up chromatography as the practical one. The affordability question has a clean answer and it is a capacity argument rather than a resolution argument. A chromatographic step's cost scales with the mass of product per cycle divided by the resin's dynamic binding capacity, times the resin price divided by its cycle life, plus the buffer volume. For a therapeutic protein at a gram per litre and a thousand dollars a gram, resin at several thousand dollars a litre with a hundred-cycle life is trivial against the product value. For a bulk chemical at a dollar a kilogram, the same resin is three orders of magnitude too expensive, and no improvement in binding capacity closes a gap that size. That is why the mode matters less than the position in the train: chromatography is affordable when it is operating on an already-concentrated stream, which is why Belter puts it in Part III after extraction and adsorption in Part II, and why a proposal that puts a column directly on clarified broth has usually not costed it.

6. Membranes, and the one place thermodynamics bites

Shuler §11.4.5 to §11.4.8 cover dialysis, reverse osmosis, ultrafiltration and microfiltration, cross-flow operation of both, and §11.4.11 electrodialysis; Belter Ch 9 puts ultrafiltration and electrophoresis together, with §9.1 basic ideas and §9.2 ultrafiltration; Stanbury's membrane-processes section is brief and practical. The selection is by cut-off and by fouling, and the fouling is the design problem — which is why cross-flow exists, and why Shuler gives it its own subsection distinct from dead-end operation. Where this connects to the thermodynamics the candidate already has is the energy duty. Concentrating a stream against its osmotic pressure has a minimum work that Smith Van Ness §15.6 derives, and the osmotic pressure of a 0.5 mol L⁻¹ solution at 25 °C is 12.4 bar — so a reverse-osmosis concentration of a broth with that much dissolved solute cannot be done below that pressure at all, regardless of membrane. Against evaporation the comparison is stark: removing water as latent heat costs about 2,257 kJ per kg at 100 °C, while removing it against 12 bar of osmotic pressure costs of order 1 to 5 kJ per kg of ideal work. Membranes win the energy argument by two to three orders of magnitude and lose the fouling argument, and which of those dominates is a property of the broth rather than of the technology.

7. Stage yields multiply, which is the week's single most important arithmetic

Overall recovery is the product of stage recoveries, so a train is penalised by its length even when every stage is good. Ten stages at 95% give 0.95¹⁰ = 59.9%; at 90% they give 34.9%; at 99% they give 90.4%. The design consequences are three and they are not interchangeable. Shorten the train, which is almost always the largest available gain and is bought upstream — a secreted product removes disruption and the clarification that follows it, two stages, worth 10 percentage points at 95% each. Fix the worst stage, which is worth exactly its own shortfall and no more, and is identified by computing the cumulative recovery stage by stage rather than by intuition. Or raise the titre, which does not change any stage yield but changes every stage's cost, because cost scales with volume processed and volume scales as the reciprocal of titre. The reason this arithmetic is worth doing explicitly in a proposal is that it converts a qualitative preference — 'we would prefer a secreted product' — into a number that can be compared against the yield penalty secretion usually costs upstream. If secretion costs 15% of titre and saves two stages at 92% and 95%, the comparison is 0.85 against 0.874 and the answer is not obvious, which is exactly the situation where the arithmetic earns its keep.

8. Where the cost actually is, and how it moves with titre

Shuler §11.1 gives the two anchors: recovery and purification above 50% of manufacturing cost, especially for intracellular products, and the price-against-dilution relation spanning seven orders in each — citric acid entering recovery near 100 g L⁻¹ at one to two dollars a kilogram against a therapeutic protein at 10⁻⁵ g L⁻¹ and of order a hundred million. Stanbury Ch 12's recovery-costs section gives the same thing as ratios: older processes split roughly 1:1 between fermentation and isolation, recombinant products at very low titre 1:8 or 1:10, so the fermentation becomes 10% of cost and recovery 90%. It also gives recovery losses to expect — 8% for citric acid, 4% for penicillin G before salt formation — and Atkinson and Mavituna's allowances, about £40 per tonne for ethanol selling at £220 per tonne at 7% w/v, £100 per tonne for single-cell protein at £300 per tonne and 3% w/v, and £300 per tonne for organic acids or glycol at £700 per tonne and 10%. Those are 1999 sterling and dollar figures of different vintages; the ratios travel and the absolute numbers do not, which is Stanbury's own caveat about his own chapter. What the ratios say is unambiguous: the downstream fraction of cost is a function of titre, so every gram per litre the strain gains buys a reduction in the dominant cost term, which is why week 52's elasticity analysis will put titre above yield for most products — and why, for a product already at 100 g L⁻¹, it will not.

9. In situ product removal as two interventions that happen to use one piece of equipment

The curriculum points Lee §7.2.2 and §7.3 here for the driving-force argument, with its own note attached that Ch 7 is the thermodynamics of pathways and contains no product-removal section — which is right, and the connection is still worth making because the two interventions ISPR performs are genuinely different and are usually conflated. The first is relief of toxicity: the product inhibits growth or the enzyme, and removing it raises the achievable titre in the broth-plus-extract system even though the broth titre stays at the inhibitory level. That is a kinetics argument and it is the one usually made. The second is thermodynamic, and it is the one Lee §7.2.2 and §7.3 actually license: for a pathway whose last step has a small or unfavourable ΔrG′, the mass-action ratio sets the maximum driving force, so lowering the product concentration raises the flux the pathway can carry at all, and the max-min driving force analysis from phase 2 is the tool. These are distinguishable by experiment: toxicity relief shows as a higher total product at the same specific rate, thermodynamic relief shows as a higher specific rate at the same biomass. They also price differently, because toxicity relief needs only enough removal to stay below the inhibitory concentration while thermodynamic relief needs the concentration held low throughout, which is a much larger duty. A proposal claiming ISPR should say which of the two it is claiming and what titre increase follows, because the two give different numbers.

10. Secreted against intracellular, decided downstream

The whole week comes to a point here, and the comparison is four lines. A secreted product's train begins with cell removal and goes straight to concentration: filtration or centrifugation, then concentration, then purification, then finish. An intracellular product's train begins with cell harvest, then disruption, then a harder clarification of finer debris, then purification against the entire host proteome under a protease clock, then finish — two extra stages, each with its own yield, and a worse starting purity for everything after. Put the arithmetic from core idea 7 on it: two extra stages at 90% and 92% cost 17% of recovery before any difference in the stages they share. Against that, the upstream case for intracellular is real — cytoplasmic expression reaches the 25 to 50% of total protein that week 40 recorded for E. coli, where secretion into the medium is the exception, and inclusion bodies are sometimes an advantage because resolubilisation doubles as a purification step when the protein refolds easily. The decision is therefore not general. It is: compute the titre ratio between the two expression strategies in your own hands, compute the recovery ratio from the two trains, multiply, and compare — and if the intracellular route wins on the product of those two, say so, because for many proteins it does and the downstream argument has become a reflex.

Worked anchor

Cost the train for a mid-value product, find the dominant term, and show what titre does to it.

Basis. 50 m³ batch from week 49, secreted extracellular product, titre 50 g L⁻¹, so 2,500 kg in the broth. Purity target 98%. Glucose at $400 per tonne, steam at $20 per tonne, product selling at $12 per kg. Stage recoveries assumed, flagged below.

Step 1 — the train and its cumulative recovery.

cell separation (disc-stack centrifuge) 0.98 cumulative 0.980 clarification (depth filtration) 0.97 cumulative 0.951 concentration (triple-effect evaporation) 0.99 cumulative 0.941 extraction / adsorption 0.88 cumulative 0.828 ion exchange 0.90 cumulative 0.745 crystallisation 0.93 cumulative 0.693 drying 0.97 cumulative 0.673

Overall 67.3%, so 1,683 kg of product leaves the plant from 2,500 kg in the broth. 817 kg is lost, which at $12 per kg is $9,800 of product value thrown away per batch, against a glucose bill for the whole fermentation of about 8,300 kg at 0.30 g g⁻¹, i.e. $3,300. The recovery losses are worth three times the sugar.

Step 2 — the worst stage, identified rather than guessed. Extraction at 0.88 is the largest single shortfall. Raising it to 0.95 lifts overall recovery from 0.673 to 0.727, i.e. 135 kg or $1,620 per batch. Raising ion exchange from 0.90 to 0.95 lifts it to 0.710, worth $920. Adding a second polish stage at 0.97 would cost 2.0 points of recovery, $590 per batch, and must therefore buy at least that much in purity value.

Step 3 — the stage-yield sanity check the week exists for. If this train were ten stages at 95% rather than seven at these values, overall recovery would be 0.95¹⁰ = 59.9%. At 90% per stage it would be 34.9%. The number to carry out of this is that the length of the train is a first-order cost driver, and the only way to shorten it is upstream.

Step 4 — the energy duty of the concentration step, from first principles. At 50 g L⁻¹, each tonne of product is carried in 20 m³ of broth. Concentrating ten-fold removes 18 tonnes of water per tonne of product. Smith Van Ness §4.2's latent heat of vaporisation of water at 100 °C is about 2,257 kJ kg⁻¹, so the single-effect duty is 18,000 × 2,257 = 40.6 GJ per tonne of product. At roughly 1.1 kg of steam per kg of water evaporated, that is 19.8 tonnes of steam per tonne of product, $396 at $20 per tonne. Triple-effect divides the steam by about three: $132 per tonne.

Against that, a membrane concentration: the ideal work against an osmotic pressure of order 12 bar is a few kJ per kg of water, so of order 100 MJ per tonne of product against 40,600 MJ — two to three orders of magnitude less energy. The reason evaporation is nonetheless specified here is fouling and the achievable concentration factor, not energy, and that is a broth property to be measured rather than argued.

Step 5 — the whole train, costed per kilogram of product. Per tonne of product leaving the plant:

raw material (glucose at 0.30 g g⁻¹, grossed up by 1/0.673) $1,980 steam, triple-effect concentration $132 other utilities, electricity and cooling $150 consumables: filter aid, resin amortisation, solvent make-up $400 labour and overhead, allocated $600 capital charge, allocated (week 52 computes this properly) $900 ------- total, order of magnitude $4,160

Against a selling price of $12,000 per tonne that is a gross margin of about 65%, which is healthy — and the dominant term is raw material, at 48%, which is a fermentation number rather than a downstream one. That is the honest answer for a product at 50 g L⁻¹ and $12 per kg, and it is not the answer the week's framing implies.

Step 6 — the sensitivity that reverses it. Redo step 5 at four titres, holding stage recoveries fixed and scaling the volume-dependent terms as 1/titre:

titre 10 g L⁻¹: broth 100 m³ per tonne, water removed 90 t, triple-effect steam $660, consumables and utilities roughly five-fold, downstream subtotal about $3,900 against raw material $1,980 — downstream is 66% of cost. titre 25 g L⁻¹: 40 m³, 36 t, steam $264, downstream about $1,700 — 46%. titre 50 g L⁻¹: 20 m³, 18 t, steam $132, downstream about $1,080 — 35%. titre 100 g L⁻¹: 10 m³, 9 t, steam $66, downstream about $740 — 27%.

So the fraction of cost sitting downstream falls from two-thirds to a quarter across one order of magnitude in titre, which is Stanbury's 1:8 and 1:1 ratios reproduced from a different direction and is the quantitative form of Shuler's price-against-dilution relation.

Step 7 — what the arithmetic chooses. Three candidate improvements, each priced per tonne of product at the 50 g L⁻¹ base case:

(i) Raise extraction recovery from 0.88 to 0.95. Worth 8.0% of output, about $960 per tonne of revenue retained. Cost: solvent screening and possibly a second extraction stage. (ii) Double the titre from 50 to 100 g L⁻¹. Worth about $340 per tonne in downstream cost, plus the capacity released — the same plant now makes twice as much, which halves the capital charge per tonne, another $450. About $790 per tonne, plus capacity. (iii) Raise the fermentation yield from 0.30 to 0.35 g g⁻¹. Worth $1,980 × (1 − 0.30/0.35) = $283 per tonne.

At this titre and this price, fixing the worst downstream stage is worth more than either of the fermentation improvements, which is the opposite of the usual instinct and is why the stage-by-stage recovery table is the first thing to compute. At 10 g L⁻¹ the ranking inverts — titre dominates everything — and at 100 g L⁻¹ raw material dominates and the downstream work stops paying. The elasticity is not a property of the process; it is a property of where on the titre axis the process currently sits, which is week 52's point arriving a week early.

What this leaves out, and it is the largest omission: every stage recovery above is assumed, and none of them is a measurement. The arithmetic's structure is right and its conclusions are robust to the assumed values — step 7's ranking survives any plausible reshuffling of the stage yields, because it is driven by the size of the worst shortfall rather than by its exact value — but the actual decision needs measured recoveries, and the first experiment of any downstream programme is a material balance across each stage on a real broth. Assumed stage yields are the single most common unmarked assumption in a process proposal.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • titre 50 g L⁻¹ in a 50 m³ batch, giving 2,500 kg of product in the broth, with the product secreted and extracellular
  • every stage recovery in the train is assumed rather than measured; the ranking in step 7 is robust to the assumed values but the absolute recoveries are not
  • glucose at $400 per tonne, steam at $20 per tonne, product at $12 per kg, all current-day figures assumed rather than sourced
  • fermentation product yield 0.30 g g⁻¹ on glucose when the raw-material line is grossed up by the overall recovery
  • ten-fold concentration in the evaporation step and 1.1 kg of steam per kg of water evaporated, with triple-effect taken as dividing the steam by three
  • latent heat of water 2,257 kJ kg⁻¹ at 100 °C, from the Smith Van Ness steam tables, with no pressure correction for the actual evaporator duty
  • osmotic pressure of order 12 bar for the broth, computed from a 0.5 mol L⁻¹ ideal solution at 25 °C, which ignores activity coefficients entirely
  • labour, overhead and capital charge allocated as round figures pending week 52's proper calculation
  • volume-dependent cost terms scaled as the reciprocal of titre in the sensitivity, with stage recoveries held fixed — in reality some stage yields improve with concentration
  • Stanbury's and Atkinson and Mavituna's recovery figures left in the currency and vintage as printed, with no indexing to the present
