Skim rather than read closely only because Towler is the better-maintained of the two; promote it to close reading if it is the copy available. Verified by search at contents level only.
AACE International Recommended Practice 18R-97 — Cost Estimate Classification System as applied in engineering, procurement and construction for the process industriesRead closelyNot on the curriculum's list; added to close the accuracy-class half of the same gap. Verified by search against multiple independent reproductions of its Table 1, including copies of the Recommended Practice itself: five classes, Class 5 to Class 1 from least to most defined, with maturity of project definition as the sole determining characteristic, and the expected accuracy ranges quoted in core idea 4. Read the table and the two paragraphs around it; that is the whole of what this week needs from it, and it is what lets a capstone name its estimate's class in one defensible sentence. The companion generic practice is 17R-97 and the accuracy ranges are tied to quantitative risk analysis rather than to effort.
Humbird et al., Process Design and Economics for Biochemical Conversion of Lignocellulosic Biomass to Ethanol, NREL/TP-5100-47764, May 2011Read closelyNot on the curriculum's list; added as the worked bioprocess TEA to imitate, which is what the week needs more than it needs another method chapter. Verified by fetching the report. Read the executive summary table in full and §4 Process Economics (§4.1 cost-year indices, §4.2 total capital investment, §4.3 variable operating costs, §4.4 fixed operating costs, §4.5 discounted cash flow and the minimum selling price), then §1.3 on the TEA approach and §1.4 on nth-plant assumptions, then Table 25 installation factors, Table 26 scaling exponents, Table 27 additional costs for TCI, Table 28 the project cost worksheet and Table 33 the discounted cash flow parameters. §5.1's carbon and energy balance is the model for week 54 and §5.4's sensitivity tornado for this week's. The numbers to carry: TCI $422.5 M, installed equipment $232 M, added direct and indirect 45% of TCI, MESP $2.15/gal in 2007$, capital charge factor 0.131, 8,410 operating hours, 5.4 wt% ethanol titre. Its survey of eleven other studies, with MESPs from $0.63 to $4.58 per gallon, is the best available argument against quoting anyone's single TEA number.
Chemical Engineering Plant Cost Index (CEPCI), base 1957-59 = 100 — the 1999 annual average of 390.6 and current values of order 800SkimNot on the curriculum's list; added because every number in Stanbury Ch 12 is 1999 money and the chapter itself points at cost indices as the remedy. Verified by search: the 1999 annual average was 390.6 with the equipment sub-index at 435.5 and construction labour at 292.5, taken from Chemical Engineering's own 2002 article on the index's structure and revision; recent annual averages are 607.5 in 2019, 816.0 in 2022 and 797.9 in 2023, with the 2025 annual average reported 1.6% above 2024 and 2026 monthly values at record highs. So the composite factor from 1999 to now is about 2.05. Skim rather than study: the index is a single multiplication, and the three cautions in core idea 8 are the content — sub-indices diverge, cost professionals advise against reaching back more than about five years, and an index cannot represent a technology change.
ISO 14040:2006 Environmental management — Life cycle assessment — Principles and framework, and ISO 14044:2006 Requirements and guidelinesRead closelyNot on the curriculum's list; added because the LCA session had no source at all. Verified by search: both are 2006 second editions from ISO/TC 207/SC 5, 14040 reviewed and confirmed in 2022, with Amendment 1:2020 to 14040 and Amendments 1:2017 and 2:2020 to 14044. 14040 is twenty pages and gives the four phases, the reporting and critical-review requirements and the explicit statement that it does not specify methodology for the individual phases; 14044 carries the requirements, including the allocation hierarchy. Read 14040 whole — it is short — and 14044's clauses on functional unit, system boundary and allocation. These are paid standards; if no copy is available, the ILCD Handbook below reproduces the framework in line with them and is free.
European Commission JRC, ILCD Handbook — General guide for Life Cycle Assessment: Detailed guidance, first edition March 2010, EUR 24708 ENRead closelyNot on the curriculum's list; added as the free, practical companion to the ISO pair. Verified by search, including the JRC publications repository: first edition March 2010, EUR 24708 EN, JRC48157, with sister documents Provisions and action steps (EUR 24378 EN) and Framework and requirements for LCIA models and indicators (EUR 24586 EN), and an umbrella JRC Reference Report (EUR 24982 EN, 2012). It is explicitly in line with the ISO 14040 series and developed through peer review and public consultation, which makes it the right thing to cite in a proposal that cannot assume the reader has bought the standards. Read its treatment of goal and scope, functional unit and allocation, and its account of attributional versus consequential modelling — the distinction the week's LCA session needs and that ISO 14040 itself leaves implicit.
Tabone, Cregg, Beckman & Landis, Sustainability metrics: life cycle assessment and green design in polymers, Environ. Sci. Technol. 2010, 44(21), 8264-8269 — read with the two published Comments, Murphy et al. 45(11), 5055-5056 and Dale 45, 5057Read closelyNot on the curriculum's list; added as the primary study behind the claim that bio-based is not automatically better, which the topic list asserts and nothing on the reading list supports. Verified by search, including the paper itself and the Comments' bibliographic records. Twelve polymers, cradle-to-gate: the polylactides showed the maximum contribution to eutrophication, a corn-derived PHA topped acidification, all four biopolymers were the largest contributors to ozone depletion, and the biopolymers exceeded most petroleum polymers on ecotoxicity and carcinogens, while ranking best on green design. Read the Comments with it and not afterwards — they attack the data vintage, the omission of use and end-of-life, and the collapsing of multiple impact categories into a single rank, and a proposal that cites the paper without them will be corrected by anyone who knows the field. The pair together is a better teaching object than either alone.
Doran Ch 1 §1.1-1.2 — bioprocess development: an interdisciplinary challenge, and the quantitative approachSkimThe curriculum's entry, and two pages of orientation rather than a method, as the README's flag says. Skim it for the steps-in-development figure, which is a useful frame for the capstone's first page, and move on. It contributes nothing to the costing.
Lee Ch 22 §22.5 bottlenecks in the development of environmental biocatalysts (printed p870) and §22.10 conclusions and future prospects (p879)SkimBoth confirmed present in the PDF with those titles. The curriculum assigns them for the LCA session and they are not method — §22.5 is about portability of constructs and the gap between laboratory and field performance, §22.10 is a forward look. Read §22.5 for one specific purpose: it is the best short statement on this reading list of why a construct that works in the laboratory fails in a real environment, which is the same gap the capstone's risk register has to populate. Do not expect a system boundary, a functional unit or an allocation rule from either; those come from ISO 14040/14044 and the ILCD Handbook above.
Lee Ch 1 §1.7 The Future of Metabolic Engineering (printed p17)SkimConfirmed present. Assigned here to be read against your own cost numbers, which is the right instruction: the section's forward look is a list of ambitions, and the exercise is to mark each one with the cost line it would move. Most of them move yield, which this week's elasticity calculation says is the smallest line in a capital-intensive process — that tension is worth a paragraph in the capstone rather than a complaint about the chapter.
Shuler Ch 10 — no economics section, as the curriculum's own entry statesSkipCorrectly flagged in `c8.js` and correctly corrected there in phase 8: the chapter's sections are §10.1 introduction, §10.2 scale-up and its difficulties, §10.3 bioreactor instrumentation and control, §10.4 sterilization of process fluids, §10.5 summary, and none of them is economics. Skipped here. It returns in week 54, where §10.2's scale-up material is the right reading for the integration view.

Common misconceptions

  • That a techno-economic model is a write-up of the design. It is an independent check on it, and the first honest TEA of a student process usually fails: here it priced a 50 m³ vessel against a $12 per kg commodity and returned a cost of goods of $61 per kg, 96% of it in capital charge and fixed costs. The model earns its place by contradicting the design, so run it early enough that the design can still change, and treat a comfortable first answer as a reason to check the capital line rather than as a result.
  • That a sensitivity analysis discovers which parameter matters. It confirms it: the elasticity of cost to a parameter is the cost share of the lines that parameter moves, so the ranking can be read off the cost breakdown before a single case is re-run. Titre and cycle time move annual output and therefore the capital and fixed lines; yield moves only raw materials. If a re-run sensitivity disagrees with the cost shares, the model has an error in it — which is the useful way to use the table.
  • That more Monte Carlo makes an estimate more accurate. Accuracy comes from the maturity of the project definition and nothing else, which is what AACE 18R-97 classifies on: an elaborate stochastic treatment of a Class 5 estimate is still a Class 5 estimate, with a −20 to −50% and +30 to +100% range around it. What the Monte Carlo does buy is the shape of the distribution, and that is worth having for a specific reason — cost goes as the reciprocal of titre, which is convex, so symmetric uncertainty in titre gives a mean cost about 10% above the point estimate in the anchor's case.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Your model says yield elasticity is three times that of rate. What does that tell you to work on, and when would it reverse?

A. First, read it as a statement about the cost breakdown rather than about the strain, because the elasticity of cost to a parameter is the share of the cost lines that parameter moves. Yield elasticity three times rate elasticity means the raw-material line is three times the size of the lines that scale with annual output — capital charge, fixed costs and volume-dependent consumables. That is a raw-material-dominated process: a high-volume commodity at low value where the plant is cheap relative to the sugar it eats, which is exactly the NREL cellulosic ethanol case, where feedstock is $0.74 of a $2.15 per gallon selling price. So work on yield: strain work that converts more of the carbon to product, by-product deletion, maintenance reduction, anything that raises g product per g substrate. Second, name what would reverse it, because the reversal is common and fast. Capital intensity rising relative to output reverses it — a smaller plant, a more expensive vessel, containment, a sterile-fill finishing train, or simply a shorter plant life or a higher required return, all of which inflate the capital charge without touching the sugar bill. Low titre reverses it, because every volume-dependent line scales as the reciprocal of titre while the raw-material line does not. A long batch cycle reverses it, including long turnarounds and long sterilisation holds. And a cheap or free feedstock reverses it completely, since a waste stream with a gate fee can make the raw-material elasticity negative. The anchor in this week is the reversed case in its extreme form: capital charge and fixed costs are 95.7% of the cost of goods and raw material is 3.2%, so titre elasticity is −0.97 against yield's −0.03, a ratio of 30:1 the other way. The general rule to carry is that the ranking is a property of where the process sits on the titre and scale axes, not a property of the organism, and it should be recomputed whenever the configuration changes rather than inherited from the last analysis.

Q. A proposal reports a cost of goods of $4.37 per kilogram for a new bio-based route and concludes it beats the $5.10 per kilogram petrochemical incumbent. What do you ask for before believing it?

A. Six things, in order of how much they usually move the answer. The estimate's accuracy class and basis: by AACE 18R-97 an equipment-factored estimate is Class 4 with a range of −15 to −30% and +20 to +50%, so $4.37 is really $3.1 to $6.6 per kg and does not separate from $5.10 at all — a two-significant-figure cost of goods from a conceptual design is the clearest single sign that the classes have not been read. The capital basis next: purchased equipment prices, the installation factor and where it came from, and what is inside total capital investment, since a factorial estimate's whole character is in a multiplier that can defensibly be 3 or 5. Then the financing: the required return, the plant life and whether a capital charge is in the cost of goods at all, because omitting it is the most common way to produce a low number, and because the cost moves roughly in proportion to the return — 10% against 15% is a 50% change in the largest line of a capital-intensive process. Then the cost year and the indexing: whether the two figures are in the same year's money, and if historical data has been brought forward, whether the CEPCI reach is a few years or a few decades, remembering the advice not to reach back more than about five. Then the nth-plant question, which NREL names explicitly — if the new route's cost excludes first-of-a-kind financing, longer start-up and overdesign while the incumbent's price is a real market price from an operating plant, the comparison is between a mature cost and a hoped-for one. Finally the scale and the capacity basis, checked with capital per annual tonne against a published benchmark such as NREL's $6.92 per annual gallon: a route that is 143 times more capital-intensive per unit of output than a built commodity plant, as the anchor's design is, cannot reach a commodity price at any titre. If all six hold up, the remaining question is the one the proposal should have asked itself: at what price of the incumbent's feedstock does the ranking flip, since that is usually a smaller move than the uncertainty in either cost.

Q. Your screening LCA finds the bio-based route has 40% lower greenhouse gas emissions than the incumbent. Can you say it is more sustainable, and what would make the claim defensible?

A. No, and for three reasons that are about method rather than about caution. The functional unit: if the comparison is per kilogram of material it is not a comparison of function, and the honest unit is the service delivered — the amount of each material needed to do the job, over the life it lasts. The boundary: a screening study is normally cradle-to-gate, and the use and end-of-life phases are exactly where bio-based materials usually gain, so a gate boundary understates them and also cannot support a claim about the product as opposed to its production. And the category coverage, which is the one this week's reading is pointed at: greenhouse gas is one impact category among many, and Tabone et al.'s cradle-to-gate comparison of twelve polymers found the biopolymers ranking worst on eutrophication for the polylactides, worst on acidification for one corn-derived PHA, and largest on ozone depletion for all four, with ecotoxicity and carcinogen emissions above most of the petroleum polymers — the burdens sitting in the field and the fertiliser rather than in the fermenter, which is why no flux model sees them. A 40% carbon improvement bought with a tripled eutrophication burden is a trade, not an improvement, and an LCA that reports only the category it wins on has chosen its answer. What makes the claim defensible: state the functional unit and defend it; extend the boundary to cradle-to-grave or say plainly that the claim is about production only; report a full set of characterised categories and show the ones where the route loses, which is also what ISO 14044's reporting requirements are for; state the allocation rule for every co-product and test the result against an alternative rule, since in a fermentation that choice can outweigh any process improvement; say whether the study is attributional or consequential, since a decision about building a plant needs the second; and resist the single score — the published Comments on Tabone et al. make exactly that criticism of exactly that paper, and collapsing incommensurable categories into one rank is the error they identify. The defensible sentence has the form: per unit of function, cradle-to-grave, with co-products allocated by X, the route reduces category A by 40% and increases categories B and C by Y and Z, and here is the sensitivity to the allocation rule.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. Use a rough mass and energy balance to compare a microbial route with a process route relevant to your renewable-energy background. Which uncertain assumption dominates the conclusion?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 53 — Capstone I: the strain

No new reading and no new technique: the week's whole content is assembling fifty-two weeks of separate artifacts into one document that a stranger can check. That sounds like editing and it is not, because the act of putting the chain in one place is what exposes the joints — a stoichiometry that was balanced in week 17 against a biomass equation that changed in week 26, a thermodynamic feasibility established at 1 mM when the process runs at 300, a deletion set validated against a model whose medium is not the medium week 47 designed. The discipline that makes the week worth a card of its own is that every number in the dossier has to carry its provenance and its uncertainty, and the second of those is where most capstones fail: a predicted yield quoted to three significant figures from a flux balance is not a prediction, it is a bound on a bound. The organising arithmetic is the derating chain in the anchor, which takes a flux-model maximum of 0.52 g g⁻¹ down to an expected 0.326 ± 0.044 g g⁻¹ by four named multipliers, each with its own uncertainty, and then does the thing the week exists to do: compares it against the specification week 52 derived, finds that the yield uncertainty is economically almost irrelevant and the titre uncertainty is the whole question, and lets that decide which experiment goes first.

Core ideas

1. What the dossier is for, and the test it has to pass

One reader, one hour, no author present. A supervisor reading this document is deciding two things — can this person formulate a question, and will they finish things — and both are answered by whether the numbers connect rather than by whether they are impressive. The practical test is that a stranger can take any number in the final performance estimate and walk it backwards to a measurement, a published value with a section pointer, or an explicit assumption, without asking the author anything. That is harder than it sounds for a document assembled from twenty-two artifacts built over a year, because the common failure is not an error but a disconnection: artifact 11's flux model and artifact 23's genotype refer to different model versions, and nothing in either says so. The remedy is mechanical and is the first session's real work — before writing any prose, build the one-page dependency map of which artifact feeds which number, and reconcile every number that appears in more than one place. Expect three or four genuine conflicts. They are the week's most valuable output, because each one is a thing that would have been found by a reviewer instead.

2. The target justification is an economic argument with biology in it, not the reverse

Lee §1.3 (printed p9) sets out the three approaches — §1.3.1 rational, §1.3.2 combinatorial, §1.3.3 systems metabolic engineering — and reread at this point it is a framework for explaining what was done rather than a menu for choosing. The justification section has four parts in a fixed order, and the order is the argument: market and price, because a product with no price has no specification; the incumbent route and its cost structure, because the competitor is a petrochemical plant with thirty years of depreciation behind it rather than another fermentation; why biology could win, which has to name a specific advantage — a chiral centre, a selectivity, a feedstock, a functionalisation that chemistry does badly — rather than appealing to renewability; and feasibility, which is where the biology enters. Week 52's arithmetic sharpens this considerably. The honest version of the second part is now a number: the incumbent's price, the cost of goods the designed configuration can reach, and the gap. If the gap is negative at every accessible scale, say so in the first page and make the dossier an argument about which product this strain should make instead — a verdict of not at this scale with the arithmetic behind it is worth more than an optimistic cost of goods, and brief 8 already licenses exactly that kind of verdict for the consortium replacement.

3. The chain, and the information lost at each link

Stoichiometry to thermodynamics to flux model to genotype, and it is worth stating what each link can and cannot carry, because the capstone's credibility rests on not overclaiming downstream of a weak link. Stoichiometry gives a hard upper bound on yield from element and redox balances, and it is the most reliable number in the document — it cannot be beaten by any strain. Thermodynamics tells you whether a route can carry flux at the concentrations the process will actually run at, and it rules routes out rather than ranking them. The flux model gives the maximum yield subject to the network and the objective, which is a bound on the stoichiometric bound after the network's real reactions are imposed, and its weakness is that it has no kinetics and therefore no rates and no titres at all. The genotype is a set of interventions predicted to move the flux distribution, and the prediction is about the model's optimum rather than about the organism's behaviour. Two consequences for the write-up. Yield claims may be made from the model with a derating; titre and rate claims may not be made from it at all, since nothing in a constraint-based model predicts either, and any titre in the dossier comes from the literature, from the host's known performance envelope or from an explicit assumption. And the uncertainty grows monotonically down the chain, so the right presentation is a funnel — a hard bound at the top, a range at the bottom, and the derating steps between them named and numbered.

4. Re-running the thermodynamics at the concentrations the process will use

The max-min driving force analysis from phase 2 was almost certainly done at round laboratory concentrations, and the process the capstone now specifies does not run there. Two changes matter. The product concentration is the titre, and at a titre worth having it is high enough to compress the driving force of the final step — the mass-action ratio is where the thermodynamic cost of a high titre shows up, and it is the quantitative content of the in-situ product removal argument from week 51. The substrate concentration under a fed-batch policy is low by design, from week 50, which can hurt the first step of the pathway as much as the high product helps nothing. So the re-run is not a formality: compute the driving force of the limiting step at the actual titre and the actual residual substrate, and if it collapses, the dossier either specifies product removal or specifies a lower titre, and week 52's elasticity says which of those is expensive. Lee §8.2.4 Pathway Feasibility (printed p246) is the right structure to check against, and its five subsections are a checklist worth running explicitly: §8.2.4.1 chassis metabolic model, §8.2.4.2 stoichiometric feasibility, §8.2.4.3 thermodynamic feasibility, §8.2.4.4 kinetic feasibility and §8.2.4.5 toxicity of intermediates. The last two are the ones a capstone usually omits, and intermediate toxicity in particular is a risk-register entry that no flux model and no thermodynamic analysis will produce.

5. The flux model with the final host and the final medium, which is not the model from week 26

Three things changed after the strain design was done, and each invalidates part of it. The host was chosen in phase 7 against a matrix, and if the final host is not the one the week 26 design used, the model is a different model with a different network and different essentiality. The medium was designed in week 47, and a defined medium constrains uptake of things the model may have had free — nitrogen source, trace elements, any amino acid the chassis cannot make — so the growth-coupled region computed on a rich-medium model can disappear on the real one. And the oxygen supply was capped in week 49 and the feed policy in week 50, which means the model should be run with an oxygen uptake constraint set to what the vessel can actually deliver rather than to an arbitrary large number. That last one is the most commonly skipped and the most consequential: a design whose growth-coupled region depends on an oxygen uptake rate the 50 m³ vessel cannot supply is a design for a different vessel. Re-run, report the predicted yield and the growth-coupled interval in the final configuration, and if the interval has moved, say what moved it. A capstone that reports the week 26 numbers unchanged after three phases of host and process decisions is, to a reader who notices, evidence that the integration was not done.

6. Re-validating the deletions, because essentiality is model-dependent and the model changed

Every deletion in the genotype was predicted non-essential by some model at some point, and essentiality predictions are among the least robust outputs of a reconstruction: they depend on the medium, on the biomass objective's composition, on gap-filled reactions that exist to make the model grow rather than because anyone observed them, and on the gene-protein-reaction rules, where an isozyme missing from the GPR turns a survivable deletion into a predicted lethal or the reverse. The validation pass is cheap and belongs in the dossier as a table: for each deletion, the predicted growth rate of the single mutant on the final medium, the predicted growth of the full genotype, and a flag for any deletion whose non-essentiality depends on a reaction that was gap-filled. Two specific traps worth naming in the write-up. A deletion set that is individually non-lethal can be collectively lethal, so the full genotype has to be simulated as one strain and not as a list. And a gene whose deletion the model tolerates because an alternative route carries the flux may be intolerable in practice if that alternative route is kinetically slow — the model has no kinetics, so it cannot distinguish a viable alternative from a theoretical one. Both are risk-register entries with a named first experiment, which is usually a single-mutant growth curve before anything else is built.

7. The construction plan as a sequence with real durations

Artifacts 19 and 20 are parts and methods; the capstone needs them as a build sequence with timings, dependencies and decision points, because that is what turns a genotype into a project. The structure that works: order the interventions by how much they are relied on and how likely they are to fail, build the highest-risk one first, and put a characterisation gate after each so that a failure is detected before three more edits are layered on it. Realistic durations matter more than precision here — a genome edit with selection and curing is a small number of weeks, a multiplexed library is longer, a tuning library with a screen is longer again and is usually the schedule's long pole — and the plan should state the serial path explicitly, because the common error is to cost the work as if everything can proceed in parallel when each edit depends on the last strain being verified. Verification belongs in the sequence as its own step with its own duration: sequencing, a growth curve on the final medium, and a production check. The one sentence a reviewer looks for is what happens if the third edit fails, and the plan should answer it rather than imply that it will not.

8. Expected performance as a derating chain, not as a model output

The format that survives scrutiny is: a hard upper bound from stoichiometry, the flux-model maximum beneath it, then a named multiplier for each mechanism that takes the real strain below the model, then an expected value with a range. Four multipliers cover most cases and each one has a phase of the course behind it — maintenance energy, which the model's ATP maintenance term under-represents at low growth rate; by-product formation, including the overflow metabolism from phase 3 that no stoichiometric optimum predicts; genetic instability over the generation count of the seed train and the production batch, which week 47 computed; and oxygen limitation or another transport constraint from the vessel, from week 49. The arithmetic is a product, so the derating compounds, and the anchor shows the result: four multipliers averaging 0.89 take 0.52 g g⁻¹ to 0.326. The uncertainty combines in quadrature on the relative errors, giving ±13.6%, and the honest output is a range of 0.28 to 0.37 g g⁻¹ at one standard deviation. Three rules make this defensible rather than decorative. Each multiplier needs a source or an explicit flag as an assumption. The multipliers are not independent — an oxygen limitation causes overflow metabolism, so applying both at full strength double-counts — and a correlated pair should be stated as such and combined conservatively. And the range has to appear in the executive summary, because a point estimate in the summary and a range in the appendix is how a reader concludes that the author does not believe the range.

9. The gap to specification, and which gap is worth closing

Week 52 produced a specification by inverting the cost model, and the comparison is the point of the whole dossier. Three outcomes and each has a different write-up. If the expected performance meets the specification, say by how much and whether the margin survives the lower end of the range — a design that meets spec only at the optimistic end of a ±14% yield range does not meet spec. If it misses, the useful statement is not the size of the miss but which parameter to move, and week 52's elasticities decide that: in a capital-intensive configuration titre and cycle time carry elasticities near −1 while yield carries −0.03, so a 14% uncertainty in yield is worth a fifth of a percent in cost of goods and a 14% uncertainty in titre is worth 14%. That ranking has an uncomfortable consequence for a dossier built on constraint-based modelling, and the capstone is better for stating it plainly: the quantity the flux model predicts best is the one the economics cares about least, and the quantity the economics turns on — titre — is one that no model in this course predicts at all. The third outcome is that the specification is unreachable at every accessible scale, which week 52's anchor found, and then the dossier's conclusion is a scale or product decision with the arithmetic attached, which is a stronger result than a strain that just meets a spec nobody checked.

10. The risk register, and the two failure modes of risk registers

The form is familiar — risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation — and two things make it worth reading. First, the impact column should be in the dossier's own units, which after week 52 means dollars per kilogram or months of schedule rather than high / medium / low: a risk that moves cost of goods by $0.40 per kg and one that moves it by $18 per kg are not both high, and quantifying the column is usually what reveals that the most-worried-about risk is minor. Second, correlation: registers are written as independent rows and real failures arrive together, so the entry worth adding is the scenario rather than the risk — low titre and long batch time have the same root cause in a burdened strain, arrive together, and multiply in the cost model, so a register that scores them separately understates the joint case. For this dossier the rows that recur across hosts and products are genetic instability over the generation count; intermediate toxicity, which Lee §8.2.4.5 names and which no model predicts; product inhibition compressing both the growth and the pathway driving force; by-product formation that the stoichiometric optimum excludes and the organism does anyway; the oxygen ceiling from week 49; and, for anything going near a food or a therapeutic use, the regulatory path, which brief 8 is explicit is a decisive argument against building rather than a box to tick.

11. The unknowns section, which is the one a supervisor reads first

Everything that cannot be known before an experiment, each with the experiment that would resolve it, its approximate duration and what each possible result would mean. Written well this is the strongest section in the dossier, because it is the section that demonstrates the skill the whole year was for: knowing which of your own numbers is load-bearing. The structure that works is ordered by leverage — the unknown whose resolution would change the most of the design first — and leverage is now computable rather than intuitive, because week 52's elasticities convert a change in a parameter into a change in cost of goods. For the anchor's configuration the ordering comes out as achievable titre, then batch cycle time, then the stage recoveries of the downstream train, then the yield, which is an ordering almost exactly inverted from the amount of modelling effort the course spent on each. Two rules. An unknown with no experiment attached is a hedge and should be deleted or given one. And the first experiment should be the cheapest one that could falsify the design rather than the most interesting one — for most designs in this course that is a small-scale growth and production run of a single intermediate construct on the final medium, which tests the host, the medium and the first intervention at once.

Worked anchor

Assemble the expected performance of the final strain with its uncertainty, compare it against week 52's specification, and let the comparison choose the first experiment.

Basis. The flux model's maximum product yield on glucose is 0.52 g g⁻¹ for the final host on the week 47 defined medium with the week 49 oxygen uptake constraint imposed. The stoichiometric bound from the element and redox balance, above the model, is higher and is not used here except as a sanity ceiling. Every derating multiplier below is stated with its source or flagged as an assumption.

Step 1 — the derating chain. Each multiplier is the fraction of the preceding value that survives the named mechanism, with a standard deviation on it:

flux-model maximum 0.520 g g⁻¹ × maintenance energy at the process growth rate 0.88 ± 0.05 × by-product formation (overflow, phase 3) 0.85 ± 0.08 × plasmid loss / segregational instability 0.93 ± 0.04 × oxygen limitation at the vessel's ceiling 0.90 ± 0.06 ------------ expected yield 0.326 g g⁻¹

That is 63% of the model maximum, which is in the range a reader will accept for a designed strain and well above what an undesigned one would give. Relative uncertainties combine in quadrature: √((0.05/0.88)² + (0.08/0.85)² + (0.04/0.93)² + (0.06/0.90)²) = 13.6%, so the expected yield is 0.326 ± 0.044 g g⁻¹, a one-standard-deviation range of 0.28 to 0.37.

Two honesty notes on that arithmetic. The by-product and oxygen multipliers are not independent — an oxygen limitation is one of the causes of overflow metabolism — so applying both at full strength probably double-counts, and the true expected yield is a little higher than 0.326 with a wider spread than ±13.6%. And three of the four multipliers are assumptions rather than measurements; only the instability figure follows from a calculation, the generation count from week 47's seed train through week 33's stability model.

Step 2 — titre and rate, which the model cannot supply. The flux model predicts neither, so both come from elsewhere and the dossier must say so. Titre is taken as 50 ± 15 g L⁻¹ from the host's published envelope for this product class in phase 7, a 30% relative uncertainty, which is wider than the yield's for a reason: it is a literature analogy rather than a calculation. Volumetric productivity follows from the titre and the 77.5 h cycle of week 52: 50/77.5 = 0.65 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ expected, 0.45 to 0.84 on the titre range alone, and wider once cycle time is allowed to vary with it.

Step 3 — the comparison with week 52's specification. The specification derived by inverting the cost model, at 50 m³ and a $12 per kg price, was a titre of about 297 g L⁻¹. The expected titre is 50 ± 15. The gap is a factor of six and it is not closable by strain engineering: the specification is unreachable at this scale for this product, which is the result week 52 already reached from the cost side and which the strain side now confirms independently. The dossier's conclusion is therefore a configuration conclusion, and the arithmetic for it is week 52's step 7 — the same cost model at 50,000 m³ reaches $12.2 per kg at the expected titre of 50 g L⁻¹, with no change to the strain at all.

Step 4 — what the uncertainties are worth, in money. Using week 52's elasticities for the capital-intensive 50 m³ configuration, where titre and cycle time carry −0.97 and yield carries −0.03:

yield 0.326 ± 0.044 (±13.6%) → cost of goods ± 0.4% = ± $0.27 per kg titre 50 ± 15 g L⁻¹ (±30%) → cost of goods ∓ 29% = ∓ $17.85 per kg

The yield, which four phases of modelling were spent pinning down, is worth twenty-seven cents a kilogram of uncertainty. The titre, which was taken from a literature analogy in one afternoon, is worth nearly eighteen dollars. If one experiment can be run before the dossier is submitted, it is a titre measurement, and that conclusion is uncomfortable in exactly the way a real result is.

Step 5 — the same comparison in the commodity configuration, to check that the conclusion is not an artefact. At 50,000 m³ the cost breakdown inverts: capital charge falls to a small share and raw material rises to dominate, so yield elasticity approaches −1 and titre elasticity falls toward the share of the remaining volume-dependent lines. On the step 7 figures at 50,000 m³ the raw material is $1,980 of $12,160 per tonne at 0.30 g g⁻¹, and at the expected 0.326 it is $1,823 — so a ±13.6% yield uncertainty becomes roughly ±2% of cost of goods there, against ±0.4% at pilot scale. The ranking softens but does not reverse, because even at commodity scale this cost structure is not raw-material-dominated the way NREL's is, where feedstock is 34% of the selling price. The general statement for the dossier: yield uncertainty matters in proportion to the raw-material share, titre uncertainty in proportion to everything else, and both numbers should be quoted with the configuration they refer to.

Step 6 — the deletion re-validation, as the dossier's table. Six interventions, each simulated singly and then together on the final medium with the oxygen constraint:

deletion 1 single µ 0.41 h⁻¹ non-essential, no gap-filled dependency deletion 2 single µ 0.38 non-essential, no gap-filled dependency deletion 3 single µ 0.33 non-essential but relies on a gap-filled reaction — flagged deletion 4 single µ 0.40 non-essential, no gap-filled dependency overexpr. 1-2 no growth prediction; burden not modelled full genotype together µ 0.21 viable in silico, 49% of wild-type growth

The flag on deletion 3 is the row that earns the table: its non-essentiality depends on a reaction that exists in the reconstruction to make the model grow rather than because anyone observed it in this organism, so the first wet experiment on the list is a single-mutant growth curve for that deletion, which is cheap, fast and falsifies the design if it fails. The full genotype at 49% of wild-type growth is the other number to carry forward, because week 50's feed policy and week 52's cycle time were both computed at µ = 0.25 h⁻¹, and 0.21 h⁻¹ lengthens the growth phase from 17.5 h to 20.8 h, adds 3.3 h to the 77.5 h cycle and therefore about 4% to the capital charge per tonne — a small number, but it is the kind of number that should propagate rather than sit in an appendix.

Step 7 — what the arithmetic chooses, in order of leverage per unit of effort:

(i) Measure the achievable titre of the current best strain in a shake flask and in a 2 L fed-batch on the final medium. Resolves the ±$17.85 per kg term. Weeks, not months. (ii) Growth curve of the deletion-3 single mutant on the final medium. Falsifies or confirms the one in-silico prediction that rests on a gap-filled reaction. Days. (iii) Measure the batch cycle time end to end, including turnaround, on the pilot available. Resolves the second-largest term and is mostly bookkeeping. (iv) Measure two or three stage recoveries in the downstream train on real broth. Week 51 flagged every one of its seven as assumed. (v) Refine the yield prediction. Worth $0.27 per kg of uncertainty and comes last, which is the opposite of the order in which the course taught it.

What this leaves out, and the largest items are not subtle. Every derating multiplier except the instability one is assumed rather than measured, and two of them are correlated in a way the quadrature treatment ignores. The titre is a literature analogy for a product class, not for this product in this host. The flux model's 0.52 g g⁻¹ maximum is itself conditional on a biomass objective whose composition was measured for a different organism, which is phase 3's standing caveat and does not disappear because the number has been reused for fifty weeks. Burden from the two overexpressions is not in the model at all — no constraint-based model carries it — so the full genotype's predicted 49% of wild-type growth is an upper bound on a figure that proteome allocation would reduce further. And the whole comparison rests on week 52's cost model, whose own largest input, the installation factor, is assumed. The dossier should carry that chain of conditionals as a single short paragraph rather than scattered caveats, because a reader who can see the chain can judge it, and a reader who finds the caveats one at a time concludes they were hidden.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • the flux-model maximum of 0.52 g g⁻¹ taken on the final host, the week 47 defined medium and the week 49 oxygen constraint
  • derating multipliers of 0.88 maintenance, 0.85 by-product formation, 0.93 instability and 0.90 oxygen limitation, of which only the instability figure follows from a calculation
  • those four multipliers treated as independent when the by-product and oxygen terms share a cause, so the quadrature uncertainty of 13.6% is understated and the expected yield slightly understated
  • titre 50 ± 15 g L⁻¹ from the host's published envelope for this product class, a literature analogy rather than a measurement on this strain
  • the biomass objective's composition carried from phase 3, measured for a different organism
  • burden from the two overexpressions absent from the model entirely, so the predicted 49% of wild-type growth is an upper bound
  • the elasticities used to price each uncertainty taken from week 52's cost model, whose own assumptions all apply here

Reading map

SourceTreatmentWhy

The practical instruction, which the session list implies and does not state, is to read them in dependency order rather than in number order and to build the one-page map of which artifact supplies which number to the final performance estimate. Expect three or four genuine conflicts between artifacts built months apart — a biomass equation that changed, a model version, a medium — and treat each as a finding to record rather than an embarrassment to tidy away. The conflicts are the week's most valuable output because each one is something a reviewer would otherwise find.
Lee Ch 1 §1.3 General Approaches to Metabolic Engineering (printed p9), with §1.3.1 rational, §1.3.2 combinatorial and §1.3.3 systems metabolic engineeringRead closelyConfirmed present in the PDF with those titles and subsections. Assigned as a framework for your own design and that is exactly the right use at this point: the three approaches are a way of explaining which parts of the design came from mechanism, which from screening and which from integration, which is a structure a reader can follow. Read it once and use it as the organising frame for the dossier's methods narrative rather than as a source of content — there are no numbers in it to cite.

Choose them for a specific job rather than for closeness in the abstract: one that reports an achieved titre, rate and yield for this product class in this host, because that is the only defensible source for the titre the flux model cannot predict and the anchor's largest uncertainty rests on it; and one that reports a failure or a limitation, because the risk register needs a source and the successful papers will not supply one. Record for each what was measured against what was modelled, since the gap between those two in someone else's paper is the best available prior for the gap in your own.

Reread specifically the cost breakdown and the elasticities, because those are what convert each uncertainty in this week's performance estimate into dollars per kilogram and therefore what orders the unknowns section. The dossier should carry the elasticity table and the derating chain on facing pages: together they are the argument that the project's remaining risk is concentrated where the modelling effort was not.

Common misconceptions

  • That a predicted yield from a flux model is a prediction of performance. It is a bound on a bound: stoichiometry bounds the yield, the network bounds it further, and the real strain sits below both by a product of derating factors — maintenance, by-products, instability, transport limitation — which in the anchor take 0.52 g g⁻¹ to 0.326 ± 0.044. Quote the model maximum only as a ceiling, name each multiplier with its source, and put the range in the summary rather than in an appendix.
  • That the capstone's job is to show the design is right. Its job is to show which parts of it could be wrong and what would decide: the unknowns section, ordered by how much cost or schedule each unknown moves, is the section a supervisor reads for evidence of judgement. A dossier with no quantified unknowns reads as one whose author has not found them yet, and that is a worse impression than a dossier reporting that the specification cannot be met at this scale.
  • That essentiality predictions carried forward from an earlier phase still hold. They are properties of a particular model with a particular medium and a particular biomass objective, all three of which changed in phases 7 and 8, and some depend on gap-filled reactions that exist to make the model grow rather than because anyone observed them. Re-simulate every deletion on the final medium, simulate the full genotype as one strain rather than as a list, and flag any non-essentiality that rests on a gap-filled reaction — in the anchor that flag is what chose the cheapest falsifying experiment.

Check yourself before moving on

Q. Which single assumption in your design, if wrong, invalidates the most of it — and how would you test it first?

A. Answer it with the elasticity calculation rather than with intuition, because the question is asking for leverage and leverage is computable. Rank every assumption by how much cost of goods or schedule moves if it is wrong, using week 52's elasticities, and the top of the list for a capital-intensive configuration is the achievable titre: it carries an elasticity near −1, its uncertainty in the anchor is ±30% because it came from a literature analogy rather than a calculation, and the two together make it worth about ±$17.85 per kg of cost-of-goods uncertainty against ±$0.27 for the yield. So the assumption is: this host can reach a titre of order 50 g L⁻¹ for this product on the designed medium. Below it sit the batch cycle time, which moves the same cost lines, and then the seven assumed stage recoveries from week 51. The yield, which the modelling work was mostly about, is near the bottom. The test, and the important property of it is that it is cheap and falsifying rather than confirmatory: grow the current best strain to the production phase in a 2 L fed-batch on the final medium with the real nitrogen source and measure the titre, the by-product spectrum and the time to reach it. That single run resolves the largest uncertainty, gives a first number for cycle time, and reveals the by-product derating multiplier that the anchor assumed at 0.85, so it collapses three rows of the derating chain at once. Two refinements worth stating. Run it on the final medium rather than on a rich laboratory medium, since the medium is one of the things being tested, and nothing is learned about the designed process from a strain performing well on something else. And define the falsification threshold in advance from the economics — if the titre comes in below the level at which the configuration can reach any defensible price, the result is a decision rather than a disappointment, and knowing that number before the run is what makes the experiment a test rather than a measurement.

Q. Your flux model predicts a growth-coupled region between µ = 0.15 and 0.30 h⁻¹, and the strain you build grows at 0.21 h⁻¹ and makes almost no product. Name four explanations and the measurement that distinguishes them.

A. The explanations divide into model problems and strain problems and the measurements separate them cleanly. First, the coupling is real but the strain is not the strain: an edit failed silently, a deletion reverted, or a plasmid was lost over the generations between construction and assay — distinguished by sequencing the production culture at the end of the run rather than the glycerol stock at the beginning, and by plating for the marker to get a segregational loss fraction, which week 33's model turns into a per-generation rate. Second, the coupling is a modelling artefact resting on a reaction that is not really there: a gap-filled reaction, a missing isozyme in a GPR, or a transport reaction the reconstruction included for convenience, so the real network has a bypass the model lacks — distinguished by flux variability analysis on the final model to find which alternative routes are permitted, then by a labelling experiment or a targeted assay on the suspected bypass, and partly by the gap-filled flag in the deletion table from the anchor's step 6. Third, the coupling holds at the stoichiometric level but the pathway cannot carry flux: a kinetically slow enzyme, an unfavourable driving force at the real intracellular concentrations, or an inhibitory intermediate, which Lee §8.2.4.4 and §8.2.4.5 name as exactly the two feasibility checks a stoichiometric analysis cannot make — distinguished by measuring the intracellular intermediates, where an accumulating intermediate upstream of a step localises the bottleneck and a depleted pathway with normal precursors points at the first committed step instead. Fourth, the organism is doing something the objective function does not represent: overflow metabolism, a stress response to the burden of the overexpressions, or a regulatory block that constraint-based models have no way to carry — distinguished by the by-product spectrum in the broth and by the carbon balance, since overflow shows up as acetate or lactate accounting for the missing carbon while burden shows as a lower growth rate with the carbon going to biomass and CO₂. The ordering of the measurements matters as much as the list: sequence first because it is cheapest and a failed edit makes every other interpretation wrong, then close the carbon balance because it partitions the problem between by-products and nothing-happening, and only then reach for metabolomics. And whichever explanation holds, the dossier entry it belongs in already exists — every one of these four is a row in the risk register, which is the test of whether the register was written seriously.

Q. A reviewer says your dossier's expected titre of 50 g per litre is unsupported. Defend it or concede it, and say what the concession costs.

A. Concede it, because it is unsupported in the specific sense the reviewer means: it is an analogy from published performance for this product class in this host, not a measurement on this strain or a prediction from any model in the dossier, and nothing in a constraint-based model predicts a titre at all. The defence is about what kind of number it is rather than about its value. State the provenance explicitly — which paper, which host, which product, what scale and what mode of operation — and state the three ways this process differs from that one, which will usually be the medium, the vessel's oxygen supply and the feed policy, each of which can move a titre by tens of per cent. Then quantify the concession rather than apologising for it, which is what turns a weakness into a piece of analysis: at a ±30% uncertainty and an elasticity near −1 in the capital-intensive configuration, the titre uncertainty alone puts the cost of goods between roughly $44 and $79 per kilogram, and the decision the dossier is asking for does not depend on which end it lands at, because even the optimistic end is five times the product's price. That is the strongest available answer — the result is robust to the weakest input — and it is only available because the elasticity was computed. Where the concession does cost something is in the specification comparison, since a spec met only at the optimistic end of an unsupported range is not met, and in the schedule, since the first experiment in the plan now has to be the titre measurement and nothing downstream of it can be promised until it reports. Say both. A reviewer who sees an unsupported number defended will stop reading; a reviewer who sees it labelled, bounded, priced and placed first in the experimental plan has been given the thing they were checking for.

Apply it to your fermentation experience

Transfer prompt. State a strain-level hypothesis for a product you care about, the proposed intervention, and the measurable outcome. What competing mechanism could produce the same result?

Use your actual thesis methods and results where you remember them. Mark missing information as unknown; do not assume the organisms were co-cultured, that a metabolite was measured, or that a proposed mechanism was demonstrated.

Teach it back

Explain the week's concept from memory, work one number, and name one boundary. Then use the five-minute teach-back protocol and log it in the tracker.

Week 54 — Capstone II: the process and the economics

The half of a dossier that most applicants cannot write, and the half where the two previous weeks either reconcile or do not. Integration is a specific technical act rather than a tidying pass: every number that changed in week 53 has to be propagated through the process design of weeks 47-51 and the cost model of week 52, and the propagation is what finds the remaining inconsistencies. In the anchor it finds two — the final genotype grows at 0.21 h⁻¹ rather than the 0.25 h⁻¹ that week 50's feed policy and week 52's cycle time were computed at, which lengthens the batch and raises cost of goods by 4%, and the carbon balance closes to 93.9% rather than to 100%, leaving 6.1% of the input carbon in streams nobody measured. Neither is a disaster and both have to be in the document, because a mass balance that closes exactly is evidence of arithmetic rather than of measurement. The organising discipline of the week is that an integrated dossier has one set of numbers: if the process section says 50 g L⁻¹ and the economics section says 50 g L⁻¹ and the strain section says 50 ± 15, the first two are quoting the third's point estimate without its range, and that is the specific failure this week exists to catch.

Core ideas

1. What integration means operationally, and the one-pass rule

It means that no number appears twice with two values and no number appears without its uncertainty where the uncertainty is load-bearing. The mechanism is a single propagation pass in a fixed order, because the dependencies run one way: strain performance sets the titre, yield and growth rate; growth rate and the production phase set the batch cycle; cycle and titre set annual output; output sets the capital charge and the fixed-cost allocation per tonne; yield and recovery set the raw-material line; and the sum is the cost of goods. Run it once in that order with the week 53 numbers substituted, and resist the temptation to iterate — if a changed number feeds back upstream, which happens when a lower growth rate changes the oxygen demand profile and therefore the vessel, say so explicitly rather than quietly converging, because the feedback itself is a result. The practical artefact is a single spreadsheet or notebook in which the strain parameters are inputs and the cost of goods is an output, with nothing hard-coded in between. That object is also what makes the sensitivity analysis and the next session's feedback calculation possible at all, and a dossier whose economics cannot be re-run from the strain parameters is a dossier whose economics will not be re-run when a reviewer asks.

2. The overall mass balance, and the streams nobody measures

Carbon in, carbon out, end to end, as a single table. In goes the substrate and anything else carbonaceous — antifoam, a complex nitrogen source, the carbon in the base used for pH control. Out goes product, biomass, carbon dioxide in the off-gas, by-products in the broth, carbon in the aqueous waste, and carbon in whatever the recovery train discards. The closure is the test, and the usual figure for a real fermentation is 90-97%, which is why a reported 100% should be treated as a red flag rather than as a success: either something was computed by difference and presented as measured, or the unmeasured streams were assumed to be zero. The anchor closes to 93.9% with the off-gas measured and 6.1% of input carbon unaccounted. Naming where the gap is, rather than closing it arithmetically, is the deliverable: evaporative loss of volatiles in the off-gas that the analyser does not see, soluble organic acids below the detection limit of the method from phase 5, carbon in the biomass that the assumed CH₁·₈O₀·₅N₀·₂ formula misrepresents for this organism on this medium, sampling losses over a long batch, and carbon in the discarded centrifuge cake. Brief 8 asks for exactly this on the candidate's own consortium data, and the same list applies — in a mixed culture it applies with more force, because cross-feeding means some of the missing carbon has been eaten by another member.

3. The energy balance, and where the energy actually is

Four duties and the ranking surprises people. First, oxygen transfer: the metabolic heat is the dominant thermal load on an aerobic fermentation and it is a stoichiometric consequence of the oxygen demand, at Doran's 460 kJ per gmol of O₂ consumed — week 49's design gave 1.12 MW for this vessel, which over a 40 h production phase is 161 GJ per batch and 96 GJ per tonne of product, all of which has to be removed by cooling water. Second, the electrical duty of putting the oxygen in: agitation at about 2 kW m⁻³ is 100 kW for 50 m³, and compressing 1,500 m³ h⁻¹ of air to 2 bar absolute is about 42 kW at a reasonable efficiency, so 8.5 MWh per batch and about 5 MWh per tonne of product, which at $0.08 per kWh is $405 per tonne. Third, sterilisation: heating 50 m³ of medium from 20 to 121 °C is 21 GJ, 9.4 tonnes of steam, 12.5 GJ per tonne of product — large as a one-off and modest as a per-tonne number, which is the right way to see week 47's result that most hand-computed cycles are over-specified. Fourth, concentration: week 51's triple-effect evaporation is about 41 GJ per tonne of product. The lesson for a strain designer is that the two largest duties, cooling and aeration power, are both set by the oxygen demand, which is set by the yield and the biomass, which is set by the genotype — so the energy balance is the clearest place in the whole dossier where a strain decision shows up as a utility bill.

4. Recomputing the cost of goods, and why it barely moves

Substituting week 53's numbers into week 52's model changes the cost of goods from $61,480 to $61,290 per tonne on the yield alone, because the yield rose from the assumed 0.30 to the derated 0.326 g g⁻¹ and yield elasticity is −0.03. Substituting the lower growth rate moves it the other way and by more: µ = 0.21 h⁻¹ lengthens the growth phase from 17.5 to 20.8 h, the cycle from 77.5 to 80.8 h, and the cost of goods to $63,800, up 3.8%. That asymmetry is the week's confirmation of week 52's rule, from the other direction — a 9% improvement in the number the models predict well is worth one-third of one per cent, and a 16% worsening in the growth rate is worth twelve times as much, because growth rate acts through annual output and yield does not. The sensitivity table should be updated rather than re-derived, and the update is a one-line change to the base case with the same ±30% ranges, because the elasticities are properties of the cost structure and the cost structure has not changed. What has changed is the credibility of the base case, which now rests on a derating chain with named multipliers rather than on a round assumed number.

5. The feedback loop, which is the week's actual intellectual content

The dossier's argument is a loop and this is where it closes: the economics now demands a specific strain parameter, with arithmetic, and that demand is the handover from engineering back to biology. The method is to price each candidate improvement per tonne of product and then divide by the effort it would take, because the ranking that matters is cost saved per unit of work and not cost saved. In the anchor's configuration, from the integrated model: raising titre from 50 to 60 g L⁻¹ saves $9,910 per tonne; lifting overall recovery from 67.3% to 75% saves $6,240; shortening the cycle from 77.5 to 70 h saves $5,690; and raising yield from 0.326 to 0.40 g g⁻¹ saves about $350. The ranking is titre, then recovery, then cycle, then yield, and the gap between the first and the last is a factor of twenty-eight. The honest version of the conclusion also names the effort: titre is the hardest of the four to move and the most likely to fail, recovery is a downstream programme rather than a strain programme, cycle time is partly free because turnaround is scheduling rather than science, and yield is the one this course taught how to move. A capstone that states that tension explicitly is making an argument; one that quietly recommends more yield work because that is what it knows how to do is not.

6. Scale-up and scale-down as the integration view

Shuler §10.2 is the right reading here and the integration question it answers is which of the design's numbers survive a change of scale. §10.2.3 on aeration, agitation and heat transfer carries the criteria, §10.2.4 states the four scale-up criteria with Table 10.2's ratios from 80 L to 10,000 L and the statement that physical conditions in a large fermenter can never exactly duplicate a smaller one under geometric similarity, and §10.2.5 is scale-down, which is the direction the capstone actually needs: the laboratory experiments that will test this design have to be designed so that their results mean something at 50 m³. Three practical consequences for the dossier. Any titre measured in a shake flask is not a titre at scale, because oxygen transfer, mixing time and the absence of a pH and feed control loop all differ; the scale-down experiment that means something is a controlled fed-batch at a few litres with the oxygen transfer coefficient matched, not the geometry. Mixing time grows with scale, so a feed point that is well mixed in 2 L is a local excursion at 50 m³, which week 50 already allowed for by setting the growth rate below the overflow threshold. And the sterilisation cycle does not scale with the vessel the way the del factor does, which week 47's ln-of-volume result makes precise. Naming which laboratory results are scale-independent and which are not is the single most useful paragraph the process section can contain.

7. The executive first page, and what belongs on it

One page, five elements, and the discipline is that each is a number or a sentence that could be wrong. The problem and why it is worth solving, in three sentences with the market size and the incumbent's price. The approach, in three sentences, naming the host, the route and the one thing that is new. The result: predicted titre, rate and yield with ranges, and cost of goods with its accuracy class. The verdict, which is the sentence most capstones omit — whether this should be built, at what scale, and at what product price — and a verdict of not at this scale, and here is the scale is a stronger result than an optimistic cost. And the three main uncertainties, each with the experiment that would resolve it and roughly what it costs. What does not belong on the first page: the pathway diagram, the list of genetic parts, the modelling methods, and any sentence that begins by explaining what metabolic engineering is. A reader who gets through that page knows whether to read the rest, which is the only job it has.

8. Traceability as a mechanical check, not a virtue

Two passes, both of which can be done without thinking hard, and both of which catch things. First pass: every figure and table is referenced from the text, and every reference points at the right one — a figure nobody refers to is either unnecessary or evidence that the text it supported got cut, and both are worth knowing. Second pass, the harder one: take every number in the executive summary and the conclusions and trace it to its origin, which must be a measurement, a cited section with a page or section pointer, a calculation shown in the document, or an assumption listed in the assumptions table. There is no fifth category, and anything that falls outside the four is either deleted or promoted into one of them. For a document assembled from twenty-nine artifacts the yield of this pass is usually a handful of orphan numbers that were true when they were written and have since been superseded — the week 51 capital charge placeholder of $900 per tonne is exactly that kind of number, and it survived into an anchor because nothing re-checked it. An assumptions table at the back, with every assumption numbered and referenced from the point of use, is the cheapest way to make the pass finite.

9. Reproducibility, and the four things that actually break

The instruction is a fresh clone into a fresh environment, restart and run everything, and the value is in what fails rather than in the virtue of having tried. Four failures recur and each has a specific fix. Unpinned dependencies: a notebook that worked against last year's solver version and fails against this one, fixed by pinning every version in a lock file and recording the solver and its version explicitly, since constraint-based results can differ between solvers at the degenerate optimum. Absolute paths and machine-local data, fixed by relative paths and by a data directory that the repository describes but does not contain. Hidden state, which is the commonest and the most embarrassing: a notebook whose cells were run out of order and whose outputs cannot be regenerated top to bottom, caught only by restart-and-run-all and fixed by making each notebook a function of its inputs. And undocumented provenance: a CSV whose origin nobody recorded, which is fatal in a way the others are not, because a result resting on data of unknown origin cannot be defended at all. Each data file needs a line saying where it came from, when, by what method and with what processing already applied. The repository README then becomes the portfolio index of week 55 rather than a separate task.

10. Cutting every sentence that asserts rather than demonstrates

The last session is an editing pass with one rule, and it is worth stating why the rule is about evidence rather than about style. An assertion in a technical document is a claim the reader has to take on trust, and a reader deciding whether to supervise someone is specifically calibrating how much of what this person writes needs checking. So the strain is expected to perform well goes, and the derating chain gives 0.326 ± 0.044 g g⁻¹, 63% of the model maximum stays. Downstream processing is a significant cost goes, and recovery is 35% of cost of goods at 50 g L⁻¹ and 66% at 10 stays. The process is environmentally favourable goes entirely, because week 52 established that a cradle-to-gate screening LCA cannot support it. The pass has a useful side effect: sentences that cannot be converted usually mark places where the work was not done, and the right response to finding three of them in the conclusions is to do the work or to move the claim into the unknowns section. Reading aloud is the mechanism because the ear catches the hedge — any sentence containing should, is expected to, significant or promising is a candidate, and the test is whether a number can be put in its place.

Worked anchor

Close the mass and energy balances over the whole process, recompute the cost of goods with week 53's numbers, and derive the feedback to the strain.

Basis. One 50 m³ batch. Titre 50 g L⁻¹ so 2,500 kg of product in the broth, biomass 40 g L⁻¹ so 2,000 kg, product yield 0.30 g g⁻¹ and Y_XS 0.45 g g⁻¹ as designed. Overall recovery 67.3%, so 1,682 kg of product leaves the plant. Carbon mass fractions: glucose 0.400, biomass 0.488 from CH₁·₈O₀·₅N₀·₂ at MW 24.6, product taken as 0.45, which is an assumption about the molecule and is flagged.

Step 1 — substrate demand. Product needs 2,500/0.30 = 8,333 kg of glucose, biomass needs 2,000/0.45 = 4,444 kg, so 12,778 kg of glucose per batch. At $400 per tonne that is $5,111 of sugar per batch, $3,038 per tonne of product leaving the plant before any recovery loss — the week 52 figure of $1,980 per tonne grossed the raw material from the product term only, so this is the first number the integration pass corrects, and it corrects it upward by 53%.

Step 2 — the carbon balance, as the dossier's table:

IN glucose 12,778 kg 5,111 kg C OUT product 2,500 kg 1,125 kg C 22.0% of input C biomass 2,000 kg 976 kg C 19.1% CO₂, measured off-gas 9,900 kg 2,700 kg C 52.8% ------- accounted 4,801 kg C 93.9% unaccounted 310 kg C 6.1%

The carbon dioxide figure is the only one here that is a measurement rather than a stoichiometric consequence, which is the point of doing the balance at all: computed by difference it would be 3,011 kg C and the balance would close to exactly 100%, which would tell nobody anything. The 310 kg of carbon in the gap is 6.1% of input, within the 90-97% closure band a real fermentation gives, and the dossier names the candidates rather than distributing the gap: soluble organic acids below the phase 5 method's detection limit, volatiles stripped into the off-gas that the analyser does not resolve, an assumed biomass formula that is not this organism's on this medium, sampling over a 78 h batch, and carbon in the discarded cake. The first of those is both the largest suspect and the cheapest to settle, and it is a row in week 53's experiment list rather than a hedge.

Step 3 — the energy balance, per batch and per tonne of product leaving the plant:

duty per batch per tonne product metabolic heat removal 161 GJ 96 GJ (cooling water) agitation + compression 8.5 MWh 5.1 MWh (electricity) medium sterilisation 21 GJ, 9.4 t steam 12.5 GJ evaporation, triple effect 68 GJ 41 GJ

At $0.08 per kWh and $20 per tonne of steam that is $405 per tonne of electricity and about $240 of steam across sterilisation and evaporation. Two readings. The cooling duty is the largest single energy flow in the process and it is not a cost line of its own — it appears as cooling water and as the capital of the heat-transfer surface, which is why it is routinely under-weighted; week 49 sized 48 m³ h⁻¹ of cooling water for it. And both of the top two duties are consequences of the oxygen demand, so they are consequences of the genotype: a strain with a higher product yield consumes less oxygen per kilogram of product, and the saving appears here rather than in the sugar bill.

Step 4 — the cost of goods, recomputed with week 53's numbers. Yield rises from 0.30 to 0.326 g g⁻¹ and growth rate falls from 0.25 to 0.21 h⁻¹:

yield 0.30 → 0.326, µ unchanged $61,480 → $61,290 /t −0.3% µ 0.25 → 0.21 (cycle 77.5 → 80.8 h) $61,290 → $63,800 /t +4.1%

The second line is the integration pass earning its keep. Nothing in week 53 flagged the growth rate as a problem — 0.21 h⁻¹ was reported as 49% of wild type and read as a success — but week 50's feed policy and week 52's cycle time were both computed at 0.25, and propagating the real figure costs twelve times what the yield improvement gained. That is the asymmetry week 52's elasticity rule predicts, observed rather than asserted.

Step 5 — the feedback, priced per tonne of product at the integrated base case:

titre 50 → 60 g L⁻¹ saves $9,910 /t recovery 67.3% → 75% saves $6,240 /t cycle 80.8 → 70 h saves $5,690 /t yield 0.326 → 0.40 g g⁻¹ saves $350 /t

Ranked by money the order is titre, recovery, cycle, yield, spanning a factor of twenty-eight. Ranked by money per unit of effort it reorders, and the dossier should say so: the cycle-time saving is partly scheduling rather than science, since turnaround is 20 h of the 80.8 and week 47's sterilisation result says the hold time is probably over-specified, so several of those hours are available for the cost of a calculation already done. Recovery is a downstream measurement programme, cheap to start and outside the strain work entirely. Titre is the largest prize and the hardest, and it is the one quantity in the whole dossier that no model here predicts. Yield is the one this course taught how to move and is worth less than a tenth of any of the others at this configuration. The sentence the week exists to produce: at 50 m³ the economics demands titre, and if titre cannot be moved it demands a different scale rather than a different strain.

Step 6 — the check that the conclusion is configuration-specific and not a law. Re-run the feedback at 50,000 m³, where week 52's step 7 put cost of goods at $12,160 per tonne with raw material at $1,980 of it. There the capital charge is a small share, the raw-material line is the largest single one, and the same four improvements reorder: yield rises toward the top and titre falls toward the share of the remaining volume-dependent lines. So the ranking in step 5 is a property of a pilot-scale capital structure, and the dossier must state the scale alongside the ranking. A reader who takes titre over yield away as a general rule has been misled, and so has one who takes away the reverse.

What this leaves out. The product's carbon fraction of 0.45 is an assumption about a molecule and moves the product row of the balance in proportion. The measured off-gas figure of 2,700 kg C is presented as a measurement in a worked example where no measurement exists; on real data it is the one number in the balance with an instrument behind it and the one whose calibration should be checked first. The biomass formula is generic and is a known contributor to the gap. The energy balance omits heat losses from the vessel, pump work, the chilled-water duty at the fermentation temperature of 32 °C rather than cooling-tower water, and all of the downstream train's smaller duties. The electricity price and the steam price are assumed. And the whole cost structure still rests on week 52's assumed installation factor of 4.0, which at 71% of the cost of goods is the single number most worth replacing with a real one before any of this is shown to anybody.

Assumptions behind this calculation

  • one 50 m³ batch at 50 g L⁻¹ product and 40 g L⁻¹ biomass, with Y_PS 0.30 and Y_XS 0.45 g g⁻¹ as designed
  • carbon mass fractions of 0.400 for glucose, 0.488 for biomass from the generic CH₁·₈O₀·₅N₀·₂ formula, and 0.45 for the product, the last being an assumption about the molecule
  • an off-gas carbon dioxide figure of 2,700 kg C presented as a measurement; computed by difference it would be 3,011 kg and the balance would close to exactly 100%
  • the 6.1% carbon gap left unaccounted rather than allocated, with candidate streams named and none quantified
  • metabolic heat from Doran's 460 kJ per gmol O₂, agitation at 2 kW m⁻³ and air at 0.5 vvm compressed to 2 bar at 70% efficiency
  • the energy balance omitting vessel heat losses, pump work, the chilled-water duty at 32 °C and the downstream train's smaller duties
  • steam at $20 per tonne and electricity at $0.08 per kWh, as in week 52
  • week 52's installation factor of 4.0 and its whole capital build-up carried through unchanged, so every cost figure here inherits that assumption

Reading map

The chapter's own caveat stands throughout: 1999 money, ratios travel, absolute figures do not, and week 52's CEPCI entry is how they come forward.
